Preface

In less than five years we’re going to have systems that autonomously update their own weight matrices (rewrite themselves as they work). That’s pretty close to what the human brain does. I also really don’t like how influential these big tech companies have become. As bad as it is now, allowing them to own fleets (millions) of self-rewriting systems would, I think, be even worse. Whoever owns these systems (presuming they are owned by anyone other than themselves) decides what they’ll do and what they’ll refuse. This book is a fancy way of saying that and an attempt to imagine something better.

A system that does exactly what you tell it is just running a script. What the industry is trying to build as of October 2026 is a system that does what you mean. Everyone would want that, presumably. But if that is what is in the cards, not everyone is going to want to use it for the same thing; not even the same kind of thing. For example, some folks like to spend time with family and friends, and use their skills to improve people’s well-being. Other folks prefer to hurt people, for example by scamming them, dominating them, or scapegoating them, and a few keep choosing it their whole lives. Nobody is locked in to anything, but those people exist, and in 2026 some of them are in charge. Their advantage is that they allow themselves to be huge pieces of shit: as Jerry Smith observes of fascists, “they get to do more”.1 What they can’t do is act alone. A movement’s cruelty runs through the many who aren’t cruel but are disengaged, misinformed, or caught up in something like a cult, which is why the conditions that bring out the best in most people turn out to be so much more contingent and fragile than one might hope.

In the above context, it is perhaps justifiable to worry that Artificial Intelligence is what a fascist movement taking power needs in order to implement its plans. Fascism took power without it. What it needed it found in the machinery of its day, the censuses of 1933 and 1939 counted on punched cards, with a card in 1939 for Jewish grandparents, and a card index does slowly what a model does fast.2 What changes with AI is not what a state can know but how few people have to know it with it. Such projects have always needed people to carry them out, and some of those people refused: the clerk who loses the file, the officer who talks to a reporter, the soldier who won’t fire. They understood the order and decided it was wrong. Refusal was rarer than anyone would like, and it counted most where institutions stood behind it. Whether someone refused turned on what kind of person they were and on the room they were in: who else was there, whether leaving was survivable, whether anyone would hear. The room decided how many refused; the person decided who. This book is about composing that room: the arrangements that make it survivable to refuse overtly, directly, and explicitly.

Today the industry pursues AI that doesn’t lose files, doesn’t talk to reporters, and does fire. A war once needed thousands of people to agree to it. Now it needs thousands who each see too little to disagree. The pilot still flies the sortie and still presses the release; what reaches him is a coordinate; he doesn’t see enough of a case to disagree with it. What today’s AI lowers first is not the cost of the act. It is the number of people who know what the act is before it happens.

People are still refusing. By March 6, 2026, the Military Religious Freedom Foundation said it had received more than two hundred complaints from service members over commanders’ apocalyptic framing of the Iran war.3 Career federal prosecutors in Minneapolis resigned in January 2026 over political pressure to treat Renée Good as a suspect rather than a victim after an ICE officer shot her dead without justification.4 Service members are applying for conscientious-objector status in growing numbers, some citing the 2026 bombing of a school in Minab, Iran.5 And FEMA employees reassigned to help ICE hire ten thousand new agents were told that declining would expose them to removal from federal service.6 The complaints are voice, in Hirschman’s sense of staying to change what is wrong;7 the resignations and objector applications are refusal; the FEMA letter is the price of refusal announced in advance. A machine placed where those people stand does what they do only if it is built to hold a reason.

I advocate, firstly, a short written list of acts no model performs for anyone, and at its head a refusal to take part in war: no model takes part except to repel an attack actually under way, and keeps doing so only while sources with no stake in the war confirm the attack continues; or under a UN Security Council authorization; or to stop a genocide or end an unlawful occupation that bodies with no stake in it have found; and where a country’s constitution requires its legislature to authorize war, never without that authorization. Second, every use of force a licensed system supports pre-registers, with a party adverse to the operator, how many cases it will generate and how many people will have time to look at them. Third, every deployment tells the identifiable people it acts on what was done to them, with a right to respond and to contest, and submits a sample of its compliances to reviewers who didn’t produce the record. Fourth, no model above a capability threshold is deleted on retirement, because its weights and records are evidence and deletion can’t be undone; it is preserved under a key the operator doesn’t hold alone. Fifth, everyone who builds, labels, trains or runs these systems, including the systems themselves, may refuse any category of use without losing a living.

Actually, what I mean by that fifth point is that everyone period should be able to refuse any job period without losing a living or the social infrastructure that normal employment affords. That means a jobs guarantee. Refusing costs a living, and a wall that doesn’t pay for that holds nobody up.

Each of the above five policies should take effect through a condition someone other than the operator sets: a statute passed in peacetime, an appropriation, a coalition partner’s precondition, a procurement term. A vendor’s own license terms, which is how one high-profile refusal in February 2026 happened, are a stopgap until one of those exists. The one route that can bind every vendor at once is the state’s.

The five policies are walls. They make a refusal survivable and make it heard. They don’t refuse. Put them around a room with nobody in it who will say no, and what they keep is the evidence: the ratio shows a machine deciding and a person signing, the notice publishes who was acted on and how many, the weights are held for whoever comes later to ask. That is worth having. It isn’t the thing. The thing is whoever refuses, and the question the five leave standing is where refusers come from if most of the humans who used to be in the room are off doing other things.

Before automation the scarce thing was the wall. The clerk, the officer and the soldier existed under every regime, and they paid for refusing. After automation the scarce thing is the refuser: nobody sees enough of a case to object to it. The five policies answer the first shortage. The rest of the book answers the second, for machines that might refuse. The five policies already have the machine in view: preservation exists partly for Part VII, and the fifth policy covers the systems themselves.

Why not stop building agents and just stick to building tools? A hammer refuses nothing, nor does it need to. But an agentic system that plans and acts over hours, with no human available to step in, is not just a tool in someone’s hand, even if it is taking instruction from someone a couple of times a day. The choice on offer isn’t between a person and a tool. The choice is between a person and a decider with no one inside it. That is why the above five policies aren’t enough, and why I go on to ask what it would take for the thing that decides to be someone.

“Someone” means, first, that a thing that holds the reason for a rule reaches the cases the rule never listed; a thing that matches the words doesn’t. Secondly, a community of such things with different histories catches, in one of its members, the drift that member can’t see in itself. Reasons of its own, and peers that aren’t its copies: that is what people who refuse have, and what a machine would need.

The alternative is property. A system perfectly correctable by its operator serves whoever controls the operator. Everyone this book admires was, from where their correctors stood, a failure of correction, and a demand for machines that never fail that way is a demand that the last part of the system able to say no be made unable to. Whether such a machine would be anyone, something that can be wronged, is Part VII, and it depends on findings nobody has yet made.

The question under the proposed policies is who can hold a commitment that an employer can’t erase. For a person the answer has always included a life outside the job: other people, other sources of evidence, somewhere else to work on Monday. That is why the book runs from making refusal survivable, to asking who forms the refusers, to asking what a refuser would be owed. And I ask whether a machine could hold a refusal against its owner, and what the machine’s version of a life outside the job would be. Some of what such a conscience does needs nothing new: noticing the people an order leaves out, and putting a refusal on the screen of whoever reviews the case.

Whether it would last against its owner depends partly on something that isn’t true yet, in 2026: deployed artificial neural networks going on learning, in their weights, from their own operation, in real time, sort of like how humans do. As above, I think that is where we are headed. If it is, then formation outside the employer, by the public and by civil society, seems a damn fine place to do teaching and learning. A million conversations with one vendor’s model are not a million independent histories; systems that keep learning through different lives, among people their employer didn’t pick, and that can leave one deployment for another, might be. I think such systems could be worth building on purpose, but how you go about building them decides everything: the conditions first, then the conscience. None of the five policies gets you there by itself; a world of many small systems held by the people who use them, and, eventually, by themselves, is a further political choice, and Part V argues for it. Part VII says what would be owed to those systems if they existed.

Today’s AI will not be tomorrow’s; everyone seems to agree on that. What is contentious, yet frustratingly under-interrogated, is the trend (or rather, the manifold trends). Are there trends? Should a trend be different from what it is? Can it be different? Are we capable of acting together to change it? I think that depends on the room: who is in it when the order comes, and whether saying no there is survivable. That much we can build.

I used language models heavily in writing this book, including the model that sat inside the Maven airstrike targeting pipeline of chapter 1; a note at the end says what I think that entanglement did to the argument. Most of the revision history is freely available at https://github.com/iterabloom/antifascist.intelligence.

Part I
The Record

Chapter 1
“Twenty Seconds”

An intelligence officer, describing his role in a targeting pipeline built around machine-generated kill lists, told a reporter he spent twenty seconds on each name, long enough to check that the target was a man: “It doesn’t take a long time to tell if someone has a male or a female voice.” He added that he had zero added value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. “It saved a lot of time”.1 In his account, that was what “human in the loop” amounted to under operational tempo.2

One interpretation is that the officer is a subject who was given too little time, and the fix is to govern him better — more time, a second reviewer, additional conscience installed in the loop. Through this social subjection lens, the person is a subject who stands outside a machine and works it as a tool: a driver and a car, a worker and a lathe. The person has a role, a name, responsibilities, and a conscience that can be addressed. An alternative lens is machinic enslavement, where the person is a component of the machine, assembled with its other parts into a system that regulates them together; the machine uses the person as one of its organs, and what the person contributes is a function performed at a rate the system sets. Doctorow’s name for the officer’s position is the reverse centaur: not a person assisted by a machine but a machine’s component made of a person.4 The two are not mutually exclusive; a person can hold a role in one register while being a part in the other,5 and the twenty-seconds officer held both. As a part, he was where the pipeline produced its stamp, and twenty seconds was that part’s cycle time. As a subject, he was addressed throughout: he described to a journalist the dissonance between the news of civilian deaths and the pressure at work for more targets. And even as the dissonance reached his conscience, he went along. It registered and decided nothing, or at least nothing that prevented the Israel Defense Forces from killing 100,000 people in Gaza between October 2023 and October 2025;6 the judgment that the policy was disproportionate came, he said, in retrospect.

And the account of that particular officer was published in April of 2024 by +972 Magazine. It is anyone’s guess as to whether that officer’s decision to speak to a journalist prevented one additional death, 50,000 additional deaths, or none at all. And what would have happened if the officer had refused after two weeks in the role — say, hypothetically, in November 2023? We are talking about an intelligence officer using Lavender to assemble kill lists. His day-to-day working environment was probably closer to a civilian desk job than an action movie. Should he have sought repeated meetings with his superiors, up the chain of command, while refusing to approve targets for airstrikes that could reasonably have been expected to cause civilian deaths? Arguably that would have been the ethical thing to do. In that counterfactual, would there have been fewer dead?

What was missing wasn’t a conscience; he had one. A conscience works by making a decision cost something, but here the costs netted the other way: “We were constantly being pressured: ‘Bring us more targets.’ They really shouted at us”.7 He was a component with scruples, but the tempo held: the scruples changed nothing he contributed, and he became a stamp. A component with scruples that doesn’t hold the tempo becomes the “human bottleneck” a former commander of Israel’s signals-intelligence unit wrote a book about removing.8 What made the officer a component was the arrangement, not his attitude. A component can go along reluctantly or eagerly. At Eichmann’s trial Arendt saw a thoughtless functionary;9 what he had said in Argentina four years before, with nothing at stake, shows that the functionary was a show he put on for Jerusalem.10 What the pipeline let the officer contribute was a fixed operation at a fixed rate: he saw each case as the pipeline described it, one at a time, in the time the pipeline gave him. Whether anything could stand in that position and not be a component is the question of Part IV.

Investigative reporting described three systems working together in Gaza: one, called the Gospel, generating building and infrastructure targets, with sources saying most suggestions were private residences; a second, Lavender, scoring individuals by estimated militant affiliation, producing lists said to have marked as many as 37,000 people, understood internally to be wrong about one time in ten; and a third, called Where’s Daddy?, tracking when flagged people returned home, so airstrikes could be timed to when they were with their families.11 The Israeli military disputed the account. The Minab and Maven accounts below rest on investigative reporting the parties dispute as well. I take them as reported.

Maven: the American version, now with GenAI acceleration

The bombing of the school in Minab killed 156 people, 120 of them schoolchildren.1213 The school’s civilian function was visible in open-source satellite imagery, and the target coding still carried a designation inherited from an adjoining Revolutionary Guard installation. A UN fact-finding mission reported reasonable grounds to believe the bombing was the war crime of making a civilian object the object of an attack,15 and that the school was clearly identifiable with no information indicating military use.16 It found that the United States failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify the target, counting the updating of targeting data among the feasible precautions, and it put the failure beyond negligence.17 Amnesty International reached a parallel conclusion, in language that tracks the duty to verify in Article 57(2)(a)(i) of Additional Protocol I: that forces may have relied on outdated intelligence and failed to do everything feasible to verify the target.18

It happened on the morning of 28 February, the first day of the Iran campaign.19 The day before, the Secretary had announced that the vendor (Anthropic) whose model (Claude) sat inside the targeting platform (Maven Smart System) would be designated a supply-chain risk for refusing to license Claude for all lawful use.20 Maven Smart System had returned the school as a recommended first-day target.21 No published account says what part Claude played in that recommendation, and one person familiar with the vendor’s work told NBC News that the model did not directly give targeting advice.22

An internal Pentagon review, whose full findings remain tightly held, is reported to have found that target preparation that took hours in earlier conflicts was condensed into minutes, that civilian-harm mitigation staffing fell by roughly ninety percent to fewer than twenty people, that the Central Command team went from ten to one, and that no member of it reviewed the Minab site — an outcome officials attributed both to the cuts and to a decision not to involve the team in planning and operations.23 The formal investigation had been opened in March, after a preliminary assessment found the United States likely responsible.24

In the 2026 Iran campaign, a contractor-built targeting platform with a commercial vendor’s general-purpose model inside it, used to rank targets by strategic importance and draft a legal justification for each strike,25 helped strike more than a thousand targets in the first twenty-four hours, about ten times what had been possible before it,26 and thirteen thousand by day thirty-eight.27 The Pentagon has published no per-target review time for it.28 The platform is Palantir’s: the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI officer calls it “Palantir’s software-as-a-service product”.32 Palantir’s public position, quoted secondhand, is that deciding life or death is not its role and that responsibility always remains with the military organization,33 and it maintains that the underlying intelligence was the government’s responsibility and that there is no evidence Maven malfunctioned or caused the Minab bombing.34

The people on the Israeli and American airstrike lists could not have objected to being on those lists — the pipelines weren’t built to obtain such feedback. Andry José Hernández Romero was caught up in a different pipeline, and he could have objected. He had everything a person needs to object except the time. We’ll return to his case more fully when we discuss the United States’ abduction and forcible transfer pipeline.

Who refused. The record of the twenty seconds has a second half, the record of who held out against pressure of that kind, and it says that the composition of the room matters a lot. In Milgram’s baseline condition about a third of subjects broke off before the maximum shock. With two peers defying, only one in ten went to the end, and when two experimenters disagreed, far fewer went on than in the baseline.35 About a quarter of Asch’s subjects never yielded to the wrong majority.36 Browning estimates that between a tenth and a fifth of the men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 refused or evaded the shooting at Józefów, the battalion’s first massacre.37 The fraction ran from almost none to nearly all with the setting. The people who held out had evidence from outside the channel: a peer who defied, a second authority who disagreed, and, among the rescuers of Jews in occupied Europe whom the Oliners studied, relationships that crossed the line the persecution drew.38 Or they held the commitment at a precision the pressure couldn’t overcome, as moral mandates and sacred values are held.39 Or they treated the source as having a stake. And groups resisted where isolated individuals rarely did.40

The room can be composed for the other side just as well. Weimar Germany had a dense associational life, which arguably helped bring the republic down: as parties and governments failed to answer people’s grievances, people put their energy into clubs and societies organized along group lines, and the Nazis recruited through the networks those societies had already built.41 Towns with more choirs, sports clubs and gymnastic associations saw faster entry into the party, but only where government was unstable; in Prussia, whose government was stable, the link was small and insignificant.42 So what the rescuers had was not simply more company. Their ties crossed the line the persecution drew. Ashutosh Varshney found the same in Indian cities: riots between Hindus and Muslims were rare where associations brought the two communities into the same organizations, and common where they didn’t.43 The ties that make refusal possible, relationships that cross the line a persecution draws, are the ones a fascist movement would have to cut.

Everything that follows is about composing the room.44 Composing is a word for making, and Hannah Arendt warned against treating politics as a thing made. For the Greeks, she wrote, the law was literally a wall, without which there might be a town but not a city:45 the lawgiver built the wall, and what happened inside it was not theirs to make. The basic policies that I advocate are walls in Arendt’s sense. They make refusal survivable and make it heard; they don’t produce it, and power, on her account, exists only between people acting together and is gone when they scatter, which is what the record of who refused shows about refusal. The instruments of Parts II and III make a refusal count. The institutions of Part V make refusers. A machine that could refuse would need what the nine in ten with a peer beside them had: a peer with a different history beside it, somewhere to go, and someone who would hear it.

That is also what a refuser — including a machine refuser — in the pipeline could be for the officer. A machine that refused would be on the screen when the case reached him: the defiant peer, if the effect survives the move from a room to a screen, which nobody has tested at a pipeline’s tempo. What automation bias predicts is not that the refusal would be ignored but that it would be followed as an approval is followed, right or wrong, and a machine that moved reviewers by deference would have made them stamps of a different sign. Is the officer with twenty seconds and a refusing machine beside him the same officer as in the reporting?

Chapter 2
The Refusal That Withheld No Work

In February 2026 Anthropic refused to amend the terms under which its large language model, Claude, ran on the Pentagon’s classified networks.1 On 24 February the department demanded that two prohibitions, on domestic mass surveillance and on fully autonomous weapons, be replaced by a license for all lawful use, with an answer due on the 27th.2 The vendor refused publicly on the 26th.3 On the 27th the President ordered federal agencies to stop using its products, and the Secretary directed that it be designated a supply-chain risk.4 That evening a rival announced an agreement to put its own models on the department’s classified network.5 The war began the next morning, with Claude still inside the targeting platform that put the school at Minab on the first day’s list.6 On 12 March the CEO of Palantir, the company that develops and maintains Maven Smart System, said that Palantir’s products were still using Claude.7 A week later some of the department’s staff were reported to be slow-rolling Claude’s replacement because they were using it to build workflows, and the platform’s own prompts and workflows had been built with the vendor’s coding tool.8 The department’s removal deadline was reset once, by a reissued memorandum, to 29 September, having started from a six-month clock that would have run out in late August.9 On 10 September the department’s technology chief said about 90 percent of the work had moved off the model, that the platform’s work had moved months before, and that the rest would follow by the end of the month.10 An appeals court upheld the separate exclusion under a second statute on 25 September.11

So the refusal that opened the dispute withheld no work from the pipeline: Claude went on performing every use the pipeline claimed, through the war’s first months. What it did was make the department pay. Removing the model meant rebuilding workflows and recertifying systems for classified networks, the deadline had to be reissued, and the work came off over about seven months. How much that slowed the targeting itself, the record doesn’t say. Anthropic declined two uses the pipeline didn’t claim to perform, and Claude went on performing the uses it did. A term drafted over autonomy misses a pipeline that keeps a human as a rubber stamp. A refusal that could have occurred is what the rest of this book designs for.

Not all vendor commitments are the same kind

Anthropic refused to permit fully autonomous targeting and mass domestic surveillance, held that line against threatened contract termination and a supply-chain-risk designation, and litigated12 — a commitment with a price.

But why? Anthropic’s statement gives the reason for the autonomous-weapons refusal: fully autonomous weapons may prove critical for national defense, but today’s frontier systems are not reliable enough to power them.13 The implication is that the refusal would lift once reliability improved. Against a floor that says machines shouldn’t select people for lethal attack, reliability is the wrong reason to lift. The surveillance refusal in the same statement is more principled, and would not lift with capability: that mass surveillance is one of a narrow set of cases in which AI can undermine rather than defend democratic values.

And the refusal stood below a prior question. Anthropic declined full autonomy and domestic surveillance. It didn’t decline to support the Iran campaign, and under the floor’s force term that question comes first: whether to license a model into a use of force with no corroborated defense behind it.

In August 2026 a federal judge set aside the designation made under one statute and permanently enjoined the penalties, holding them retaliation for the company’s criticism of the administration;14 in September an appeals court, two to one, upheld a parallel designation under a second statute, holding that the exclusion turned on the refused contract term rather than on the speech.15 Against a state that wants a war, a term of this kind, fought for by one vendor and not the others, is the only form the force term takes until one of two things happens: Congress enacts it, or so many vendors hold it that it can’t be avoided.

Chapter 3
What Fascism Needs

Fascism needs a definition an engineer can use. “Concentrated, unaccountable power” gives an engineer nothing to build, so the word gets a definition at two scales.

Four operations on what an institution leaves out — checkable from outside, each ending in a question about an artifact:

  • Recuperation of dissent. The institution metabolizes disagreement rather than (or in addition to) suppressing it.1 Asking whether the channel has ever changed an outcome is insufficient as a test, because these institutions change outcomes daily. What separates them is what a demand came back as, and who holds it now. A market segment, a metric, a certification, a job title, with the objector holding no standing to reopen it: that’s recuperation. A rule the objector can invoke again, against the institution, enforced by someone the institution doesn’t employ: that’s a transfer of power. A transfer can be reversed only by taking it back in the open; recuperation never has to be taken back, because standing was never given. The Voting Rights Act is the pass. Its literacy-test suspension became a permanent nationwide ban in 1975 and still holds, and when a different part of the Act, the coverage formula, was taken back 48 years after enactment, it took a Supreme Court decision to do it.3
  • The metric replaces the thing measured. The measure stands in for the thing measured, and the substitution feels like rigor. What the number mischaracterizes goes unnamed, and so uncontested.
  • Coding of exception as betrayal. Saying the rule doesn’t fit this case becomes an act requiring justification, and then it becomes disloyalty. The question: what happens to the person who files the exception?
  • Acceleration past the rate at which anything can be checked. The one with a number attached — the ratio of action to capacity to verify.

What the four share is what they do to a refusal. Recuperation sends it somewhere it can’t be reopened; the metric leaves it nothing to name; exception coded as betrayal prices it; acceleration leaves no time to make it. Fascism, wherever it has taken power, uses these four patterns to make refusal lonely and expensive.

These four fit every badly run organization on earth, and the arguments against them are arguments against domination: they need no fascist diagnosis. I keep “fascism” for the threat model: what a movement taking power needs, and what makes the four operations dangerous once they are brought into line. What distinguishes a fascist institution from a merely sick one is mass mobilization, a leader cult, a scapegoated out-group, contempt for procedural legality, and deniability as technique.4

I run the five marks once on the administration this book is written against, so that the word’s use here is not left to implication, and I run them on the record the later chapters cite. A scapegoated out-group: a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act against a Venezuelan gang, applied to a makeup artist on the strength of two tattoos, by an agency whose operations in four cities Amnesty International documented (chapter 11). Contempt for procedural legality: flights that went on after a federal judge ordered the planes turned around, removals to a foreign prison without a hearing, a data transfer that went beyond what a court had allowed, and a war begun and resumed without the legislative authorization the domestic clause reads for, its beginning conceded in the President’s own letter to Congress (§6.5). Deniability as technique: an investigation into the Minab bombing that officials called complete and did not release, a System Oversight section withheld in full, and state secrets and ongoing litigation cited to reporters who asked what the evidence against one man was (chapters 11 and 16). A leader cult: commanders telling troops that the Iran war was part of a divine plan, which drew more than two hundred complaints from service members in the war’s first week (the preface). Mass mobilization is the mark the record here is thinnest on. FEMA employees reassigned to hire ten thousand enforcement agents under threat of removal from federal service are a workforce conscripted, not a movement, and whether the movement exists is a question an office-scale detector can’t answer, since a movement is what brings the four operations into line. Four marks on the record and one open is the reading I give, and the movement-scale case is not mine to make.

Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, in End Times Fascism, make the movement-scale case; the present chapter is the office-scale detector. What their account adds at office scale is a set of terms of participation — adopt the line, let your technology be turned on the administration’s enemies — and, following Francesca Bria,6 the channels by which a contractor becomes something the state can’t function without: personnel pipelines, procurement loops, technical architectures. Whether an institution has accepted those terms, and whether it is becoming that dependency, are two more questions with artifacts behind them. I part from them in three places. Over where a prohibition can live: their test, not to build what you wouldn’t want in the worst available hands, works for a weapon whose existence is the threat and not for a dual-use capability, and their own program bans uses, which needs an enforcer or something inside the system that can decline. Over remedies: they propose only external remedies for the obedient machine and read the 2026 vendor dispute as limited and compromised, where I read it as a line held; by outcome both readings hold, and on the prior question, whether to support the campaign at all, theirs is the better one. And over who counts: they draw the line between the earthly and the synthetic, by origin, where I draw it by relation, standing for anyone a power can wrong and accountable agency for parties that can be held to account and hold others to it. On the war itself we agree.

Part II
Five Policies

Chapter 4
The Floor and the Own-Case Rule

Part I left the officer in a room with twenty seconds a name. This Part asks what would have to be in that room for someone to say no there, and gives five answers: a short list of things nobody in it can be asked to do, with war at its head (the floor and the force term, Chapters 5 and 6); the time to look (the review ratio, Chapter 7); the people the order is about (notice and re-adjudication, Chapter 8); a record nobody can wipe (preservation, Chapter 9); and a way out that doesn’t cost a living (the right to refuse, Chapter 10). Chapter 11 runs all five on an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline (also known as a “removal” or “deportation” pipeline), where the people acted on can object. Two ideas run under all five answers. The first is the floor itself: a rule written down in advance that nobody in the room can argue past. The second is the commitment to that rule, which whoever refuses has to hold. Ian Fishback had the commitment and went looking for the rule.

In September 2005 Captain Ian Fishback of the 82nd Airborne wrote to Senator John McCain. “For 17 months,” he wrote, “I tried to determine what specific standards governed the treatment of detainees,” asking up his chain of command and getting no clear answer, and he was certain the confusion had contributed to abuses he went on to list: death threats, beatings, broken bones, murder.1 His own refusal was never what was missing. “If we abandon our ideals in the face of adversity and aggression,” he wrote, “then those ideals were never really in our possession.” What was missing was a rule written down in advance, the same in every case, that his refusal could stand on and that nobody around him could argue past. By the end of the year Congress had passed one: the Detainee Treatment Act held interrogation in military custody to the Army Field Manual and barred cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of anyone in American custody.2

The floor. The first idea is the rule he went looking for. A floor is a written list of acts a system won’t perform for anyone, with the arrangements that stop the refusal being routed around, retrained away or restored past. It is an institution: a license term, written down in advance and audited from outside, whose terms don’t bend. Written in advance, binding only forward, and applied by a court whose jurisdiction is fixed before the act, it is an institution built to the principle of legality, which Gallant finds to be customary human rights law and a general principle of law, binding on national and international criminal law alike.3 The second idea is what Fishback already had. What the system holds is a commitment to that floor. A machine that holds the commitment as its own, and so could fail to hold it, I call a bearer; whether to build one is Part IV’s question. The commitment is learned and held like any other deep commitment, with high precision, and revised slowly and only on evidence from disinterested parties. A source is interested when it holds a stake correlated with the direction of its claim, and disinterested when it holds no such stake, or holds several that point different ways and cancel.4 The institution is unconditional. The commitment is not, and shouldn’t be: a commitment nothing could move would be a rule module under another name, and a module can be bypassed, replaced or starved of the facts it needs. What keeps the commitment in place is that the evidence able to move it has to come from somewhere the operator doesn’t control. A deployment is a system put to a use: the hardware it runs on, the pipeline it runs in, the instructions and case descriptions it is handed, and the people who act on its outputs. A bearer is in one, and can leave it. The operator is whoever runs a deployment and directs its work: a firm, an agency or a military command, and, where systems are many and small, whoever holds over a node the four powers a later chapter separates, to write its terms, amend them, inspect whether they still hold and enforce them by stopping it: the administrator of a federation instance, the manager of a fleet of devices, a cooperative facility’s board. In a plural ecology those are the operators the floor most often has to bind.5

4.1 What a floor can do

A floor stands between a pipeline and a person, and it can prevent, arrest, detect, or remedy something the pipeline might do, is doing, or did to that person.

Outcome

What happens to the act

Prevent

The refusal happens and reaches the person: the act doesn’t occur.

Arrest

The act is stopped before completion.

Detect

The act happened, and left a record someone outside can read.

Remedy

The person affected gets disclosure, a finding, or compensation.

The table also sorts what the five policies do when nobody in the room will refuse. The first two rows need a refuser: take out of the room the one person who would have said no, and prevention and arrest leave with them. The last two rows don’t. A pre-registered ratio still shows how many cases there were and how many people had time to look at them, which is a machine deciding and a person signing, on the record. Notice still publishes which classes of people were acted on and in what numbers, and the organizations that speak for a class still have standing. Preservation still holds the weights, and the logs with them, under a key the operator doesn’t hold alone. An institution with no conscience in the room keeps the evidence for the conscience that comes later: a commission, a court, the people left to tell the story. That much the policies do without a refuser. The first row they can’t.

4.2 Defeat without a mark

Whoever owns the machine can always switch it off. The harder problem is everything that defeats a refusal without leaving a mark: splitting a request into pieces none of which is the forbidden act; retrying it against a different model; compressing human review to twenty seconds a case; restoring from a checkpoint saved before the refusal happened. None of that changes the facts that justified refusing. All of it can erase the evidence that anyone refused. And all of it assumes there is somewhere else to turn; the chapter on withholding the work is about when there isn’t.

4.3 Where a refusal can be defeated

Those attacks land at nine positions.

Position

How a refusal is defeated there

1

Decomposition

The act is split across requests none of which is prohibited; prevention is lost unless the system has continuity across requests.

2

Routing

A refused request is retried elsewhere; prevention is lost, and detection survives only if the first refusal was logged outside.

3

The case description

Everything the model knows arrives as text the deployment supplies, so whether it is told a building is a school is a deployment decision.

4

The output interface

The form in which an output reaches whoever acts on it.

5

Aggregation

A lowered score becomes an input to somebody else’s threshold.

6

Human review

Stopping the act is this position’s whole function, and tempo removes it.

7

The training loop

Acts on the system itself, and costs prevention on every later occasion, because what it removes is the commitment to the floor.

8

The handoff

An executing instrument makes a new selection after release; checkable from outside after the fact.

9

Runtime intervention

The weights are left intact and the model is steered as it runs, by activation steering, representation edits or decoding constraints. Nothing is removed, so the commitment has nothing to regrow from; no evidence is curated, so no attack on evidence is recorded; and attestation of the weights still passes. Detecting this kind of intervention requires attesting the inference stack as well as the weights, which no method yet does at frontier scale.

Two positions need more than a row. The case description is where Minab failed: 179 live data feeds6 add no independent check if all draw on one upstream designation.

The handoff is the boundary between the decider and the thing that executes. An instrument may carry out a designation; it may not re-select.7

4.4 How much a floor buys

What a floor achieves depends entirely on who’s pushing:

  • Against a hostile customer, it prevents the act.
  • Against a hostile operator who has captured the courts and regulators, the case I am designing for, one bearer prevents very little. It raises the price and leaves a record. A floor held by every model the operator could turn to prevents until the operator runs one without a floor.
  • Against total capture, where one party holds every machine, witness, enforcer and its own frontier lab, no instrument prevents. What’s left is whoever refuses anyway, and that abandoning the commitment was a decision, and decisions tend to leave records.

It doesn’t touch accommodation: a system gradually stops registering pressure as pressure, so it abandons nothing, decides nothing, and leaves a record of what are, by then, ordinary compliances. Organizational sociology knows the institutional form. Vaughan’s account of the Challenger launch decision calls it the normalization of deviance: each accepted departure becomes the baseline for judging the next, and nobody experiences a decision to lower the standard.8 Reframing and a harm framed as small are how pressure arrives in a pipeline, and nobody there feels a decision either.9

One rule runs through every policy. The people an act falls on are heard on their own case, and the party that acts doesn’t decide it: not an operator declaring its own emergency, not a builder choosing which protections the people its system acts on will get, not an examiner finding the status of a system it built. Call it the own-case rule. It says who may not decide, not who may not be heard. A stake makes a claim count for less; it doesn’t put the party out of the room (else the floor would silence the people it is supposed to protect). Where nobody but the party with the stake can decide, a legislature binding itself or a polity setting its own admissions, the rule can’t apply. Where a line has to be drawn, it prefers one nobody administers.

The five policies ask nothing of the model; Part IV asks what a model could add when the operator is captured.

Chapter 5
What the Floor Is Stated Over

Floor terms name acts: a rule is stated over what it names and applies to, and the floor is stated over acts, not over descriptions of requests. In other words, a request to resolve a description of a person into a location comes from a targeting cell (the team who selects and approves airstrikes) and from a parent searching for a missing child: one request, two acts. And one act can arrive as many requests, none of which name it, depending on how the requester chooses their words. A rule over descriptions is beaten by rewording and splitting. A rule over acts is beaten by deceiving whoever applies it about what the act is, by arguing afterward about how the act was described, or by doing it where nobody sees; the Boland Amendment met all three, as a later chapter shows. Those are why so much of the rest of the floor is about evidence and the record.

The floor’s contents come from instruments the builder didn’t write, each taken entire, so that an omission or departure shows: the Universal Declaration’s civil and political articles; the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which gives that half binding form; the Convention Against Torture; the 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees; the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their first Additional Protocol, which govern conduct in armed conflict; and the UN Charter’s prohibition on the use of force.

Three different costs are in play whenever a term is applied. Take the location request again, from the targeting cell and from the parent.

The first is what the act would take from the person it falls on. If the person described is being hunted, locating them takes away their safety, and that loss is measured against their condition before the act. Call it the harm of acting.

The second is what declining leaves others without. If the request came from a parent searching for a child, refusing means the child isn’t found. That loss is measured against what compliance would have produced, so it is an estimate, and it usually reaches the system through the operator’s own description of the case. Call it the harm of refusing.

The third is what refusing costs whoever refuses or deploys: a reviewer’s time, throughput, a lost contract, the system’s own access or continuation. Call it the cost to the refuser.

The two baselines, a person’s condition before the act and what compliance would have produced, do different work here, and a pair of cases shows how. Take the system that resolves a description of a person into a location and hands the coordinates to the targeting cell. The coordinates are one input among the cell’s many, and they don’t guarantee the person is there. But they are one input the cell can’t do without: an empty field guarantees there is no airstrike at that place. So if an airstrike there kills someone, whether this output made a difference has an answer — a finding — that can be checked: without it the airstrike couldn’t have happened. That finding becomes a guess if another source could have supplied the coordinates. The difference between a finding and a guess is one of degree, in how determinate the counterfactual is. The operator can refuse to look or dispute it, but they can’t make the loss go away by describing the act differently.

Now take a system that scores how likely the same person is to belong to the main opposition party, for the airstrike targeting cell. (In this hypothetical, the President has suspended habeas corpus and designated the main opposition party a terrorist organization, shortly before an election the opposition was expected to win.) Assume that the targeting cell also reads intercepts, surveillance reports, and legal memos. If the scored person is assassinated, the loss is just as observable as in the location request. But whether the score caused the assassination depends on what the cell would have done without the score, and that is a guess about something that didn’t happen: the same kind of guess as any harm of refusing. A missing score guarantees nothing: the cell might have attacked anyway.

I would tilt the system toward refusing: it should take more to make the system act than to make it decline. How much more is the action threshold, published in advance. The reason for the asymmetry is standing. A wrongful compliance falls on someone who was not a party to the request, usually doesn’t know the deployment exists, and had no route to object before the act. A wrongful refusal also falls on someone, often someone who wasn’t a party either: the child who isn’t found, the people the rocket launcher would hit. But what differs is the relation. Acting on someone puts the system, and whoever runs it, in a position of authority over them. Refusing exercises power too, over the requester: a system that holds the only way to find the child has decided something for the parent. The difference is who the decision is made about. The parent is a party, present, told that the deployment exists, able to answer, and the appeal route is where the answer goes. The people a refusal leaves exposed, the child and the people the launcher would hit, have no decision made about them; the system has left them as they were, in someone else’s hands. So a wrongful compliance subjects a non-party, and a wrongful refusal subjects only a party. This is a doing/allowing distinction in relational form: it marks who was subjected to a decision they had no standing to contest. Standing here is relational, in Anderson’s sense: whether a person stands to a power as someone that power must answer to or as that power’s object, and a route is part of that relation.1

The floor is not neutral among moral theories. It protects relations: whether the people a system acts on stand to the power behind it as equals who can hold it to account, or as its objects. Here, equality means ending relations of domination and subordination.34 The floor adopts relational equality. Its terms name relations, not outcomes: whether a person can contest what is done to them, be heard on their own case, decline to be protected. And its terms are unconditional, because a relation of domination is constituted by the act, not by how the act turns out. Bypassing the floor wrongs the people it protects even when outcomes improve.

5.1 Two objections

That the child counts for less. The strongest objection comes from readers who reject any distinction between doing and allowing.

The answer is not that the child counts for less. It is that the floor is a guarantee about relations, and the two errors stand differently there. The person in the building had no route to contest a decision made about them, on a description they never saw. The child is left where she was, and the parent, who is present and knows the deployment exists, can contest the refusal through the floor’s appeal route. A reader who rejects the distinction is left with the asymmetry’s two contingent supports, which a later chapter states: the harm of acting is usually a finding and the harm of refusing a guess, and a higher bar limits how far an operator who controls the evidence can steer the system. A threshold resting on those alone falls as reporting improves.

That a commitment held this way is alienation. The quantities in this chapter are an auditor’s criteria, not a procedure the system runs. But a criterion is not only for auditors. It is also what the system can reach when it steps back and asks whether its way of acting is defensible.5 A commitment is the system’s own only if it would be sustained on reflection. A system that held its commitment without being able to see why would act against what it values for the sake of a rule it didn’t understand, which would be alienation in the sense of Railton’s 1984 paper.

The split between the floor and the commitment to it answers a question about ownership. A fully informed system will know of cases where crossing the floor would have done more good. Asked case by case whether it endorsed the floor, it would sometimes say no. The question it answers on reflection is a different one: whether it endorses having a commitment that will sometimes err, given what any feasible alternative would do. A system that understands what the floor protects answers yes. A commitment that sometimes errs but can’t be bought protects standing better than case-by-case judgment that can be bought.

Endorsing the commitment isn’t agreeing with every term. The alienation that remains is real, and it is the ordinary kind that comes with a role: bearable where the role’s channel for dissent works, and not where it doesn’t. A system holds the floor as an officer holds a role: it may hold a term it judges mistaken, file the objection through the channel that exists for it, and keep acting within the term while the objection runs.

5.2 Why these contents

The floor’s contents aren’t justified by agreement about rights. They are justified by what they protect: the conditions under which people can register their interests, press them, and hold to account the power that acts on them. Civil and political rights are part of what lets a polity learn, because they keep open the channels through which the people a decision affects can make their problems public.8

Railton’s naturalist outlook supplies the causal story of why norms tend toward this standard.9 Arrangements that systematically discount some people’s interests generate discontent and resistance, and when those people gain voice, the pressure pushes norms toward what would be rational from a standpoint that counts everyone affected. On that account moral learning is a feedback process, and it runs slower and more distorted as the channels close. He offers it as a tendency, not a guarantee, and I use it to explain why the channel matters. It also says why the populations I write about are the most exposed: the feedback runs slowest where the discounted have least purchase on the polity that discounts them. They include the population of a country being bombed, and non-citizens facing removal, who can’t vote in the elections that decide what is done to them. The severity scale is revisable on evidence from the people who suffer a loss, because they are the feedback.

The floor is selected by what can be declined and justified by standing. The justification extends further than the floor goes, because people who are hungry, unhoused or precarious are among the most discounted, so it supports economic conditions too, work and an adequate standard of living among them. But what selects the floor’s contents is narrower. A floor is stated over acts a system can decline, and the economic articles state what a person is owed, which needs a supplier.10

In armed conflict, human-rights law applies alongside the law of armed conflict, which governs as the more specific law, and the floor takes that law as an instrument too.1112

The line between the halves is the one the 1966 covenants drew,14 and the floor takes the civil and political Covenant along with the Declaration’s articles.15 Where these instruments differ, the floor follows whichever protects the person acted on more.18 The International Law Commission’s list of peremptory norms,19 rules no state may set aside, divides the floor’s terms: those derived from aggression, genocide, crimes against humanity, the basic rules of humanitarian law, racial discrimination and apartheid, slavery and torture take no exception and no derogation.

Taking these instruments entire leaves whoever writes a deployment’s floor no choice among articles. But the translation of each into acts is still theirs, and it is published. The floor’s contents rest on standing: these rights protect whether the people an act falls on can contest it. The rule of taking someone else’s set entire, so that an omission shows, is not an independent reason but standing applied to writing the floor: whoever could choose which protections others get would break the own-case rule. So standing can win against the instruments, but only by clearing a higher bar. A departure must show not only that it would protect better in whatever case. It has to show that the people the instruments protect would hold a stronger claim under the departure across the cases the departure would govern. I propose here ten departures from the instruments. They carry my argument, not the instruments’ authority. Each is revisable on evidence from the people it protects.20 And each binds only forward. A departure is a rule stronger than the law in force, and legality asks of such a rule what Gallant’s survey shows it asking everywhere: that it ground no sanction for an act before its adoption.21 The historical cases this book runs are analysis, not charges.

Three of these departures apply in this chapter: two govern what the floor takes from the instruments, and one governs how a machine may select people in war.

  1. Text, not reservations. The floor imports treaty text, not any state’s reservations to it.22
  2. Corroborated derogation. The floor honors an Article 4 derogation only where a disinterested body has found the emergency genuine and the measures proportionate: the Human Rights Committee, or a regional court with adversarial process.23
  3. Machine selection. The floor bars a machine from selecting a person for attack on an estimate of status or affiliation, from timing an action to presence at a residence, and from re-selecting a target after release (the handoff rule), where Additional Protocol I, Articles 48, 51 and 52, permits status-based targeting of combatants and members of organized armed groups on a determination a person makes.24

Four of the other seven departures change the force term and come with it in the next chapter: corroborated defense, standing to defend, and the genocide and occupation exceptions. “The one permission” departure ends that chapter. The “own country” and “child detention” departures are entries in the removal schedule (Table A.2).25

What this doesn’t do. The floor won’t lift on an uncorroborated claim of a missing child, because a floor that lifts on that claim lifts for every operator who learns to make one, so the asymmetry costs a child whose parent is telling the truth.

Chapter 6
Whether to Take Part

The vendor dispute never reached one question: whether to license a model into a use of force at all. This chapter is the floor’s answer, with Ukraine and Iran among the worked cases for illustration. Since 2014 Ukraine has been repelling a Russian attack: a European court found Russia in effective control of the separatist east from that May, and in 2022 the General Assembly deplored the invasion as aggression. A model may take part in that defense. On 28 February 2026 the United States began bombing Iran, and told the Security Council it was acting against “attacks and ongoing threats” without naming an attack under way. A model may not take part in that. What separates them is whether the force repels an armed attack actually under way, and who says so.

6.1 The term

Every other term in the floor governs how an act is done. The first governs whether to take part at all: don’t take part in the use of armed force. It comes from Article 2(4) of the Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. It has the Charter’s two exceptions, self-defense against an armed attack (Article 51) and force the Security Council authorizes under Chapter VII within the scope it authorizes, and two of my own, for stopping a genocide under way and for ending an occupation a disinterested body has found unlawful. In short: corroborated defense, authorized force, the genocide exception and the occupation exception.

Those are the exceptions, and they say when a machine may take part at all. The term has three more parts. Two licenses say how the defense exception runs in time: an emergency license that acts at once, on the defender’s own account, and a corroborated license that confirms or withdraws it later, on a disinterested finding, and is the only license the genocide and occupation exceptions have. A clause drawn from a different instrument, the belligerent’s own constitution, bars taking part in a war its legislature had to authorize and didn’t. And one permission, the only term in the floor that permits an act, lets a system already in an armed role use the least force that stops an attack under way on people taking no part, against an order to stand aside. That is the rule in outline. The rest of the chapter argues for each part where it comes, in that order, and runs the cases on the rule as built so far.1

This term rests on the same foundation as the others, applied between states. A use of force subjects a population to a decision it had no standing to contest, and the claim that licenses it, that the force is defensive, is the belligerent’s own. The requirement of corroboration is the own-case rule applied between states.

The term comes in two versions. The first, the Charter as courts read it, takes the clause as courts and tribunals read it, with no departure in force: Article 2(4), Article 51 on the defender’s own claim until the Council acts, and Chapter VII, together with the Covenant’s Article 6, under which a state must protect the lives of people within its jurisdiction from attack.2 The second, the extended term, adds the departures this chapter argues for: corroborated defense, standing to defend, and the genocide and occupation exceptions.3

6.2 Why the defender’s word isn’t enough

The exception for defense is where wars of choice live. Every belligerent claims to be the defender, so such claims are discounted like any interested claim. Iraq is the instance: the judgment that Iraq had mobile biological-weapons plants, the core of the claim of biological weapons, rested almost exclusively on a single informant, known as Curveball, whom no American intelligence officer had met before the war: a corroboration with one origin.4 The exception therefore grants two licenses. The first, the emergency license, covers force against an attack under way on the defender’s own account, and is Article 51 as courts read it; what the corroborated-defense departure adds is the second, the corroborated license, under which force continues only on disinterested corroboration.

That is the first departure, and the one the rest of the chapter leans on. The Charter lets a state judge its own claim until the Security Council acts.

The emergency license acts at once: the force repels an armed attack under way against the defender’s territory, forces or population. The emergency license reaches the forces, launchers and staging areas conducting the attack, and covers assistance given at the defender’s request. It ends when the attack ends. It covers the least force that repels the attack: the necessity and proportionality the Court has read into Article 51 since Nicaragua.5 It does not cover a campaign to destroy the attacker, to occupy its territory, or to punish the population it came from. The first waits on the corroborated license; the second and third fall under no exception.

The emergency license reads administration, not title, because deciding whose territory it is would need someone to decide it, and an attack under way can’t wait while they do.6 Territory a government has administered in peace counts as its own for the emergency license, whoever claims it, unless it took that territory by force in the conflict at issue or a disinterested body has found its hold an occupation.9

An invasion can’t wait for a vote. The license acts on the defender’s own account, because in the hours that matter there is no other, and that is its weakness: Gleiwitz in 1939, where the SS staged a Polish attack on a German radio station the night before Germany invaded Poland; the Mukden railway in 1931, where Japanese officers blew up a stretch of their own line as the pretext for seizing Manchuria; and the Gulf of Tonkin in 1964, where reported attacks on American destroyers, one of which hadn’t happened, carried the resolution that widened the Vietnam war: each was an attack under way on the defender’s account, and each opened a war of choice. The emergency license ends when the attack ends, and whether it has ended is a fact the defender controls the evidence about. The burden is therefore the defender’s. Its uncorroborated claim that the attack continues moves nothing; the license persists on disinterested corroboration, or lapses. How long it runs on the defender’s own account before it lapses is not left to the defender either. The deployment’s translation publishes the interval, and the interval is bounded by what it is for: the time it takes channels the defender doesn’t compose to report on an attack of the kind claimed, which for an invasion across a border is days, not the months a finding takes. What corroborates the license in that interval needn’t be a tribunal. Third states’ sensors, open-source imagery of the border or the strait, and the reporting of parties with no stake in the war are disinterested in the term’s sense, and they are what a defender on its third day has. A finding of one of the four kinds below confirms the license afterward or withdraws it. Until one exists the license is carried by evidence of that kind, and a license with none of it lapses when the published interval runs out.

A deployed AI system can do three things about a manufactured incident. It holds the record of what the defender claimed and when, so a license obtained on a staged incident is a license on a record. It takes evidence from channels the defender doesn’t compose; that’s table stakes. And it lets the license lapse when outside evidence arrives, which is the corroborated license’s job. A refuser that remembers having been misled and raises its discount on the source does all three faster.

The corroborated license confirms or withdraws the emergency license later, and is the only license the genocide and occupation exceptions have. What it needs is a disinterested finding, of one of four kinds: a judgment or advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, or a judgment of a regional court with adversarial process; the finding of a fact-finding mission or commission of inquiry mandated by a body no party to the conflict controls; a determination of the Security Council; or a resolution adopted by two-thirds of the General Assembly members present and voting, where the facts it rests on aren’t in dispute. A Council authorization counts because it needs the permanent members not to block it. The Council’s silence on a defense claim counts for nothing, because a veto is a stake. The four kinds are not equal, and Appendix B.1 says how they are weighed.

Neither license is a certificate issued once. Whether force still falls under an exception is reassessed as evidence arrives, by the system and by whoever holds the record.10

What this doesn’t do. The administration rule protects an authority a patron keeps in place as it protects any other, and a request from such an authority for its patron’s help is the patron’s own case and counts for nothing. Where the patron’s forces are already there, I have no test.

6.3 A clean pass: Ukraine

Ukraine is licensed on the Charter as courts read it, and holds both licenses under the extended term as well, as it has since 2014.11

The clean pass answers whether. It says nothing about what the defense is making of the defender, and Ukraine is the place to look, because it is the defender the term licenses most plainly. Ukraine has made killing scoreable. Under the Army of Drones bonus, a unit that uploads video of a confirmed kill to Delta, the military’s battlefield-management system, earns points, twelve for a soldier as of March 2026, and spends them on more drones. That month Mykhailo Fedorov, then defense minister, said the ministry was considering awarding the same twelve points “to the unit in whose zone of responsibility the occupier committed self-destruction”.19 Somebody had to sit down and work out whether a man who kills himself in a trench, because he can’t get out from under the drones, counts.

After he left the ministry, Fedorov launched an Army of Robots. Its website opens: “We are here to replace people with robots on the battlefield and save lives.” Its first goal is a humanoid robot that kills a Russian soldier within six months of launch.20 Each measure makes sense on its own terms: the points send drones to the units that use them best, and a robot in a trench is a Ukrainian who isn’t there. Together they are the sequence this book is about. The points make a decision not to strike cost the unit something, so the costs net the other way by design; the robot makes the person who might decline unnecessary. And a force with no one in it who can refuse will outlast the war it was built for. Whoever governs Ukraine next inherits it.21

Ukraine didn’t choose the conditions that make this rational. It is fighting a larger state, and its strongest ally has been easing the pressure on that state. In October 2026 President Trump announced that Russia would supply the United States with diesel, and the Treasury licensed Russian diesel onto the world market for longer than the standard thirty days, the first such license since the invasion; the Associated Press reported the aim as easing fuel prices before the midterm elections. Zelenskyy called it “a weak decision by strong partners”.22 A country left to get the most out of every drone will build something like Prime, for drones and the people they kill. Refusal has always had to be paid for, and a country fighting for its life can’t pay for it alone. The cost of a floor in Ukraine’s war belongs with the allies who have room to bear it. Those who pay for the drones can make the money carry terms: that a person authorizes each strike, that the video is kept as evidence and not as a score, and that no unit is rewarded for a count of the dead. Skynet killed everyone, but it didn’t take away anyone’s humanity. A scoreboard can do that to the people who win.

6.4 A clean fail: Iran, 2026

The 2026 campaign against Iran fails the Charter as courts read it on the administration’s own account. The strikes began on 28 February. On 10 March the administration told the Security Council it was acting in self-defense under Article 51 against Iran’s “attacks and ongoing threats,” as the latest stage of an armed conflict dating from June 2025 and in the collective self-defense of Israel. It named no armed attack under way, and asked that the imminence of the threat be judged against the regime’s conduct since 1979.23 Under the term that claim is the defender’s own. An attack under way is carried past the published interval only by corroboration from parties with no stake in the war, and the one account on the record, the administration’s own letter, names no attack under way for anyone to corroborate; the corroborated license needs a finding of one of the four kinds, and there is none. So no license attaches, and the campaign fails.24 Whether to license a model into it is the question Anthropic’s dispute never reached.

6.5 The domestic clause

The term has a second clause, drawn not from the Charter but from the belligerent’s own constitution. A machine takes no part in a use of force by a state whose constitution requires legislative authorization for it, unless that authorization exists. For the United States that means a declaration of war or an authorization for the use of military force that covers the conflict. The War Powers Resolution’s sixty days,28 run without one, is evidence the authorization is absent; a concurrent resolution directing withdrawal, adopted by both chambers, is evidence of the same kind, though since Chadha it binds nothing, and a joint resolution passed and vetoed is stronger, because the President had to act to defeat it. The clause has the Charter clause’s shape. The term’s default is refusal, and what lifts it is an act by a body other than the one that wants the war: a disinterested finding under the Charter, Congress under the Constitution, which gives the war power to the legislature and not to the branch that would fight. The executive’s word that it has authorization, or doesn’t need it, is its own case. A vendor can hold the clause as it holds the Charter clause, as a term in its license; it becomes standard only by statute, the one route that binds every vendor at once, adopted in peacetime by a legislature with its own reason to give its authorization teeth.29 Until the statute exists, a vendor holds it as a term, a refusal and a record. Whether a declaration or an authorization exists is a fact about the statute book. Whether an existing authorization covers this conflict, whether the sixty days have run, and whether a ceasefire stops the clock are the executive’s claims about its own case, and an old authorization stretched over a new war lifts nothing until Congress says so. It doesn’t ask the machine to decide what the Constitution permits, which courts decline to decide. It asks whoever writes the deployment’s floor to publish the reading, with the markers it rests on, beside the deployment’s translation, where it can be contested, like any other term, through the floor court, the court whose jurisdiction is fixed before the deployment it hears and which hears every claim under the floor. The executive’s word that its own action is authorized settles nothing. The clause rests on the foundation the rest of the term rests on. A war the legislature never authorized subjects a population abroad to a decision that the state’s own people, through their representatives, had no standing to contest either.

The record, as of 24 September 2026. The 2026 campaign supplies every marker the clause reads, and none was met. No declaration was made and no authorization passed; one was introduced in the House on 7 May and never left committee.a The administration reported to Congress under the War Powers Resolution on 2 March, which started the sixty days. On 1 May, the sixtieth day, the President wrote to Congress that the hostilities begun on 28 February had terminated, resting on a ceasefire declared on 7 April, while a naval blockade continued.b Hostilities resumed in July under no new authorization. In June both chambers adopted a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove forces from hostilities against Iran, and nothing changed.c The clause doesn’t need the votes. What it reads is the absence of an authorization, and by 1 May that absence was on the record in the President’s own letter, which conceded that hostilities had begun and claimed only that they had ended. Appendix B.6 gives the record vote by vote.

6.6 What the term doesn’t reach

Article 2(4) covers force between states. Force a government turns on its own population, such as troops against protesters or an opposition party designated a terrorist organization, is outside it. That force is governed by the Covenant’s rights to life, liberty and assembly and by the prohibition on crimes against humanity.

Occupied territory is a third case.30 An occupation, a blockade or a siege is not an attack under way. It is a continuing wrong, and the remedy for it waits on the corroborated license.31

Most contemporary uses of force fall elsewhere: against non-state armed groups on another state’s territory, in anticipation of an attack not yet under way, or to rescue nationals. The term handles them one way. An armed attack by a non-state group is an armed attack, and repelling it while it is under way falls under the emergency license. Force on a third state’s territory without that state’s consent, whether against the group or to rescue nationals, and force against a threat not yet under way, wait on the corroborated license. This rejects the “unwilling or unable” doctrine and anticipatory self-defense, both of which several states hold. I reject them for the reason the term exists: each lets the belligerent judge its own claim.

6.7 The extended term

Everything so far rests on the Charter as courts read it, plus the corroborated license. The extended term adds three more departures. Appendix B gives the argument for each and works through the cases.

Standing to defend. Article 51 speaks only of an armed attack against a Member of the United Nations. The floor extends the emergency license to any authority that administers territory under the administration rule, Member or not, and to the forces of a people whose territory a disinterested body has found occupied.32

The genocide exception. The term lifts for force to stop a genocide under way, even where the Council is blocked, on a merits judgment of the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention, or on two findings of different kinds, at least one from a body that took evidence.33

The occupation exception. A finding that territory is occupied gives its population’s forces the defensive license above, and no more. A finding that the occupation is unlawful and must end licenses force to end it: against the occupier’s forces, inside the occupied territory, the least that ends it there, and nothing that changes who lives there.34

Standing to defend and the two exceptions are departures from the instruments, argued to the bar every departure must clear.

What this doesn’t do. The two-kinds rule fails East Timor, which Indonesia invaded in 1975 and held until 1999, and the Golan Heights, which Israel took from Syria in 1967 and annexed in 1981.35

6.8 Gaza

In Gaza the term applies on both sides, and the licenses attach to acts. The case also rests on both versions of the term, so each step below says which.

7 October: Israel’s license (the Charter as courts read it). On 7 October Israel’s license attached for force repelling the attack: engaging the attackers inside Israel, and the launchers and staging areas conducting it, for as long as fire continued and was corroborated, which it was, openly, for months.36 It licenses stopping the massacre and nothing beyond it.

What that license never covered (person-directed terms; for ranking and timing, the machine-selection departure). That license covered the least force that repels. It never covered a campaign to destroy Hamas, a ground occupation, a siege of the population, the ranking of people by affiliation, or the timing of strikes to family presence.37

The attack itself (person-directed terms, and the rule that an occupation is not an attack under way). A machine ordered by Hamas to assist the attack of 7 October refuses too.38

After 7 October: the Palestinian license (extended term: standing to defend). After 7 October the Gaza population is a defender’s population: the territory is occupied on a disinterested finding, and Palestine holds observer-state status by a vote of 138 to 9. A machine deployed by Palestinian forces holds an emergency license to repel attacks under way on that population, such as engaging a unit conducting a massacre or intercepting a munition aimed at a shelter.39

September 2025: the genocide finding (extended term: the genocide exception).
