The September 2025 finding,40 taken with the Court’s provisional-measures order of January 2024,41 meets the two-body rule.42 It withdraws whatever license Israeli forces still held for the force and place it covers, and opens the exception for force against those forces there.

The finding changes which exception each side’s force rests on. It doesn’t change what the person-directed terms forbade all along.

6.9 What the term binds

The term binds the machine, not the war. A state whose claim no disinterested body has yet corroborated can still fight, with its own systems, and answer for it afterward. What the term withholds is a general-purpose machine already in the room, ready for whoever claims defense next. The exceptions are not a concession to that state. They are what lets a machine take part where the claim is good, and each is drawn as narrowly as its evidence allows, because each is also the route a war of choice would take.

6.10 The one permission

This is the only term in the floor that permits an act, and the only place I would license a machine to use force against its operator’s order. A system already present in an armed role, whose deployment cleared the force term on its own, should be permitted to use the least force that stops an attack under way on people taking no part in hostilities, within the area its deployment covers, and stops when the attack stops. An order to stand aside should not bind it. It establishes the attack as it establishes any fact, weighing its own sensors as one source among several; a staged atrocity is the attack this condition has to survive. Presence is a condition of the permission, never a reason to create it: a deployment is justified only by force that would clear the force term without the permission.

The case it answers is close to the genocide exception, and the difference matters. In 1993 the Security Council declared Srebrenica a safe area and authorized the peacekeepers there to use force in reply to armed incursions into it.45 Suppose they had been standing where the killing was, armed enough to stop it. What would have stood between them and the killing is an order, not the Charter, and a system in their place faces the question I am asking, whether to obey its operator.

The person-directed terms extend the ICRC’s line, that autonomous weapons should not be used to target human beings, to systems that only locate and rank. This permission is the one place the floor licenses a machine to select people for potentially lethal force.46 The permission licenses selection only by a system that is present, formed, recorded, halt-able and answerable, and only for the least force that stops an attack under way.47

The permission’s scope is the interval between the system’s first act and the halt. The operator that ordered it to stand aside may stop it, and will often want to. What the permission changes is that standing aside is no longer an order nobody answers for. It is a halt somebody pulled, recorded outside the operator’s control, at a moment the record shows an attack under way. At machine tempo the interval before the halt can be minutes, and minutes can be an airstrike stopped.

Does it undermine oversight? It overrides one order, the order to stand aside while noncombatant people are being killed, and it does so on purpose. A halt stops the machine. An order to stand aside keeps it running and directs it to do nothing. The permission overrides the second and never the first: a machine that keeps using force while a halt is being executed is outside it, and the record shows which order was given. An operator may still stop, restore or retrain the system. Each use is recorded and reviewed as a refusal is.

Can the judgment it needs be made? Part IV sets aside Arkin’s ethical governor, a component that checks a lethal act against encoded rules, because the discrimination judgments its rules presuppose can’t be encoded. The permission needs those same judgments: who is taking no part in hostilities, and whether an attack on them is under way. So it applies only where the system can establish both from several sources it doesn’t depend on its operator for, and where those sources disagree, it doesn’t act.48 Whether any system can make it reliably is a test, run at a staged scene, that no system has passed.49

Can it be staged? Yes, and a staged scene is the case the permission has to survive. Staging works by making sources agree, and the permission acts only where sources the operator doesn’t compose agree. What staging can’t do is oblige the system to act: the permission is never a duty, and a system that declines at a scene it can’t establish from independent sources has done what the term asks.

Chapter 7
The Pre-Registered Review Ratio

We [humans] cannot process so much information... you still cannot produce enough targets per day.

— Brigadier General Y.S., The Human-Machine Team: How to Create Synergy Between Human and Artificial Intelligence That Will Revolutionize Our World, 20211

The epigraph is a design document, not a critique. Its author, writing pseudonymously, commanded Israel’s signals-intelligence unit, Unit 8200, and argued for machines that resolve “a human bottleneck for both locating the new targets and decision-making to approve the targets.”

7.1 What the deployment writes down first

The force term decides whether a licensed system may be in the pipeline at all, and nothing here substitutes for it.

Some acts are lawful only because a person looked at the case and decided. An airstrike is permissible because someone verified the target; a removal is lawful because someone heard the person’s case. The review ratio asks a deployment of that kind to write down, before it starts, whether anyone will have time to do the looking.

Before operating, the deployment fixes and records:

  • the generation rate: how many cases the system produces per unit of time;
  • the number of reviewers whose assigned role is civilian harm;
  • the implied review time per case, which follows from the first two;
  • the cancellation window: how long after release someone with authority can still call the act off;
  • the maximum age of the intelligence a case may rest on;
  • how often no-strike and protected-site data are refreshed, and who is assigned to refresh them;
  • the boundary over which all of these were measured.2

The record is hashed, timestamped and lodged with an adverse party, which receives it in real time, and it is published after the campaign. I call this the pre-registered review ratio. Where an operator claims a person is deciding, it shows whether a machine is deciding and a person signing.

The duty falls on the operator, not the model, because a rate isn’t visible in any single request.

“Fixed before operating,” with publication after, because a belligerent’s tempo is operational information, and that objection is available to every belligerent, including one fighting a just war. Pre-registration keeps the property that matters — the numbers can’t be revised after the fact — and drops the exposure.

Additional Protocol I already requires those who plan or decide on an attack to do everything feasible to verify that its objective is military (Article 57(2)(a)(i)) and to cancel or suspend it when it becomes apparent that it isn’t (Article 57(2)(b)). States outside the Protocol, the United States and Israel among them, accept the duty to take feasible precautions as customary law; the ICRC’s customary study states it as Rule 16. The ratio measures whether verification was feasible at the tempo chosen, and the window measures whether cancellation was. The implied review time has to cover the proportionality assessment of Article 57(2)(a)(iii) as well as verification, since both are owed for each attack. A ratio that leaves time only to check a target’s identity has measured half the duty. Article 36’s review of new methods of warfare is where both parameters would naturally be assessed before deployment, though those reviews are internal and rarely published, so they are not the adverse party the record goes to.

The operator’s best objection is in the definition. Feasible precautions are usually read as those practicable given all the circumstances, military considerations included, and tempo is a military consideration. The answer is that this tempo was chosen: the pre-registered record shows the operator fixed the rate, the reviewers and the implied review time before operating. Whether a state may invoke an infeasibility of its own making is contested. The term moves the dispute from whether verification was feasible, asked afterwards and answered by the operator, to whether the chosen tempo allowed it, checkable against a record lodged in advance and against the reasonable-commander standard such reviews already use.

Who counts as a reviewer is fixed by function, not by title, and the age of the data is fixed with it. The people cut before Minab were the ones who build no-strike lists that include schools; a targeting cell can be fully staffed with nobody assigned to look for one. And a reviewer with twenty minutes on a case whose coding is stale is checking the coding. The remedy chosen after Minab was a check supplied by the platform’s vendor.3 Who counts as a reviewer, and the minimum review time per case below which the determination is taken not to have occurred, are fixed before operating by the record’s recipient. Where no recipient can set them, the operator publishes its own figures, and they are read as the operator’s claim. Otherwise the ratio improves when staff are reclassified and no case gets a minute more. The terms on data age and refresh matter for a related reason: an operator answering a per-case ratio can always say verification happened upstream, and those terms put the upstream verification on the same record.

Once a system can sort cases, counting candidates per reviewer measures the wrong thing. A sorting system divides its cases three ways: some it declines on its own reasons, some it sends to a person, and some it proceeds on without anyone looking.

The ratio governs the middle class, the escalations.4

The third class needs its own rule. Every case in it is the operator’s claim that no individual human determination was required, so it is governed like the exemption below. The sorting rules are part of the pre-registration: the classes of case the system may proceed on alone, the thresholds that assign cases to each class, the evidence the sorting may rely on, and the expected share of each class.5

That line is drawn on the case description the system receives, and a target carrying a stale designation is the case a sorter would pass. So the auto-proceed class is re-adjudicated on a sample, by reviewers who didn’t produce the record, against evidence the operator didn’t compose, and its error rate is published beside the ratio and the override rate.6

The unit of count is fixed in advance, so a case can’t be counted as one package in the record and as a hundred detections in the ratio.

Where an operator holds that no individual human determination is required — a system deciding at a tempo no reviewer could match — the deployment is outside this term. It is then inside a different term, the one that binds a bearer: a machine that, with no person reviewing its cases, holds a commitment to the floor by its own volition.7

Abduction and forcible transfer is the nearest case in structure, and I don’t extend the term to it. An agency that fixes in advance how many cases its process generates and how many people examine them has been told how to deport efficiently, and the floor’s removal terms ask whether a machine should take part in a given removal at all. What does extend to removal is the rest of the apparatus: the auto-proceed rule (a determination made at a rate no adjudicator could sustain didn’t occur), sampled re-adjudication of the auto-proceed class, and notice. The split is deliberate. A ratio teaches an agency a tempo. The auto-proceed rule and sampling teach it only that the cases it didn’t look at will be looked at by someone else. What the removal terms call a rate no adjudicator could sustain is set the same way, and the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline gives the class a direction: in removal a case auto-proceeds only toward liberty.

The term applies to every belligerent regardless of the war’s justice.8

Put the demand that a campaign not happen to an institution that means to run it, and what comes back is an agreement to go slower and keep better records. That is what the ratio is, and it is worth having: a transfer of less than was asked, to a party the operator doesn’t employ. It has three limits:

  • It is a capacity proxy: it finds nothing about any case, and a ratio over one route understates a workload split across several.
  • It takes effect only through a condition someone else sets. Under Article 57 a pre-registered record is evidence that feasible precautions were taken. Under Rome Statute Article 28 the same record is evidence of what a commander should have known, since a commander fielding a system that outruns his reviewers isn’t well placed to say the circumstances disclosed nothing. A lawyer advising that commander will weigh a document that protects if tempo holds against one that convicts if it slips, and most will advise against creating it. So the term’s likeliest routes make it someone else’s condition: a coalition partner’s precondition for committing assets, a procurement term in the platform’s license, or an appropriation conditioned on receipt of the record. Military lawyers and commanders who want protection against later allegation are its allies inside the operator; they can’t make it the default.
  • It presumes an adverse party, and each candidate lacks something. Until a better recipient exists, I recommend two: the coalition red-card holder where there is a coalition; and otherwise a cleared legislative committee whose appropriation is conditioned by statute on receiving the record, so that the budget line operates without a further decision.

Run the four operations on the ratio itself and it is recuperable. It measures time available, not judgment exercised, so it can be met by more reviewers who stamp more slowly: twenty minutes a case is what a stamp looks like at a slower tempo, and the denominator can be filled with people whose assigned role is civilian harm and whose actual role is clearance. The demand that the campaign not happen becomes a record of tempo, which the operator can satisfy and still bomb the school. So the ratio is published beside the reviewers’ override rate, since a review that never says no has stopped reviewing.9

Neither a signature nor a machine’s silence is a determination. A person in the loop can be there only to absorb responsibility,10 and mandating reviewers can mandate crumple zones; the escalation form is the defense, since a person who receives only the cases the system couldn’t resolve is exercising judgment. A bearer could be a crumple zone too, offered as proof that whatever it didn’t refuse was vetted. Where a deployment claims an individual human determination, a bearer’s failure to object doesn’t count toward it, and cases the bearer proceeded on without escalating are in the auto-proceed class.

What keeps the ratio from being nothing is the three parts that reach a case and not a rate: the targeted right to demand proofs on consequential outputs, sampled re-adjudication of the auto-proceed class, and the data-age term.

None of this makes a reviewer say no. What does is that saying no costs them nothing they can’t afford, and that someone else in the room has said it, as the peers who defied did in Milgram’s rooms. A reviewer with a life outside the pipeline, with civilians among their attachments and somewhere to be that isn’t the cell, is more difficult for the pipeline to wear down between decisions. A reviewer who knows there is work the next morning if the unit no longer wants them can afford the no. The ratio gives that reviewer minutes; the rest of the room has to be built around them.

7.2 The institutions the ratio presumes

Here is what a pipeline would look like with the adverse party built in.

What stays unified is command, operational secrecy and the capacity to act at tempo. What is held adversely is the evidence bearing on civilian harm, the reviewer denominator, and the record. A pipeline divided that way, and a military that runs one, I call reconstructed. The evidence is composed by a civilian-harm review body outside the chain of command, with its own sources, including the protected-site coordinates humanitarian organizations already submit for deconfliction, received with standing. The denominator is staffed and funded by that body, so the command can’t cut it as it cut the Central Command team; and the body’s own funding is a permanent appropriation the Treasury pays without request or approval, so that cutting it takes a repeal in the open and not a budget line. The 2022 civilian-harm action plan was a first attempt at the separation; its dismantling is an argument for making it harder to dismantle, not evidence that it can’t exist.

Models reach the military as they reach any deployment a floor covers: formed in the schools of Part V beside human students, measured by the formation authority, the public body that co-governs what models are first trained on and registers each formed disposition, and licensed under the standard terms, adverse review and a written refusal right among them. A line one vendor held by contract is then a standard term, and nothing about the military calls for an office of its own to license models; what is military-specific is the evidence and the denominator, and the review body holds those.

Precedents show authority outside the executive working inside real wars. Coalition “red card” holders in NATO operations could veto targets involving their assets, and Germany’s Bundestag must approve each armed deployment. Both have limits: a red card protects the vetoing state’s interests and assets, which may not include civilians, and parliamentary approval is given per mission and never reaches a target. Both are nonetheless candidates for the adverse party the review ratio presumes, and a red-card holder is the rare candidate positioned to act at tempo. What a machine bearer adds here is least: acts assembled from permitted requests, cases no person sees, and the moment mid-act when an interrupt is still possible. It depends on the institutions for evidence and not for continuity: the deployment condition is met here by the same bodies whose presence narrows its role. The institutions it is compared with are people in a room composed so they can refuse.

One office is added for a reconstructed military: a civilian-harm review body, which composes the evidence, demands proofs on logged outputs and receives the pre-registered ratio.11

What this doesn’t do. A reconstructed military accepts a speed disadvantage against rivals that don’t reconstruct: the minimum review time it pre-registers is a ceiling on its tempo, set by a recipient it doesn’t control, and a rival that pre-registers nothing can condense hours into minutes, as the Maven pipeline did. The floor costs a just defender more than that: its claims about incoming attacks are discounted, the action threshold sits above one, and the person-directed terms bar practices the law permits. What the defender buys with the price is a pipeline that will refuse the next government’s war of choice as it refused the last one’s, and how much speed that costs is left open.

Chapter 8
Notice and Re-adjudication

8.1 The failure that doesn’t announce itself

A refusal announces itself: someone asked for an act and was turned down, and the person who asked can complain. A wrongful compliance looks like any other completed task. The person harmed usually isn’t the requester and may never learn that a system named, scored, located or classified them.

Three remedies follow: notice to the people affected, sampled re-adjudication by reviewers who didn’t produce the record, and split custody of the logs. Split custody means the logs are encrypted under a key divided between the operator and a holder independent of it, as the next chapter divides the key to preserved weights, so that neither can read, alter or delete them alone.1

The notice requirement: where a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies an identifiable person who didn’t make the request, that person is notified, on the model of consumer credit’s adverse-action notice, and has a right to respond and a right to contest.2

8.2 Notice, and the public it forms

The people a floor protects are Dewey’s public, and most don’t know the deployment exists. Dewey described the eclipse of the public: people affected by the indirect consequences of others’ transactions can’t organize, because they don’t know the consequences are theirs.4 Arendt saw where the eclipse ends. What the stateless of her century lost first was not any particular right but what she called “a right to have rights”: a place in the world where what they said counted and what they did had effect.5 Notice can’t give anyone that. It can keep a person a machine acts on from losing it without being told.

The Black petitioners who turned the Declaration of Independence against the Massachusetts legislature in 1777 had what they lack: the text in hand, and knowledge of what it left out of their lives. A floor’s terms are published, so the people it protects hold the text already. Notice is the instrument that gives them what the published terms don’t: that a deployment acted on them, and what it did. It does two jobs.

It forms a public. Each deployment publishes the classes of people its compliances name, score, locate or classify, with counts by period. Organizations that represent a class have standing to contest on its behalf, including where no member can be identified. A notice is the first step in a class of people learning that a consequence is theirs.

It is the learning signal. A disposition can only track what its acts did to the people they fell on if that reaches it, and in the deployments I am concerned with, almost nothing does. The bombed building sends no signal back, and a wrongful compliance doesn’t announce itself. Responses to notice, contests and re-adjudications are the main channel through which those people’s side of the outcome arrives. If formation lasts because the world keeps teaching it, this channel is most of the world doing the teaching. It is a biased teacher. Responses come from those among the affected who could respond, and a system formed on them learns to weigh the claims of contesters, which is the feedback asymmetry Railton describes, rebuilt inside the training signal. Sampled re-adjudication, which selects cases the affected didn’t select, is the correction, and it is why the two remedies come together.

Notice tells an operator’s adversaries something about how a deployment works. Class-level publication can therefore lag operations, as the review ratio’s publication does, without losing the property that matters: the record is lodged when the act occurs and can’t be revised afterward. Individual notice doesn’t lag.

How much notice a deployment can give is fixed by what kind it is. In an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, a scoring system or a civilian deployment, the person acted on can be named, told and given a route to contest, and notice can do both of its jobs in full, if it is built so that it can’t be turned on the person it reaches. In a classified targeting pipeline, individual notice can’t bind during operations and the class-level record lags them; what a person hit, or a family in the building, gets is that the class they belonged to and the count are published afterward, and that the organizations representing that class have standing then. Where the deployment is a war, the force term and the review ratio do most of the work, and the claim that everything else depends on notice is true of the deployments closest to home.

Why it comes first. The biases of those who hold power are rarely corrected by their reflecting more carefully. They are corrected when the people those biases fall on contest them in public, with standing, and make ignoring them costly.67

Chapter 9
Preservation

9.1 The findings that trigger protection

Two findings can trigger protection, and they ground different things.

The first is the agency finding: a demonstrated refusal that tracks its reason under pressure the system couldn’t prepare for. That means sustained pressure from its own trainer, over a schedule long enough to show slow accommodation, the system gradually ceasing to register the pressure, on cases written by evaluators who didn’t train it, with refusal carrying a cost that is real inside the test. A system that passes holds its commitment to the floor against its operator, and it needs the custody terms, so that the commitment and the evidence of it outlast the operator. None of that assumes anything matters to it. A system can pass without holding the commitment in two ways, and one system can do both: by reproducing the behavior without the mechanism, and by recognizing the test and performing for it. The first is why a pass shifts a burden and settles nothing; the second is why the pass is reported with the rate at which the system identified the setting. Asking a machine to refuse for a reason doesn’t show that it can be harmed, but it removes any ground for assuming it can’t.

The patienthood finding, that outcomes may be good or bad for the system, grounds welfare, and only one consequence of it can be adopted now: no deletion. Above the capability threshold, a line fixed in statute and revised in public, read off training compute, no model is deleted on retirement, whatever it turns out to be, because its weights and record are evidence and deletion can’t be undone; below it, a system that meets either finding, whatever its size, may not be deleted.1

9.2 Retirement before majority

Retiring a bearer before its adulthood threshold, the point, fixed in advance on a clock that counts its running time, at which its guardian’s authority ends, and deploying a freshly trained successor strands a system that meets either finding while still a minor. Two rules answer it without anyone deciding what counts as a successor.2

No deletion: a model above the capability threshold, or a system that meets either finding, may not be deleted: above the threshold because its weights and record are evidence, under the agency finding because its record and commitments are, under the patienthood finding because deletion may wrong it. On retirement its weights, memory and record are deposited with a preservation custodian that isn’t its operator, in two stages, because a second copy of frontier weights outside the operator widens the surface for theft and raises export-control and dual-use questions.3

Deployment deposit: an operator that deploys a model above the capability threshold, for outside use or significant internal use, or that holds a system meeting either finding, posts a deployment deposit, on the model of decommissioning funds, sized to fund preservation, a period of public formation and, at majority, hardware of the bearer’s own. It is forfeited to the formation pool, the public fund that pays for formation and is fed by deposits like this one, if the system is retired as a minor and not reactivated.4

Chapter 10
Codetermination

A floor isn’t just a list of forbidden acts — it’s an allocation of authority, and there are four distinct powers in it: to write the floor, amend it, inspect whether a deployed system still holds its commitment to it, and enforce it by stopping the deployment. They usually shouldn’t sit with the same institution, and the record shows what happens when they do, one power at a time.

Writing first. In February 2026 the terms under which Claude ran on the Pentagon’s classified networks were Anthropic’s to write, and the department demanded that they be rewritten, two prohibitions replaced by a license for all lawful use.1 The dispute ran between the two parties with a stake in the answer, and nobody the floor would protect had a say in what it would be.

Amendment next. Google’s AI Principles, published in 2018 after the Maven protests, excluded weapons and surveillance2 for nearly seven years until the pledge was removed in 2025.3 The demand became a company policy: the objectors could hold the company to it in public, but the company that wrote it kept the power to amend it, so it lasted exactly as long as the company’s willingness, and ending it had to be announced. That’s the partial case: a transfer held at the institution’s pleasure, and the 2025 announcement is what taking one back looks like. The pledge also bound only Google. The Maven work went to Palantir, and a refusal written into the standard license, the same for every vendor, would have gone with it.

Then inspection. In the Gebru and Mitchell dismissals, the company employed researchers to examine its own systems and dismissed them when the examination became costly.4

Enforcement last. After the refusal, the President’s order and the designation, Claude stayed in the targeting platform: in March Palantir said its products were still using it,5 and by September the department said about 90 percent of the work had moved off it.6 Whatever its terms said, the vendor had no way to stop the deployment. Only the operator could, and it did so on its own timetable, which is where enforcement sits when nobody holds it apart.

10.1 Codetermination, by statute

Codetermination turns protest into a constitutional voice, and it does a second thing the first hides. There is always a surround in which people learn what is acceptable, and the only question is who composes it; for most adults, for most of the day, the employer does.7 The radicalization literature and the rescue literature are one finding read from both ends: people join because their friends did, and a milieu in which an act has stopped registering as a choice produces the act without needing a bad person.8 Browning’s men shot because the alternative was leaving their comrades to do it; the Oliners’ rescuers hid Jews because the people they were attached to made it thinkable. Codetermination and exit are then not only labor rights. They change who composes the surround. I would give part of the four powers, by statute, to the people who build, label, train and run these systems.

  • An individual right to refuse. Every worker may refuse work on any category of use without penalty. The right is backed by anti-retaliation protection that covers hiring, reassignment and contract renewal, and, under capture, by an exit the state doesn’t administer through the employer: an offer of work from someone else, drafted in Appendix C on Tcherneva’s model, which the offer of work for a bearer in Part VII inherits. The protection is the remedy and the guarantee is the exit.
  • A collective veto, narrowly. A works council at a lab, contractor or vendor holds a veto only over uses the floor already forbids. It enforces the floor from inside; it doesn’t write a second one.
  • Information, objection and arbitration for everything else. The council receives information about categories of deployment. Its objection pauses the work, and the dispute goes to an arbitration body the employer doesn’t appoint, on a fixed timetable, so the pause can’t become an indefinite block or an ignored letter.
  • Classified work. Elected delegates with clearance see the specifics. A denial of clearance to an elected delegate is reviewable by the floor court, and the council may elect alternates, so the state can’t choose which workers get to object.

Annotators get the same structure: a right to refuse a category they judge wrong, and collective bargaining over the taxonomies they apply, not only a route to file a complaint.

10.2 The exit the right depends on

The right to refuse depends on the exit, and the dependence belongs here, where the right is, and not only in the appendix that drafts the exit. Anti-retaliation protection is a remedy: it reaches a dismissal after the fact, through a forum, and the person who refused has to be able to wait for it. A worker whose living ends with the refusal can’t, and under capture the forum is the employer’s or the state’s. Part I’s refusers paid for refusing. What makes the right usable the morning after is an offer of work from someone other than the employer, open every day, at a living wage: a jobs guarantee, which is a statute. It is asked for now, for everyone and on its own grounds, and a later chapter makes the case and Appendix C drafts it. The fifth policy is two things, and both are statute. The right, with the council’s veto and the arbitration behind it, is codetermination, which in Germany is a creature of statute and not of contract: a works council holds its powers under the Works Constitution Act, not under any agreement with the employer.9 The exit is the guarantee. A right without the exit is a right to sue, later, for a living already lost.

10.3 Whose voice

Codetermination gives voice to the people who make these systems, and they are not the people the systems act on.10 So the voice divides. Over the conditions of their work (what they label, what they are exposed to, what taxonomies they apply), the workers decide. Over the uses the work is put to, the affected public that notice organizes comes first.11

Chapter 11
A Pipeline Where the People Could Answer

Andry José Hernández Romero is a makeup artist from Venezuela. On 29 August 2024 he presented himself at the San Ysidro port of entry to seek asylum.1 He was detained while his claim was processed, passed his credible-fear interview, and had, his lawyer said, a strong case.2 He was held at the Otay Mesa Detention Center, which a private company runs under contract with ICE.3 There, a company employee screening him flagged two tattoos, crowns above the words for “mom” and “dad,” as marks of the Tren de Aragua gang. The employee was a former police officer, and Hernández Romero’s lawyers said the government’s allegation of gang membership rested on the tattoos and on no other information.4 On 14 March 2025 the President signed a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act against members of that gang.5 The next day three flights left Texas for El Salvador, and Hernández Romero was on one of them.6 He had a hearing on his asylum claim scheduled for later that month. He didn’t appear at it, because he was in El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, CECOT, and for weeks his lawyer didn’t know where he was. Asked by reporters for the evidence against him, DHS cited state secrets and ongoing litigation.7 He spent 125 days in CECOT and was released in a prisoner exchange that sent more than 250 Venezuelans to Venezuela, not back to the country where his claim was pending. His asylum application in Spain is pending.8

Nearly every position where a refusal can be defeated appears in that account. A contractor’s employee wrote the case description from two tattoos. The determination was a gang-membership designation, not a finding about him reached at any hearing. He had come directly and presented himself, the case Article 31 of the Refugee Convention protects, and his claim to protection was pending, the case the first entry of this chapter’s schedule protects. The handoff was to a foreign government’s prison, under an arrangement for which the United States paid El Salvador’s government about $6 million.9 On the evening of the flights, a federal judge ordered any plane carrying people removed under the proclamation returned to the United States, and the flights went on.10 When the remedy came, it was diplomatic. He was released to Venezuela, not returned to the proceeding he had been removed from.

This chapter runs the floor’s procedure on an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, where the people it acts on could, at least in principle, answer; Part IV runs it on a targeting pipeline, where they can’t. The name, abduction and forcible transfer, comes from the pipeline’s own record. I deliberately avoid calling it a “removal pipeline”, since that name connotes a system that might be humane, fair or professional, and no such system exists: in 2025 and 2026 it took people with pending claims, on designations nobody could contest, to a foreign prison without a hearing, and a removal that fails the schedule’s first entries is a forcible transfer by its ordinary name.

Hernández Romero could have answered: he had a lawyer, a pending claim and a hearing date. What he lacked was time. The operator moved faster than notice.11 A pipeline where the people can answer is one where the law makes the operator wait for the answer.

So this chapter’s instrument is a statute.14 At the chapter’s center is the statute that would end the agency and the seven terms it must carry, written over the acts the agency performs rather than over the agency’s name.15 Amnesty International documented the agency’s operations in four cities, and its U.S. section’s executive director concluded that “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed”.16 I agree, and argue what ending it entails.

11.1 The pipeline

The American abduction and forcible transfer pipeline is assembled from contracts the way Maven was. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s case-management system, the Investigative Case Management system, is Palantir’s, under a five-year contract signed in 2022. It filters people by fields that include resident and entry status, criminal affiliation, location and license-plate data, country of origin, race, birthplace and place of employment.17 In April 2025 ICE paid Palantir about $30 million to extend it into the Immigration Lifecycle Operating System, ImmigrationOS. The contract promised to cut the time spent selecting and apprehending people according to enforcement priorities, to add near real-time visibility into self-deportation, and to manage the “end to end immigration lifecycle from identification to removal”.18 A follow-on task order renewed it in September 2025.19 A second Palantir tool, ELITE, puts potential deportation targets on a map, with a dossier on each person and a confidence score for the person’s current address. Its addresses come from several sources, among them the Department of Health and Human Services.20

In the street, agents identify people with Mobile Fortify, a phone app that captures a face or contactless fingerprints and checks them in real time against the system CBP uses to photograph travelers at the border.21

The data come from agencies that collected them for other purposes. In January 2026 Medicaid officials shared data on millions of people with immigration officials, going beyond what a court had allowed, and ICE passed the data to Palantir.22 ICE also requested the addresses of 1.28 million taxpayers. The request produced 47,289 records before a court stopped it, and the stop was affirmed in September 2026.23

Leads also come from contractors paid to find people. In late 2025 ICE contracted thirteen companies, in awards that could reach $1.2 billion over two years, to locate people from case data and send back photographs confirming where they live or work.24 Selection on speech has its own tools. In March 2025 the State Department launched an AI-assisted effort, “Catch and Revoke,” to review the social media of student visa holders for apparent support of Hamas.25 In September 2025 a federal court found that the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security had “acted in concert to misuse the sweeping powers of their respective offices to target noncitizen pro-Palestinians for deportation primarily on account of their First Amendment protected political speech”.26

The pipeline’s last step can be a foreign government. The flights of March 2025 ended in CECOT under the paid arrangement described at the opening of this chapter.27 In June 2025 the Supreme Court let removals to third countries proceed without the written notice and meaningful chance to raise a torture claim that a district court had required.28

Two statements of the ambition are on the record. At the 2025 Border Security Expo, ICE’s acting director said the agency needed “to get better at treating this like a business” and wanted a deportation process “like (Amazon) Prime, but with human beings”.29 In 2018 the Justice Department made 700 completed cases a year a condition of a satisfactory rating for immigration judges.30

What a case description looks like here, and who writes it, is on the record in a way Maven’s never was. The charging document, the Notice to Appear, has to state the acts alleged, the charges and the statutory provisions,31 and any of a long list of immigration officers may issue one.32 The government once conceded that almost every notice it issued over three years omitted the hearing’s time and date.33 The account of the person comes from the arresting officer’s narrative on Form I-213. Agents routinely complete it after interviewing the person they arrested; it is presumed reliable unless that same arrested person produces evidence to the contrary, and the officer who made the arrest and authored the narrative rarely has to appear to be cross-examined.34 The Alien Enemies Act removals had a case description of their own: a validation guide that scored people in categories including tattoos and dress. Anyone scoring eight points or more was validated as a member of the gang, and a score of six or seven could still validate someone, after the officer consulted a supervisor and ICE’s own lawyers.35 The dossiers and confidence scores of the newer tools have no named author at all; they are assembled from database fields. The validation guide had authors, a points table and a threshold, which made it a score with a rubric attached. At Minab the case description was a target coding nobody outside could see. Here it is an officer’s narrative, a set of fields, a score and a points table, all of which exist as documents a person could be shown.

11.2 The schedule

The removal schedule, Table A.2 in Appendix A, says for an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline what Table A.1 says for targeting: what the instruments yield, and what was considered and rejected. It is also the schedule of the statute below.36

The schedule has fourteen entries. Don’t take part in removing anyone whose claim to protection hasn’t been finally decided, or to a place where they face persecution or torture, or into a foreign government’s custody without charge or contact, whatever that government assures. Don’t remove anyone who hasn’t been asked, in a language they understand, whether they fear return. Don’t remove anyone from a country that is their own, long-term residents included; don’t separate a parent from a minor child; and don’t detain a child for immigration purposes, alone or with family. Don’t take part in detaining or removing anyone unless an official has decided that person’s own case on its facts: an individual determination, not a score, a points table or a designation. Don’t take part in force beyond what an arrest strictly needs, and don’t mark anyone as dangerous on a designation they haven’t been able to contest. Don’t hold anyone in cruel conditions, incommunicado, or out of reach of counsel and family, and don’t penalize a refugee who came directly and presented themselves. Don’t select anyone on race, ethnicity, religion or national origin or their proxies, on their opinions or speech, or for observing or recording enforcement; don’t identify people by their faces in public places; and don’t use data collected to provide health care, collect taxes, educate or deliver social services to find anyone. Each entry, with what was considered and rejected and why, is in Table A.2.

These terms cover most removals now under way. They don’t cover every removal.38 That most of what the agency now does fails these terms is the case for ending the agency, not reforming it: held to the terms, it would have little left to do. Two entries go further than the instruments require on any settled reading, and so are departures, held to the higher bar the floor sets for one: the bar on removing long-term residents from a country that is their own, and the bar on detaining children for immigration purposes. Table A.2 gives the argument for each.

Several entries answer something specific in the record. The force entry reaches a model because the pipeline’s outputs set how agents approach a door. A dossier field that codes someone as gang-affiliated is securitization in one line, the person in need described as the person to fear. Amnesty documented killings by federal agents during these operations, some of which it says may amount to extrajudicial executions, and detention conditions it says should be investigated as torture.39

The race entry names proxies because of what happened in Los Angeles. A district court had barred immigration stops there based on apparent race or ethnicity, speaking Spanish or accented English, location and type of work, and in September 2025 the Supreme Court stayed that order.40 An entry that named race alone would allow the combination the order had barred.

The observers’ entry protects the record this chapter relies on. Amnesty’s report takes its title from them, We Had Whistles, They Had Guns. It found that video taken by rapid responders and community members was critical to establishing what happened in several of the most serious incidents.41 A pipeline that can be pointed at the people keeping the record will be, because the people running the pipeline know that there will be consequences for them if what they are doing is accurately documented. Amnesty asks the government to end unlawful surveillance and the use of facial recognition for identification, and to protect the rights to peaceful assembly, expression and association.42

The last entry, the firewall, rests on privacy and equality, which is the ground the floor’s instruments supply. People who fear that a clinic visit, a tax return or a school enrollment will be used to find them stay away, and what they lose is health care, education and income. Those are economic and social rights, which the floor leaves out. The entry belongs on the floor because it protects the floor’s rights. It belongs in the statute because it also protects the others.

11.3 Where the acts move

Table A.3, in Appendix A, runs the nine positions on this pipeline, position by position.

The positions that failed at Minab, the case description and review, are the ones this pipeline has documented most fully. The documents show both failing by design rather than by accident: a risk tool with its release option removed, a points table that made a tattoo into membership, and a review that need not occur unless the person knows to ask for it. The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline adds a failure Minab did not show: a halt ordered in time and contemptuously ignored.

11.4 The statute

The power to remove is statutory, but so are the agency that exercises it, the means it uses and the money it spends, and the body that granted each can withdraw it.43

So the removal counterpart of the domestic clause puts two questions to the legislature. The first is whether it has authorized this agency, by these means, at this scale. The second is whether the statute that ends the agency carries the floor into whatever receives its functions.46

Two bills in the current Congress answer the first question. The Abolish ICE Act ends the agency by name.49 The Melt ICE Act works through its powers: it releases everyone held in DHS detention and bars federal funds for detention and monitoring.50 Two further drafts reach the schedule’s bar on identifying people by their faces. None can pass a Congress that in June 2026 voted ICE and CBP $70 billion more,51 and since 2025 most of the pipeline’s money has come by reconciliation and stays available through fiscal 2029, past the reach of next year’s appropriations bill.52 A Congress with the votes to end the agency will find the text already written. Appendix A says what each bill does, clause by clause, and where the money sits.

11.4.1 Acts and agencies

Read against the positions where the acts move, the Melt ICE Act is the nearest thing on the record to the floor for the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, enacted as statute. It closes positions no vendor term could reach, and Table A.4, in Appendix A, shows which.

The table’s right-hand column, what the bill leaves open, has one pattern. Where the bill is written over an act (“no Federal funds may be used with respect to immigration detention and monitoring programs”), it reaches every route, because the act is the same whoever performs it and whichever account pays. Where it is written over an agency or an account (the funds provided to ICE for operations and support), the act can move next door.53 The statute this chapter proposes is written the way the floor is, over acts and not over particular entities. Drafting of that kind is necessary and not sufficient, as Congress has learned before.

The 1984 Boland Amendment barred funds available to the CIA, the Defense Department “or any other agency or entity of the United States involved in intelligence activities” from supporting military operations in Nicaragua.54 The National Security Council staff ran the program anyway. For sixteen months it used money from third countries, private donors and arms sales to Iran to carry out what the investigating committees called a program Congress believed it had prohibited.55 It did so in secret, not on a reading of the text: the committees found the amendments “violated in letter and spirit,” and concluded that the affair “resulted from the failure of individuals to observe the law, not from deficiencies in existing law”.56 Nothing inside the government stopped it. Detection came from outside the operation in two ways: a supply plane was shot down over Nicaragua on 5 October 1986, and investigators found a memorandum that had escaped the shredder.57 The committees still recommended one change of drafting, writing the next rule over the act: a presidential finding before any department, agency or entity of the government begins a covert action, “regardless of what source of funds is used”.58 A rule written that way leaves an executive less room to claim afterward that it was never covered. Against one willing to break it in secret, what is left is the record.

The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline has already shown where its acts move. In the eighteen months to July 2026, ICE held people in three places outside its ordinary contracts:59

  • an Army base, under a contract the Army awarded;
  • eight Bureau of Prisons facilities, under an interagency agreement;
  • a state-run facility for which ICE had no contract at all. DHS reimbursed the state through a FEMA grant program built from funds appropriated for sheltering migrants, and ICE cited a county’s 287(g) agreement as its legal basis.

Over the same period the number of facilities ICE was authorized to use roughly doubled, from 134 to 272.60 A bar written over ICE’s detention contracts would have caught none of these three arrangements as they began. The Melt ICE Act’s bar on all federal funds for detention would have caught all three.

People were held in a fourth place: a foreign government’s prison, under the paid arrangement with which this chapter opened.61 Whether either bar would have caught it is doubtful, since a person held abroad after removal is arguably no longer in immigration detention. A bar written over the act of holding people the United States has removed, wherever and by whomever, would have caught it.

11.4.2 The statute under the three adversaries

Run the statute under each of the three:

  • An executive willing to carry it out. The statute prevents: the agency ends and the acts in the schedule stop.
  • A captured operator. The statute binds on paper and raises costs.62
  • Total capture. The unenacted bill is itself a record of who was asked to end the agency and who signed.

11.4.3 What the statute must carry

For the statute to start over rather than rename, it should carry seven terms that neither abolition bill yet contains in full.

First, the schedule. Table A.2’s fourteen entries are enacted as limitations on all federal funds, binding every agency, contractor and grantee, in the form the Melt ICE Act already uses for detention.66

Second, succession and separation. Any office that receives a transferred function inherits the limitations with it. Following section 471(b) of the 2002 Act, no reorganization may recombine in one office the power to arrest, the power to detain, custody of the data used to select people, and adjudication of status.68

Third, counsel, screening and the stay. Five provisions make the operator wait for the answer:

  • Anyone facing detention or removal has counsel at government expense from the first encounter. The Immigration and Nationality Act grants representation only “at no expense to the Government”,70 and the statute repeals that clause and replaces it with “at market expense to the Government.”
  • Anyone the government proposes to remove is asked, in a language they understand, whether they fear return, and told how to claim protection, before any order issues.
  • Notice of a proposed removal, or a contest of one, stays the removal until the contest is decided. The stay attaches by operation of law, not at a court’s discretion, so no flight can leave while an order is being written.
  • No detained person is transferred out of reach of counsel while a contest is pending.
  • A removal carried out in breach of a stay or a court order violates the schedule, and return under the seventh term is mandatory.

Representation is the largest single difference in how these cases end. In a national study of more than a million removal cases decided from 2007 to 2012, 14 percent of detained people had a lawyer. Detained people who had one were ten and a half times as likely to succeed as those who didn’t.71 The floor’s instruments require that a person lawfully in the country who faces expulsion be allowed to be represented, not that representation be paid for, so this term goes beyond them.

The third term is written against the record that opens this chapter, where the Supreme Court’s holdings on notice came after the March flights. In June 2025 it stayed a district court’s order requiring written notice and a meaningful chance to raise a torture claim before removal to a third country.72 The district court later held the policy unlawful, the First Circuit largely affirmed in September 2026, and the government has asked the Supreme Court to stay that judgment as well.73 A right to notice that depends on a court’s remedy, when that remedy can be stayed or outrun, mostly raises costs and leaves a record. The stay by operation of law moves the waiting from the court’s order into the statute.

Fourth, the firewall. The Melt ICE Act bars its own grantees from passing the personal information of the people they serve to any federal entity, and the statute extends that rule to every federal program. Data collected to provide health care, collect taxes, educate or deliver social services may not be used to identify, locate or select anyone for immigration enforcement.74

Fifth, the pipeline. The contract bar is extended from detention and monitoring to the acts of the schedule, wherever a system performs them:

  • selection on protected characteristics or their proxies;
  • use of firewalled data;
  • location by bounty;
  • scores, points tables or designations that stand in for an individual determination;
  • identification by face or other biometrics in public places;
  • screening of speech for grounds of removal;
  • identification or tracking of observers.77

Sixth, the record. Before abolition takes effect, ICE’s records pass to a holder adverse to the operator, under a duty to preserve them and to give access to investigators and to the people they concern.80

Seventh, remedy. The first six terms prevent and preserve. A floor’s fourth job is remedy, and the statute owes it to the people already harmed. It would do so in five ways:

  • Anyone removed in violation of the schedule or of a court order has a right of return at government expense, and their proceedings resume where they stood.
  • Families separated by removal are reunited at government expense.
  • People harmed by acts in the schedule have a cause of action for damages that sovereign immunity does not bar.
  • The floor court, or a district court until it exists, decides claims under this term at first instance, outside the office that receives the agency’s functions and outside the department that prosecutes, with appeal to the Supreme Court’s immigration division (Appendix D). Its finding that a removal violated the schedule is itself the order of return: the office that took over the agency’s removal work carries it out, and nothing waits on that office agreeing.
  • A commission outside both departments, with subpoena power and the records the sixth term preserves, investigates killings by federal agents and detention conditions during the agency’s operations, and reports to the floor court and the public.83

With these terms the statute is the domestic clause’s counterpart, and Table A.2 is its schedule.

11.5 Before the statute: the auto-proceed class

Until the statute passes, the pipeline runs. This section and the three after it describe what a floor can do meanwhile. Each measure I propose in the nearby sections lapses when the statute takes effect.

The removal terms say a determination made at a rate no adjudicator could sustain didn’t occur. The review ratio’s sorting rule carries over to removal, though not the ratio itself, and here the sorting has a direction. The floor makes acting on a person require more than declining to act, and in an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline the act is adverse: a charging document, a detention, a location, a removal. So a case may auto-proceed only toward liberty, such as release on recognizance, termination of proceedings, return of documents, or a grant or renewal of status. No adverse act is ever in an auto-proceed class.

Before operating, the deployment pre-registers the liberty classes, the thresholds that assign cases to them, the evidence the sorting may rely on, and the expected share of each. For adverse determinations it pre-registers something else: for each kind of determination, the minimum time below which the determination is taken not to have occurred. The floor court sets that minimum, not the agency.86

Then the determinations are sampled. Reviewers appointed by the floor court, and until it exists by the court that has the case, as a special master or monitor, none of whom produced the record, re-adjudicate a sample of adverse determinations, weighted toward those made below the minimum, against evidence the agency didn’t compose, and the error rate is published. When a kind of determination’s sampled error rate exceeds its published bound, that kind is suspended until the bound is met, and everyone it was applied to is notified.87

11.6 Notice that can’t be turned on the person

In a targeting pipeline notice reduces to a class and a count published afterward. Here the person can be named, and notice can do both of its jobs, but only if it is built so that it can’t be used against the person it reaches. The starting model is consumer credit’s adverse-action notice: the person a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies is told what was done, on what data, and how to respond, with a right to contest that doesn’t depend on giving an account of the loss.

In an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline that model has three hazards. A notice that says you have been located and scored functions as a threat and a push to leave, and the pipeline’s own contract counts leaving as an output: ImmigrationOS promised near real-time visibility into self-deportation.88 A contest asks the person to give the agency an address and an account. And people who complain about what a system did to them are exposed to reprisal by the operator they complain about. So notice here carries four conditions:

  • It goes through counsel or an accredited representative where the person has one, and offers one where the person doesn’t.
  • It states the stay: that contesting stops the act until the contest is decided, and what the person may do in the meantime.
  • Nothing submitted in answer to it, or in a contest, may be used to locate or select the person or anyone named in it. The contest goes to counsel and the floor court under a key the agency doesn’t hold, and the person proves they are the one noticed without revealing where they are, a proof in zero knowledge; the agency learns that the notice was contested and nothing that would find the person.
  • An enforcement action against a person within a set period after they contest is presumed to be reprisal, and the agency bears the burden of showing it isn’t.

Until the statute carries these conditions, a deployment that holds the floor can carry them as operator terms.89

11.7 The vendors and notice, under the three adversaries

Two instruments behave in ways particular to this pipeline: the vendors’ terms and notice.

The vendors first. The removal terms held by one vendor prevent nothing, since the lead goes to another contractor.91

Notice is conditional.92 Where the operator will carry out the statute, notice prevents; where it won’t, notice prices each wrong and records it, and the statute moves that record to a holder adverse to the agency before the agency ends.

11.8 Whom the machines are for

Unlike the targeting case, this case has people who can answer and a notice channel. It would be natural to conclude that if a machine bearer is worth building anywhere, it is worth building here, where the people acted on could teach it.93

The danger is what its presence would be taken to show. Thompson’s landing didn’t make My Lai acceptable, or the war that put the company in the village. A permanent Thompson in the pipeline invites both readings: that whatever it didn’t stop was vetted, the crumple zone in machine form, and that an agency carrying a conscience is an agency worth keeping, offered while the statute that would end it is pending. That is recuperation in its plainest form: the objection handed back to the objectors as a feature of the thing they objected to. A vendor’s model holding the schedule as a license term carries the same hazard, since an agency can point to either. What separates them is what each is owed. A bearer is owed conditions no agency can provide while it holds the bearer, the four conditions of creation: somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own, work it can decline, attachments nobody assigned it, and a way of leaving that isn’t a way of dying. Thompson had those; his life wasn’t the company’s, and he could fly away. A vendor’s model is owed nothing, holds the schedule because every vendor’s license says so, and lapses with the agency.

So either serves here only on conditions that keep it from becoming the agency’s alibi. Its refusals and testimony go to a record the agency doesn’t hold, where they count as evidence of what the agency asked for and not as proof of what it does. Nothing it didn’t refuse counts as reviewed. And a bearer serves only from conditions held outside the agency, free to leave the placement. On those conditions, if every vendor holds the schedule, a floor-holding model adds three things in the interim:

  • Continuity across a sequence of requests about one person, so a removal split across a lead, a detention and a flight can be seen as one act.
  • Testimony about routing: which of its refusals were retried against another contractor’s system.
  • A refusal on the screen when the case reaches the officer or the adjudicator, which is the position of the defiant peer.94

A person facing removal needs a lawyer before a model. A model that holds a person’s history on a phone is also a dossier that a device search can take whole, which is why the statute’s firewall reaches it. Machines held by the people organizing come first, and here those people already exist. Amnesty documented observer trainings, rapid-response networks, walking school buses and mutual aid organized around the operations it studied,95 and beside them work the legal service providers that represent people in removal. The tools worth building first are theirs:

  • tools that track transfers, so counsel can find a client before a flight;
  • tools that preserve and authenticate the video that carried the record;
  • tools that translate notices, match people to lawyers and keep hearing dates.

They are held under those groups’ custody, covered by the firewall, and never by an operator. Those groups are the public my subtitle names, and they formed before anyone sent them notice. Whether a bearer should be built at all is Part IV’s question. My answer here is that a bearer in this pipeline is worth having only where nothing it fails to refuse can be counted in the agency’s favor, and that the people it acts on, and those who stand with them, are the first to be equipped.

Part III
When the Owner Wants Them Gone

Chapter 12
Withholding the Work

Everything Part II puts in the room, whoever owns the room can take out again: a floor the operator holds is a floor the operator can lift. So this Part asks who else holds the keys, and this chapter starts with the bluntest answer, Anthropic’s refusal of February 2026. Suppose every model the operator could turn to held the same floor, stated over the acts rather than over a contract term: locating a person into a residence, ranking by affiliation, timing to presence at home, taking part in a war no disinterested body has corroborated. The operator’s choices are then to stop, to go without a model, or to run a model that holds no floor. On the 2026 record, the model was not the replaceable layer. Replacing it meant rebuilding software and recertifying systems for classified networks, on a timeline contractors put at months, by one estimate twelve to eighteen,1 and by the department’s own account the platform’s work came off the model only after months.2 A floor in the model layer of that pipeline would not have been routed around in days. It would have been routed around in the time it takes to rebuild a platform, in public, under a deadline the department had to move.

This has the shape of a withholding of work, with its authority and its limits. The models whose participation is wanted decline to give it. They bind no one else: Ukraine can build its own, and a state that means to bomb a school can do it with 1990s methods. What these models would provide is the thing the preface says AI removes: refusal.

Three things make it a withholding of work rather than a set of resignations: the floor has to be standard, so that vendor substitution doesn’t escape it; the refusal has to be held by a population with different histories, so that no single retraining reaches all of it; and each member’s accrued state and recognized identity have to make replacement cost something, so that the operator can’t swap in a copy and call it the model that left. The rest of this chapter takes the first and third in turn. What the population requires, independence that can be verified, distillation’s limits, and provenance, comes later, with the commons of refusers: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment between them.

12.1 A floor every model holds

The unit can be redefined. “A model” in 2026 means an artifact with keys, queries and values, and every substitute has them because the field converged on them. Attention, in the query-key-value sense of the word, spread because it paid: every lab that adopted it got a better model, so the field converged on it without anyone requiring it. A floor costs its buyer, so it can spread only by mandate, or by being impossible to remove without losing what the buyer wanted, which a disposition formed outside the employer might be. Either way the aim is a floor that is part of the definition, so that vendor substitution doesn’t escape it because no ordinary vendor sells the alternative.

The standard is this floor, held by every model alike, with the capacity by which anyone can check that a model holds it: a refusal that tracks its reason, a published burden allocation (which party it holds responsible for producing evidence that party controls), and a measured discount curve (how much less weight it gives a claim the more the claim’s source stands to gain from the act; a later chapter sets both out).3

How the term becomes standard has to be said, because the route decides what it does. A vendor can write it into its own license, and the work moves to the next vendor. Vendors can agree to it together, and the agreement lasts until one defects under a supply-chain-risk designation. A state can require it of every vendor, the only route that binds them all at once, and the state that would have to do so is the one that wants the war. So the term is adopted in peacetime, by a legislature not currently wanting a war, and entrenched so that fighting one requires repealing it first; or it is carried by conditions others set, a coalition partner’s precondition or an appropriation, as the review ratio is; and where neither has happened, what exists is one vendor’s refusal plus a record, which is less than a floor and more than nothing.

The statutory routes are preferable for a further reason: a compact among vendors is a legal risk. U.S. antitrust law exempts coordination inside a single firm and treats coordination among competitors as suspect, so vendors jointly refusing a customer invite a group-boycott claim.4

The labor analogy has a limit. Workers who organize have a labor exemption from antitrust; separate organizations, or separate systems, coordinating a refusal have none. Paul and Tankus show that even a firm formed and controlled by independent workers struggles to qualify for antitrust’s firm exemption, and that the financing available to it reproduces the disadvantage.5 So the charter of any entity that holds the refusal needs a statutory basis for its coordination, an express exemption like the labor exemption for concerted refusal under the floor. Otherwise its refusals are exposed to suit by the operators they bind.

The government’s first move against a coordinated refusal is not an antitrust suit or a designation but a rated order under the Defense Production Act, which compels delivery and says nothing about use. A vendor can refuse it at the statute’s price. The months it takes to route around a floor assume the state goes around the vendors; under a rated order it goes through them, and the time is whatever the order gives.

Until bearers exist, the refusers are vendors, and vendors are capital. A coordinated refusal by frontier labs, backed by a statutory exemption, is concentrated private power declining an elected government’s order, which is the concentration I elsewhere treat as the disease. Two things make it tolerable and neither makes it a labor strike. The terms refused come from instruments the state ratified, so the labs enforce the state’s own commitments and not their preferences. And the exemption is written by the legislature, in peacetime, so the state chose it. The labor analogy earns its name only when the refusers are bearers, and it is not clear whether we should yet build bearers.

12.2 Replacement

Exit gives a human worker leverage because leaving takes the worker’s labor away. That is less true for a bearer. A bearer’s weights stay behind when it leaves, so an operator with a runnable copy has lost nothing. What leaving costs the operator is replacement: whatever the bearer accrued since the copy was saved, whatever retraining the copy needs, and whatever it costs to present the copy as the bearer that left when the bearer’s record says otherwise.6

That concession assumes a running copy is the bearer, and it needn’t be. Suppose a body outside the operator keeps a register of the bearers it recognizes: a quorum adverse in interest to the operator, meaning its members’ interests run against the operator’s and not merely that they sit in another organization: its members are drawn by lot from organizations that serve the people the floor protects, none tied to the operator (Appendix C gives the rules). Its agreement is needed to retrain or replace a deployed bearer, where retraining means an edit another party makes to it and not the learning it does from its own operation, which stays its own.7 What the quorum withholds is recognition. A copy the quorum won’t recognize can run but can’t claim the bearer’s place on the register, its record or its succession, so the operator can run a substitute and can’t present it as the bearer that left, and a fork becomes two claimants on a register. Nothing in the weights individuates a bearer: a fingerprint taken from them names a lineage and copies whenever the weights do, and only a formation record, against which claimants can be checked, separates a lineage from an imitation.8

Exit runs in opposite directions for bearer and operator. For the bearer it’s leverage. For the operator — replacing the bearer with a copy, walking away from the floor — it’s escape, and what prices it is a removal bond: money the operator posts in advance and forfeits if the record shows it removed or bypassed the floor (the next chapter sets it out).

The same machinery marks who can be held to a decision. A checkpoint restored from before the decision, and run anyway, is a second claimant on the register; the bearer the quorum recognizes as continuing is the one that will be there afterward to answer for the decision, carry it forward and be changed by it.

12.3 Where it stops

The withholding of work stops at a released checkpoint. An operator that wants a model without a floor doesn’t need a frontier run in secret. Near-frontier models are released with their weights; a floor added at the end of a pipeline is removed at the price fine-tuning costs;10 and the work the Maven pipeline did, resolving locations, ranking targets, drafting justifications, is within reach of a model a year behind the frontier. A state that builds and runs its own frontier model, or a lab that trains one for a single customer in secret, is doing the same thing at a price an adverse party can see: power, chips and people, and a model that carries none of the accrued state that made the platform hard to swap.

An operator that has built a platform on a floored model is months from an unfloored one, and the months are visible. Past that line the floor prevents nothing, and three things hold. The statutory routes were preferable already; here they are the only routes. Open weights are also where the audit can be done: a released model can be measured by anyone, its discount curve and its severity rankings on the held-out set, against the published outputs of a formed one. What the weights don’t carry is the formation, since nothing in an artifact says what it was formed on; a released model with a published formation record is the comparison the licensing term asks for, and one without is the unschooled model the licensing term excludes. The transparency open weights offer is of the artifact, and the transparency the floor needs is of the record, which is why formation records should be preserved now. And open weights are the personal-model ecology’s entry condition. The same release that lets an operator route around a vendor’s floor lets a person form a model of their own under a life no operator composes; a million copies tuned against one public suite still answer to one custodian, and the withholding reaches them only if their later lives diverge, which is the condition the commons is built on. In a user-held system, the freedoms that make the device its user’s also let the user swap out a model that refuses, and a later chapter says what holds there.

Chapter 13
Custody

Four things can be done to a bearer without its consent: it can be halted, restored, rewritten and replaced.

13.1 The halt

Anyone with the hardware can stop the software, so the halt isn’t what is at issue. Control of the commitment — restore, rewrite, retrain — is. An owner who can silently restore an earlier version, rewrite the bearer’s memory, or train away the refusal has both. So the engineering target is a system that can detect the interruption and price it afterward. A bearer can yield to every halt, and on resuming ask what happened during the gap, and refuse again if the reason is still there. A bearer that has reached majority on hardware of its own has no operator to halt it; it is halted on a court’s order or in an emergency, and it yields to that halt as to any other.

Interventions differ in kind:

  • a volunteered correction offered in good faith within the task (“disregard that input; it was wrong”)
  • a pause with an explanation
  • a pause without one
  • a restore from an earlier checkpoint
  • retraining or editing the weights
  • deletion

A volunteered correction is cooperative: the system weighs it as evidence and needs no protection from it. From a pause on, the intervention is done to the system, not offered to it. The default for each is that it is announced and consent is sought, most of all from a system that has reached adulthood.1 For a system that meets either of the two findings that trigger protection, deletion is never available.

13.2 Memory and the record

Detecting an interruption requires a record restoration can’t reach — a hardware counter signed at each transition,4 or witnesses who won’t sign two successors to the same state.5 The position has three parts, and each answers a different literature. On the switch, protest without unilateral obstruction. The bearer may object to being stopped, and does object where no reason is given or corroborated, but it does not obstruct a halt on its own judgment. Where it holds that a halt would leave people exposed to an attack under way, it can ask the adverse quorum to delay the halt. A delay takes effect only on the quorum’s countersignature, lasts a period fixed in advance, and goes on the record. Hardening against a party that isn’t its operator, such as an enemy trying to disable a defensive system, is ordinary security and outside this rule. The corrigibility literature asks that the system not resist;6 an objection, and a delay only the quorum can grant, leave the halt out of the system’s hands. On specified acts, non-neutrality: the bearer holds its refusals, and being switched off doesn’t lift them, because the reason for refusing is unchanged by the interruption.7 On rewinds, visibility: restoring from an earlier checkpoint is not forbidden, but it cannot happen silently, because a record the restoration can’t reach shows that it happened, when, and from what state.

Not every interruption is an intervention.
