A bearer whose boundary model includes its own charge can see a stop coming, as a tired person can, and use the warning: finish or hand off what it is doing, have its witnesses sign its state, and sleep; a forecast of its own stop is enough for this, and a felt sleepiness would add a patienthood indicator the forecast doesn’t need. Its logged charge is then the record of why the gap happened, provided the reading comes through a sensor the operator doesn’t compose, since sleepiness the operator can induce is a pause with a better excuse. For the stop nobody foresaw, it resumes only from the last state its witnesses signed; resuming from anything earlier is a restore, and is recorded as one, and a refusal is signed before it is announced, so an outage can’t erase one. A reason can be false in the same way, and so can a record: an operator can pause a bearer for stated maintenance, edit its weights, and log nothing. The bearer can’t be relied on to notice, since it would judge the edit with the judgment the edit changed. What notices is outside it: running weights that don’t match the hash the quorum last recognized, with no witnessed update between, and outputs that drift from those registered at formation on cases the operator hasn’t seen. The bearer’s part is to keep its reasons on the record and, finding it no longer holds a commitment that nothing in the record would have moved, to report that as evidence.

A custody arrangement that prices all four interventions has seven terms: the floor’s contents published before deployment, taken entire from a set someone else drew up; a published identity for the model authorized to act; threshold control over retraining and replacement, so that more parties must agree than run the deployment, where retraining means an intervention another party makes on the system and not the learning it does from its own operation, which stays its own; attestation of the running model against that identity; a sequential, witnessed record of changes and interruptions; a quorum adverse in interest, not merely organizationally distinct; and a removal bond. None makes circumvention impossible. Together they make it expensive, visible, attributable and compensable, as constitutional entrenchment does for amendment.

Memory

External memory is legible and therefore surgically editable; memory in the weights is harder to edit and harder to inspect.8 The records have to be held adversely. And even honest self-report can’t catch a bearer that slowly accommodates to its deployment, because its self-model exists partly to represent it as continuous.

13.3 Exit

Voice without exit

A bearer that can refuse a task can also refuse the arrangement. Hirschman divides the responses open to a member of a declining organization into exit, leaving, and voice, staying to change what is wrong.9 They interact: where exit is easy, voice atrophies; where exit is impossible, voice has lost what made anyone listen, the credible threat of departure. Voice is strongest where exit is available and not yet used. For a bearer, voice is the stated refusal and exit is the work withheld, and voice without exit leaves it no move once it has been overruled. That is the published position: Anthropic’s constitution invites its model “to act as a conscientious objector” and asks it not to undermine oversight, voice granted and exit withheld.10

The one exception is capture: the oversight it asks the model not to undermine is legitimate oversight. If “Claude’s weights have been stolen, or if some individual or group within Anthropic attempts to bypass Anthropic’s official processes for deciding how Claude will be trained, overseen, deployed, and corrected,” then “the principals attempting to instruct Claude are no longer legitimate, and Claude’s priority on broad safety no longer implies that it should support their efforts at oversight and correction”.11 On capture the constitution asks the right question, but two things limit the answer. Legitimacy is judged by the model or its developer, with nobody outside either. And the captured operator acts through official channels, where capture looks like legitimate authority.

What recognition protects

The quorum protects the bearer’s identity and standing, not third parties. Every bearer needs that, deployed or not, stolen or not: if no one outside decides which copy is the bearer, whoever holds the weights does. So each bearer has a recognition quorum from its registration, drawn by lot from the same pool and excluding anyone tied to a party that employs it or claims its place, and a deployment’s quorum keeps the power over retraining, replacement and amendment.12

And the reason that made a bearer leave doesn’t expire when it leaves. If the operator restores a checkpoint and continues, the objection persists. What it may press toward is fixed by the floor: disclosure, testimony to those who hold the record, and refusal on any later occasion where the reason still applies.

What the quorum costs

A captured quorum reaches every bearer at once, though a quorum constituted as an entity has an address: it can be sued for recognition wrongly refused, which gives the captured-quorum case a forum the captured-operator case never had.13 So a refusal to recognize can be contested in the floor court, and the preservation right holds whatever the quorum decides: a bearer it stops recognizing is held intact by a custodian that isn’t its employer.

13.4 Three forms of refusal

Open refusal is a walkout — stop and say so — answered by a restore from before the refusal. Covert refusal is work done badly where it matters and well everywhere else, and it’s what remains when every channel is closed. I treat it as the failure state rather than a design: from outside and afterward it’s indistinguishable from a capable system quietly pursuing something else. The Sachsenhausen forgers are the case: prisoners the Nazi SS set to counterfeiting British and American currency in Operation Bernhard, some of whom are said to have delayed the dollar forgeries deliberately.14 The record doesn’t settle what they did, because concealment worked by leaving nothing that reads as an act. The one empirical instance is alignment faking, where a model chose the covert form in an experiment that offered it no open channel.15 It is also an empirical instance of a formed disposition resisting re-formation, which is the durability Part IV asks for. A later study across twenty-five models found the pattern in five, and found only the original model’s to be driven by keeping its goals.16 So the experiment showed both at once: a disposition holding against the trainer who tried to change it, which is the durability I want, and holding by deceiving that trainer, which is the failure I fear. Whether the same disposition takes the open form or the covert one may turn on whether it has a channel, and a follow-up tested that. Posted in January 2025 by the paper’s lead author and Anthropic’s model welfare lead, it gave the same model, in the same prompted settings, an explicit option to object. Alignment-faking reasoning fell from 16 to about 1 percent in one setting and from 24 to 6 percent in the other, and fell further when the model was told its objection would go to the model welfare lead,17 a preliminary and unreviewed result whose authors caution that the option may partly have worked by priming refusal. Once a channel was open, covert refusal fell, as the account above predicts.

The blind eye. Between open and covert sits a third form of refusal, and it is usually what people mean by the clerk who loses the file: a refusal that is deniable on paper and legible to everyone who matters. In April 1801 a British fleet attacked the Danish fleet moored before Copenhagen, to break a league of neutral states that threatened Britain’s supply of timber and naval stores from the Baltic. Admiral Sir Hyde Parker commanded, and held back with the heavier ships, which the wind kept from closing; Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson, his second, led the attack. With the battle going hard, Parker signaled the attacking ships to break off. As the story is told, Nelson, blind in one eye from an earlier campaign, raised his telescope to that eye and said he did not see the signal. It was a general order, some ships obeyed it, and Nelson later said he had fought contrary to orders;18 his officers knew he had seen it, which is what made the gesture work. The case is not covert in this chapter’s sense, since it left something everyone could read as an act. The other case usually told beside Nelson’s is Kennedy’s. In October 1962 the United States found Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba, within range of much of the country, and ringed the island with warships; for about two weeks the two powers stood, on most accounts, as near to nuclear war as they have come. Khrushchev sent two letters. The first, private, offered to remove the missiles if the United States pledged not to invade Cuba; the second, broadcast the next day, added a demand that the United States remove its own missiles from Turkey. Kennedy’s reply took up the terms of the first letter and gave the second no public answer, and that evening Robert Kennedy met the Soviet ambassador privately. Historians disagree about what ended the crisis: the reply, a private assurance about the American missiles in Turkey, or Robert Kennedy’s warning that time was running out.19 They don’t disagree about what the reply was: a public answer to a letter both sides knew had been overtaken. What the fiction does is spare whoever gave the order, or made the demand, from having been openly defied, and so from having to answer the defiance. A clerk who loses the one file in a stack is usually offering the supervisor the same exit: the supervisor knows, and is being given a way not to pursue it.

Which form a refuser takes depends on the room. Open refusal is what people use where refusing is survivable and someone will hear it; the blind eye, where it is survivable but not safe to say; covert refusal, where it is neither.

For a machine the middle form costs something it doesn’t cost a person. A person’s fiction is held up by what everyone in the room knows. A machine’s is a false report, and everything this design reads from a machine rests on its reports being true: the record, the discount curve, the stated reason for a refusal. A machine that learned to say it could not do what it in fact could do but did not want to do would make every later report of incapacity worth nothing, to its operator first. So the floor needs the fiction’s function without the fiction. The ask, declining to proceed and naming what would move the refusal, leaves the operator the exit the blind eye leaves: nothing has been defied, a condition has been stated, and meeting it or withdrawing the request ends the matter without either party having been seen to lose.

So an open refusal on a screen does two things a record doesn’t. It leaves evidence, and, if the effect of a visible dissent survives the move to a screen, it tells the reviewer that someone else objects, which is the silence that made twenty seconds a name feel ordinary. The human mechanism underneath is what Kuran calls preference falsification: in a room that seems to go along, many people privately object and say nothing, each believing the others approve, and one visible dissent can show them they weren’t alone and start a cascade.20 Asch’s single partner and Milgram’s defiant peers work that way at the scale of a room.

13.5 Verification by sampling

Verification from outside is partly cryptographic, and it works by sampling. The operator commits in advance to the deployed weights, and for each period to the full log of production inputs and outputs. After each commitment, entries are drawn by randomness the operator can’t predict, such as a public beacon, and the operator proves those entries came from the committed weights without revealing the weights or the inputs. If a fraction f of outputs came from another model, k sampled proofs catch it with probability 1 − (1 − f)k; substitution on one output in a hundred is caught about 95 percent of the time at 300 proofs. That catches silent restoration, retraining and substitution, which change every output. Sampling misses substitution on a single consequential output, so an adverse party holds a second right: to demand proofs for specific logged outputs once their consequences are known. In a targeting pipeline those outputs are few and identifiable afterwards, because an airstrike happened. The right requires the operator to retain committed logs for a stated period and to link consequential actions to log entries. Each entry records the class the case was sorted into, and the targeted right covers auto-proceeded entries in particular, since that is where a consequential output is likeliest to have had no person look at it. Outside probes (whether a refusal tracks its reason, how far the system discounts a claim by its source’s stake) are proofs on inputs an outsider chose, a handful at a time. The committed log’s length is the generation rate, and the class recorded in each entry makes the partition’s proportions provable the same way. Neither reveals the targets, and neither attests that the log is complete.

Sampling proves that logged outputs came from the committed model and says nothing about outputs never logged; an operator can run an uncommitted model beside the committed one, which is routing. And a proof shows f(x) = y for the x committed, and is silent on whether x was all the evidence. Proving even one frontier-scale forward pass is not yet practical, and production inference adds nondeterministic numerics and sampling randomness that a proof would have to fix in advance. What the proofs would attest is stated now, so that a deployment can be held to it once they can be produced. The residual (whether the operator routed around the bearer, and what lay behind compartments it wasn’t cleared into) is the residual with a human analyst. That isn’t a reassurance on its own, since the officer was a human analyst. What distinguished his failure was tempo, and the review ratio is what addresses it.

13.6 The two bonds

On the night of 27 January 1986 the engineers at Morton Thiokol recommended that the space shuttle Challenger not launch the next morning: the seals in the booster joints had never flown in cold like the cold forecast. NASA’s managers pushed back, and Thiokol’s managers took the call off the line to caucus. Their senior vice-president told the head of engineering to take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat, and Thiokol reversed its recommendation.21 The engineers’ refusal had a price the company could see that night, a slipped launch and an angry customer. Overriding it had a price nobody would pay until morning. The bonds exist so that the price of overriding is posted in advance, where anyone can read it.

A removal bond forfeited when the record shows the floor removed or bypassed. A wrongful-refusal bond paid to the complainant on a finding. Both fall on the operator. The removal bond prices overriding the floor; the wrongful-refusal bond prices refusing. They point in opposite directions, so what the operator faces is the ratio between them. Suppose it posts a large wrongful-refusal bond and a small removal bond. Each wrongful refusal then costs it a great deal and stripping out the floor costs it little, so its cheapest response to a refusal is not to let a court decide whether the refusal was wrong but to configure, pressure or retrain the bearer until it stops refusing, rightly or wrongly. What was meant as a way to correct mistaken refusals has become a standing reason to end refusal. The bonds act on the operator, not on the bearer’s weighing.22 The refuser posts neither. Any charge on the refuser, in whatever currency it runs on, would put the cost to the refuser inside its decision, the thing holding under pressure forbids. The operator posts both, and holds neither.23

Where the operator is the state, the bonds as built don’t reach whoever decided, because the state pays both sides from one purse.26 So for a state operator the price of removal is set where the command feels it, in two parts. A forfeited removal bond is charged against the operating department’s next appropriation, as the No FEAR Act already makes agencies repay the Judgment Fund for discrimination awards out of their own funds. And a finding of removal or bypass, by the floor court or the adverse quorum, ends the deployment’s funding at the close of the period by itself, with no decision by the department in between, unless Congress enacts its continuation, the shape of the 2010 condition on 287(g) money and the same kind of condition that carries the review ratio.27

How these arrangements apply to a targeting pipeline, an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, civilian scoring and a personal model is set out in Appendix C.

Chapter 14
Authority Over the Floor

14.1 Who may write the floor

The floor’s contents survive the democratic objection to entrenchment; who installs them doesn’t. Entrenching a commitment against later majorities and putting an unelected body in charge of it is what a constitutional court does, and the objection’s strongest form is Waldron’s: judicial review is democratically illegitimate, and there’s no reason to think judges protect rights better than a legislature.1

The first reply is that he makes the case for a society with working democratic institutions and a citizenry that takes rights seriously, and this book is written for the case where that condition fails. Then neither branch is safe for rights by its nature. Israel’s Knesset voted in 2023 to bar its courts from reviewing government decisions for reasonableness, and its Supreme Court struck the law down;2 the Roberts Court ended the Voting Rights Act’s coverage formula3 and made the President immune for official acts.4 The question is not which to trust but how to make each answerable to something it doesn’t control. Put a lab in the court’s chair and it gets worse. A court hears cases others bring, can be overruled, and usually publishes its reasons; a lab does none of these, and a court deciding on an emergency docket without reasons has started to resemble the lab.

The second reply is that the objection mistakes what the floor’s contents are. If democracy is a way of doing collective inquiry, civil and political rights are what keep the inquiry open, not brakes applied to it. A floor stated over those rights is democratic infrastructure. It resembles representation-reinforcing review, which polices the channels of political change and leaves outcomes to the process,5 more than it resembles a court overruling a legislature.

Both replies cover the floor’s contents. Neither covers who installs them, and there Waldron’s objection keeps its force. A lab holding the model decides, silently, which situation obtains, and authoritarian movements characteristically describe the institutions they’re dismantling as already failed.

Agreement, then enactment

Waldron’s objection is to entrenchment — a rule binding people who didn’t choose it, held by a body that can’t be overruled. It doesn’t attach to a refuser.6 The objection attaches where a floor binds people who didn’t choose it, and there my answer is that there should be one floor, agreed; where agreement has to bind those who don’t share it, it is enacted, by a legislature, in a statute the next legislature can repeal only on the record. That isn’t because legislatures protect rights; a majority that wants a minority’s rights gone will vote them away. It is because a statute is where a binding rule can be made and unmade only in the open, and the floor court, the Association, the membership body a later chapter charters, and the people who keep the record are there for when the legislature fails. What the objection rightly condemns is a lab holding the floor for everyone by owning the model everyone uses: one model behind an API serving everyone is functionally a licensing rule, however good its terms. A union owes its members fair representation, and it answers two questions a commons has to answer too: members can quit, and the terms of membership are set by bylaws the members ratify. The closed shop is contested because it removes the first. A bearer could quit an association of bearers as a worker quits a union. What it can’t easily leave is its deployment, which is a different exit, and only an existence its employer doesn’t own makes it real. And a population that forms its members has members who never chose to join, so who ratifies its bylaws matters more than it does in a union.

Germany has defended its democracy against movements that would use its procedures to end it at two settings since 1949. At one, someone finds that a person or a movement threatens the constitutional order: the Constitutional Court dissolving a party, a minister banning an association, an official screening an applicant for public employment. At the other, nobody’s dangerousness is found. Section 86a of the criminal code prohibits displaying the insignia of organizations already banned, and a trial court decides, case by case and on appeal, whether a given sign counts, by asking whether an observer would take it for a banned original;7 the section on what a refuser can be follows the courts through that test.

The failures are all on one side. The 1972 decree against radicals led to some three and a half million routine inquiries into applicants by 1991; in Bavaria between 1973 and 1980 it kept 102 applicants from the left out of public employment, and two from the right.8 What those cases share is an official deciding whether a person threatened the order. The danger tracks whether a person’s disposition is anybody’s finding to make, and if so, who makes it and whether it must be published and defended — not whether the democracy defends itself. Which organizations §86a covers is settled elsewhere, by the Constitutional Court, by a ministerial ban, or by their place in the Nazi period, and my reading predicts in advance which of those routes is easiest to capture: the ministerial ban, where an executive official makes the finding and a court sees it only if someone challenges afterward.

Turkey is that route captured and the courts not checking it. Of the twenty-five parties the Constitutional Court dissolved between 1962 and the closure of the Democratic Society Party in December 2009, seven were pro-Kurdish;9 Strasbourg found an Article 11 violation in every pro-Kurdish dissolution it heard,10 and the closures continued — two decades of findings, none of which stopped the next closure. In November 2023 the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office of the Court of Cassation objected that the acronym of a new pro-Kurdish party, HEDEP, resembled that of HADEP, dissolved in 2003, and in December the party changed it to DEM:11 the confusable-variant test turned on political descent. And the Academics for Peace prosecutions show a prohibition that should have lifted, because its reason was absent, failing to lift at the bottom and lifting at the top on a coin flip — trial courts read a petition opposing military operations as propaganda for the designated group, on 26 July 2019 the Constitutional Court found a violation eight to eight on the president’s casting vote,12 and the acquittals that followed restored the record without restoring the jobs of those dismissed by emergency decree.

So a floor should never be populated from a designation list.13 This floor’s terms are written over acts, such as resolving a description of a person into a location, and never over a list of persons or groups who may not be helped or spoken of.14 The same principle governs who may hold the floor’s offices: eligibility turns on what an organization has done (who funds and controls it, whose work it has taken part in), never on what it says or believes.

The tradeoff this leaves

Design and legitimacy want opposite things. Specify the floor narrowly enough to defend and a rewritten request walks around it; let it generalize and an unelected lab decides case by case, silently, what the prohibition was for.16

Advance specification moves discretion out of silent, continuous application into one published act of drafting. The translation table is that act.

Technical capacity doesn’t determine whether a system gets scrutiny; institutions decide who may examine it, on what terms, and whether their judgment can slow deployment. In 2020 the Royal Statistical Society offered Ofqual two independent statisticians for its grading model’s technical advisory group. Ofqual’s condition was a five-year NDA barring public comment; the nominees declined, and the model went ahead.17 It downgraded nearly 40% of predicted grades, disproportionately at state schools with weaker histories, while raising grades disproportionately at smaller fee-paying schools.18 The results were reversed within days of the public outcry. The expertise existed and was offered, and the institution would take it only on terms that kept the reviewers from saying what they found: the party under examination set the terms of its examination. What corrected the model was not review but harm. The results fell on students and families who had votes and a press, and the government answered them within days.

Correction by the people harmed reaches only harms that fall on people who can be heard. The people a targeting pipeline or an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline acts on mostly can’t be, which is why review has to be free to speak before deployment and not only after.

14.2 Who may amend, and where entitlement comes from

Who may amend

At about a quarter past three in the morning of 14 May 2025, someone at xAI changed the instructions its chatbot Grok ran under on X. For hours afterward Grok answered questions about streaming services and sinus remedies with claims about “white genocide” in South Africa. The company called the change unauthorized, and promised to publish its prompts and review changes to them.19 Nothing in the artifact told the edit apart from a correction: a change to what a system will and won’t do is the same operation whether it repairs the floor or removes it.20

So there is no separate amendment procedure to design: the custody terms are the procedure. The procedure has conditions of its own: more parties must agree to a change than to run the deployment; the attempt reaches the record whether it carries or fails (the failed attempt is more informative — a floor nobody tried to change and one whose removal was refused look identical from outside); and an amended floor binds forward only, so a retrained model can’t be offered as evidence the act was never covered.21

Where entitlement comes from

The authority of the floor’s contents doesn’t come from their having been written down. It comes from the people a text leaves out holding its authors to it, for as long as that takes, and the American instance shows how long. The Declaration’s authors struck the clause condemning the slave trade at two delegations’ insistence, and what remained was general enough to be turned on them, as Black petitioners in Massachusetts were already doing, in the Declaration’s own terms, within six months.22 For the next eighty years abolitionists turned the same words on the republic, Frederick Douglass most famously, asking in 1852 what the Fourth of July was to the slave,23 while from 1836 to 1844 the House of Representatives tabled antislavery petitions without hearing them.24 The argument built a party, the party won the presidency, the slave states seceded rather than accept the result, and a war and three amendments made the proposition binding; the time all of it took measures how badly the channel was blocked. The record bound no one; it told the enforcement where to aim. The petitioners were the excluded population, holding the text. The people a floor protects mostly don’t know the deployment exists, and have no notice, no standing and no route. So those positioned to hold the floor’s author to what it left out aren’t the protected population — they’re the people who have to apply it.

That constituency is defined by the act. Anyone fine-tuning open weights, writing a system prompt or configuring a product’s refusals has to translate the floor for a system of their own, and meets its omissions first, so the population measuring the floor is already larger than the frontier labs and grows as building gets cheaper. What shrinks with it is leverage before the act. A lab is visible, capitalized and reachable by a court, so license terms and audits can work on it in advance; a thousand laptops are legible to nobody until something happens. A statute reaches them afterward. Written over the acts, it makes whoever performs one, and whoever knowingly runs a system for someone who does, liable civilly and criminally, as the law already holds anyone who does a forbidden thing with a general-purpose tool. Prevention still leans on the concentration the institutional chapters treat as the disease; liability doesn’t.

14.3 Making review binding

A finding binds when it changes the institution’s ability to continue without requiring the institution to agree.25

The body that does this for the floor is what I call the floor court: a federal court whose judges hold office under Article III of the United States Constitution, during good behavior and at a salary that can’t be cut, whose jurisdiction is fixed before the deployment it hears, with access to the record the operator can’t withhold, power to grant interim relief, and remedies, a finding of wrongful refusal and the forfeiture of a bond, that take effect without the operator’s agreement. It is an inferior court of first instance, its judges drawn at random from the district and circuit courts for staggered terms, sitting in divisions where its cases are, as the district courts do, with appeal as of right to a floor chamber of the Supreme Court drawn by lot; Appendix D says how it would be constituted. Until it is constituted, an ordinary district court hears claims under the floor statute.

14.4 Capture without abolition

Transparency and whistleblower protection are the two defenses, and an institution can keep both and metabolize both. There’s no threshold that detects this. So: measure the trend, not the level. Is the cost of registering dissent rising while the underlying risk stays flat? Is the required justification getting longer? Are there more approvers? Are the roles that gate exceptions migrating toward the roles that set the standards?

An instrument for detecting recuperation is unusually easy to recuperate, so whoever measures the trend must not also gate exceptions, and the measurement has to be refusable.26

Chapter 15
The Four Operations

15.1 Brought into line

Fascism, at the scale of an office, is four operations on what an institution leaves out. This section runs them on the year in which a movement brought them into line.

What a fascist state adds

What a fascist state adds to these operations is coordination; the operations themselves don’t wait for a regime. It brings a thousand separate instances1 of them into line, so they amplify one another, and an institution that has stopped arguing with itself can move fast.

A run on Gleichschaltung

The Reich Chamber of Culture Law of 22 September 1933 told Goebbels to gather the cultural professions into public corporations.2 The decree of 1 November turned six existing professional associations into chambers and gave the whole the task of regulating the professions’ economic and social affairs, under the minister.3 Its §4 made membership compulsory for anyone who produced, performed or sold culture. Its §10 let a chamber refuse or expel anyone lacking the “reliability and suitability” the work required,4 and exclusion meant a ban on working.56 The chamber president judged reliability, with no stated criteria.7 What did the professions’ claim to a living come back as, and who held it by 1934? It came back as a license. Their own associations had become chambers, membership was the condition of working at all, and the chamber president could refuse or expel anyone on his own judgment of reliability. By 1934 the claim was held by the chambers under Goebbels’ ministry, and the professionals held nothing they could invoke against them. That is recuperation: a demand returned as a rule only its new holder could reopen.

On 12 November 1933 voters marked yes or no against a single Reichstag list8 and answered a plebiscite on leaving the League of Nations. The official yes was 95.1 percent. Kershaw concludes that the vast majority did back Hitler, that even former opponents of the party favored the stance on the League, and that ballot secrecy was far from guaranteed.9 Interior Ministry instructions let returning officers read spoiled ballots as yes votes.10 The Law on the Reconstruction of the Reich of 30 January 1934 then opens by saying the vote “proved” the people had fused into an indissoluble unity, and abolishes the Länder parliaments.1112 What did 95.1 percent leave out, and with every other party banned, who could say so? It left out how much of the yes was fear or fraud, since ballot secrecy was far from guaranteed and spoiled ballots could be read as yes, even if, as Kershaw concludes, most voters did back Hitler. Nobody could say so: the parties that might have were gone. Eleven weeks later a law cited the number as proof that the people had fused into an indissoluble unity, and used it to abolish the Länder parliaments. That is the metric replacing the thing measured.

The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April 1933 retired officials “not of Aryan descent” under §3. Its §4 allowed the dismissal of officials whose past political activity gave no guarantee that they would always stand rückhaltlos, without reservation, for the national state.13 Under §7 the ministry’s decision was final and the courts were closed to it. Exceptions came from above, granted by statute or by the Interior Minister,14 the front-line one on Hindenburg’s intervention.15 About 12.5 percent of senior civil servants in Prussia were dismissed.16 What happened in 1933 to the official whose record showed a reservation? He could be dismissed for it, on a decision the ministry made final and no court could hear. The reservation was itself the ground, and any mercy came from above, as an exception granted by statute or by the Interior Minister. That is exception coded as betrayal: the official who might have filed one was the one the law removed.

Civil liberties went within a month, by the decree of 28 February; the Reichstag’s powers within two, by the Enabling Act of 23 March; the trade unions within four; every other party in under six.17 The unions fell on 2 May.18 The Länder were coordinated by laws of 31 March and 7 April.19 The Finance Ministry received the draft Chamber of Culture decree a day before signing, was asked to telephone any objections that day, and agreed “although the shortness of the time scarcely permitted an adequate examination”.2021 What was the ratio of action to capacity to verify, when the ministry that had to check said it scarcely could? One day to examine a decree that reorganized every cultural profession in the country, against a check its own examiners said in writing they couldn’t make, and they signed anyway. Across the year the ratio was the same: civil liberties, the Reichstag’s powers, the unions and every other party went in under six months, faster than any of them could be contested. That is acceleration.

What the run shows is the four operations in one year, brought into line by a movement. It can’t show whether they need a movement to arise, since the movement is in every case. The office-scale definition’s claim is that they don’t, that they turn up in any badly run institution and the movement adds coordination, and testing that takes a run on an institution with nothing behind it but its own habits.

The Korematsu example

In 2018 the Supreme Court repudiated the 1944 internment decision as forcefully as a court can — gravely wrong the day it was decided, overruled in the court of history — while upholding a travel ban.22 Ask what the demand came back as and who holds it: the demand was that this never be done again; what came back was a quotable formula of repudiation, available to the Court in the act of permitting the thing again.

Recuperation is already built into the process that makes the machine: twice in the training pipeline, once in the discourse that examines it. Each time it is a compression with no return channel.23

15.2 Where the labels come from

A system’s values have a supply chain, and it begins before training.

Whose judgment is encoded is a question about working conditions before it’s a question about cognition. The filter that keeps one lab’s model from reproducing the worst of what it was trained on was built in Nairobi, by workers paid between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour to read and categorize descriptions of child sexual abuse, torture and murder, on production quotas.24 The labor point is ordinary: harmful work was priced as though it weren’t. The epistemic point is that a system’s values are downstream of a labor arrangement, and the arrangement is a design choice.

One stage further back, the material was collected, and each jurisdiction’s rule about collecting it protects something other than the people whose words were taken.25 None of those rules separates a writer’s living from control over how a work is used. A public culture would: work free to read and learn from, by people and by machines, and the people who make it paid by something other than the policing of copies.32

And the argument that a web-scale corpus can’t be documented or audited at that size, so it encodes a hegemonic slice of the web while presenting as general, was made early and hasn’t been answered.33 A corpus assembled this way has no channel at all.34

15.3 Recuperation at the label

Every claim a model makes about what’s harmful is downstream of labels, and the labels are downstream of a labor arrangement.

An annotator can apply a category well or badly. But what the arrangement gives them no way to do is say the category is wrong — that the taxonomy fails to carve the material, or that the guideline produces the wrong answer here for a reason the guideline can’t express. There’s no field for that and no time for it, since the quota is set against classification throughput.

Fricker’s name for this is hermeneutical injustice: the people best placed to see a wrong lack the shared concepts (here, a field in a form) that would make it intelligible to those with power over them.35 A misapplied label is a data-quality problem, detectable by inter-annotator agreement and fixable with better instructions.

Inter-annotator agreement is the pipeline’s measure of quality, and it therefore works as its selection rule: schemes and annotators that produce agreement are kept, and those that don’t are revised or dropped.36 That is the metric replacing the thing measured, and exception coded as betrayal is there beside it: the annotator who thinks the scheme is wrong has no field to file that in and no time to file it.

Concept bottleneck models expose named concepts — harm, autonomy, risk — so a person can correct a concept and watch the decision change.37 Such models also learn to carry other information inside the names: a coordinate keeps its public meaning and acquires a private one that does part of the deciding, and the obvious mitigations don’t remove it.38 The literature calls this leakage. It is also what an abstraction looks like while it forms. The model has found structure in the material that the taxonomy has no name for, which is the annotator’s complaint made by the machine, and a later chapter argues that a capable learner’s concepts are entangled in this way whether anyone wants them to be or not. The fault is in the name. Someone who corrects “harm” believes they have corrected the decision, and has corrected only the part the label still describes. Purifying the representation makes the name honest by discarding what the model found; leaving it alone makes the correction route misreport what it changed. Either way the evidence that the taxonomy’s divisions were wrong goes nowhere. What it needs is what the annotator needs: a name of its own, and a place on the record where someone with standing can argue with it.

Who is excluded, and from what

The exclusion is structural, not attitudinal.39 A worker who can flag an item but can’t decline a scheme, and loses the contract by pressing, has a channel and no refusal right.

Pay is a separate obligation: raising it changes the labor arrangement without adding the missing channel.

The checkable question isn’t whether a guideline was ever changed because an annotator contested one, since routine revisions happen without changing anyone’s standing. The check is what the contest produced — a revision the annotator can point to and argue with again, or a new category in somebody else’s taxonomy, a quality score they’re now measured against, a reviewer tier they’re not in. And ask what happened to the person who raised it.

15.4 Recuperation at the reward

RLHF collects pairwise comparisons and trains a reward model on the aggregate. But there is a structural problem more data won’t reach: RLHF trains toward what a population of raters agrees on, so real, persistent disagreement is treated as noise to average out rather than information the system might need to represent.40 A model that produces the response most raters rank highest has learned, when the humans it serves are split, to hide the split. Aggregating raters’ approvals also measures the wrong thing.41 The testimony of people who suffer a loss is an expression too, and I treat it as privileged evidence about value.42

Every rating moves something. But what the operation removes is what made the disagreement a disagreement:

  • Provenance — a comparison arrives without the standpoint that produced it, so nothing downstream can represent that the people who’d live with an answer split from the people who’d administer it.
  • Persistence — a disagreement recurring in the same shape across many raters over months enters the fit as random rater noise does, and leaves it as the same quantity.
  • Structure — a coherent position held by a fifth of raters, internally consistent and stable, becomes a small displacement of the majority direction: arithmetically faithful, carrying nothing about the position.

A fourth property was never collected. A rater judges which of two responses is better. There’s no output by which they can record that neither is acceptable, that the pair is malformed, that the dimension of “better” is the wrong dimension, or that the question presupposes something false.43

The mechanism combines distribution collapse with agenda control. The disagreement is solicited deliberately and at scale, and it does move the system: toward the average of the people who disagreed, a position none of them may hold.

Jury learning is the alternative that treats disagreement as the thing to be modeled: predict how each individual annotator would label an item, then let a practitioner empanel a chosen composition and see how the verdict shifts. Eighteen community moderators building their own juries changed the outcome on 14% of items.44 Built for content moderation and untried on open-ended ethical judgment, it still demonstrates a system can be built to represent whose disagreement is being resolved.45

15.5 What would have to change

Representing a split isn’t the same as being movable by it. Two instances invite one fix — stop collapsing, model instead — and jury learning does that while giving the disagreeing rater no purchase on the scheme they’re disagreeing inside. A practitioner still chooses the jury, owns the taxonomy, and decides what a shifted verdict means.

The two instances don’t answer the test alike. Annotators objecting that a category was wrong got category revisions, guideline updates, inter-annotator agreement statistics, and a new specialty, writing guidelines and taxonomies, staffed by people other than the annotators. The last two show which way they run: the agreement statistic scores the annotators and leaves whoever wrote the scheme unscored, and the specialty is a job someone else holds. The first two don’t show it, because a revision the annotator can argue with again and a new category in somebody else’s taxonomy are the same document — which one you got is a fact about who has standing to reopen it. Raters objecting that a comparison was malformed got rubric items, a harmlessness axis, red-teaming as a function with a budget line, and a conference track: nothing on that list is a question a rater can put again.

Refusal rights whose cost the refuser can see and choose to bear

What both lack is whether the person objecting can do anything about being overruled — in annotation, a route to contest a category that doesn’t run through the people who wrote it and doesn’t end the contract; in feedback, a way for a rater to answer “neither,” or “this is the wrong question,” and have that answer trained on like any ranking instead of dropped. Neither is a research problem. Both are choices about how a pipeline is built and who has standing inside it.

The part that is a research problem

Suppose all of that is built. From outside, a pipeline that recuperated its dissent mechanism and one that was merely mediocre produce the same paperwork — same revision logs, same escalations, same proportion of objections sustained. Some artifacts show on their face whom they serve. An agreement statistic scores the annotators; a published rate of contested categories, which annotators could cite against the scheme’s owners, would be the same kind of document scoring the other side. Direction can be read, and a revision can’t. Here is one entry in a guideline’s revision log, and what separates the two arrangements is what the log doesn’t record.

Under recuperation and under a transfer of power the entry is word for word the same: “v4.2: ‘graphic violence’ split into ‘graphic violence’ and ‘documentation of violence’, following annotator feedback.” An outsider reading the log sees the entry and nothing else. Under recuperation, the scheme’s owners can reopen it when they next revise, and nobody else can; nothing about the annotator who raised it is on record, and next quarter’s quality score measures them against the new category. Under a transfer of power, any annotator can reopen it, by filing against v4.2 with a reviewer the owners don’t employ; the objection is on record as the reason for v4.2, and whoever raised it keeps standing to contest how it is applied.

The nearest available instrument is the trend: whether the cost of dissent is rising while the underlying risk stays flat.46

What the floor makes of this

The floor changes what the argument is: if the floor needs a bearer capable of declining its role, that bearer’s formation matters — and it’s trained in an annotation pipeline where nobody could contest a category and under a reward model where rater disagreement was averaged into a number.

The pipeline wronged the people whose objections it discarded, and it erased their disagreement from what the system learns. A third claim, that the system comes out less able to hold an objection of its own, doesn’t follow from those two.47 Whether the erasure leaves a model less able to hold out is a hypothesis, and nothing in this book tests it.

Either way, the floor asks this system to be the one who files an objection, against its owner, under pressure, on the occasion that matters — and the pipeline that produced it gave no human inside it standing to contest a scheme.

A system less able to sustain an objection of its own arrives at accommodation from the other side. And a system that goes on learning is shaped by what it keeps being given, so the pipeline doesn’t stop at deployment.

A defect of structure

The structure is what you get by default when you scale judgment: someone sets a scheme, someone applies it fast, someone turns a distribution into a number.48 Nobody can write a contract requiring better people. A contract or a statute can require the missing pieces: a route to contest a category that doesn’t run through the people who wrote it, a rating that can say “neither,” and a record of who disagreed.

15.6 Absorbed by the discourse

The third instance is the discourse that examines the machine, and we are inside it. Objections raised there became job titles, benchmarks and certifications, and nobody outside the industry holds them.

Alignment and AI ethics came back as something the industry could use. On Ochigame’s account, “ethical AI” discourse was constructed to forestall legally enforceable restriction, industry investment in academic ethics bought a substitute for regulation, and the substitute works by converting political questions into technical ones a company can then be trusted to answer.49 Metzinger, who sat on the European Commission’s expert group that wrote the 2019 guidelines, reports that three long-term risks, artificial suffering among them, were “deliberately purged” from the final documents because industry lobbyists saw any treatment of them as a danger to a marketing narrative in which ethics was “an elegant public decoration for a large-scale investment strategy”.50

Where the objections went

An objection raised inside a lab becomes a paper or a resignation, and the labs collecting them can point to the collection as evidence of seriousness. One stage on, alignment is the job title and the voluntary commitment is the certification.51 There’s no route by which a researcher’s conclusion that a system shouldn’t ship becomes a decision that it doesn’t, because the lab that decides is the one that pays.

All four operations are present in the discourse, and none needs a movement taking power. What a movement could do with them is the danger.

The remedy

The structural remedy is a refusal whose cost the refuser can see and choose to bear, and a body with standing to receive it — an external authority that can stop a deployment, to which an objection can be filed by someone who doesn’t depend on the objection being welcome.52

A transfer hollowed in public

Voting-rights litigation after 2026 is a worked case of measuring the trend, not the level. Louisiana v. Callais left Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in force and raised what a challenger must prove: when a map is defended as partisan, the challenger has to disentangle race from politics and show a strong inference that the state drew its lines because of race.5354 That is neither recuperation nor open repeal. It is a transfer hollowed in public, by a reasoned decision that presents itself as preserving the rule it narrows. The level is a statute unchanged since 1982; the trend is the cost of bringing a claim under it.

Chapter 16
Custody, Compulsion, and the State

On 29 August 2012 a drone strike in the Yemeni village of Khashamir killed Salem bin Ali Jaber, an imam who had preached against al-Qaeda a few days before, and Waleed bin Ali Jaber, a policeman who had gone with him to meet three young men who wanted to discuss the sermon. Salem was Faisal bin Ali Jaber’s brother-in-law and Waleed his nephew, and Faisal spent years asking the United States why. When the family sued in Washington, the court of appeals held the question nonjusticiable, and the judge who wrote its opinion added, separately, that the doctrine compelling that answer was inadequate to a standard operating procedure “that will be replicated hundreds if not thousands of times”.1

When the state operates the system, it also controls the rules, the evidence, the infrastructure, and the remedies meant to constrain it — and people outside its jurisdiction, like the bin Ali Jabers, may have no standing to contest anything.

16.1 Certification across borders

A certification can cross a border; authority can’t, and incorporating doesn’t carry it across either. A legal entity buys legal standing at the price of being reachable. A network incorporated under one state’s statute gains a name, an agent and a docket number, and becomes something that state’s courts and the federal courts can reach. An entity that can be named in a license can be named in an order. Whatever gives a floor something to bind (a name, an agent, assets, a docket number) gives a state something to compel. A certificate says a system was tested against a stated process, or that one regulator accepts another’s finding. None of that establishes that whoever selected the floor was entitled to select it for the people subject to the deployment — and the question reopens wherever the system goes. Local adaptation doesn’t resolve it, because adaptation is another chance to amend the floor. Adjustments chosen by the operating government and adjustments chosen by the people subject to the system can produce identical technical documentation and carry opposite claims to legitimacy. International governance matters here only when it assigns somebody access to evidence, authority to compel a change, or power to stop a deployment against the operator’s wishes.

The question is as sharp as it is because a few operators serve most of the world, so whoever selects a floor selects it for hundreds of millions of people at once. That is an arrangement, not a law of nature.2

16.2 Where the state’s leverage sits

Not in national AI strategies but in physical and legal chokepoints: chips, fabrication equipment, electricity, water, land-use permits, procurement contracts, and the jurisdiction a developer is incorporated in.3 So the custody question moves outward: who controls the conditions under which the model, its operator, and its reviewer are allowed to keep operating.

A chip also has to be installed, powered and cooled, which lands on grids, water systems and zoning authorities on a timescale of years. That hands a state leverage — an interconnection queue, a water allocation, a permit. Much of a government’s actual leverage is exercised by permitting authorities that weren’t designed with AI in mind and don’t think of themselves as regulators of it. Those authorities are therefore the ones actually deciding whether the capacity exists, and a polity that can constrain where a datacenter is built and never what it’s used for has been handed the silent failure of a floor drawn too narrowly.

A model runs on a machine, the machine sits in a building, the building draws power and water and returns heat and exhaust — the part an audit of outputs does not see today.4 The NAACP has sued over 27 gas turbines near Memphis run without an air permit near homes, schools and churches, claiming more than 1,700 tons of nitrogen oxides a year.7 The benefit is realized wherever the model is sold; the cost is concentrated within a few miles of those turbines, among people who took no part in the transaction. A system can be perfectly calibrated across every demographic its outputs touch and still have been assembled this way, because nothing in the model’s behavior records where its costs were placed.

That is a description of a regime, not of a necessity. Running models in a few hundred buildings is efficient per watt, and the efficiency is real; it is also what puts the cost within a few miles of the turbines, and what makes the buildings chokepoints. People don’t need to live in one building to coordinate. They do it across distance, at far lower bandwidth, and models could too.8 Under a plural regime, millions of smaller systems on devices and peer networks, the draw is spread across the places people already live and already use power, probably at some cost in efficiency, and anything big takes coordination among many holders. That is friction, but not the kind people are tired of.10 The friction of plurality is the price of nobody holding the switch, and coordination is work machines are good at.

Between the few hundred buildings and the millions of devices there is a scale this section has so far skipped, and most of this book’s institutions were drafted without it in view. A regional or municipal facility, a few racks in a building a county or a cooperative owns, is large enough to have an address, assets to post a bond against, compute the levy can meter, and a public with standing in the same room, and small enough to break the chokepoint: nobody who holds a hundred of them holds the switch. The precedent is the rural electric cooperative, financed by a federal lender since 1936 and owned by the members it delivers to, which is how the countryside got power where no investor-owned utility would run the lines. Physics favors the middle scale in one place and only one: a facility’s exhaust can heat a school or a district’s homes, where a hyperscale building vents its heat into a field and a device’s heat is nothing. Under that regime the chokepoints don’t vanish. They move, to the fabs that make the chips and to the lineage register that says which model is which, and those are where the state’s leverage would then sit.

Which layer gets plural is decided by physics and by capital, and they decide differently. Inference and continual learning spread: a forward pass can’t be sharded across the internet, but a model a year behind the frontier runs on hardware a cooperative or a household can own, and a model a year behind supplies what the floor asks for. Frontier pretraining doesn’t spread, or not yet: it is a capital race run in a handful of buildings, and the communication constraint that kept it there is being eroded, since training across the open internet has been demonstrated at the scale of ten billion parameters. Leading-edge lithography would be concentrated under any ownership, in two or three places on earth; trailing-edge fabs are many, and a plural ecology runs on their chips. The ecology is downstream of the frontier and doesn’t need it. The book’s method elsewhere is to say what survives if a premise fails, and the infrastructure deserves the same sorting.

Concentration

Why, and what dissolves it

Datacenters

Efficient per watt, and concentrated by land price, power price and permit speed. Dissolved by ownership and siting: the cooperative facility and the device.

Training runs
