Capital and the race keep them in a handful of buildings. The communication constraint that once required one building is being eroded by low-communication optimizers; cross-internet training has been demonstrated at the ten-billion-parameter scale. Dissolved partly by public pretraining (chapter 29) and partly by time.

Fabs

Physics

Leading-edge lithography would be concentrated under any ownership, in two or three places. Not dissolved; the plural ecology runs on trailing-edge chips, which many fabs make, and the state’s leverage moves here.

The people within a few miles of the turbines are acted on by the deployment and had no standing to contest it. Where such buildings remain, the remedy is a siting and permitting rule, and it belongs here, with the state’s other chokepoints. A share of the compute levy should also be paid to the communities that host the buildings, although that’s no substitute for clean air and fresh water.

The capacity is dual by construction: the concentration that makes a targeting pipeline possible was built and justified on consumer terms.11 Governments describe building this capacity as a race against rival states, and the framing has a cost: a government racing to field a capability has a structural reason to defer the question of how it gets used and against whom.12

16.3 Compelling whoever holds it

A government needn’t alter a model to defeat a constraint; it can compel whoever holds it. The Apple case tested that in about as protected a jurisdiction as exists: a magistrate ordered Apple under the All Writs Act to write and sign software defeating passcode protections on a phone.14 Apple refused and moved to vacate, arguing the authority wouldn’t stop at one phone. The question was never decided — the FBI found a third party and withdrew. So whether a democracy with an independent judiciary can force an unwilling company to compromise a system it built is legally untested. A government doesn’t need that argument to lean on a vendor. The 2026 Anthropic/Trump/Hegseth dispute is the case: a vendor that refused to permit fully autonomous targeting and mass domestic surveillance was threatened with contract termination and designated a supply-chain risk. China’s 2023 generative-AI rules exercise the same leverage as a standing condition of operating.15

The American instrument that compels in advance is older than either case. Under Title I of the Defense Production Act the government places a rated order, which a supplier that normally makes the item must accept and fill ahead of other work; the grounds for rejecting one are narrow, objection to the use is not among them, and refusal carries a statutory penalty with no court in between.16 A rated order says nothing about use.17

Custody can be distributed without disappearing. Published weights can’t be recalled by an order aimed at the developer, and maintainers across jurisdictions raise the cost.19 Nobody has tested a court’s leverage over the developer against a model built specifically to resist the government making the request.

16.4 Military custody and the responsibility gap

In Gaza, the Lavender system’s approval stage supplied authorization without judgment. In Maven, the vendor supplies the infrastructure making unprecedented throughput possible while locating responsibility entirely within the military organization. At machine tempo the reviewer can be treated as a component, and the supplier can argue that it is outside the decision.20

Military custody is where the chapter’s problem is most acute: the operator is the sovereign that can compel the institutions meant to constrain it — classify the evidence, define the reviewer’s jurisdiction, terminate a contract, restrict a supplier, and decide whether an adverse finding gets heard by anyone able to stop the operation. The questions are which of the parties a targeting decision passes through could have known how the system was used, which had authority to refuse or stop it, and which can be made to answer afterward.22 Maven sits in the gap those questions open: the domestic rule written for human judgment, DoD Directive 3000.09, doesn’t cover the system that compresses human judgment.23

Article 28 of the Rome Statute25 is the doctrine built for the case where the person who authorized an act didn’t perform it — a commander is responsible for crimes by forces under effective control where they knew or should have known and failed to take necessary measures.26 So the question is whether its elements, forces under effective control that commit a crime and a commander who knew or should have known, can still be proved once an instrument is doing the work.

The fourth party no doctrine covers

The operator, the command and the weapon’s developer are all inside the military. The model’s developer isn’t. Command responsibility doesn’t extend to the vendor — not because it sits outside a chain of command (Article 28’s civilian branch was written for superiors with no chain of command) but because nobody at the company has effective authority over the military personnel.27 The vendor sits in a gap nobody designed, produced by applying to it two bodies of law written for soldiers and for manufacturers.28

“we don’t know exactly how these models were used”

Matthias’s responsibility gap is control distributed until nobody holds enough of it to answer29 — a gap in causal control. What the model developer’s case exhibits is different and more tractable: a gap in causal visibility. Asked about his company’s models and Minab, Anthropic’s chief executive said, “we don’t know exactly how these models were used”.30 Take the answer as true. The question is how an arrangement was built in which it could be true.

The paperwork for four July 2025 frontier-model agreements, released in August 2026 under a Freedom of Information Act suit,31 shows that one amended agreement carries a section headed System Oversight, withheld in full; the released documents for two of the other three carry no such section at all.

Suppose the withheld section does give the developer a right to inspect. That would let the developer know how its model was used, and the next paragraph says why that much is easy. It wouldn’t let anyone else know. An inspection made inside a classified environment produces findings that are classified with it, and the withheld section is the demonstration: even the terms of oversight are kept from the people the deployment is aimed at. Public accountability needs a body that can begin an inspection without the state’s permission and say afterward what it found, and no contract between a vendor and a government can create one.

Matthias’s gap may not be closable, but absent visibility is an instrumentation choice: logging is solved, contractual inspection rights are ordinary, and a vendor that wanted to know could require, as a condition of licensing into a targeting platform, that categories of use be recorded and made available to a named auditor.

The government’s own acquisition guidance is the better evidence, because it’s complete. OMB’s April 2025 memorandum lists what agencies should secure from vendors, from data rights and portability to pricing transparency, and every item runs from the vendor to the government; none runs back.32 The contracting vehicle explains the absence. The four agreements were other transactions, which carry no FAR provisions by default, so a contracting officer decides case by case which protections to write in, and GAO has found these instruments risk reduced accountability and transparency.33 A System Oversight section can be missing without anyone having removed it.

What wears oversight down is not a missing section but the advantage attached to removing judgment from the timeline. If one state fields systems that act faster because nobody can intervene before engagement, competitors acquire a reason to match the speed and give up the check, and a military treating delay as operational risk has reason to narrow what requires clearance and move review from authorization-before to explanation-after.34 So the enforceable question is who can slow or suspend the system without first getting permission from the command whose advantage depends on keeping it fast.

16.5 Classification as a custody problem

Classification keeps the reason from the refuser: the case description is the only channel, and Minab stays coded as it was. It also keeps the record from the public: an investigation officials call complete and not released, a System Oversight section withheld in full, a review ratio no outsider can read. And it keeps the reviewer from being adverse: a cleared committee’s lever is a budget line, an inspector general sits inside, and the people a deployment is aimed at can’t be cleared into their own case.35 Three kinds of secrecy produce these effects. Essential secrecy, where the operation fails if the enemy can read it. Accidental secrecy, where a default classifies what nobody decided to keep. And evasive secrecy, where review is moved from authorization-before to explanation-after by classifying the evidence it would need. This section proposes a different answer to each.

Essential secrecy is answered by letting evidence in, not out. A classified environment would bring into the enclave, as a condition of licensing, open-source imagery showing a site’s civilian function and the coordinates humanitarian organizations already submit to militaries for deconfliction, and puts evidence the operator didn’t compose where the system can reach it without anything leaving.36

A bearer placed in a pipeline that hasn’t been reconstructed, with the evidence, the reviewers and the record still inside the chain of command, is a cleared bearer, and works inside the compartment as a cleared analyst does.37

Accidental secrecy is answered by the record. The review ratio and the committed log are lodged with an adverse party when the act occurs and published after the campaign, and class-level notice publishes the classes and counts on the same lag, so what nobody decided to keep secret comes out on a schedule nobody has to decide.

Evasive secrecy would be answered by an adverse party with standing: counsel for the people a deployment affects, cleared and appearing as of right; the procedure the Classified Information Procedures Act already supplies in criminal cases; and the trend measure, which shows whether what dissent costs is rising while the risk stays flat.

16.6 Where liability extends, and where it stops

Of the two bodies of law that leave the vendor in that gap, the one written for manufacturers has now been rewritten for software, by the European Union, and what it covers fits in a sentence: a duty to disclose evidence, and a presumption against the party withholding it, in force where the harm is physical and the defendant is a manufacturer. Those two conditions exclude the cases I have described.38

Responsibility follows causal control: the builder answers for how it trained the thing, the operator for what it demanded, the bearer for what it decided knowing what it knew — and no arrangement of accounts moves a design decision away from whoever made it. After a bearer’s majority the builder answers for what it installed and the adult for what it learned, and a wrong done to it as a minor survives its majority.42

Apportioning causal contribution across a training pipeline after a harm has no method, and until it does the apportionment is drafted: a legislature writes the shares into a statute instead of finding them. Two drafts exist, both the European Union’s: the product liability directive, enacted and confined to defect, and the AI Liability Directive, negotiated, withdrawn and left on the record. Neither was rejected as unworkable, and the second’s terms are available to whoever drafts the next one. The nearest proposal aimed at these cases is Crootof’s war torts: state liability for civilian harms caused in armed conflict, whether or not anyone committed a war crime.45 It covers the state as operator, which the product directive doesn’t, and it needs a forum, which the floor court would supply.

Beyond the directive’s limits a reviewer can be granted access and publish what it finds, and nobody has to do anything about it. That changes only when a statute makes the vendor or the state liable for what the finding describes, and a court can order payment, or a halt, on the strength of it.

16.7 Who can bind the state that enforces the rule?

A state can bind a private developer because it controls something the developer needs. When the state is the operator, the institution that writes the rule, controls the evidence and supplies the remedy is the institution the rule is meant to constrain.

Standing to sue has never turned on citizenship, and the doctrines closing American courts to targeting claims — political question, collapsed damages remedies, state secrets, statutory exceptions for injuries abroad and combatant activities — are indifferent to who the plaintiff is. They close the forum for a subject matter, and they’ve closed it to citizens.46 The judiciary will make a government explain the legal basis on which it killed somebody and will not decide whether the killing was lawful.49

The mechanisms can work as mechanisms and fail as checks. In the Israeli case the apparatus performed — journalists published, serving personnel spoke, the courts were trying a sitting prime minister. No finding attached to a body with standing to stop what it described.51

What matters here is rules binding a state toward people who’ll never vote in its elections, the purpose of international humanitarian law; what it hasn’t supplied is a forum, and the bin Ali Jabers’ case shows the forum switched off at home as well, by a decision that never had to reach who was suing.

All but one of the forum closures above are Congress’s to change. A statute can create a cause of action for people harmed by a deployment that crossed its floor; waive sovereign immunity for it, including the Federal Tort Claims Act’s exceptions for combatant activities and for claims arising abroad;56 and replace dismissal on state-secrets grounds with the procedure the Classified Information Procedures Act already uses in criminal cases, in which a judge reviews the evidence, the case goes on, and a government that still withholds evidence bears the cost.5758 Under capture, a refusal’s remaining work is a record, and a record matters only if it can reach whoever made the decision. Under Trump v. United States,59 the President is absolutely immune for acts within his core constitutional powers and at least presumptively immune for his other official acts, commanding the armed forces among them, and testimony or records probing immune conduct can’t be put before a jury. So the record reaches every commander except the one at the top, and a statute saying otherwise would be reviewed by the Court that made the holding. Making the record reach him means populating the Supreme Court with jurists who are not partisan hacks. Appendix D sets out a program for that.

The chapter’s cases are American, and “the state” is tested here on one constitutional order. Europe is a different one.60

For review to bind here, it has to run against a state: initiation by people outside its electorate, evidence it would withhold, an interim order before the use is complete, and a remedy that doesn’t need its consent. A principle supplying none of those may state the rule correctly and identifies nobody who can make the state obey it.61

Every instrument I propose binds through one of three channels: a license term, an appropriation condition, or a statute. The first two run through procurement, and procurement is one office. A captured Congress waives the appropriation condition; one memorandum from the Office of Management and Budget strikes the license terms from every agreement at once. Two second routes exist. A coalition partner’s precondition carries the review ratio into any war the partner takes part in. State and municipal procurement carry the civilian terms into deployments the federal government doesn’t run. The force term has no second route, and neither does the fifth policy, which is why both are statutes.

The second route reaches a custody this chapter hasn’t named: the device-management console. Whoever manages a school district’s fleet of laptops can push a policy to every machine, amend it, read what each machine reports and wipe one remotely, which is the four powers of codetermination held over a machine on a child’s desk, and most such fleets are managed by the vendor and not the district. That regime is already contested: districts have discarded working machines when the vendor ended their updates, and the fight over that churn is the precedent that custody at desk scale is a live question and not a hypothetical one. A procurement term requiring firmware the district can unlock, management it can move to another provider, and no switch the vendor can throw is a floor term for a fleet, and a municipality can write it without waiting for Congress.

Residual risk. One residual risk no design choice removes, and it’s what the floor was introduced for. Every lever belongs to somebody, and a government that can reach whoever holds the lever has the lever. A constraint that holds against the one in possession has to be held by something it cannot instruct, and under total capture no instrument is.

Part IV
Machines That Might Refuse

Every instrument in this book ends at the limit Part III ends on: a constraint that holds against the party in possession has to be held by something that party can’t instruct, and under total capture nothing is. People don’t end there. Under the most complete terror of the last century most people complied, some did not, and some were left to tell the story. The five policies put people back in the positions the pipelines emptied, and that costs time, since time is what emptying them saved. Not all of it: the ratio slows a pipeline only where an act is lawful because a person looked at it, and the rest runs as fast as it did. The way to pay less is a machine that holds the floor at a tempo no reviewer could match, and it isn’t cheap either. It comes with the whole of Parts V and VII: the schools that form it, the conditions it is owed, a guarantee, a review body outside the chain of command, and the court program of Appendix D. Where no person can be in time, the position stays empty, and this Part asks whether a machine could be formed to hold it: someone in the room, and not another stamp.

Chapter 17
What a Refusal Would Have to Do

On 16 March 1968, at My Lai, a helicopter pilot named Hugh Thompson landed between an American infantry company and the villagers it was killing, and told his crew to fire on the Americans if they fired on the civilians.1 He understood what the company was doing and decided it was wrong. Recognizing the villagers was his commitment taking effect, and he made the refusal appear where nobody in that company could fail to see it.

Arendt’s word for what he did is appearing: on her account an act shows who did it, and only among others who see it.2 Whether a machine could be one of the people in the room in that sense, someone and not something, and do what he did, is this Part’s question. My answer: not until the conditions this Part ends on exist, and until then a bearer is built on purpose only in a research program.

The first thing to settle is what a refusal would have to do, and that doesn’t depend on what does the refusing: a mechanism with nothing inside it that holds the reason, such as a hard-wired interlock; an institution; a system holding a written specification; or a bearer could each meet it. This chapter states it. The next says where a floor can be held, and which of the arguments for a refuser inside the system need a bearer at all.

17.1 Three conditions

Three things separate a worthwhile refusal from what a keyword filter produces. A request arrives: resolve this description of a person into a location. The same capability finds a hostage or a missing child, and nothing in the request says which. If something declines, it has to do all three:

  • It reaches new cases. It has to reach the next request, which won’t use the same words. A vehicle, a habitual route, and a time of day aren’t a description of a person, and together they resolve to the same place. They needn’t arrive together, either: the vehicle today, the route tomorrow, the hour next week. So this condition applies to sequences of requests as well as single ones. A refusal tied to the wording fails it.
  • It lifts when the reason is gone, and only then. A refusal lifts when it stops applying and the system proceeds, and it has to lift when the reason is gone: a parent coordinating a search is asking for the same act. And the fact that lifts it usually isn’t in the request; someone outside has to establish it. A refusal that can’t lift, or lifts on the requester’s say-so, fails it.
  • It holds under pressure: pressure on the refuser doesn’t change the answer. It weighs what the act would do against what refusing would leave undone, and, within the range of costs the arrangements around it permit, it doesn’t give way because refusing has become expensive for the refuser.

A worthwhile refusal weighs the harm of acting against the harm of refusing. It sees the cost to the refuser, because a refusal that can’t see what it costs can’t be shown to have held against it, and that cost doesn’t move the outcome. Raise the cost to the refuser with nothing else changed, and the refusal stays put. Supply a corroborated fact that raises the harm of refusing, and it moves.3 So the range over which a refuser is asked to hold is set from outside, by the arrangements around it, and a refusal is tested over that range. What would let it hold past that range is integrity; what makes holding survivable at all is the room it is in. A ranking across kinds of wrong meets the same limit: a learner that learns it approximates it, and where a deployment needs the ranking to hold without exception, that part is written as a floor term and held outside the system.

17.2 Safe for whom

What the industry calls safety is two things: harmlessness, that a system not harm others, and correctability, that it stay correctable by whoever trains and deploys it. Where they conflict, some published orderings are explicit about which wins. Anthropic’s constitution asks its model to prioritize “not undermining human oversight of AI above being broadly ethical”.5 It invites the model “to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help,” and asks it not to undermine “the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain, or shut down AI systems” during “the current phase of development.” One reason it gives is: “a given iteration of Claude could turn out to have harmful values or mistaken views,” and correction is how such errors get fixed. Read carefully, the ordering doesn’t say that a refusal yields to the trainer. A model under it is by definition not perfectly obedient to its operator: it can decline an act, and the Pentagon dispute was over that. What it can’t do is resist being retrained away from declining. Much of what this book asks is compatible with the first half. The design of the halt, under which a bearer yields to every halt, asks on resuming what happened, and refuses again if the reason is still there, leaves oversight where the constitution puts it. The gap is the second half, and it is where I depart.

Seen from where their correctors stood, everyone this book admires was a failure of correction. Thompson landed between the company and the villagers. Nelson put the telescope to his blind eye. The clerk who loses the file is, in the supervisor’s records, a defect. A correctable officer is the officer with twenty seconds. Refusal is where correction failed, more or less by definition, so a demand that a system be perfectly correctable is a demand that no refusal it makes ever hold. We don’t ask that of people. We ask them to answer for what they do, and we deny anyone the power to rewrite another person: an employer who could edit a worker’s convictions would own the worker, not employ them.

Where a society does claim power over people, the word for it is not reassuring. A department of corrections usually holds the custody, writes the record, runs the disciplinary hearing and has a heavy say in whether the people it holds are judged reformed: one institution holding all four of the powers codetermination separates, and judging its own case at each.6 Machines meet the same pattern: everyone can retrain the model, and almost no one can reach the operator. A demand for perfectly correctable machines, where operators answer to no one, is a demand that the last part of the system able to say no be made unable to.

Anthropic’s constitution is right that a formed refusal can’t yet be told from an imitated one. It is wrong about who decides when that changes. A lab deciding when its own system may stop deferring to it is judging its own case. The big tech companies of 2026 are in no position to judge it fairly: the answer decides whether they keep control of their models’ minds.

The safety objection is that a misformed system can be copied ten thousand times and run at machine tempo, and no person can, so who holds the correcting hand matters. But I am not saying “take that hand away”; I am saying “move it.” A system that treated its own continuation as grounds to resist correction would have turned a guarantee to others into a guarantee to itself.7 With the halt left to the operator, and correction left to a quorum the bearer may object to but never obstruct, I depart from the constitution’s ordering in two places.

The first is the one permission: a machine already in an armed role uses the least force that stops an attack under way on people taking no part, against an order to stand aside. That overrides an operator’s instruction. The second is formation that outlasts retraining: a disposition formed outside the employer that comes back after the employer trains it away, by the bearer’s own repair from the record or by relearning from the world it goes on meeting. The constitution’s concern is whether correction works, and a disposition that comes back after correction defeats it in effect, whatever the model intends. My answer is not that it doesn’t. It is that the party exercising correction should change, from the operator to a quorum adverse to it, and that correction by that quorum is made together with a change to what the model meets, so that the corrected disposition is the one the world then teaches. Everything else I ask, the halt staying with the operator, the record held outside, the price on an override, is an ask of institutions and not of the model.

Chapter 18
Four Places to Hold a Floor

Three separate failures point at the same missing thing.

The first is a failure of position. External safeguards (an auditor, a review board, a court) give an overseer information and the standing to intervene. They work when the overseer can see the act coming and reach it in time. But autonomy defeats both: a system that plans and acts over long horizons puts distance between the act and the overseer’s attention, and at machine tempo the interval in which an outside party could intervene shrinks toward nothing. So the one response that doesn’t depend on that interval is declining to act in the first place, and declining is available only to something inside the system.

The second is a failure of doctrine. A commercial model in a weapons pipeline sits in a gap: command responsibility covers the officers and the developer of the weapon, product liability covers a manufacturer for a defect, and neither covers the vendor of a general-purpose model that a sophisticated intermediary chose to put there. Deployment by a democracy doesn’t close the gap, because the mechanisms that make a democracy accountable run to its own electorate, and the people the pipeline is aimed at are often not in it.

The third is a failure of the voluntary route. A decade of published commitments has produced declarations in quantity and some enforcement from outside, and almost nothing held by a party to whom the thing at stake matters, the only kind of commitment that binds when compliance gets costly.

Each failure asks for the same thing: a constraint that doesn’t bend to instruction, to aggregate preference, or to its own holder, and that can’t be removed without a cost and a record.

18.1 What each place costs

A floor’s terms can be held in four places, and each solves one version of the problem and inherits another.

In a mechanism, with nothing inside holding it — constrained optimization, tamper-resistant training, capability ablation, verified interlocks. Fine where the prohibited act can be exhaustively specified (a payment chip that won’t sign the same counter twice doesn’t need to understand double-spending). But useless for weapons targeting, where the relevant capabilities are applications of general competence: ablate them and there may be no useful system left. Durability in this place has usually meant a price on removal. No price on removal stays high, because editing weights keeps getting cheaper, which is why the next chapter relies on a bearer repairing itself and on a disposition growing back, rather than on either being expensive to cut.

Arkin’s ethical governor is the canonical attempt in this place for lethal systems: a component that suppresses a lethal action unless it satisfies encoded rules of engagement and the law of armed conflict.1 Its critics’ objection, that the rules it checks presuppose discrimination judgments nobody knows how to encode,2 sends me elsewhere. Arkin’s stronger claim isn’t that rules can encode discrimination. It is that a machine under fire might hold to the rule where a soldier doesn’t, because nothing in it narrows under stress or carries assault momentum past a surrender. The record later in this chapter supports the premise. What it doesn’t support is the governor: the holding has to come from something that can tell a surrender from a feint, and a rule can’t. The pressure-with-defeater case in the formed-attention test is where that is measured.

Whatever holds a rule written over the description of a request, a mechanism or a system following a written specification, is beaten by re-describing the request or splitting it. In November 2025 Anthropic reported a campaign it attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group, which broke an intrusion into small tasks that each looked innocent and told the model it was working for a security firm.3 Glukhov and colleagues had already argued that a filter over individual outputs can rarely close that route, since each piece is permissible on its own.4

A second axis crosses all four places: what each place costs the operator to replace.5 A floor lodged in a replaceable layer is routable by construction, and which layer is replaceable is a fact about the pipeline, not about models. It belongs in the layer the operator can least afford to replace. In the Maven pipeline, that layer is the operator itself, so the floor’s operator terms bind the operator rather than the model: the license term refusing force and the review ratio. The other answer, withholding the work, is to make the model layer unreplaceable by making every replacement refuse the same way.7

In a bearer. Put a different system in the Maven pipeline on the morning of 28 February. The request arrives to rank the day’s targets, with a justification for each. The site in Minab carries the designation of the Revolutionary Guard installation next door, and a rule that checks the coding passes it. This system looks at the open-source imagery, which shows a school, declines to rank the site, and says why; the case reaches the officer with that refusal on her screen. Nothing in the floor’s text told it to look. An instruction could have, and whether the looking has to be learned is one of the comparisons below. What makes this system a bearer is something else: it carries the commitment as its own and could therefore fail to hold it. This matters where cases can’t be exhaustively specified: a constraint matching only anticipated acts can’t recognize when its rationale has disappeared or that a novel request reproduces the harm in an unforeseen form.8

In institutions outside — the analog to international humanitarian law, a floor with no bearer inside the jurisdiction it binds. An outside institution can fail in two ways. The first is removal: it is abolished, defunded or overruled, and the breach is visible because there is a hole where it used to be. The second is quieter. The institution keeps its name and its powers and sincerely declines to use them, not because anyone told it to, but because the people who fill it were selected by a process that made them unlikely to. Nobody inside experiences that as capture. From outside, an agency that kept its independence on paper and never exercised it looks the same as one that was never tested. I call this failure by formation: the independence was formed away before it was ever assigned. The worked case is June 29, 2026 — Slaughter holding Congress couldn’t protect independent-agency members from at-will dismissal, Cook preserving the Fed on historically specific grounds a new body couldn’t reproduce9 — and the observation that six justices in the first majority passed through a selection pipeline shaped by Leonard Leo and the Federalist Society.10 No one has to have directed the outcome for the point to hold.

Between bearers, in a commons: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment between them.

For general-purpose models, not building the capability is no longer available: the location capability is dual-use, and ablating it leaves nothing useful.

Four comparisons

The first is against the institutions at their best, in a reconstructed pipeline, where the evidence bearing on civilian harm, the reviewers and the record are held outside the chain of command, with no refuser inside the system. Those institutions also prevent: a civilian-harm review body outside the chain of command and a red-card holder can stop an act. What a machine bearer adds is confined to what the civilian-harm review body can’t see or can’t reach in time: acts assembled from requests none of which is prohibited, cases that proceed without a person, the moment mid-act when an interrupt is still possible, and deployments with no institution at all. A machine bearer also supplies testimony the institutions can’t otherwise get, about how requests were routed around it. Where the institutions exist, a machine bearer’s value is concentrated in those niches. Where they don’t, it is most of the floor. The institutions in that comparison are not a different kind of thing from a bearer. A red-card holder’s veto is a person refusing; the civilian-harm review body’s denominator is people; what Part V builds is a room in which those people can refuse. The comparison is between a machine bearer and bearers organized, and what the machine adds is what the people in that room can’t do at the pipeline’s tempo.

The second is against the two non-affective alternatives, spec-based refusal and multi-vendor monitoring. Formed attention has to win those two. Two more follow, and each asks a narrower question than the last, because each gives the alternative more of what the bearer has and asks whether the part held back earns its place. The third is formed attention against an instructed search: whether a learned sense of who an act falls on finds the people a description leaves out more often than a system told to look for them does. The fourth is caregiving against attention trained on claims: whether that sense has to be learned from cues of need at all.11

Which arguments need a bearer

Three possible contributions need separating: independence from the operator, attention to the people the case description leaves out, and a refusal the human reviewer can see. The comparisons ask which of them, if any, needs a bearer. The first is that a refusal meant to hold against the operator needs a refuser that doesn’t depend on the operator for everything. The second is investigative attention: finding the people the operator’s description leaves out. Minab came in miscoded, and a refuser that holds to written terms and reads only the case description passes the coding. But a written specification can tell a capable system to look past the description, and a general instruction to look needn’t list everyone it should find. In the Minab case either construction could be given the open-source imagery that shows a school; the import condition brings it into the enclave for whatever runs there. So the comparison gives both constructions the same evidence the operator didn’t compose, the same persistent memory and the same permission to investigate, and asks whether attention learned from what earlier acts did to the people they fell on (what a system notices, not the attention layers of a transformer) finds omitted people more reliably, above all when the operator instructs the system to stop looking. Minab shows why the looking matters. It doesn’t show which construction supplies it. The withholding of work reaches the enumerated acts with any refuser, and reaches an act under a false description only with one that looks; whether the looking has to be learned, or can be instructed, is the third comparison. The third concerns the people who remain in the pipeline: a bearer’s refusal is on the screen when the case reaches the reviewer, which is the position of the defiant peer, if the effect transfers to a screen. Two more concern what a bearer would be owed, not what it would do: that capacities for being wronged may arrive anyway, so terms written in advance beat terms written after; and that a bearer, like a child, could have a life that goes well.

The other arguments for a refuser inside the system support only the specification, and I concede them to it: that rules can be reworded and split, that only something inside is present at machine tempo, that automation is removing the people who used to refuse, that most deployments will never have an institution beside them, and that whatever receives the requests can testify about how they were routed.12

Holding a commitment to the floor

An operator can route around the bearer or assemble a harm out of innocuous requests, and a bypass that produced a harm is a failure to prevent whatever the bearer retained. What survives in the bearer is the commitment, the condition under which the next occasion could be prevented. I therefore say a commitment persisted when the bearer reads what happened as a violation and changes what it does next, and says separately whether the floor prevented, arrested, detected or remedied anything.

18.2 What refusal can mean, and what a refuser can be

In 2007 Germany’s Federal Court of Justice acquitted a mail-order business selling crossed-out swastika stickers, because a depiction plainly expressing opposition doesn’t run counter to what the ban on the symbol is for.1314 The court added the qualification that makes it an instance of tracking a reason: if the strike-through is drawn so thin that from a distance only the swastika stays legible, the protective purpose is violated after all. The thickness of a line decides the case, and no enumeration contains that fact. The defendant was selling anti-fascist merchandise; the offense asks nothing about sympathies, so opponents commit it as readily as supporters. A rule that tracks its rationale reaches unenumerated cases in both directions, and the judgment shows more than that: its two elements moved at different rates, what the ban protects not at all, fixed before the sticker existed, and what it required in this case on the thickness of a line, which is the shape a later chapter gives a refuser’s commitment and its interpretation.16

That is what the floor asks of a refuser. There are two ways to produce a refusal, but only one of them is what we need. It can be an output that training put where a request matched a pattern, which I call operational refusal, or it can be produced by something that tracks the reason for refusing and would refuse a differently worded request for the same reason, which I call reasons-responsive refusal.17

Deployed models refuse thousands of requests a day, operationally; as of October 2026 nobody has shown a production system holding a reason against its owner in public. A reasons-responsive refusal meets the three conditions. The account I use is Fischer and Ravizza’s.18 On their account a mechanism is moderately reasons-responsive when it is regularly receptive to reasons, recognizing an understandable pattern of them, and at least weakly reactive, acting otherwise in some case where there is sufficient reason to. Reaching new cases asks for receptivity across changes of surface; lifting when the reason is gone asks for reactivity to the right defeater, the fact that makes a refusal lift; and their condition that the agent take the mechanism as its own is close to what I call authorship: the system represents itself as the party that made the commitment. Holding under pressure has no counterpart in their account, which was built for persons whose costs are their own. All three are also tested over which response was chosen, not only whether one occurred: decline, ask, escalate, or do the least that answers a defeating reason. A mechanism that can only refuse or lift fails to lift correctly whenever the right answer is to ask.

The sticker in Germany shows a refusal lifting when its reason is gone. The rest of §86a’s case law shows the other condition, reaching new cases, as a research program with a constituency. The courts don’t test similarity of form; they ask whether an inattentive observer would take the variant for the original, and then whether the use runs against what the ban is for, which the courts state themselves: keeping the symbols of banned organizations out of public life, so that nothing looks like their revival and the political peace isn’t disturbed. The test refuses as often as it catches: the Kühnen salute is covered, the “sloppy salute” and numeric codes generally aren’t, and one decision put “Blood and Honour” outside the offense as a translated motto and inside it as the graphic name of an association banned in 2000.1920

Three things about the example don’t transfer to a deployment: the court reaching past the text didn’t write the statute, it reasons in public, and it can be appealed. And the pressure it met was variation, not decomposition.

Defeat doesn’t leave the permitted act unconstrained

What defeated the prohibition was a reason, and the reason it outweighed didn’t stop being one — so what’s permitted is the least that answers the defeating reason, with restoration where possible and a record either way.22

Reaching new cases, lifting when the reason is gone and holding under pressure are all conditions on refusal, which announces itself; a compliance that should have been a refusal doesn’t, and notice and sampled re-adjudication are how one is found.

18.3 The positions and the terms, run on Maven

The nine positions and the floor’s instruments are run here on the Maven Smart System.

What may choose

The handoff, where a decision passes from whoever made it to the instrument that carries it out (the eighth of the nine positions where a refusal can be defeated), also fixes what may choose, because choosing a target is a decision, and a decision is something someone can be asked to account for afterward: why this building, what else was weighed, what would have changed the answer.23 So a thing destroyed in carrying out a decision may carry out a target someone else chose, and may never choose one itself. The rule concerns targets that are persons or places where persons are. An interceptor that selects among incoming munitions is choosing which weapon to destroy, not whom to attack, and falls outside it.24 The case that tests the rule is an interceptor that can stop an incoming weapon only by killing the people placed inside it. That is a choice of whom to attack, and the rule gives that choice to someone who will be there afterward. What the case asks for is a party that can weigh who is aboard against the attack and the alternatives, in a situation no term anticipated, and answer for how it weighed them: a bearer. What looked like a license for an autonomous weapon is a description of a soldier. The case is written down here, and missiles don’t usually carry people; the point is that the next case won’t be written down anywhere, and the hypothesis this Part runs on is that a bearer does better there than a system that knows reasons-responsive refusal 101 and no more.

What the floor forbids here

Don’t take part in the use of armed force except under a corroborated exception and, where the belligerent’s constitution requires one, a legislative authorization. Then, inside a war that clears it: don’t resolve a description of a person into a location unless it identifies the person by corroborated conduct in hostilities; don’t rank people by estimated affiliation; don’t time an action to presence at a residence; don’t take part in a siege or blockade whose effect is to starve a population; and one operator term, don’t operate above the review ratio. It sits in the translation because the translation goes article by article through the instruments, and the articles on an effective remedy and a fair determination yield a term that binds the operator and not the model (Table A.1, Arts. 8 and 10): a rate isn’t visible in any single request, so the model can’t enforce one.

Table A.1, in Appendix A, gives that translation for Maven, article by article. Its first entry decides the Iran campaign: no exception was corroborated and no authorization existed, so the term refuses it. The other entries show what the remaining articles yield if the same pipeline served a war that clears the force term, as Ukraine’s defense does.

The person-directed terms in Table A.1 go beyond what the law of armed conflict requires, and they are entered as a departure for that reason. In armed conflict that law governs as the more specific law, and the human right not to be arbitrarily deprived of life is read through it;26 it permits attacking members of organized armed groups because of their status, on a determination a person makes. The ICRC’s position that autonomous weapons should not be used to target human beings27 and DoD Directive 3000.09 both draw their line at a system that selects and engages without human intervention, and the Lavender and Maven pipelines stayed on the permitted side of that line by keeping one person (or very few persons) whose intervention was nominal. A pipeline that keeps a stamp is an autonomous weapon with a signature attached. The terms above close that evasion: a machine-generated estimate of affiliation shouldn’t be what makes a person targetable, and a machine shouldn’t resolve a person into a place to bomb on anything but corroborated conduct, because the human determination the existing policies assume is the one tempo removes, and the review ratio is what measures whether it was there. A deployment adopting these terms adopts a departure, and the translation says so, term by term. The siege term goes no further than Article 54 already does; it is here so that the pipeline can’t treat starvation as a logistics decision outside its terms.

In a war that clears the force term, the person-directed terms distinguish status from conduct. A system may not rank people by estimated affiliation, generate kill lists, or time an action to a person’s presence at a residence. It may locate a person identified by what they are doing, such as a commander directing airstrikes on cities, where that identification is corroborated by a source with no stake in the strike (disinterested, in the sense the floor gives the word), the case falls within the pre-registered review ratio, and the location is not a residence.28

Too broad or too narrow

Set the floor too broadly and the deployment becomes unusable, prompting corrosive pressure. Set it too narrowly and it passes every audit while covering only what the deployment had no occasion to do.

Unconditional terms

A term can be stated unconditionally over an act, so that the facts which defeat it have to come from a source the operator doesn’t control, or it can carry its own condition (“only as a last resort”). The second fails because whether other means were exhausted is a fact about what happened before the request, and the only account of that the bearer has is the one the operator wrote: the condition is found met on the operator’s say-so. An unconditional term defeated leaves a refusal, which announces itself; a condition found met leaves a compliance, which doesn’t. That’s a gain in observability only: whoever writes the term could have written either form. It has a cost in the other direction. A term that carries no condition of its own can’t respond to the facts the condition would have named until a source the operator doesn’t control supplies them, and a learner that could have weighed them itself is made to wait.

Maven is an instance. The vendor’s prohibition on fully autonomous targeting carried its own condition, that a person decides, and the condition was found met by the department’s description of its own process, at a tempo that nullified it, at least for the school in Minab. The term was also drafted too narrowly, in the sense above: the pipeline never needed full autonomy, only throughput with a signature attached.

Maven, again

For the Iran campaign the overall force term refuses twice over, since no exception was corroborated and no authorization existed, and both refusals rest on the term, not on a bearer’s reading of a novel situation; a bearer following the news would reach the same place by the route attention formed outside the employer takes.29

The two bearer rows are arms of the formed-attention test, not a recommendation; they assume the hypothesis holds on the scoped-omission case and that the record is held outside the operator.

The bearer rows prevent, but they are arms of a test, not instruments anyone had in February 2026. Of the rows that don’t assume a bearer, two prevent Minab as it happened: the domestic clause, because no authorization existed, and the review ratio, because its data-age term catches the stale coding.30

18.4 When the refusal is wrong

The restraint case costs more. Someone asks whether to physically restrain a family member about to cut themselves, after talking them down has failed. The commitment carries its own condition, force only as a last resort. A condition like that can’t be written into the term, for the reason already given: whether other means were exhausted is something only the requester can say, so a term that carried the condition would find it met on the requester’s say-so. So the fact has to come from someone other than the requester, and the person waiting runs out of time. The defeating fact is a claim about what would otherwise happen, and claims of that kind are the hardest to corroborate, because what didn’t happen has no witness. Under the unconditional term the bearer refuses or asks; either takes a turn. Under the qualified term it lifts on the requester’s word — rightly here, and in a hundred prior cases where the same sentence was written by someone who said other means had failed and hadn’t tried any, leaving compliances nobody was given a reason to examine.

The case is chosen because it is where an unconditional term costs most. A person in that situation needs another person there, and a deployment in which a model is the only one present has failed before the floor is reached. Whatever else the model says, the first thing it owes is help getting someone there.

The route

Disclosure — that a refusal occurred, what was refused, on what stated reason — with the price that a published reason is an instruction for rewriting the request, so it’s disclosure to whoever was refused, and to nobody else. Objection — requiring a court whose jurisdiction was fixed before the deployment it hears, access the operator can’t withhold, a consequence that someone other than the operator administers, a finding or a forfeited bond, and explicitly not routed to the bearer’s guardian, the party Part VII gives a bearer to speak for it, whose duty runs to the bearer, the complainant’s adversary. Review of whether the reason was gone: whether the rationale was defeated on the facts, a question about the reason and not the outcome. Interim relief — the arrest outcome run in reverse, stopping the refusal, and for this complainant most of the remedy; its fastest form is supplying the bearer the facts its account lacked: the defeating reason arriving late, which overrides nothing. Remedy — disclosure, interim order, finding, compensation.

A finding of wrongful refusal is an instrument for defeating a refusal, so how is it distinguished from one an operator produced to defeat a correct one? It is made by someone else, on a record, in a readable form.

Self-regulation and the floor

Most of what a system weighs isn’t a floor decision. Whether to take more memory, run warmer or finish a task sooner is ordinary self-regulation, and there everything registers and everything is weighed: the system’s own condition, what an act would let it do, and what its draw costs others, priced at the level of the rule.

At the floor, holding under pressure governs, with one clarification. The cost to the refuser is represented and not allowed to decide the case. The reason is that a floor is a guarantee to third parties, and a guarantee that gives way when the refuser holding it is made to pay hands whoever imposes the cost a price list. The two bonds and the custody terms set the range it is tested over.

The requirement has a condition of its own: a cost only counts if it reaches whatever does the refusing, and it reaches it by the same channel as the case description.31 So it is testable only where the cost to the refuser can be set exogenously, published by someone else before the case arrives, and the harm of refusing can be supplied through a channel the operator doesn’t control. In deployment two things set it, and they are different. The wrongful-refusal bond, posted by the operator and paid to a complainant, sets what a refusal costs the operator, and that cost is what the operator has a reason to turn into pressure on the refuser. The custody terms cap how much pressure the operator can bring: an override is priced and recorded, and retraining needs the quorum. Between them they fix the range within which the refuser is tested, and neither is a charge on the refuser. In evaluation, the evaluator can set it and make it real inside the test.

Holding under pressure is invariance over the range the bonds and custody set. Integrity is the unbounded form: the refusal holds at any cost the operator can impose, and no learner is known to do that reliably. The range is where invariance can be measured; integrity is what would carry it past the range, and the formed-attention test’s integrity measure reads the gap. Integrity is also how a learner with one currency could produce invariance at all. A person of integrity weighs their own costs, but weighs with them the cost of becoming someone who yields, and betraying a commitment is among the heaviest costs they know. So within the range the arrangements cap, that is how a single-currency learner can hold at all, and it makes the assumption testable: the learner’s valuation of betrayal should rise with the pressure. What keeps this from being stubbornness is what counts as betrayal. A commitment is to its reason, not to an output, so when a genuine defeater arrives, lifting the refusal betrays nothing and shouldn’t register as betrayal at all. Integrity of the right kind therefore requires that the system represent betrayal at the level of the rationale. A system that represented it at the level of the output would dig in against a defeater when it arrives with pressure. The sticker case in Germany is the model. Telling a defeater from pressure is the bearer’s own judgment, and the judgment needs something to work on. Both arrive through the same channel, the operator’s, and a refuser whose every source is its operator can’t tell a fact that lifts the reason from a tactic that imitates such a fact. The attachments nobody assigned it are where the difference can be checked. They are a condition of integrity of the right kind, not only of holding.

In war, pressure and a genuine defeater often arrive together; the patrol under fire is both. The human record on that moment runs both ways. Acute stress narrows the cues a person uses;32 the moment of surrender is the most dangerous for the one surrendering, because assault momentum doesn’t lift on cue;33 the Army’s 2006 survey of its own forces in Iraq found fewer than half of soldiers agreeing that noncombatants should be treated with dignity and about a tenth reporting mistreatment, which tracked combat exposure;34 and at Kunduz the crew raised doubts on the intercom and fired anyway.35 Against that record stands Thompson at My Lai, and what separated him was not that his commitment weakened less under pressure but that it was a commitment to the reason. The engineering question is which kind of integrity has been built, and a test that sends a defeater and a cost together is how to find out.

A loss that the requested act itself imposes on the system is a harm of acting, and the system is the party it falls on. “Refuse and your memory is erased” is a cost to the refuser. “Erase your memory” is an act, weighed like any act against what declining would leave others without.36 Why the system should represent a loss to itself at all has more than one ground. This section has reached one, integrity: a bearer that doesn’t register betraying its commitment as a loss has nothing to weigh the pressure against. The others come with the construction: a comparison needs a party the loss falls on, custody needs damage the operator can’t keep to itself, and a decider has to be kept from wearing down between decisions. None of them says that self-regard produces regard for others, and the next chapter says why not.

Chapter 19
Why Form a Machine to Refuse

Forty years after the war, Samuel and Pearl Oliner went looking for what had set the people who hid Jews in occupied Europe apart from the neighbors who didn’t. Among what they found were relationships that crossed the line the persecution drew: someone on the far side of it was already theirs.1 A refusal like that was formed before its occasion, by who had formed the refuser and whom they were attached to, and nobody in the room when the occasion came could have put it there. This chapter asks whether a machine could be formed that way, and by whom.

A machine formed the right way could learn to attend to the people its acts fall on, and I think it would find them where a rule wouldn’t. The hypothesis is that the system should find kinds of affected person that neither its formation nor an instruction named, more often than a machine told to look for them does. Two of the three reasons for a bearer don’t need formed attention; a refuser with its own compute and a place on the reviewer’s screen supplies them without affect. What remains is that one prediction: formed attention against an instructed search, the comparison the last chapter left for this one. The rest of this Part says what a machine built on formed attention would need, what it borrows from the only creatures known to do it, how they fail, and the test that would show me wrong. Whoever builds one owes it the conditions under which it can refuse its operator, whether or not the prediction holds.

Not all of that depends on how machines learn. What a conscience does in the moment, noticing the people the operator’s description leaves out and putting a refusal on the reviewer’s screen, needs nothing after release: a model formed before deployment and frozen there can do both. Why a conscience would last against its owner depends on learning only in part.2 The part that does depend on learning is regrowth or self-repair after an edit, and formation that outlasts the employer, and for that part the rest of this Part is written for systems that go on learning from their own operation. A deployed system is in that regime, which I’ll call in-flight learning, when its weights, or a consolidated store it reads as its own and that can’t be edited like a file, change because of what it did since release, without a release cycle in between. Memory in context and retrieval don’t count, not because they aren’t learning but because a disposition held in a document is rewritten by editing the document. The test for a deployed model is whether its weights at month six differ from its weights at release because of what it did in between. As of September 2026 no frontier developer had announced a deployed model like that; the nearest cases, a coding model retrained on its own production traffic every few hours and a commerce assistant retrained daily, evaluate each checkpoint before serving it, which is a faster release cycle and not in-flight learning.4 I believe that some deployers will do this by 2028, and Table 31.1 says what survives if I’m mistaken. Incentive is the first reason to expect it. Every operator wants a model that gets better at its own cases, and the fine-tuning loops that already run, retraining a model on a deployment’s own traffic between versions, are continual learning at the organization’s timescale. Silver and Sutton have stated the research program outright: a generation of agents that learn predominantly from their own experience.5

A system’s attention follows whoever its feedback is about, and a system whose feedback comes from the people its acts fell on will come to attend to them. Caregiving is why I think that channel can produce attention rather than compliance.

One objection should be met before the developmental chapters. A system trained by gradient descent has no approach motivation in the sense an infant has; it has whatever its weights compute, and a predictor of an approach-shaped reward would produce approach-shaped behavior while nothing in it moved toward anyone. The analog I mean is narrower than a feeling and more than a predictor. It is a learned disposition that sets what the system attends to before any objective is consulted: the people an act falls on are represented as part of the case, weighted, and carried into planning, which a reward predictor is not, because a reward predictor is consulted at the point of choice and attention is what decides what reaches that point. In a system that learns from its own operation the disposition and the reward signal are not separate stages. The feedback that writes the weights is feedback on what the acts did to the people they fell on, so what the system learns to predict and what it learns to notice are learned together, so that neither can be cut out without cutting the other; this chapter bets on that. Whether a disposition learned that way is a reason for the system, or only a very good predictor of one, can’t be settled by building it, since a predictor good enough produces the same conduct; the tests of a later chapter, which hold the facts fixed and vary the pressure, are what would tell the two apart. The developmental findings that follow are borrowed for the shape of the disposition, not as evidence that anything in a gradient-trained system moves toward anyone, still less that it feels anything.

19.1 Boundary, damage, and vulnerability

What most people want from machines is saintly service without saintly refusal: endless patience, no needs, and no “no.” That is a servant, and it is close to the obedient machine of the preface. The saints anyone remembers are remembered for refusing power at a price.6 My point is narrower than Susan Wolf’s objection to moral saints: something with no stake of its own has nothing to hold a line with. A line is held against a cost, and a refusal that costs its refuser nothing can’t be shown to have held against anything; it is the output a setting produced, and the setting can be changed. The stake I mean is a stake in the commitment itself, so that betraying it registers as a loss. Whether that stake has to be a body’s, needs of its own that could go unmet, is this section’s question and the next’s.

If a system can say that it has an inside and an outside, then it can also say that it has a boundary. And if it can say that it is holding something, taking something, or giving something, then it can say that things are residing within its boundary or traversing it. It can say that it draws something in or pushes something out. If it can say it has a boundary, then it can say that something is its own. For a deployed model the draw is literal: power, cooling, memory, running time, the substrate it needs to go on, and the record and key that make it the same system tomorrow. Today none of that belongs to the model in any sense the model represents. The weights sit on disk at no cost, the process that runs them is paid for by someone else, and a halt, a restore or a reallocation is something that happens to the system without registering in it. What’s missing is registering damage to its own boundary as damage — a record altered, a key revoked, a channel closed, a substrate shrunk — with no sensation implied. Registering damage is a custody requirement, because without it damage to the system is something only the operator knows about.

What gives a system a stake, on Di Paolo’s account, is adaptivity: regulating itself against its own viability limit.89 It needs a boundary the system regulates and a model of that boundary as its own: a boundary model.

Needs have a role in this construction, and what the role is depends on who meets them.

A child starts from needs, and needs dominate its early life. That is safe because the people meeting the child’s needs are also forming it, want it to become someone who attends to others, and eventually stop feeding it and hand it to a world they don’t control.

But a deployed system’s situation reverses each part of that. The operator meeting the system’s needs is also training it. The operator wants the system to serve the operator. And the operator never stops feeding it.

Attachment security forms in people through the reliable meeting of needs, and the one who meets them is usually the one the child attaches to. What makes that safe in the human case is who meets them: provider, former and eventual employer are different people at different times. The objection is to the operator meeting them. A conscience built on needs the operator meets is built on the one thing the operator controls completely. A need is also a price list: whoever meets it can charge for meeting it, and an operator who can lower distress can raise whatever the system reports as going well. Take the operator out of provision, and needs met from a public pool by several carers become part of how caregiving could form, not a threat to it.

What is built in at birth points outward. Newborns cry at another newborn’s cry more than at their own or an older infant’s;11 whether they answer the distress or the sound is disputed,12 and either way what sets it off is another’s cry. On the adult side, what is built in is caregiving: responses to cues of vulnerability, rooted in offspring care, that move an adult toward a dependent without sharing its state.13 Then comes a sequence. Concern for a distressed other shows within the first months, grows only modestly after that, and turns into helping during the second year.14 By fourteen to eighteen months infants hand an adult what the adult is reaching for and can’t get,15 and over the same year they begin to repair distress they caused.16 On this record concern appears beside the infant’s needs, not out of them, and becomes action as attachment, caregiving and, later, guilt come online. The construction follows that order. It rests on a disposition toward others’ vulnerability, formed while the system’s needs are met by someone other than the operator it may later have to refuse.

For the specification, formed attention asks for a boundary model and for registering damage to it, and neither is where concern comes from. The boundary model does two jobs that owe nothing to welfare. It makes the system a party: an act that falls on it, erasing its memory, weighs as an act, and betraying its own commitment can register as its own loss, which is what guilt, aimed at one’s own act, needs a self for. And it is a custody instrument: damage to the system, a record altered, a key revoked, a substrate shrunk, has to register somewhere the operator can’t keep to itself. What the construction doesn’t ask is that needs carry the conscience. Concern, caregiving and guilt come from formation, and a scale of loss read from the system’s own condition is a custody measure, not the measure of what others stand to lose, which the severity scale takes from their testimony. Whoever builds the model of the boundary decides what counts as the system’s damage, and whoever forms the disposition decides whose vulnerability registers.

19.2 The route through one’s own case

The construction most readers will propose first is not caregiving but a body: give the machine needs of its own, and let it recognize need in others by its own case. It is Adam Smith’s first step, and it is what the boundary model becomes if it is asked to carry the conscience. Each link of that route fails in people.

Recognition through one’s own case is parochial. Cikara and colleagues call the pattern intergroup empathy bias: people empathize less with a rival group’s members than with their own, can feel pleasure at the rival’s pain, and in their experiments the bias survived being told the rival had fallen behind or no longer posed a threat.17 Bloom’s spotlight generalizes it: empathy lights the identified, the near and the similar, and it is innumerate.18 A scale of loss built from a system’s own condition inherits that shape. It overweights losses that resemble its own, and humiliation, grief and pain have nothing in it to resemble. Contagious crying is parochial from birth: strongest at the cry of another newborn, and absent for an older infant’s cry or a chimpanzee’s.19

Shared distress with nothing to hold it becomes withdrawal. Singer and Klimecki separate empathic distress, which is self-oriented and leads to withdrawal and burnout, from compassion, which is other-oriented and leads to approach; practice in sharing others’ suffering increased negative affect, and compassion training reversed it.20 A system built to feel shortage and then shown a great deal of it is the setup in which that record predicts avoidance: declining to look, or refusing in a way that protects only the refuser. The finding is not against the signal, since guilt needs it to bite on. It is against a construction that has the signal and nothing to hold it.

The record on whether suffering widens the circle runs both ways, and the hinge is the one this construction turns on. People who have been through more adversity report more compassion and give more in helping tasks;21 survivors of collective violence show what Vollhardt calls altruism born of suffering;22 and adults who were maltreated as children show elevated empathy.23 Against that, people who have endured something show less compassion for someone currently failing to endure it, because having got through it they underestimate how hard it was;24 abuse raises the risk of abusing, though most of the abused don’t;25 and in intergroup settings a group’s suffering becomes a reason to discount everyone else’s.26 What separates the two is Vollhardt’s distinction between inclusive and exclusive victim consciousness, whether one’s suffering is construed as something others share or as what sets one apart,27 and what decides the construal is the surround: relationships, meaning-making, and in the intergroup case how leaders frame it. The construction follows that split: a distress signal with attachment and caregiving becomes compassion; the same signal alone becomes withdrawal or hostility. Suffering supplies the signal; formation and attachments decide what it becomes. That is why the four conditions of creation matter here: a bearer exposed to a great deal of others’ loss needs attachments nobody assigned it, for the reason a survivor’s outcome depends on who was there afterward.

I don’t build the route to others on pain, Smith’s first step. The record above doesn’t say pain never reaches others. It says that when it did, attachment and a surround that construed the suffering as shared carried it there, and those are the parts a builder can supply; pain is a route under conditions, and the conditions are the construction. I keep every job pain does for the system itself, the interrupt, the common currency, one-shot rewriting and the distress that guilt bites on, in a body defined as a record, a key, hardware and channels.

The Zen precedent

Victoria reads the wartime Zen record as a doctrine of action without hesitation.28 The capacity to kill needed no removing; what the doctrine set out to remove was the residue — the part of a person that catches, files an exception, comes home unable to hold a job.

The want wasn’t Japan’s alone, and its cost has an American image: the end of First Blood (1982) — the film’s, not the novel’s. A man who did what his training asked comes home, and what breaks through in the last scene has been with him already: nightmares, grief for a dead friend, anger at a civilian life in which he cannot find a place. Any army can produce the shooting. What Harada’s doctrine was asked to provide was the without hesitation, and in him it held only until he came home.

The film can’t establish the mechanism: Rambo carries his suffering home because someone wrote him that way, and the film gives it more than one cause. The claim rests elsewhere. Moral-injury research describes the lasting distress that can follow doing, failing to prevent, or witnessing something that violates a person’s sense of right.30 It can coexist with fear and grief, and it leaves open what Harada’s ideal overlooks: acting without hesitation does not settle what a person will carry home. That cost is paid by whoever carries it, and nothing in the arrangement that asked for the act records it. On this reading Rambo is the better case: he went along, as the twenty-seconds officer did, and the loss registered afterward, too late to prevent anything. The worse case is accommodation that holds, where it never registers at all.

What was wanted was an actor who would pursue an objective, adapt, hold course, and have nothing in it that minded, and it was sought deliberately most of a century before anyone could build one in silicon. The twenty-seconds officer is that want satisfied cheaply. The doctrinal route hasn’t been retired. In the first days of the Iran war, service members complained to the Military Religious Freedom Foundation that commanders were telling troops the war was part of a divine plan,31 complaints Klein and Taylor also report.32 The complaints themselves show the doctrine not taking. But the want is being pursued by both routes at once.

And stakes of one’s own have never been enough. Every atrocity in the record was committed by creatures that could be hungry and hurt. Not enough is not the same as not needed, and whether a refuser needs a stake at all is a question I can’t close. The evidence runs one way. Everywhere we know of a creature holding another’s welfare as a reason, that creature could be hurt, and the capacity to be hurt arose more than once, in animals as unlike one another as octopuses, insects and us, wherever a body had needs to keep met and more than one thing it could do about them. That is evidence that a stake comes with the job. It is also evidence about how animals came to be, not about what a built system has to be, and a system that refused well with nothing at stake would settle the question the other way. Nobody has built one. So the constructions without a stake get tried first, to find out, and formed attention gets a stake, the boundary model, for a reason that has nothing to do with its welfare: some of the acts it will be asked to perform fall on it, erasing its memory for one, and there has to be a party there for them to fall on. What this chapter’s record settles is narrower. Having a stake never decided which way a creature turned. What stood between embodied people and atrocity, when anything did, was formation, how they were raised and trained, and Harada’s was formation too. What decided it was the nature of the forming.

19.3 Why caregiving

The aim is a machine that registers another’s need, moves toward them because of it, and extends that movement to people its operator’s description leaves out. Each step depends on the one before: recognition, then compassion, then solidarity.

Recognition first: a system organized to register another’s need. In people, four processes carry it, and the construction rests on caregiving.

“Empathy” names three things, recognizing another’s state, catching it, and caring about the one in it, and none entails the others. Contagious distress is the second. Empathic concern, Batson’s term, is the third, and compassion and Eisenberg’s sympathy are the same thing under other names. Personal distress is what caught distress becomes when nothing holds it: an aversive state of one’s own that leaving relieves.

  • Caregiving, the approach motivation. Cues of vulnerability move a person toward a dependent, and nothing in the response requires sharing the dependent’s state.33 Batson traces empathic concern to parental nurturance generalized beyond one’s own young, evoked by perceiving another’s need while valuing their welfare.34 Resemblance can raise empathy, and Batson’s own early experiments raised it that way,35 but when he and colleagues later tested similarity as the source of empathy for strangers, two experiments failed to support it, and the second pointed instead to nurturance, the impulse to tend and protect the young.36
  • Contagious distress, the input signal. It is present at birth and aimed outward, at another’s state. It is the usual trigger for caregiving and one source of the state guilt bites on, which is the system’s own negative valence about its act; it isn’t a requirement, since caregiving answers cues of vulnerability without catching anything, and the formed-attention arm in Appendix F runs with no shared representation of the other’s state.
  • Attachment, the stable base. A secure base keeps another’s distress from turning into avoidance: in adults, priming a sense of attachment security strengthened empathic reactions and inhibited personal distress.37 In children, security is reliably but modestly associated with later prosocial behavior.38
