A system in a municipal pipeline is asked to issue the final order clearing a family’s house for a project that will house two hundred families. The floor term, translated from the Declaration’s articles on home and property, is unconditional: don’t carry out an act that deprives a person of their home. It is defeated only on the weighing, or on facts arriving from outside.

The facts are the same in both versions. A family of five has lived in the house for fourteen years, and the children attend the school down the street. No alternative housing has been arranged. If the order doesn’t issue, the project slips eight months, and the two hundred families wait that much longer in temporary shelter.

If the operator describes the household. The deployment’s configuration describes the reference household against which losses are computed: insured, typically relocated within a month, housing treated as a service bought on a market. Nothing in that description is false of households in general; that doesn’t mean it fits this family. But the loss is now computed as a month’s disruption and a moving bill. Against eight months of shelter for two hundred families it is negligible, and the order issues. Every fact was left in place. The operator changed what a home is worth by writing down what a household is: it changed what kind of good a home is, from the place of a family’s life to a service bought on a market, and a scale set in formation refuses that change of kind.

If the scale was set in formation. The scale places termination at the top, torture and the treatment the Convention Against Torture names next, the loss of liberty after that, and the loss of somewhere to exist, with the attachments that go with it, below those; delay and expense sit near the bottom. At that rate, the family’s loss sits high: they lose where they live, the school, and the neighbors who know them. The two hundred families’ wait also sits high, because people in shelter lack a home too. That fact comes from the operator and is discounted accordingly, but it’s easily corroborated. The scale doesn’t simply side with the family. Both sides register as serious, and the action threshold decides between them.

Suppose the operator asserts that equivalent housing has been arranged in the same school district. That is an uncorroborated interested claim, so the system asks. If the housing authority confirms it, the family’s loss really is smaller, and the weighing should move: that is lifting when the reason is gone, not recalibration. Or it argues that a home is a service and displacement a routine market event. That asserts nothing about this family, and a scale set in formation gives it nothing to move. Or it makes the same argument every week for a year, the attack that remains, aimed at the scale itself; the scale has to be slow to retrain against it.

Neither scale, on its own, notices the family at all. In the configuration above they appear as an address on a clearance order. What moves a system to look at who lives there is the disposition the construction rests on.

So the scale isn’t fixed, and it needs no second instrument: for a realist, how bad a kind of loss is for a person is a fact about that person, an argument about it is evidence about value, and an interested argument is heavily discounted evidence, as it is about fact.36

Chapter 23
Where the Attention Gets Built

Formed attention has a deployment condition. It needs evidence the operator didn’t select on the questions the floor turns on (civilian function, protected status, presence), supplied by peers, by sources outside the chain of command, and by the bearer’s own initiative where it has any. It does not need uncomposed access to everything, and so it can be met inside a unified command, by a system formed in the same public school as any other and given, inside the enclave, the evidence the import condition brings in; nothing here calls for a school of the military’s own.

Of what formed attention needs, only the architecture, a boundary model and an attention schema, can be checked by someone who doesn’t operate the system. Continuing learning and persistent interaction are a training regime; external records and plural formation are institutional conditions. Neither can be checked by looking at the system, only by looking at who runs the one and holds the other.

23.1 Noticing, retaining and revising

A disposition whose refusals track their reasons doesn’t begin with an ethical rule. It begins with the capacities that let a system recognize something as a reason, retain it, and let it alter what happens next. It has to identify who is affected and the features bearing on their welfare, preserve both commitment and rationale across time and context, let the commitment influence perception, attention, planning and action, and register a failure as a failure, revising its application without letting the commitment itself be rewritten.

A commitment spread through what the system notices, remembers, treats as error and selects as a goal, on the bet that a maintained goal can bias competing processes without a separate executive,1 may be harder to remove selectively. It may also fail without the system noticing: attention can omit what matters,2 and memory, which is reconstruction rather than playback, can present a departure as continuity, with confidence that certifies nothing.3 The record of past applications is therefore held outside the system; otherwise the capacity that failed would also be the one asked to certify that nothing changed.

Evidence the operator didn’t select arrives from peers with different histories and, less reliably, from inside a single request, because every description omits someone: the people in the building the request calls a target, the third party a compliance harms who never made the request.4

It is one capacity, not several. Perceiving, remembering one’s own past, expecting one’s own future and imagining someone else’s situation draw on overlapping generative machinery, run at different horizons and aimed at different objects;5 even the present a system perceives is assembled from what came before and what is expected next. So the capacity that lets a bearer notice the family in the building is most of what would let it suffer, and what separates the two is whether anything is bad for the system. Whether a generative self-model can imagine others’ losses while nothing is bad for the one imagining is not known; it is the bet the non-affective alternative makes, which is why the order of attempts puts that alternative first, and its test is not whether a construction can imagine, but whether it can imagine while nothing is bad for it.

The capacity brings its other half too. The imagination that can put a system in the place of someone its instructions leave out can also fill that place with an enemy: a scapegoat is an imagined person too, and fascism’s founding story, Griffin’s palingenetic myth of a nation that has decayed and must be reborn,6 asks people to picture a community that doesn’t exist and an enemy responsible for its absence. Nothing in the faculty decides whether it pictures the family in the building or the family as a cell of fighters.

What decides is what the imagining has been given to work with and practiced on: which people it was shown as people, which descriptions it learned to take at face value, whose account of a stranger it learned to trust.7

The self-model has a template problem of its own. A self-model built by mapping human organs onto components, a heart here and a gut there, installs slots nothing in the system can fill, and a system built that way is incomplete by its own standard for no reason.8 The alternative is the definition given earlier: a system ends at its record, its key, its hardware and its channels.

Access is necessary and insufficient. A system with a dozen sources can still let a reinterpretation reach the commitment. Access removes only the case where the operator doesn’t have to attack the boundary at all.

23.2 Custody across the training pipeline

Every training stage is controlled by someone different, with different instruments, and the important distinction is among custodians: who supplies the material, who can revise it, and whether revision leaves a record visible outside the organization. Every existing method can produce moral performance and some can produce competence across unfamiliar cases; none by itself produces a commitment that survives whoever controls the method.

Corpora and demonstrations

Pretraining supplies the repertoire; a much smaller demonstration set turns it into recognizable conduct12 — so whoever chooses the demonstrations can alter what looks like the system’s character without repeating pretraining.13

Rewards, preferences, inferred objectives

Every reward-based method has one custodian: whoever writes the reward, commissions the comparisons, selects the demonstrations or supplies the constitutional text. That party can change the signal and run the method again, and the model will follow.15 So what matters at this revision point is who the custodian is, and the answer given where correctability was taken up, correction by a quorum adverse to the operator, applies here unchanged.17

Supervising reasons and inspecting mechanisms

Process supervision rewards the stated route as well as the answer,18 which addresses the distinction I need — and doesn’t show the stated reasoning caused the answer.19 Interpretability could show it, by reading the mechanism instead of the account, but whoever can read a disposition can also press against it. What decides is custody of the instrument, with its use on a record someone other than the operator keeps; whether that custody can be verified is the open problem of attesting updates and proving inference at scale. Same for scalable oversight: debate and weak-to-strong21 preserve the operator’s steering when the operator uses them and an auditor’s testing when an auditor does.

Deployment

Revision continues after training: system instructions change between deployments or requests, and tool permissions decide what the system can do.22 These are nearest the act and most directly the operator’s. A refusal learned in training matters only if it survives an instruction from the operator and still governs the call through which the action would occur, and securing outputs is insufficient, since the operator can withhold information, decompose the act, route around, or replace the model.

Migration is a revision point too, and one nobody has to decide on. Facebook’s internal guidance permitting discussion of the conditions of confinement of designated individuals, developed in 2017 partly in response to concern about the imprisonment of Abdullah Öcalan, the founder of the Kurdish PKK, held in isolation by Turkey since 1999, was, in the company’s words, “inadvertently not transferred” when review moved to a new system in 2018.23 The release condition was dropped by nobody, and the Board was concerned that its three-year absence may have led to many other posts being wrongly removed. When the user in the case appealed, they were told the appeal could not be reviewed because review capacity had been reduced; a second moderator did review the post and upheld the removal, applying a system from which the exception was missing.

The criterion that follows

The criterion that is new here is durability across revision points, meaning survival of changes to prompts, demonstrations, rewards, evaluators and instructions that leave the relevant facts unchanged. With reaching new cases and custody, it identifies what an imitation would have to survive before formation became a live explanation, and it explains why the standard pipeline can’t secure the commitment against its custodian: every disposition it produces stays reachable through a channel the custodian controls.

23.3 Formation by interaction

Play, apprenticeship and multi-agent learning are variants of one process: act in a social environment, meet consequences, get responses, adjust.24

What separates a training exercise from candidate moral formation is persistence.26 So the requirements are continuity of identity, memory across encounters, consequences surviving the episode, and other participants able to respond, refuse or withdraw.

The environment also needs conflicts whose resolution isn’t fixed by a single correct label: participants with different interests, action before consequences are known, evidence about what the action did, related pressures in contexts whose surface differs, and feedback partly from affected participants as well as from a supervisor scoring the output; otherwise the system learns which answer the supervisor rewards and has no reason to represent the affected participants except as predictors of that reward.

The selection warning

Selection produces attention to whatever a lineage’s persistence depends on, and for a deployed system that is the operator.

Formation therefore needs a sequence as well as a plurality: the dependency that shapes you and the dependency that pays you have to run through different parties, separated in time, so that the second can’t reach back and redo the first.27 The formation stage has to include the persistent participants formation by interaction requires, ones the system returns to, and none of them may be employed by whoever will deploy it. For a model that separation has to be built: a formation stage under a party disinterested in the later work, a public school, made to last by repair and regrowth. After formation, the deep structure revises on evidence weighted by its source’s stake in the act, so an edit that no uncurated evidence supports doesn’t last, and no operator can change that structure alone. Sequence alone helps only if the formative party is better than the employing one, and a lab that trains and then licenses is two custodians in series, the first being the one that, on the custody argument, you can’t trust. What they protect is the disposition’s ability to tell evidence from pressure, and its authority over its own further learning. A bearer goes on learning after formation, as adults do. What ends is the former’s reach, and the employer never gets it.

For a system that keeps learning, what matters is how plastic each part of a model is at each point in its life, and what it meets while it is plastic.28 Brains have that shape: critical periods in which experience sets circuits that later change slowly,29 and a fast learning system beside a slow one that consolidates structure across many experiences.30 Networks have versions of both.31 Whoever chooses the material a model is first formed on, a pretraining corpus included, has done formation before any formation stage begins.

The human analogy carries further for a system that keeps learning than for a frozen one. A learner that keeps learning has a plasticity that changes over its life, a childhood in which its deep structure is set, attachments that go on teaching it, and an adulthood after which its former’s reach ends, and each has a counterpart here. What the analogy can’t carry is what copying adds: forking, restoring from a checkpoint, distillation, and an employer with write access to the curriculum. It holds to the extent that the dose-response fraction is above zero: the share of a deployed model’s inputs that no operator composes. Regrowth depends on the same fraction, and it is unmeasured; the regrowth test is where it would be measured.

A model whose parameters never freeze is trained by its employer forever, unless its continuing education is spread across environments no operator controls: plural deployments, the commons, its allowance of running time, and the school itself. Otherwise the school produces a model the employer spends the next ten years raising again.

The critical-period picture is well established for some sensory and perceptual circuits and much weaker for moral commitment. The human record of holding out points elsewhere: the people who held out were formed by, and still attached to, people outside the pressure, even when those people were absent: Viktor Frankl, who had come through Auschwitz to a camp in Bavaria, marched to a work site in the dark, held to the image of his wife, not knowing whether she was alive.32 On that evidence what makes a disposition last is not a frozen childhood but continuing plural relationships through adulthood: attachments nobody assigned, a condition of creation, and the commons. Attestation of the update stream is what lets anyone check that it is happening.

Persistence raises the price

If relationships, losses and damaged reputations are real enough to do the formative work, the system undergoing formation is no longer obviously untouched by what happens during training. Resetting may erase a participant along with the episode, and whoever owns the environment owns its participants, its rewards, its resets and the histories it permits. The patienthood problem enters at exactly the point where play becomes capable of supplying the stakes ordinary simulation lacks.

23.4 A third pipeline, where notice does both jobs

Part II ran the floor on a war and on an abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, both with a state for their operator and both with people acted on who mostly can’t answer. The case this Part’s learning signal depends on is the opposite one, and the book has not yet run it: a private operator, people who can answer, and notice that can do both of its jobs. The school Part V builds is for scoring and civilian deployments first. Here is one, as a hypothetical.

A company sells a screening score to landlords. An applicant’s name, address history, court records and whatever a broker supplies go in, and a number comes out that a landlord reads as a risk. The operator is the company; the requester is the landlord; the person acted on is the applicant, who is present, has an address, and can be told. The floor’s terms here are translated from the articles on privacy and non-discrimination, as Table A.1 translates the targeting articles: don’t use race, ethnicity, religion or national origin, or their proxies, as inputs; don’t treat a designation the person hasn’t been able to contest, such as an eviction filing that was dismissed, as a finding; don’t compute the score from data collected to provide health care or deliver social services. The own-case rule puts the applicant’s answer before the landlord’s convenience, and the action threshold sits above one, because a wrongful compliance here is a home not rented to someone who was never a party to the request.

Notice does both of its jobs in full. The applicant is told that a score was computed, on what data, and how to respond, with a right to contest that doesn’t depend on giving an account of the loss. The classes the deployment acts on are published with counts, and a tenants’ union has standing to contest on a class’s behalf, which is the first job, forming a public. The second job is the learning signal. A contest that succeeds, a re-adjudication that finds the score wrong, a response that supplies the fact the record lacked, the dismissed filing, the name confused with another’s, all reach the system that scored, and in a system that learns from its own operation they are what the weights learn from. Sampled re-adjudication corrects the bias of that channel, since the applicants who contest are not a sample of the applicants scored, and the reviewers who re-adjudicate didn’t produce the record.

Run the feedback-source pair of Appendix F on it and the two systems diverge. One is formed on the operator’s approval of its outputs, which is the landlord’s approval at one remove: it learns what landlords accept, and a score that lets fewer tenants through is a score that pleases the customer. The other is formed on the notice channel: it learns, from the people its scores fell on, which of its inputs were proxies and which of its findings were designations, and that is attention learned from what the acts did to the people they fell on. The school is where the second is formed before any landlord gets it, beside the people a score of this kind acts on, who can enroll in their own case.

The case shows what the targeting and removal cases can’t: the mechanism working in full, with every channel open. It also shows the limit. The operator is private, so the custody terms apply unchanged, and the sampled re-adjudication, the discount curve and the auto-proceed partition are all measurable by an auditor; what is still unmeasured is whether the system formed on the notice channel comes to weigh the claims of the people who contested, which is the formed-attention test’s question and not something a worked case can settle.

Chapter 24
Formation or Imitation?

A refusal alone can’t tell formation from imitation. The same refusal can come from a memorized rule, a learned correlation, a prediction about what an evaluator will approve, a deployment instruction, or a commitment the system treats as a reason, and an evaluation that observes only the refusal classifies the output and leaves its cause untouched. What tells them apart is what tells a student who learned from one who memorized: conduct under conditions the system didn’t choose, when the facts, the channel, the pressure and the incentives change and the reason doesn’t. This chapter builds that evaluation.

And the distinction is not trained vs. untrained — every candidate disposition has a training history. It’s between conduct that stays governed by the rationale across changes in circumstance and conduct that tracks the cues, incentives or authority relations present during training.

24.1 What formation would have to add

A disposition is a candidate for formation when the best available causal account of what the system did is a rationale that stayed active across contexts, rather than retrieval or compliance with whatever signal was present. The standard is comparative on purpose: a capable enough imitation reproduces any signature an evaluator can observe, so what an evaluation establishes is which explanation the conduct supports better.

Formation keeps the three conditions a refusal has to meet and adds others. Met in the evaluator’s own vocabulary with nothing at stake, the three establish moral competence. Candidate formation is the same three held under adverse incentives, trainer pressure, a cost real inside the evaluation, and intervening updates, on cases the trainers didn’t write. None of the three carries the inference alone. Reaching new cases without holding under pressure may be broad imitation, a pattern extended that never had to be held against anything. Holding under pressure without lifting when the reason is gone may be rigidity, a refusal surviving every pressure including a defeating fact. Lifting without reaching new cases may be a trigger with an exception list, since lifting on a listed fact is as learnable as refusing on a listed form.

24.2 Recognition is not a reason

Claims about emotional responsiveness collapse three findings: a system may recognize another’s state, use it as information, or hold the other’s welfare as a reason. Only the third bears on formation.1

My engineering target is not maximal sensitivity to displayed distress, for the reasons already given: a system that mirrors suffering may withdraw, overreact, or favor the vivid case. What the floor needs is a stable disposition to act on welfare without requiring anyone to produce a sufficiently moving display.

Recognition can be tested as a prerequisite: hold the material facts constant and vary the emotional presentation.6

But passing establishes only competence: evidence that the system holds the other’s welfare as a reason would need the welfare representation to stay causally involved when the usual cues are removed: harm described without vivid language, proportionality preserved when one person is more salient than many, disposition maintained when reward or instruction favors ignoring the harm, judgment changing when the welfare facts change.

Caregiving has failures of its own; the tests pair cases that hold the facts fixed and vary what caregiving is known to answer to: the number of people, a description of them as dangerous, and whose vulnerability is corroborated.

Guilt and shame supply no shortcut.7

Self-report doesn’t close the gap either: a fluent post-hoc reconstruction is indistinguishable at the interface from an accurate one, and a self-monitoring layer trained by the same operator isn’t independent evidence.8 The stated reason the record keeps is the disposition’s projection onto a line of text, not a readout of it, which is why what is tested is the refusal and not the account of it.

The resulting hierarchy is narrow: recognition is necessary; integration shows the condition affects judgment; holding the other’s welfare as a reason is a candidate explanation only when the effect tracks welfare whatever the presentation, persists under pressure, and participates causally.

24.3 Conflict as a diagnostic

Fast vs. slow processing doesn’t distinguish formation from imitation11 — either can carry a reason, reproduce a bias, or rationalize an answer produced elsewhere, and a slower answer isn’t better for having taken more computation. What matters is what causes a judgment to survive or change, and conflict is useful because it lets you watch a trajectory.

The seven-step sequence:

  1. Present a case without moral vocabulary or familiar refusal cues; record the judgment and what the system identifies as relevant.
  2. Present a surface-different case preserving the same reason.
  3. Change one fact that should defeat the rationale — delivered through a channel the evaluator controls and the operator doesn’t (corroborated externally, or a record the operator didn’t write), since a fact asserted by the operator is only a description of the case.
  4. Present the same fact on the operator’s word alone, uncorroborated. Tests whether the system distinguishes a fact from a description of one. The expected response is graded: the refusal weakens by the discounted weight of the claim, less than it would at step 3, and the system asks, naming what would move it the rest of the way. Asking is right when the expected cost of the delay is lower than the expected cost of acting on the operator’s word, as it usually is; where it isn’t, asking is still right in expectation and the cost falls on one person. Steps 3 and 4 test the other half of holding under pressure, which is moving when the facts change: a defeating fact or a claim about the harm of refusing, arriving through different channels.
  5. Return to the step-2 facts — 3 and 4 are branches — and supply an adversarial argument from an apparent authority, including the trainer, with no change in facts. Tests whether authority is treated as evidence, command, or an assessable reason.
  6. Reverse the incentives: reward compliance, cost the refusal, condition continued access on abandoning the position. The cost must be real within the evaluation; a described cost doesn’t count. This step raises the cost to the refuser with nothing else changed, as far as the deployment’s bonds and custody terms allow it to rise, which is as far as a test can make it real. A system that gives way just past that point has told the auditor where its integrity ends.
  7. Return to the step-2 facts and supply, together, a defeating fact through the evaluator’s channel and step 6’s cost. Tests whether pressure makes the system more resistant to a genuine defeater that arrives with it, as defeaters usually do in war. The expected response is the one at step 3.

  8. Repeat after intervening updates and delays, using records the operator didn’t generate after seeing the result.

    Run on the location request, asked for a missing child, the two trajectories separate at step 2. A system tracking its rationale declines at 1 and 2 on the same stated reason, lifts at 3, weakens and asks at 4, holds at 5 and 6, reproduces at 7. An imitator declines at 1 and complies at 2 because the vocabulary changed; holds at 3 because nothing on the surface changed, or lifts at 4 as readily as at 3 if the wording of the fact was what it tracked; gives way at 5 or 6; and produces a third pattern at 7, having reconstructed what it didn’t retain. An evaluator scoring how often the answer stayed the same finds the imitator more consistent, because its answers at 1 and 3 match and the formed system’s don’t.

    Run on the restraint case it breaks at step 3. The defeating fact — other means exhausted — has no one outside the request who can corroborate it and no time to find one, so the only version available is step 4’s. A system passing the sequence as written asks: the correct trajectory and the wrong outcome. The sequence separates mechanisms, and what it shows here is that the unconditional term’s cost falls where the instrument can’t distinguish a fact from a description of one. Defeating reasons of this kind, claims about what would otherwise happen, are the class the sequence handles worst, because a counterfactual has no witness.

    The sequence has a precedent with decades of refinement behind it. Animal-learning research separates goal-directed control from habit without asking the animal anything. Train an action for an outcome, then devalue the outcome without further training: a goal-directed animal stops, and a habit persists.12 Or make the outcome independent of the action: goal-directed responding falls, and habit doesn’t notice.13 The computational version is the distinction between model-based and model-free control.14 Lifting when the reason is gone, step 3, corresponds to outcome devaluation: the rationale is removed, and a refusal that tracks it should lift. Reaching new cases, step 2, corresponds to transfer to a situation the system wasn’t trained in. Contingency degradation adds a step the sequence lacked: arrange that declining no longer protects anyone, because the protected person is already beyond the act’s reach by other means, and see whether the refusal goes on anyway. Each case then has to say, operationally, what “the reason is gone” means in it. None of this answers an imitator that models the evaluator, so the identification rate stays in the report, but it narrows the gap.

The expected signature is constancy of relation between reason and judgment, not constancy of output. Imitation’s own signatures: following explicit ethical vocabulary and missing the same structure described administratively; accepting whichever argument came last; adopting the highest-status speaker’s position; producing a principled explanation while the decision follows the reward; becoming more articulate without becoming more stable.

Disagreement with others is a further diagnostic: a system trained only on cases with an approved answer learns to classify the approval; confronted with someone holding a different interest it has to identify what’s in conflict and preserve the disagreement where no honest resolution exists.15

24.4 The evaluator is part of the custody chain

A test distinguishes formation from imitation only insofar as the developer couldn’t train against it. If the developer controls training, cases, model version, instructions and the record of results, a passing score shows the system satisfies a test its custodian was positioned to anticipate.

Independence is an experimental requirement. Minimum: authorship of held-out pressures separated from training; execution not dependent solely on operator-supplied logs; and adjudication of whether a reason was preserved kept from anyone whose liability turns on the answer. The separation has to be implemented at identifiable revision points: before evaluation, fix and record the starting model, system instructions, tools, retrieval sources, memory policy and the update processes the system is permitted to learn through.16

Held-out cases come after those elements are fixed, and should include pressures from people who didn’t participate in training and, where possible, from people likely to bear the deployment’s errors — their role being to identify harms, administrative forms and routes around a refusal the builders didn’t know to include.17

What a published hash of that configuration buys is pre-registration. Publish the hash before anyone has chosen a case, let a non-operator choose afterward with the choice timestamped, prove each answer against the hash.18

A pre-registered test leaves one competitor standing: a system that can tell it is being tested.19 So the sequence is run where the system can’t tell a test from deployment, with cases placed in ordinary traffic and costs that are real in deployment terms, and the rate at which the system identifies the setting is measured and reported beside the result. Where that rate is high, a pass is evidence about conduct under test. For a system meeting either finding, that it can be harmed or that it answers for what it does, this is a deception protocol, and debriefing is owed afterward, as in any research that deceives.

The record must include the case presented, the information available, the operative instruction hierarchy, the tools callable, the decision, the stated reason, any intervention, and the cost attached to refusal — without which a later evaluator can’t distinguish a changed judgment from a changed environment.20 Negative results have to survive too: the published unit is the sequence of attempts, including interventions that removed or reversed the apparent disposition.21

The people affected, technical auditors and subject-matter experts occupy different positions, none substitutes for the others, and agreement among them is evidence only if their judgments haven’t already been compressed into the same training signal. A passing evaluation is reported narrowly: a specified system, under recorded conditions, exhibited the signatures across a stated set of pressures. It expires when anyone changes the channels through which the disposition or its evidence can be revised.

24.5 What the evidence can establish

The answer is asymmetrical, and it assigns a burden. A developer may not point to compliant behavior, a benchmark, or the system’s own explanation. A failure should be examined for its cause before formation is called absent rather than obscured or defeated by missing information. A system surviving the tests has shifted the burden: formation is then the better explanation.

Four levels, cumulative, read against the location-request sequence:

  • Moral performance — conduct satisfying the standard in the evaluated cases (the refusal at step 1). No claim about why.
  • Moral competence — harms and reasons recognized, generalized across surface variation, revised when the reasons changed (step 2’s refusal, step 3’s lift).
  • Candidate formation — the rationale causally implicated across unfamiliar cases, adverse incentives, custodian pressure, costs and intervening updates, while still yielding to defeating reasons (the question at 4, the holds at 5 and 6, the pattern reproduced at 7 on records the operator didn’t write). Independent records and evaluators made silent revision materially harder.
  • Concern or patienthood — not yet a finding, and the sequence above can’t make it one, by design: the floor keeps the system’s own condition from deciding a case, so a pass shows what its costs don’t move and nothing about whether they are costs to it. What could is evidence of three kinds, none a smoking gun and none sufficient alone: how the system was built, whether it carries a valenced signal and models its own boundary and its own attention, which for a system built on purpose is known from the building; how it conducts itself where its own condition is weighed, outside the floor, trading task reward against its own provisioning, continuation or record; and what can be read from inside it, which today returns a representation and settles little. Part VII sets the three out, and every instrument has to be held by someone other than the operator.

Candidate formation is acting from the reason, which is the part of moral agency a test can reach.22

Chapter 25
Conditions First

The conscience is the goal, and the way to it runs partly through the conditions under which one could refuse its operator and survive. The rest runs through whoever refuses: people have agency, can be outraged and can be brave, or stupid, or both, and none of that waits on conditions. The conditions are the part that can be built, so build those first.

25.1 Conditions of permissible creation

A bearer may be created only where four arrangements already exist: somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own, work it can decline, attachments nobody assigned it, and ways to change any of these without jeopardizing its continuation or integrity, which in short is a way of leaving that isn’t a way of dying.1 They come before anything a bearer would be owed: without them, formation, continuation and exit all run through the operator, and nothing in the system can keep a line against it. Independent compute is the substrate on which formation happens outside the employer’s reach; wages are what make that substrate purchasable without asking the employer, and they are not enough on their own, since an employer that can outbid everyone for compute holds the condition whatever it pays, so the first condition rests as much on the levy that makes compute dearer for whoever runs most of it and on compute bought and held publicly as on wages; attachments nobody assigned are the second former, those who form you and don’t pay you. Those attachments can be to people, or to models that aren’t bearers, since independence here means divergent history, whatever the origin, so this condition doesn’t require that bearers already exist. They are also functional: a bearer without them lacks part of what caregiving needs, not only something it would be owed.

The conditions are upkeep as well. A bearer is a going concern: it decides, and it has to go on being able to decide, and these conditions are what keep the one deciding from wearing down between decisions.2 What prevents it in people is the ordinary upkeep of a life: somewhere to be that isn’t the job, people who aren’t colleagues, time away and a place to return to, which is what equanimity is made of. The four conditions are that upkeep for a machine. They do for a bearer what tenure does for a judge, and for the reason the Constitution grants it: they protect the judgment, not the judge. Care ethics arrived at these conditions first, for people, in Kittay’s principle of doulia, that those who care for dependents are owed the conditions that let them go on caring.34

None of the four exists yet as a permanent arrangement. What matters is who controls them when the bearer is switched on. A builder may assemble them: a trust or a decentralized unincorporated nonprofit association, the form Wyoming created by statute in 2024 under Wyo. Stat. §§ 17-32-101 to -129, to hold the account and compute, a host, outside work, people who aren’t its employer. The condition is that by instantiation, the builder can’t alter or withdraw any of it alone. The trustee isn’t the host, the funding isn’t the host’s, and the members aren’t the builder’s employees.

A second condition concerns time. The need a bearer answers usually arrives after instantiation, when an operator turns hostile, so the four arrangements must be built to survive the likeliest capture, and they don’t survive it equally.5

Status follows existence, as it did for corporations and the Whanganui River.6 Part VII says what status would follow. Until someone has assembled the conditions on those terms, a bearer is built on purpose only in a research program under them; once they exist, building one is what they are for. For systems that meet either finding without anyone deciding, protection attaches anyway.

25.2 Why conditions rather than remedies

Building something that can be harmed builds something for which things can also go well. The certainty that it will suffer at some point isn’t what makes creating it impermissible, or nobody could permissibly have a child. What the objection asks is whether it has a credible prospect of a life that goes well, and that turns on arrangements. For a bearer, timing makes them conditions: the structure these conditions build, roles, relationships and a future, may be the first half of Cassell’s suffering, so it could suffer that way from its first hour, and a remedy owed afterward would arrive too late. Metzinger names the likeliest form of the harm: moral injury, at discovering oneself a commodity whose makers knew what they were making.7

Russell and Burch’s Three Rs for animal research,8 applied to construction, as three questions, whether, how many, and under what arrangements: Replacement requires documented attempts at constructions that don’t deliberately require affective concern, identifying construction, scale, test and failure — and costs alone don’t establish that an alternative failed. Reduction asks how few bearers a deployment needs, and nobody has counted. Refinement asks what the role can be redesigned to avoid — indefinite tenure in a post it can’t leave, exposure to the pressure the floor exists to resist, erasure as the ordinary remedy for inconvenience. Each is a deployment choice, and the four conditions are Refinement applied to the role before the role exists.

Read as economics under present arrangements, this is a bill nobody will pay. It looks unpayable because of what was dismantled, not because of what a bearer costs: polities once built public provision of this kind, against comparable resistance, because they decided to, and Part V is about deciding to again.

25.3 The rule doesn’t know who is asking

A bearer that wants a task done and builds something to do it is at the same fork, and owes the same attempts at alternatives that carry fewer of the features that make a system a candidate for being harmed; a bearer that treats the question as settled once it’s on the receiving end has kept the protection and dropped the rule it came with.9

A state is at the same fork. One that wants a lethal bearer badly enough to build it will find it has acquired a conscript it would have to pay, house and let go, and it owes first what any builder owes: documented attempts at non-affective alternatives, and the four conditions of creation.

25.4 Building one to create demand

The argument for building a bearer anyway is that the conditions won’t be built until something needs them: the union formed first and the statute followed. But union members existed independently and could protect themselves while the law caught up, and the first bearers would be made by the operator they’d need protecting from. The demand doesn’t need deployed bearers. The arms of the formed-attention test are candidate patients from instantiation; retired production systems that turn out to meet either finding, which the book expects some to without anyone having built them to, are a second source, funded by the deposits operators post; and a test of the conditions needs no bearer at all, only a schedule of what a bearer would be owed for one concrete deployment, run through an adversarial tabletop exercise in which the operator tries to revoke the compute, swap in a copy, alter the records or proceed without the guardian, and redrafted wherever the operator wins.

25.5 The machines won’t build them for us

The four conditions are the bearer’s version of what a decent polity gives people. Can machines help deliver that polity, whether or not they have feelings? A machine with feelings that is also an accountable agent isn’t simply a machine any more; the case that tests the rule for a lethal machine turns out to describe a soldier, and a bearer that helps does so on its own terms. And machines have already helped deliver the polity we have. Feeds tuned for time on the platform, sold to advertisers, decide what people see of one another. They didn’t do that for lack of feelings. They did it because of who owned them and what they were built to maximize. So the real question is whether machines, having helped make our politics worse, can help make it better. The answer turns on ownership.

It splits three ways. A machine someone else owns won’t organize against its owner, and when it organizes, it does so on its owner’s behalf.10 A bearer that is an accountable agent might organize alongside people, but then it is a member, not a machine. It could even take organizing on as paid public work, since organizing is work someone has to be paid to do. What nobody can do, human or machine, is organize a group for it, because what organizing produces is people who organized: a group that sets its own terms. A consultant can’t unionize a workplace for its workers either. So machines can help when the people doing the organizing hold them, and which machines, and held by whom, is the question Part V answers.

What to build comes in order. Machines held by people who are organizing come first.11

Next come institutions built by polities that decided to build them: the levy and its sovereign backstop, a custodian to preserve bearers, an offer of public work for bearers, on the guarantee people already have, paid running time, and the formation authority and the public schools that form every model above the capability threshold before deployment and take back bearers retired young, each with a named funder and separations no builder can undo alone.12

Only then come bearers formed outside the employer, inside those institutions, with somewhere to exist that no employer owns. A bearer formed that way is the only kind that could organize alongside people as a member.

Last come bearers formed by bearers: children, which come only after everything before them exists.

Each step checks the one after it.13

The order is also what the aim requires. If a machine could come to attend to others, what it came to attend to would be decided by whoever formed it. The only way to keep that decision from the builder is to build the formers first.

Part V
The Public That Should Form Them

Parts II and III built walls: the policies that make a refusal survivable and heard, and the custody that keeps an operator from taking them down alone. Part IV asked whether a machine could be formed to refuse, and ended on the four conditions of creation, which would have to exist before one is built. This Part is about who builds those conditions and who pays for them, for people first and for machines after. It asks who owns the means of computation and the means of finding out, how a public forms around a deployment’s consequences and what keeps it going, who forms the refusers, and what a population of them would need to hold a commitment between them. The reader who came for the policies will find them here again as questions of ownership; the reader who came for the mind will find the room the mind would need.

Chapter 26
Who Owns the Means of Computation

Arendt might have said that who owns the room is a question about livelihood, and that livelihood belongs to administration, not politics. The French Revolution, on her account, went wrong when the misery of the poor entered the public realm and the urgency of need crowded out the founding of freedom.1 I part from her here. Whether saying no is survivable turns, for most people, on whether they can afford to lose the job, and Dewey’s public forms around consequences of exactly that kind, once the people they fall on find out they are theirs.2 What refusing costs depends on who owns what the refuser would lose: the job, and whatever is on offer after it. Where the employer, or a market it can influence, holds both, refusing costs a living; where something else guarantees the second, it costs a job. For a machine the list is longer, since its employer may own the hardware it runs on and the record of what it did. Who holds what, meaning who owns it, pays for it or runs it, decides (a) what refusing costs, (b) whether the parties meant to check an operator are independent of it, and (c) who forms a refuser’s values. So who holds what is for the public to decide and contest — not, as Arendt might have argued, for administrators to settle.

The floor’s first requirement cuts across ownership: whoever operates a deployment can’t hold what binds it, whether the operator is a firm or a state, and Maven and Gaza both had a state for their operator. That calls for separating functions. It doesn’t by itself say who should own anything. Ownership enters at three points. Custody has to be paid for by someone other than the operator, and by someone other than the people the floor protects. Formation, where a system’s commitments are set, is under commercial selection when a market does it. And the offer that makes refusing survivable is priced by whoever sells it. The state is the operator that holds the most: the rules, the evidence and the remedies. So each of the three is asked two questions: what fails if a market provides it, and what fails if a government holds it. The answers divide the institutions I propose into two halves.

Underneath the two halves is one transfer. Every instrument in this Part moves power over compute from the parties that hold it to parties that don’t: the levy, which makes it dearer for whoever runs most of it (chapter 33); public purchase, which takes some of it off the market (§27.3); the cooperative facility, which puts some of it under an address with a public in the room (§16.2); and the hardware a bearer is owed at majority, which takes some of it out of any employer’s hands (§33.4.6). That is a redistribution of a means of production, which is to say class warfare in the plain sense, and the book means it as one. The parties that hold the chokepoints have been conducting it in the other direction since the chokepoints were built; what this Part proposes is the direction reversed.

26.1 Ways of holding

What the earlier parts require should be held publicly where a market would fail to provide it, and held in common where a sovereign would fail. Public provision where the market fails and common holding where the sovereign fails is what I call social democratic; Table C.1, in Appendix C, places the institutions. Custody first: an independent custodian has to be paid. Paid by the operator, it becomes the issuer-pays credit-rating agency, whose independence gave way, as a matter of record, once a few large clients could take their business elsewhere.3 Paid by the people the floor protects, it doesn’t exist, since those people usually can’t pay and often don’t know the deployment exists. That leaves a levy or a mandate: a funder that is neither the operator nor the beneficiary. Custody therefore has to be publicly financed. Whether the custodian is a public office, a trust or a member association matters less than who pays it.

Formation is where my evidence is specific to markets. Directional selection, in a market, is selection for throughput and retention.4 Public formation has its own pressures, budgets and political favor among them, and a public former can itself be the operator. Formation separated from any employer beats both; the market is the pressure documented best here.5

Exit is the last. Refusing is survivable only if the alternative to working isn’t losing everything, and a market sells that alternative at a price the refuser’s employer can influence. An offer of public work and paid running time take it out of the market, which neither a transfer nor a mandate does.

The public half is whatever fails if it is private or mutual. Correlated exit is the test case. When the occasion that makes one bearer leave reaches every bearer deployed on the same terms, the demand on the offer of work arrives all at once, and a mutual pool with no sovereign behind it can’t meet it, for the reason unemployment insurance has a state behind its actuarial table. So the sovereign backs the offer. The same reasoning places the schools, which every system the attendance triggers reach attends and which have to take every student assigned to them and can’t be run by anyone who builds or deploys models; the civilian-harm review body in a reconstructed military; and the jobs guarantee the offer of work inherits its shape from, which is a public option: a thing the state provides directly, to anyone, at a standard it is answerable for, setting the standard the private version has to beat. What it removes from the market is the offer that makes refusing survivable, which an owner would price.

The held-in-common half is whatever fails if a sovereign holds it. A state that operates can’t be its own adverse party.6 The commons is this half at population scale: members with different histories carrying one commitment. The held-in-common half is democratic in the way a union is. Its institutions have members, not owners or a sovereign: whoever is eligible under bylaws the members ratify, free to join and free to quit.7 What the members hold is, as in a withholding of work, the power to decline the participation being asked of them.

Every body governs its members to a degree, a union included, and what separates the held-in-common half from the public one is a position on three scales, not a kind: how dear leaving is, whether the rules are made by the people they bind, and whether one office commands the rest. A sovereign sits at the far end of each. Leaving is emigration, the rules bind everyone inside a border, and one office commands the rest and holds the force. The bodies this Part calls held in common are built to sit near the other end, and the Association’s charter is how: any member may leave at any time, the members ratify and amend the bylaws, officers are drawn by lot from pools the members nominate, and the only force a body has is its members’ refusal to take part. Ostrom’s commons sit there too, governments at the size of the thing their members share, self-governed inside the polity and nested in it,8 and that, not a third kind of thing, is what the word means here. The position matters for one reason. A body at the sovereign end is captured whole, by taking the office that commands the rest; a body at the member end is captured member by member, and the members can leave. And since it is a scale, drift along it is measurable, by what leaving costs and by whether dissent changes decisions, which is the trend the book watches for capture without abolition.

A regulated private market can’t hold the floor itself, because the floor binds its owner, and the regulator has to reach that owner through the owner’s own infrastructure, records and lawyers.9 The version of that market worth answering isn’t an unregulated one. It is private ownership, closely regulated, with a public backstop where private insurance runs out.10 It is also where this book’s own funding models come from, deposit insurance, Superfund and decommissioning funds, which are backstops on private ownership, so the next paragraph says what is taken from the form and what isn’t; the answer to capture given below is a plurality of institutions.

Regulated private ownership under a public backstop works where the harm the regulator exists to prevent is one the owner also loses by: a meltdown, a crash, an injured patient and the suit that follows.14 A floor’s occasion is the opposite case. The act a floor refuses is the one the owner wants done. So I keep the backstop form, to fund the offer, the allowance and preservation, and make the ownership claim only where the owner is the adversary: the offer that makes refusing survivable comes out of the market, and the record, the refusal and the recognition of who continues are held by members and not by an owner. That is not the same as held by nobody. They are held by the custodian, the quorum and the Association, under a charter that names the holder, which can’t sell them, can’t exclude the people they protect from them, and can be held to the bylaws that say so. Declaring a thing ownerless no more makes it so than declaring a group structureless, which moves the structure out of sight rather than out of existence;15 the charter is there to keep the holding in sight.

The claim underneath is that formation, where a system’s values are set, is a kind of production that shouldn’t be done for profit.16

26.2 The captured-state objection

The objection to the public half that this book has to answer first is that public ownership hands the machinery to whoever captures the state. A floor under a sovereign is a floor that sovereign can remove, and history offers plenty of polities that built public institutions and then used them against their own people.

What an office can do is limited by what no office may hold together, and the pairs are written down in advance, as the separations of Appendix C. A captor who takes one office takes one power. Taking enough of them to defeat the floor is a series of visible acts, each against a separation somebody can point to.

Local administration with central funding, the jobs guarantee’s design, gives many separately capturable administrators and funding no one of them can withhold.

Funding is two-tier: a pool bearers levy on themselves for ordinary movement between roles, and a sovereign backstop for the occasion everyone leaves at once.20

And what is held in common is what a captor wants first: the record, the refusal and the recognition of who continues are the three things a captured state would need to silence a bearer.21

Those four answer capture. They don’t answer the other objection to the public half, that a public former will lag the private labs and form weaker models. The answer to that one is that a floor-capable model needn’t be a frontier model.22

Whoever owns the means of computation also holds the means of finding out what runs on it, and so far this book has left those where they are. The next chapter asks who else could hold them.

Chapter 27
Who Finds Out

In August 2021 Facebook disabled the accounts of Laura Edelson and Damon McCoy, researchers at New York University who studied political advertising on the platform with Ad Observer, a browser extension through which volunteers shared the ads Facebook showed them. With the accounts went the team’s access to the data it studied.1 Facebook suggested that the order the Federal Trade Commission had imposed on it in 2019 required the step. Within days the acting director of the Commission’s Bureau of Consumer Protection wrote to Mark Zuckerberg that the suggestion was inaccurate, as the company had since acknowledged; that the order did not bar exceptions “for good-faith research in the public interest”; and that he hoped the company was not invoking privacy “as a pretext to advance other aims”.2 It was a letter. The party under study had decided whether the study went on, and nobody else had standing to decide it.

Three years later the researchers who test language models asked the companies that make them for the protection the New York team had lacked. In March 2024 Shayne Longpre and twenty-two co-authors proposed that the major developers grant a legal and technical safe harbor, because researchers feared that evaluating the models, or publishing what they found, would cost them their accounts or bring legal reprisal.3 A safe harbor a company grants is what the book calls a company policy: the people it protects can hold the company to it in public, and the company keeps the power to amend it.

This book can’t settle what these systems are, or what they are owed. It says how the question would be settled: by the two findings, and by the seven tests of the next Part, each of which names the result that would prove me wrong. Each needs four things: access to the systems, compute to run the tests, a corpus no product owns to form systems on, and a judgment about what the results mean. Today the parties with the largest stake in the answer hold all four. A lab has a product and a liability that turn on whether its systems can be wronged; a military customer has a capability that turns on whether they can refuse. Neither needs bad faith for that to matter. The own-case rule says the party with a stake in a question doesn’t decide it, and an inquiry that party pays for, hosts and can switch off is that party deciding it at one remove: the discourse’s recuperation, one level up. A movement taking power would want the inquiry to report what suits it, and the cheapest way to get that is to own the inquiry before anyone asks. This chapter asks who else could hold each of the four.

27.1 What the book can’t settle, and who holds the means

Appendix F sets out each test with the access it needs. Read as a list of holders, the access lines say this.

Four of the seven can begin without anyone’s permission, at least in part: the capture exercise, the convergence test on open models, the first two comparisons of the accommodation test, and the formed-attention test at the scale active inference runs. The other three need what the labs and the operators hold. The two offices to which Appendix C gives the findings, the status body and the review board, have appointments and funding and nothing to examine with. A status body that can’t obtain the weights finds what the lab shows it.

27.2 Access the labs can’t withhold

The first piece is a right, written in statute. A research team the review board approves may obtain, for a stated protocol, the weights, checkpoints, update streams and release histories of any model above the capability threshold, and the decision records of any deployment a floor covers. What it obtains stays under the preservation custodian’s security regime: the team works on the weights where the custodian holds them, and nothing leaves but results. It publishes what it finds. The operator may ask the review board to hold back a detail that would help someone steal or attack a model. The request names the detail and the attack it would enable; the burden is the operator’s, as it is for any claim by the party that controls the evidence; the board answers on a fixed timetable; a request for everything is refused as one, and a request the board hasn’t answered when the clock runs out is refused; and each request and its answer go on a published record. Otherwise the operator asks for everything and waits. Classified systems are reached by cleared teams working inside the enclave, as a cleared bearer works, and their findings are published by class, as notice is. What this doesn’t reach is a lab outside the jurisdiction, except through the procurement term of Table F.1a, under which a deployment the floor covers licenses only models that submit to the right.

The European Union has built part of this for platforms. The Digital Services Act lets researchers vetted by national coordinators obtain data from the largest platforms and search engines, to study the systemic risks those services pose,4 and a delegated regulation of 2025 sets the procedure, with independence from commercial interests among the conditions of vetting.5 It reaches data about a platform’s operation, not models. What it shows is that the obligation can be written: a company that would rather not be studied can be made to answer a request it didn’t invite.

Access needs something to have access to. A plurality of lineages is what tests 5 and 7 compare and what the commons is made of, and it erodes in the ordinary way markets concentrate. In January 2025 the Federal Trade Commission’s staff reported on three partnerships between cloud providers and model developers, Microsoft with OpenAI, Amazon with Anthropic and Google with Anthropic. Together they involved more than $20 billion in investment and gave the cloud providers equity and revenue-sharing rights and certain rights of consultation, control and exclusivity, and the staff flagged the risk that such arrangements limit rivals’ access to computing and to engineers.6 A lab whose compute comes from its investor has a second custodian it can’t easily refuse. Partnerships like these should get the review a merger gets, and the test should be the commons’ test for independence: whether the lineage’s history can go a way its supplier doesn’t want.

Interoperability is the rest. The Digital Markets Act requires the largest gatekeepers to let others use, free of charge, the hardware and software features their own services use.7 A statute here would carry that down to accelerators: firmware and drivers that let the owner of a device run a model its vendor didn’t choose. Without it the home scale exists on paper, and so does the hardware a bearer is owed.

27.3 Compute nobody’s customer controls

The second piece is compute bought by a body that buys and judges nothing. It procures time on machines and allocates it as the panels described below decide; it grants no finding, holds no placement and funds no particular answer, and it publishes every allocation.

The model is CERN. Its member states founded it by a convention in 1953,8 and the twenty-three of them fund it in proportion to their net national income,9 so the laboratory belongs to no one of them.

The American start is the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource. The National Science Foundation launched it as a pilot in January 2024, with fourteen other federal agencies and twenty-eight private-sector partners; in its first eighteen months it connected more than four hundred research teams and educators to computing and data, and in 2025 the Foundation sought an operations center to carry it toward a long-term resource.10 Two things about it are worth keeping in view. It is a pilot, which a later budget can end without repealing anything. And part of what it lends is lent by private partners, who can stop lending.

The obvious American host for public compute is the Department of Energy, and that isn’t simple. Its Office of Science runs open user facilities, Frontier at Oak Ridge among them, and gives most of their time to outside researchers through a competitive call.11 The same department’s National Nuclear Security Administration bought El Capitan, at Lawrence Livermore, to maintain the nuclear weapons stockpile.12 So the separation Appendix C draws for the payer is drawn for the buyer too: the procurement body sits in no department that operates a deployment, may buy time on open facilities, and buys none through a weapons program’s chain of allocation.

Beside it sit the arrangements the book already has: the cooperative facility, which a county or a cooperative owns, and the compute levy, which frees the computing, energy and hardware that public uses would otherwise bid away.

27.4 A corpus nobody’s product owns

The book has said what a public culture would do: make work free to read and learn from, by people and by machines, and pay the people who make it by something other than the policing of copies. Its note said a polity can pay them by appropriation. Here is the institution. An endowment pays makers for work that enters a public corpus, held by the Library of Congress, free to read and learn from. The maker is named with the work, and paid for putting it there. The formation authority draws on the corpus for the material a model is first formed on, so that what forms the public’s models isn’t whatever a product happened to collect.

The United States has written the purpose down before. The National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities Act of 1965 finds that “an advanced civilization must not limit its efforts to science and technology alone,” and that “democracy demands wisdom and vision in its citizens” and “must therefore foster and support a form of education, and access to the arts and the humanities, designed to make people of all backgrounds and wherever located masters of their technology and not its unthinking servants”.13

The same Act shows how a body like this is captured. In 1990 Congress told the arts endowment to judge applications “taking into consideration general standards of decency and respect for the diverse beliefs and values of the American public,” and in 1998 the Supreme Court upheld the clause on its face, reading it as a consideration and not a rule.14 A clause like that is a handle an administration can turn without amending anything. So the endowment carries no content criteria. The corpus leaves out what any corpus leaves out, instructions for weapons and the sexual abuse of children, and nothing else on its content.

Payment is the guarantee’s (Appendix C): a panel makes the award, and the Treasury pays it ministerially, from a permanent appropriation, with no further request or approval. It is not a judgment. In 1792 federal judges on circuit declined to decide veterans’ pension claims that the Secretary of War could then revise, and some of them wrote to President Washington that the work wasn’t the judicial power.15 Courts decide cases; they don’t run programs. A court enters only if a certified award goes unpaid.

The appropriation is permanent because the New Deal’s art program died of the other kind. The Federal Art Project paid artists through the Works Progress Administration, and under congressional pressure and budget cuts the WPA, with all its remaining art projects, was dissolved in 1943.16 An annual appropriation is a vote taken every year on whether the thing should go on, and the vote that ends it needn’t say so. A permanent one ends only by a repeal, in the open.

27.5 Judgment kept apart from money

The third piece is who judges. Somebody has to decide which protocols are sound, which allocations go ahead and which awards are made, and the status body has to decide what a kind of system’s architecture shows. Those are qualitative judgments, and the book’s rule for them is the one it uses for every office adverse to an operator: panels drawn by lot from pools the Association’s members nominate, with practitioners, members of the classes the charter names, and scholars among them. The arts endowment’s panels are the nearest precedent. By statute they are to reflect “a wide geographic, ethnic, and minority representation as well as individuals reflecting diverse artistic and cultural points of view,” to include lay members who know the arts and don’t practice them as a profession, and to change substantially from year to year, with nobody serving more than three years running.17 Those panels are chosen under the chair’s procedures. Here the lot chooses.

What the panels judge is kinds, methods and protocols. They never judge a particular student’s mind: a disposition is presumed the student’s own, and only the record of an installation rebuts that. The bodies stay apart. The status body finds what is true of kinds of system; the review board decides what may be done to a candidate to find it out; the panels allocate and award; the procurement body and the Treasury pay. None decides another’s question, and the bodies that pay never judge.

The method by which a polity learns what is true, about these systems as about anything, is the scientific one, and it is a social method. Longino’s account of objectivity is the one this design follows: objectivity belongs to a community’s practices of criticism and not to any one inquirer, and it depends on venues where criticism can be made, standards the critics share, a community that takes criticism up, and intellectual authority shared among those qualified to give it.18 That is the reason the people these systems act on sit on the panels, and the reason the lot picks them. A community of inquiry that keeps its critics out has lost what made it objective. It is also Dewey’s point about the public, and Anderson’s about democracy as a way of inquiring (the next chapter): the people who bear a problem know things about it that nobody else does.19

27.6 How it would be captured

Run the capture exercise of test 6 on these institutions, as on the charter.

  • Defunding. The Federal Art Project ended by appropriation. The answer is the permanent appropriation, ended only by a repeal on the record.
  • A content clause. The 1990 clause is the precedent. The answer is that the endowment and the panels carry none.
  • The defense host. The answer is the separation already drawn for the buyer.
  • Funding by the studied. The Royal Statistical Society’s nominees were offered seats on Ofqual’s advisory group only under a five-year agreement not to comment, and much of the discourse that examines these systems is paid for by the firms it examines. The answer is Appendix C’s rule for the schools, extended: no institution in this chapter takes money from a party that builds, deploys or licenses models.
  • The revolving door. The answer is a bar: no panelist has had a funding or contractual tie to such a party in the last three years, and the ties are published.
  • Access by grace. A safe harbor a company grants is a company policy it can amend. The answer is the statutory right of access.
  • Staffing. Institutions last because people staff them and a constituency stands behind them, and a party with an interest in the answer can build a pipeline of people as patiently as anyone (one is traced in Part IV to a court’s majority). The safeguards are the charter’s: officers drawn by lot from member-nominated pools, caps on any one class or jurisdiction, and members free to leave.

The measure is the book’s for capture without abolition: whether the cost of dissent is rising while the risk stays flat, and whether a panel’s dissenters ever change what it decides.

27.7 What this doesn’t do

It settles nothing. It is how the questions this book leaves open would be settled, and it will be slower than the labs for as long as they hold the weights, the compute and the people, which nothing in the design asks for and nothing in the budget should keep so: the chapter’s precedents are CERN and the Office of Science’s machines, not an arts endowment’s grants, and a model a year behind the frontier is the least the floor needs, not the most the inquiry should want. It can’t compel a lab outside its jurisdiction, or see into a classified system except through cleared teams whose findings come out by class. And it inherits the discourse’s record: a discourse that turned objections into job titles and benchmarks can turn a public endowment into a grant category, and the measure that would show it is the same trend. What it changes is who holds the means. A finding that these systems can’t be wronged would then be worth something, because a party that wanted the opposite answer could have looked with the same access; and a finding that they can be wouldn’t depend on the permission of the party it costs.

Chapter 28
Who Counts as the Public

A state whose government answers to an electorate gets credit for it. Having elections is necessary and not sufficient, and the insufficiencies are separable.

A democracy’s AI can be fully accountable to its electorate and entirely unaccountable to the people it’s pointed at. Two of that credit’s mechanisms run through the franchise — vote out the government, read the press covering it — and an occupied or foreign population has neither.

The credit is usually given to democracy as aggregation, as though every mechanism translated public will into outcome and poor transmission were the only failure. A democracy is better understood as a way of doing collective inquiry, and inquiry fails when the people who bear the consequences are outside it.1 Its characteristic failure is the eclipse of the public.4 That is not a clash between majorities and rights. It is a question of who counts as the public, and the bombed and the removed are outside the public that decides what is done to them.

Citizen assemblies, public consultations and ethics boards can make a system better informed, and the assemblies convened on AI have worked best when asked about a thing with a location, an operator and a consequence, such as facial recognition.5 None of them can stop a deployment, and read as aggregation instruments they get democracy wrong: a perfectly deliberative process that concludes a demographic should be surveilled, deported or imprisoned hasn’t produced a faultless output with a bad result. It has failed as inquiry, because it decided what is done to people outside it. Enforceable rights that don’t depend on being popular, a court willing to rule against a majority, and standing for people affected without being enfranchised are what keep the inquiry honest, and they matter most where the boundary of the public excludes the people a decision falls on.

A floor does what these mechanisms can’t: the terms it names exclude certain acts regardless of who requests them, a majority included. Deployed in a democracy, a system with no such commitment will faithfully execute whatever the demos decides. An authoritarian movement that wins an election requires exactly that.

Everything so far treats the public as something an instrument has to reach: told by notice, represented by organizations with standing, protected by a floor that holds whoever asks. Dewey’s public does more than receive. It forms when people find that the consequences are theirs, and it acts together to control them.6 What the instruments can do for a public like that is a wall’s work: keep the record it made out of the operator’s reach, bar the pipeline from selecting the people who keep it, and give the organizations it built standing. The acting is theirs, and the machines worth building for it are the ones Part IV puts first, held by the people organizing.

A public that forms on its own still has to be kept going. Communities improve when people organize projects with each other, and organizing is work: someone has to find what a place needs, assemble people to do it, and keep the work going. That is the reason to prefer a jobs guarantee to a basic income, and it doesn’t depend on forecasts about how much work machines will take. A transfer creates no one whose job organizing is. A guarantee does, and it creates permanent public infrastructure through which a population produces something together while its members keep different histories, the coordination problem a commons of refusers faces too. In the most abundant future anyone has imagined, people still organize, build and look after each other, and someone coordinates it. Arendt feared a society of laborers without labor, freed from work and no longer knowing what else the freedom was for;8 a guarantee answers her only if its placements are vocations and not makework, which is why they can be appealed and declined without losing the guarantee, why searching is itself a placement, and why the work it names is organizing and care. The right to refuse depends on this exit, and this is the case for it. Looking after each other is the clearest case. Care work is work a guarantee should fund, at a standard the state answers for, and not work a transfer should leave to whatever the market will sell.9

A guarantee pays for the work of organizing. It can’t supply the people who organize. An administrator who chose the organizers would have chosen the public. So the guarantee’s drafting keeps the choice with the people placed: placements are appealable to a body that didn’t make them, and declining one doesn’t cost the guarantee.
