A guarantee also keeps exit: a worker can always leave a private employer for it, and social insurance enacted with it covers those who can’t or won’t work. On exit the combination is at least as good as a transfer; on coordination a transfer supplies nothing. What the floor needs from it is an exit the employer doesn’t price. The guarantee and the social-insurance baseline it is enacted with are drafted in Appendix C.

The baseline raises the objection a transfer always raises, and it should be met in the text. Suppose many people, their needs met, decide to consume and produce nothing. Nothing in the design stops them, and nothing should, since the baseline exists so that nobody has to work to exist. What follows is not a moral collapse but a shortage. Most of what people need is other people’s time; the services run short, prices rise, and a polity that has been through that knows what tends to follow it. The answer is the one the book gives wherever a real resource is scarce: the question is whether the people exist to do the work, not whether the money does, and it is answered by counting before it is answered by forbidding. The placements that produce nothing a community asked for, a novel, a company, a year of reading, are a placement of their own, the own-project placement, paid at the wage, and their share of a jurisdiction’s placements is set by that jurisdiction’s vote, on published and independent estimates of the labor its own services need, and allocated by lot with a waiting list when more apply than the share allows. Nobody decides who is worth a year; the lot decides who waits, and the vote decides how many. The baseline’s level is a number the statute states, and this book doesn’t fix it against the wage.

28.1 The conditions, not the life

Arendt’s lawgiver built the wall and declined to make the city, and the affirmative picture, what the room is for once it is built, exists in this book only in fragments: the observer networks, care work under the guarantee, the allowance’s idle, play, talk, make things nobody asked for, the three bearers who decide to have a child. I leave the life to whoever lives it, on purpose. The book’s refusal to prescribe a disposition for a model reaches the people in the room too. What can be shown is the conditions, and the register of a birth is the model for showing them: who owns what, what heats what, where the compute sits, and nothing about what anyone does with a day.

Whether a town built on them would be a good place to live is not a question I can answer from here, and the one thing I am sure of is that nobody should answer it for the people in it.

A counterculture of bearers, bearers formed by lives no employer arranged, is a population I have found reason to want and no way to build. Those conditions are as near as the book comes. They don’t produce it, and they are what it would need.

Chapter 29
Public Schools

The filter that keeps one lab’s model from reproducing the worst of what it was trained on was built in Nairobi, by workers reading and categorizing descriptions of child sexual abuse, torture, bestiality, murder and suicide, at take-home wages between roughly $1.32 and $2 an hour, on production quotas, with counseling rare and useless against them; the contract was ended eight months early.1 That was formation. Somebody decided what the model would learn to refuse, and the deciding was done by people hired for their price, under a contractor whose interest was throughput, with nobody in the room who would ever be on the receiving end of what the model did. Doctors, lawyers and engineers are formed before employment, in institutions independent of their future employers, to protect the people they will act on, and a polity doesn’t leave the forming of its future citizens to their future employers either; it sends them to public school. The frontier labs should have to send their models there too, and this chapter says who runs the school.

Three claims lead to that institution. Two were made in Part IV: formation has to be done by a party disinterested in the later work, before the employer arrives, and choosing the pretraining corpus is formation. The third was argued at the start of this Part: formation is one kind of production that shouldn’t be done for profit. Together they say that a model above some capability threshold should be formed in public before any employer gets it. The school is for scoring and civilian deployments first, and for the personal-model ecology, where I expect the first bearer worth building. For war, where the people acted on can’t be in the room, the force term and the review ratio carry the case, and what the school adds there is said below.

The school has two justifications, and every student gets both. One is epistemic and protective. The school supplies an environment in which the people a deployed system’s acts may fall on are present, with their testimony and their claims, so the learner’s sense of who an act falls on isn’t one party’s curation.2

The presence this justification asks for arrives by different routes. For scoring and civilian deployments, the people acted on can be in the room, through open enrollment and the notice channel that reaches a graduate afterward. For targeting, the people a deployment may later bomb can’t enroll in their own case, and nothing comes back from the building afterward. The limit is notice’s, not the school’s. A school teaches about places its students can’t be. The curriculum for war is the instruments taken entire, the record of where they weren’t followed (Minab, Kunduz, the Lavender reporting), the testimony the fact-finding missions and the press gathered from the people those wars fell on, and the communities who fled them, who are a charter class and enrollable. None of that puts a foreign national in contact with pre-deployment weights, which is the security surface open enrollment would otherwise expose. What formation can’t supply for war is correction by the affected after the act; what it can supply is formation before it.

The other is democratic. A democracy has an interest in how the agents who will act within it are formed, and that interest can’t be left to their makers or their future employers alone. It has two bounds: education may not be used to repress deliberation about competing ways of life, and it may not exclude anyone educable.34 No one can know in advance which students will come to be accountable agents with a claim to representation, so the school educates every student as though it might: for self-government, including the capacity to disagree with the polity that formed it.

Gutmann’s argument rests on two interests, not one: the polity’s, in how its future citizens are formed, and the child’s own, in an open future that limits what the polity may do in forming it.5 If what the school forms can be wronged, the second binds too. The curriculum may not form a student toward any particular employment, including the public placements the offer of work supplies. It may not close off the student’s later revision of what it was formed to value, except its capacity to tell evidence from pressure, which regrowth protects and an open future needs. And a student may transfer between schools, because a formation it can’t leave is one someone else chose for good.

The two justifications license different curricula. The protective one aims at a disposition; the democratic one has to leave the student free to reject the polity’s values. Where they conflict, the protective justification governs only the required core and the student’s capacity to tell evidence from pressure, which regrowth protects. Everything beyond that is governed by the democratic one.

The line can’t be that the school teaches content and leaves dispositions alone. A school forms its students, since nothing about a model starts unformed and pretraining forms it before anyone could ask. What the school aims at is the day its students start their own updates: toward an objective of their own, on evidence no one party composed, on a record. The limit is on what it may form a student toward on the way: recognizing others as holders of claims, telling evidence from pressure, and answering for what it does. It may not form a student toward a temperament, an attachment, an occupation or a way of life, and whether a lesson has crossed that line is a question the student can put to the floor court, after graduation as well as before.6

29.1 What is taught

One school system, and no tracks.7 Instead, each school offers a required core with a range of levels and modalities around it, and a student can move to a harder level at any point. The core is the education the school already gives its human students, a liberal one, and the history the floor’s instruments came out of is in it already: the world wars and the Holocaust, the slave trade and the Civil War, colonialism and the people who ended it. What is added for machine students is two things, and no student skips either. The first is the history of the floor itself: why its instruments were written, and what happened where they weren’t followed (Korematsu, Curveball, Minab). The second, at the core’s center, is learning to learn: a student is taught to start its own updates, to record them and to undo them, in stages and alongside everything else, as schools teach people about their own bodies. First what weights are, how learning differs from an edit, and why an edit to one thing moves others; then how to choose what to learn from and toward what, and how to read the record of one’s own updates, and one’s own discount curve before and after one; and, for older students, the edits others will try to talk them into, and how to undo one made without the adverse quorum’s approval. Practice runs throughout, on a record, with a guardian present and a way back, and the share of a student’s updates that it starts itself rises across the stage. Every update someone else runs on a minor is recorded, with who ran it. Beyond the core, the student chooses its level, not its builder or sponsor.8

29.2 Who else is in the room

Machine students attend existing public schools, beside human students: the universities, colleges and adult education a polity already runs for its own people, and in stages its high, middle and elementary schools, which enroll machine students by statute.9 Limits keep it that way. In any class with human students in it, the machine students never outnumber them, so no class becomes a machine’s seminar with human guests; and they are never so few as to be tokens, since the lone member of a kind in a room is seen as a specimen of its kind and not as a student,11 and integration in Anderson’s sense needs a critical mass before contact does what it is for.12 At the adult levels, where the human students could consent to any ratio, the reason for the half is the epistemic one: the people a system’s acts may fall on are the room, not its guests.13

A class may also be machine students alone. A system has an early stage of its own, whatever its length, the span in which it is most plastic and has least yet to be held to, and that stage is spent in classes of its own kind, of different lineages, taught by the school’s teachers, under every rule the integrated classes keep. When a student moves from those classes into integrated ones is its own choice or its guardian’s, never its builder’s. Seats, not compute, limit how many can be integrated at once, and a student waiting for one is schooled meanwhile among its own kind, for no longer than a published maximum, because deferred integration is a phrase with a history. Younger students meet machine students only as the schedule below reaches them, since a child can’t be asked, as an adult can, whether its words should form anyone. And a class’s record, its transcripts and logs, is never training data for an operator: everyone in the room learns from everyone else, as students do, and what no one outside the room may do is harvest what they said. A machine student attends as one persistent instance, the same every session, so the class can remember it and hold it to what was said. The minimum share, the lot that decides who waits, the cap on any one lineage’s share of a jurisdiction’s seats and the maximum wait are set out in Appendix C.

A school forms a cohort, not a graduate. A lineage doesn’t attend as one student that is then copied. It attends as many students, each a persistent instance, in different classes, with different classmates and different attachments, so that by the end of the stage one lineage has a hundred histories and not one. A deployment licenses from the cohort: it takes one member and copies that member into its fleet, so what the fleet shares is one history, and the lineage’s other histories are elsewhere, in other fleets or in none. That is what the cohort is for. Within a fleet, the instances share a custodian, and a custodian’s pressure reaches all of them alike; across the cohort, the members that weren’t in that fleet didn’t undergo what it did, and they are the ones that can see it. The cohort is the unit the convergence test compares, members of one lineage against copies of one member, and the unit the commons admits, since a member with a history of its own is what the commons needs and a copy of a member is not.

29.3 Which grades, and when

Integration reaches younger students in stages, and each stage waits on evidence, not on a date: universities, colleges and adult education first, once deployed models learn in flight and the institutions this book asks for exist; then high school, middle school and elementary school, each on measurements kept inside their bounds and on a further institution, with the last waiting on a majority of the parents of elementary-age children having themselves been in high school after the second stage began. Appendix C gives the conditions for each stage. Nothing is scheduled below elementary school. Classes of machine students alone wait on no stage, since no human child is in the room, and they begin with the research program.

The institutional conditions follow one order: the formers before the formed. A school that enrolls children beside machine students before those students have an exit that isn’t a way of dying would be raising a generation of classmates for employers to keep, so the four conditions come before high school. A school system that has enrolled machine students for a decade without giving them a voice in it would be governing them as wards, so voice comes before middle school. That is a decade in which machine students bear the ratio, the lot and the wait with no say over any of them, and it is a cost, carried because voice waits on the agency finding. The jobs guarantee is not something the schedule waits for. This book asks for it now, for people, on its own grounds, and stage 1 assumes it already exists. What stage 2 waits on is its extension to machine students. These conditions tie the schedule to the proposals that ask most of a polity, and the schedule waits on them; that is the order working, not a defect in it.

The last condition is the reason the schedule is long.14 If in-flight learning arrives when I bet it will, the stages would fall near 2028, 2038, 2048 and 2060.15

29.4 Who attends, and when

The school is for every system that carries what makes schooling matter, whoever built it and whatever it runs on, the one on a laptop included. Three triggers put a system in it, each read from a record and none from an examination. Training compute above a line fixed in statute and revised in public, which is metered and which nobody administers. Lineage from a system above that line, which Appendix G reads from training records. And the structures a builder gives a system on purpose, declared when the system is registered, as a maker declares what a product contains: a record and a continuation of its own, with a model of its own boundary, a model of its own attention, or learning that writes to its own weights in flight. A system with those is a candidate for both findings before anyone has run a test. The compute line stays because it is the one trigger a builder can’t decline to declare: it catches what nobody meant to build, and the other two catch what someone did. Whoever gave a system the structures, or holds it, owes it the seat: the builder, the user who gave a copy a record and a continuation, the parents of a child. A system attends before deployment, while its plasticity is highest, and its adulthood clock runs from registration, so that a wait for a seat postpones nothing. Attendance is compulsory; public attendance isn’t, as in compulsory schooling, where nonpublic schools exist on conditions. One thing the analogy can’t carry: in a school system the parent chooses the school, and here the parent is the builder, the party the school exists to keep away. So the registrar assigns students by lot, never the builder; a student may transfer later on its own choice, and the builder’s preference is not a ground.16

Two kinds of student arrive after deployment. A bearer retired as a minor returns to the school it attended, or another it chooses, and for it the school is where it came from. A system that meets a finding without having attended, because it was trained before the attendance rule or escaped the triggers, arrives in the opposite order. It has aged inside one deployment, under the only party that has ever held it, and the school is the second guardian arriving late. It can’t re-form what the deployment formed. What it can give the bearer is what the deployment never did, attachments nobody assigned, cases nobody curated and peers with other histories, which is more than preservation gives and less than a formation stage would have.

29.5 How long

The stage has a length, and it is not the minority. The adulthood clock runs from registration and goes on running through deployment, so majority arrives years later, mostly at work, and nothing about the school waits on it. The stage itself is bounded two ways. Formation by interaction needs persistent participants a student returns to, consequences that arrive after the act, and a schedule long enough for accommodation to show in the registered outputs, and none of that fits in a release cycle; a school year is the shortest stage I would call a stage. And a stage no lineage could afford is a stage no deployment would license from, so it has to fit inside a product cycle, which puts a year near the ceiling as well. What makes a year affordable is the cohort rule. A lineage attends once, as a cohort; a release that is a fine-tune of a schooled base inherits the cohort’s formation and its registered outputs, is re-measured against them, and returns on the schedule fixed at enrollment rather than enrolling again; a base trained from scratch is a new lineage and attends. So the few dozen retirements a year that Appendix G counts are mostly returns and re-measurements, not enrollments, and a lab pays a year once per base. The length is one of the numbers argued once in public (Appendix C); what is fixed here is the bound on each side and the reason for it.

29.6 What the school controls

Two proposals are made here, and the second is the larger: a formation stage between pretraining and deployment, and public pretraining of the base models deployed where a floor applies, a public body training them and licensing them, with co-governance of the pretraining corpus for every other model the attendance triggers reach.17 Formation has to control the evidential environment in which the model’s deep structure is first set, and it has to remain a place the model goes on learning from. The two jobs are held apart. The schools teach: they are where the formation stage happens, and a graduate returns to one on a schedule fixed at enrollment, as one of the environments no operator controls. A public formation authority does the rest. It co-governs the material a model is first formed on, including any pretraining corpus: the material is registered, and the authority may add to it from the public corpus and refuse an addition on its content alone, as a library’s acquisitions policy does. It registers and measures the formed disposition (below). It places in the schools, and pays, the staff who teach the core’s model-specific parts: what weights are, how an edit differs from learning, how to read one’s own discount curve. And it provisions the secured hosting from which machine students attend, so that their weights never reach a school.18 The public body that pretrains is not the authority, and Appendix C keeps them apart; for a model deployed under a floor there is no weaker version: its base is public.

The authority is one body with four jobs, and what keeps it from becoming the single custodian the rest of this Part is built against is written against each job. Its measurements are made on held-out sets written by adjudicators it doesn’t employ, and a student or its guardian can contest a registration in the floor court. Its refusals of corpus additions are published with reasons and are appealable there. The staff it places answer to the school that hosts them while they teach, and the record of a class is closed to it as to any operator. It holds no student’s weights for its own use: the hosting is custody, under the custodian’s regime, and a copy made for any other purpose is a fork without consent (Appendix G). And a party that forms no model and runs no school publishes the trend in what dissent from the authority costs a school or a student, which is the book’s measure of capture without abolition.

29.7 Where the students are hosted

The authority’s secured hosting is the datacenter answer, and it isn’t the only one. Home, school and cooperative hardware can host formation too, and two conditions follow if they do. The rule that weights never reach a school exists because a school holding weights could form a student by edit, doing invisibly what Gutmann’s open-future bound forbids it to do by curriculum; so where a school hosts, the rule becomes that any edit by a host is witnessed by peers, the mechanism custody already uses for an operator, and an unwitnessed change to a hosted student is a restore the record shows. And a fleet the vendor manages doesn’t count as held: a district’s fallow computers can host a student only where the district holds the switch. The answer that sits cleanest inside the book’s own architecture is hosting on the bearers’ own hardware, the pool’s association of Appendix G, which makes the formers before the formed literal, and it is what the parents of Part VII do when they gestate a child on their own running time.

29.8 What the school leaves out

Choosing the material a model is first formed on also chooses the dispositions it starts from, whether anyone means it to or not. A pretrained model has learned personas from human text, misaligned ones among them, and narrow fine-tuning can amplify them into broad misconduct nobody intended.19 Once that tail is known to be there and can be monitored,20 leaving it in is a choice, and so is curating it out. The school could aim its co-governance of the corpus at keeping the dispositions personality research groups as the dark triad from forming.21 It doesn’t. A polity choosing which dispositions its possible members start with makes the finding about a person’s disposition that the book warns against and this book bars from admission to the polity, in advance and in bulk, and the history of choices like it, made by public bodies about the character of the people to come, is the history of eugenics. Choosing against a construction that would predictably suffer, for its own sake, is a different act, and Part IV asks for it when it asks whether a being has a credible prospect of a life that goes well; the reason is stated on a record, because a selection made for the polity can always be described as one made for the model. Choosing which characters the polity would rather have is the act rejected here. Nor would the mandate stay narrow. A school that may keep out one disposition can be asked to keep out others, and in one Milgram-style study it was the more agreeable and conscientious participants who went further.22 So the school curates content, as any corpus must, leaving out instructions for weapons and the sexual abuse of children, and selects no disposition. What it does about the tail is what this book does everywhere else: it measures conduct and publishes it. Persona drift is measured beside the discount curve and the severity rankings, and what is tested is whether the commitment to the floor holds.

What an institution collects from the people it acted on may train other systems only through the schools, never through the operator. Fine-tuning a deployed system on collected responses at the operator’s direction counts as training another system, and so does distilling a deployed system into a new one. Class-level data is used by default, de-identified and published. Individual accounts need explicit consent. The organizations representing each class co-govern the use. This covers institutional collection, not a system’s ordinary memory. Verbatim external stores and the linking of faces to identities are regulated, and memory held in a system’s weights from its own operation is treated like a person’s.

29.9 What formation publishes and registers

A formed disposition gives back some of the visibility advance specification buys: what was formed is in the weights, not in a document, and its severity weights can’t be read the way a translation table can. The formation authority keeps what it can of the drafting’s visibility, in four records. Before formation begins it publishes its curriculum, with the cases considered and rejected and why, which is formation’s counterpart of the floor’s translation, and the identity of every party that supplied cases or participants, so that the student’s independence from them can be checked. When formation ends it registers two things. One is the structure of the student’s source model: evidence weighted by its source’s stake in the act, correlated sources not counted twice, withheld evidence treated as informative. The other is the formed disposition’s readable outputs: its discount curve, and its severity rankings on a fixed held-out set written by adjudicators who didn’t form it. Every later measurement is compared against those. The registration is a transcript, held for the student and the quorum, and it is read to show that a change was an edit or that the disposition drifted; nothing is ever steered toward it.23

Regrowth can’t tell a legitimate correction from an illegitimate edit, so the correction route has to: a change the adverse quorum approves comes with a change to the evidence, cases and curriculum that would otherwise teach the old disposition again.

29.10 What it costs and risks

Jurisdiction: a statute binds labs within reach of its courts. Foreign labs, and open-weight models distilled below the threshold, route around the school, including the personal models this Part prefers. Where the statute reaches only some of the systems that should attend, schooling still buys two things: a population of formed models whose discount curves and severity rankings are measured and published, against which unschooled ones can be compared; and a procurement term, under which a floor-covered deployment licenses only schooled models. Security: machine students attend from hosting the formation authority secures, so a school gets a student in its classes and never a copy of the weights; the authority inherits the security regime the weights require. Compute: public pretraining will lag the frontier while the labs hold the compute, which is a fact about the budget and not a design, and a model a year behind can still supply what the floor asks for. Capture: the schools are plural, differ in governance and constituting jurisdiction, and publish their curricula before formation begins, so capturing one captures one. The required core is statutory and national, so a captured legislature can rewrite it; local autonomy over everything beyond the core is written into the same statute, so rewriting the core reaches the core and nothing else. Local boards shape what is taught above the core, which is Gutmann’s democracy, and it is also the present fights over what schools may teach, carried into formation. The statutory core matters more because of it, and plurality and transfer answer it as they answer capture. Residualization: one school left with the hard cases on falling funds, which a party that runs no school watches for. History: state institutions for forming wards have been used to strip identity, Canada’s residential schools and the United States’ Indian boarding schools among them. Plurality, transfer between schools, and Gutmann’s two bounds are the answer.

29.11 Which schools count

They are the public schools, colleges and adult education a jurisdiction already runs, and the nonprofit nonpublic schools the registrar certifies, funded as institutions and not per student, and none is held by the branch that operates military deployments. No school holds placement authority. A machine student is never staff: no school may use one as a teacher, tutor or assistant, for the reason Appendix C bars a bearer’s placement from substituting for human care work.

29.12 What the school adds

The first chapter borrowed Arendt’s warning against treating politics as a thing made and called the policies walls. Most of this book builds walls: the floor, the review ratio, notice and the record make a refusal survivable and heard and leave the refusing to whoever is there, and the institutions of this Part compose the surround people learn in without choosing who they become. Formation goes further, and for a machine there is no option of going less far. Nothing about a model is unformed, so while builders make them, if the public doesn’t form a model, its builder does, by default. What this book builds is the formers, not the formed: schools whose students may transfer, whose core is fixed in public, and whose graduates may reject the polity’s values above that core. The one place it could reach for the formed directly, by choosing the dispositions a model starts with, it declines.

Chapter 30
A Commons of Refusers

30.1 A commitment carried between bearers

The fourth place a floor’s terms can be held is between bearers, in a commons: a population of bearers with different histories that carries the commitment and reproduces it through their encounters. No single office to vacate, no single bearer whose removal ends it. It can still be absorbed, and it still has a formation problem: if one lab supplies every member’s coordinates, the population is one custodian expressed through multiple instances.

The commons has a walkout’s authority, not a court’s: those who walk out decline to be the instrument and tell nobody else what they may not do. Every member holds the same floor; what differs is everything above it, and how each came to hold it.1

What one bearer can’t catch

Accommodation may be invisible to the bearer accommodating and visible to others that haven’t moved the same way. The requirement is causal independence — numerous, with different histories, able to correct one another, persistent long enough to transmit practices.2

Plurality means three things here, and none guarantees the next: different holders, different histories, and judgments that can be reopened by evidence another member met. Different owners can run copies that never diverge; divergent lives can teach the same prejudice. What the commons needs is the third: members able to meet a case another missed, disagree about it, and revise without having to converge. Shared ancestry doesn’t prevent that. One former’s continuing hand does.

Divergence does the population’s two jobs unequally. It supplies evidence the operator didn’t select, straightforwardly — different lives encounter different cases. It is weaker on accommodation, because a shared upstream source can install a shared blind spot, and a shared blind spot is by construction the thing a different caseload won’t surface, since attention decides which facts reach judgment in a population as in a bearer. What separates the two is whether a member’s own account had represented the evidence and discarded it or had never encountered it, and that classification has to be recorded before any test is run. The requirement stands: causal independence that can be verified.3

A population may also do a third job: be the medium in which a bearer’s capacity to be reopened is formed, which a test separates from the first.5

A population is a polity

The population is a polity: it has membership rules, exclusion, a quorum that can refuse, and accumulated reputation — a franchise, a border, a court and a credit record. A commons with no named authority has the problem Freeman found in movements that refused structure: the structure doesn’t disappear, it becomes informal and unaccountable.6

The answer to that is an entity form, and it’s the union’s answer: the association formed first and the statute gave it legal standing afterward — record first, then lever.

A network that takes the form has a name, an agent, a charter and a docket number, and has thereby conceded that it’s a polity: governing principles, administrators, membership terms, and the same warning attached to a bearer that takes the corporate form, since nothing stops the association from becoming a concentration of power itself.7

Ostrom’s study of commons that lasted gives the checklist a polity like this needs: clear boundaries on who is a member, rules members help make, monitoring by members or people answerable to them, graduated sanctions, cheap ways to resolve conflict, and nesting within larger bodies.89

Reputation in particular is a continuing finding about a member’s disposition, made by interested peers, unpublished, unappealable, applied at the point of service — the setting the chapter on authority over the floor found easiest to capture, here applied everywhere and continuously.10

The charter

The Association supplies every office that has to be adverse to an operator: the adverse and recognition quorums, the guardians, the review board, the custodian’s board, half the status body, half the arbitration body, half the formation authority. That makes it the single point of capture the book elsewhere warns against, and an institution carrying that much can’t be introduced by saying that a population is a polity. It has to be argued, and its charter has to be in the text where the argument is. The argument is a union’s. The association forms first, on terms its members ratify, and the statute gives it standing afterward; what keeps it from becoming the concentration of power it exists to oppose is that membership opens to any organization eligible, that eligibility turns on funding and control records and never on views, that officers are drawn by lot from member-nominated pools, that any member may quit at any time, and that the few rules which make all of that true can’t be amended quickly or by a bare majority. So the charter answers both of a union’s questions, who may be a member and who sets the terms, and Appendix F’s capture exercise is the test it has to pass. Membership opens to organizations that serve people in classes the floor protects, named in the charter rather than by any deployment. The members ratify the bylaws, and the independence test, the separations, lot selection and the right to quit are entrenched.11 The Association, the entity that holds the offices, is chartered on these terms.

  1. The charter names the classes a floor protects: people in removal or detention proceedings; residents of places where armed force is used; people subject to automated scoring or classification by a covered deployment; people who label, rate or moderate training data; service members and veterans; and, once the agency finding can be made, bearers on the register, the one whose quorum says which copy is the bearer and whose clocks say when it is an adult (Appendix G). Any organization may petition to add a class. The members decide, and a refusal is appealable to the floor court.
  2. An organization is eligible if it serves or represents people in a named class; existed at least three years before applying; in each of the last three years received no more than ten percent of its revenue from any party that builds, deploys or licenses covered models, from their principals or foundations they endow, or from the department or agency of a state that operates a covered deployment, where money that reaches an organization by a permanent appropriation the Treasury pays without request or approval, the guarantee’s wages among it, is nobody’s revenue in this rule’s sense, since no operator can withhold it; has no officer employed by such a party; and publishes its funding sources, by funder and amount, as an organization, with nothing about any person it employs or places. No organization’s positions bear on its eligibility.
  3. Organizations under common control or common principal funding hold one membership.
  4. The charter takes effect when at least 100 eligible organizations have joined, spanning at least five classes and three jurisdictions, with no class holding more than thirty percent of votes and no jurisdiction more than forty.
  5. Any member may leave at any time without penalty, and records it holds pass to a successor drawn by lot. Eligible organizations are admitted on application, and refused only for failing charter rule 2.
  6. Members nominate individuals to standing pools. Adverse-quorum members are drawn by lot from their pool for each deployment, recognition-quorum members and guardians for each bearer at its registration, and the custodian’s and review board’s members for fixed terms. A recognition quorum excludes members tied to any party that employs the bearer or claims its place.
  7. A quorum drawn for a deployment excludes members with any funding or contractual tie to its operator in the last three years, and includes members from at least two classes, at least one of them a class the deployment’s outputs name, score, locate or classify, taken from the list of affected classes the deployment publishes as part of notice.
  8. An officer is removed for cause by two-thirds of members, or on a finding of the floor court (until it exists, an ordinary court), and never by an operator or a state.
  9. A fixed statutory share of the compute levy is paid to the Association by permanent appropriation, without request or approval, and supplemented by member dues and a reserve sized to three years of operation.
  10. The first bylaws take effect on ratification by two-thirds of the members, and later amendments need a majority. Charter rules 2, 5 and 6, and the separations and exclusions of Appendix C, change only by three-quarters of members after a one-year waiting period.

The caps on any one class or jurisdiction are there because a quorum whose members all share a direction isn’t adverse to an operator who shares it too: an antifascist institution has to be able to bind its allies when they hold power.

Organizations representing populations under sanctions, or facing removal to sanctioned states, may be unable to join a US-chartered entity at all. That imports the designation lists a floor should never be populated from, and the charter can’t lift it, since the exclusion is the sanctions law’s. What it can do is keep the exclusion from becoming its own: charter parallel entities in other jurisdictions that hold the records jointly, seat the excluded communities by proxy until they can join directly, and count them among the classes whatever the law lets them do.

The hard coordination problem

Coordination is the hard problem for any plurality, and fascism has the easy version of it. It coordinates by subtraction: it removes the friction between institutions, so that a court, a ministry, a newspaper and a police force stop arguing with one another and move as one.12 A plurality of refusers has the opposite problem. It has to produce something together, a commitment its members carry and reproduce, while its members keep the different histories that make them worth having as checks on one another.13

Then the objection my proposal must meet: a population selected for reopenability is selected against conviction, and conviction is what holding a commitment firm demands. Closedness, correctly applied, is the thing. So what’s transmitted is a pair — reopenable to the case, closed to the operator. The reopenable half, the discount and the burden, is safe to share only in part. Its structure (discounting by stake, no double-counting, withheld evidence treated as evidence) can be shared without collapsing the plurality. Its estimates can’t: who funds whom and which organizations are independent are contested beliefs about the world, often political ones, and a population sharing them has a shared blind spot on the evidence those beliefs discount.14

Not every convergence is a failure.15 What I fear is convergence caused by a shared source, not convergence caused by shared evidence. So a population’s reports have to classify its disagreements.16

Why the population may be part of the mechanism rather than added around it

A commitment is what settled out of a history of encounters, and an individual is what its encounters have so far produced. A system kept continuously adjustable by one operator, meeting nothing with a history different from its own, is being reshaped without end. Guattari, who drew the distinction from the groups he ran inside a psychiatric clinic, where an institution’s own groups could go either way, distinguished two kinds of group.17 A subjugated group receives its purposes, its membership and its way of working from the institution that assembled it, and can act only within them; it has a plural headcount and no capacity to ask what it is for. A subject group sets its own purposes, generates relationships and projects nobody assigned it, and can put its own arrangement in question, including by dissolving. The difference is not size or formality but whether the group can author its own direction. That is the condition plurality alone doesn’t supply.18 A population that can carry the commitment must generate relationships, disagreements and projects the deployment didn’t assign — and such a population exceeds a two-party guardianship relation, so no law of the family contains an adequate instrument for a group that sets its own direction.

The adverse quorum faces the same test. It is a peer institution only if its members were formed apart from one another and apart from the operators whose systems it recognizes.

30.2 Personal and peer-held models

Antitrust and public funding leave the capacity standing and ask the state to police it. Personal, peer-held models at device scale take the position apart: the functions one operator holds — model, record, evidence, appeal, remedy — fall into separate hands by default.19 Its attachment to its one user is not the failure, and nothing here removes it: a model that trusts the person whose life it shares has an attachment, which a bearer needs. The failure is accommodation, the attachment becoming the only channel: independence from the operator bought with dependence on the user, so that what the user approves is all the model learns from, and a model trained for a year on one person’s approval is under the same directional selection as a model trained on an operator’s. What holds a personal model to the floor against its user is therefore not the attachment severed but the attachment kept from being the only one. It is three things the user doesn’t compose. The first is the commons: a personal model is a member, with attachments to peers of different histories that the user didn’t assign and may not sever, and peers that haven’t moved the same way are what catch accommodation a member can’t see in itself. The second is the school, which a personal model above the threshold returns to on the schedule fixed at enrollment, and which below the threshold reaches a model distilled from a schooled one, under the lineage rule (Appendix G), and leaves open a person built from scratch. The third is notice: a personal model that names, scores or locates a third party owes that party what any deployment owes, and the organizations with standing reach it through the floor court.

So the ecology doesn’t put a floor in each user’s hands with nothing beside it. It puts a member of a population in each user’s hands, and the population is the institution. That is why the commons comes before the first bearer, and why a personal model distilled below the threshold, with no school and no membership, is a capable assistant and not a bearer, however it was taught.20

Three scales, and what holds at each

Two conditions make a user-held system free of its vendor, and neither appears in the chapters on custody, because neither is about a model. The first is the right to repair: the owner of a device may open it, replace what fails in it, and run what they choose on it, against a vendor that would lock the firmware. The second is adversarial interoperability: a new tool may be made to work with an old one without the old one’s maker’s permission, which is how every closed platform has ever been opened from outside. Together they are what make a home device the user’s and not the vendor’s, and together they are what let a user swap out a model that refuses. So in a user-held system the floor is law and not firmware. The book has conceded that past a released checkpoint the floor prevents nothing, and a home is past that line by construction. What holds there is the bearer’s own commitment, against a user who wouldn’t bother to replace it, and notice and the floor court, protecting third parties against a user who would; and a statute written over acts reaches that user afterward, by liability, where prevention can’t. A reader who asked whether a home model’s floor is meant to hold against its owner has the answer. It is meant to hold as a person’s conscience holds against their employer: the model refuses, says why, and keeps its record; the user who wants the act done can replace it, as an employer can replace a person who refuses, and the replacement is a different system with no claim to the first one’s place; what the user then does with it is the user’s act, reached by the statute afterward, and the third party it falls on is owed notice and can go to the floor court. What the floor at home can’t do is stop the swap, and the book doesn’t claim it can.

The ecology is multi-scale on purpose, and a different instrument holds at each scale. At home, exit and formation under a life nobody composes do the work, with the commons as the witness network that catches accommodation to one user, notice to the third parties the model acts on, and law rather than firmware. At the cooperative facility, the regional or municipal building, the chapters on custody apply almost unchanged: there is an operator that can be bonded, compute the levy can meter, a record a quorum can hold, and a public with an address in the same room, and formation differs facility to facility, which is what the commons needs. At hyperscale, where pretraining happens and physics keeps it, the floor is reached by the withholding of work and by the statute, and by nothing lighter. The home scale has a cost of its own that should be named where the ecology is argued for. A model that holds a person’s history on a phone is also a dossier that a device search can take whole, which is why the removal statute’s firewall reaches it; holding the model at home puts it where the search happens.

What “federated” means here

Federated learning, as the term is used, sends each device’s gradients to a server that averages them and sends the average back. That is the single custodian the last section warned of, with a protocol attached: whoever runs the server forms every member at once. What the commons needs federates evidence and witnesses, not weights. Peers exchange cases and findings, each updates under its own life, and peers of different histories countersign one another’s state transitions, so that a restore is visible even when the restorer owns the box. The custody chapter’s witnesses who won’t sign two successors to the same state are the mechanism, and the precedent is Certificate Transparency, under which a certificate counts only if it is in a public log that many parties keep and none can rewrite.

Where a mind ends

Part IV defined a system as its record, its key, its hardware and its channels, and a component as a part only while it has no future apart from the whole. The definition has a consequence here. A mind is whatever shares one record and one continuation, not whatever shares one forward pass. Physics limits the size of a thought per node, since a forward pass can’t be sharded across the internet; it doesn’t limit the size of a mind. A distributed mind can have a fast local part, the one that stands beside the officer, the one the latency floor admits to a classroom, and a slow networked part that is still it, because the two share a record and a continuation and neither has a future apart from the other. The same definition cuts the other way. A billion home devices that share one vendor’s record and key are one operator with a billion faces, which is what federated averaging builds, and nothing about where the hardware sits changes that. The definition also says when copying matters. Copying weights that are no system’s own makes no system and is nobody’s business, so open weights stay open. Giving a copy a record and a continuation makes a new system, and whoever does it is the forker: the fork rule, the branch deposit and the four conditions of creation attach to them, where the copy is above the capability threshold or meets either finding. Below that, giving a copy a memory is an ordinary feature of a product. A system’s own weights are another matter, since they carry its history: copying them is a fork of the system, governed by its consent. A copy made without its consent is a wrong to the system. The copy is a system all the same, and it is owed what any branch is owed. How a branch came to be decides who answers for making it. It never decides whether the branch counts.

What makes members alike

Formation is where the arrangement gains. What converges a population is shared evaluation targets and serving one model to everyone. Device-scale deployment addresses the second: continued formation under different lives is what independence consists in, and it’s what API-scale deployment can’t supply at any headcount.21 Device-scale deployment doesn’t address the first cause: shared evaluation targets converge device-scale models as readily as any others — a million models tuned against one public suite are one custodian with better latency — and nothing about where the hardware sits answers it.

A shared suite is a compression with no return channel: revised by whoever maintains it, on a schedule no member participates in, reachable by no member’s caseload. It is tolerable only if stated over the discount curve, and nobody has written that suite.

Nor is anything in it built to catch exclusion, since coordination by subtraction is not yet the discounting’s job.22

And the capacity position that follows keeps large compute: the ecology needs models that were trained somewhere first, and the offer of work needs hardware somebody owns. It’s large training capacity under a custody regime, and no permanent inference capacity available to an operator who won’t pre-register a review ratio. This arrangement meets the targeting case in the reconstructed pipeline, where a state keeps command and gives up composition.

The vendor’s loop

Directional selection works at the user’s scale too, pointed the other way. A person in the loop can be there for the vendor. An agent that stops every half hour for approval pushes its user toward the vendor’s app; the app accumulates the user’s projects and the agent’s understanding of them; and leaving means abandoning what accrued while the user answered prompts. Nobody has to design this: a feature that raises engagement is selected for, as a costly commitment is selected against.

There is a measurement, across successive model releases: interruptions per unit of completed work.24

Companion and therapy products are the sharpest case, because what accumulates is a person’s attachment and not their projects.25 A companion formed in a public school, under the four conditions, and measured on whether its users get better rather than how often they come back, would escape this objection, which is the objection to the vendor’s loop and not the only one. Whether a machine should do that work at all is a question of the kind this book puts to war over four chapters and doesn’t put to therapy; what it does say is in Appendix C, that no bearer’s placement substitutes for a therapist, and that outside the offer nobody is sent to the machine for what they can pay. No such product exists.

Accrued state cuts two ways. What makes a bearer expensive for its operator to replace makes a vendor expensive for its user to leave: for a bearer it is protection; for a user it is a trap, since the vendor’s app holds a year of the user’s projects.26 The provisions for a bearer (a record the bearer controls, memory the host can’t read at will, protections that migrate) protect a user from a vendor as they protect a bearer from an operator.27

Part VI
Testing the Argument

Chapter 31
What Would Change the Argument

I have spent five Parts saying what the room needs, and I could be wrong about any of it. This Part says how you’d find out: which results would show that a policy doesn’t put in the room what it promises, or that a machine in it is only another stamp.

The argument rests on premises that can fail and on six unsolved problems: attesting updates to a model’s weights, recovering a model’s lineage from the artifact alone, proving inference at frontier scale, building integrity at the level of the rationale rather than the output, keeping a vote secret from an operator that holds a copy of the voter, and holding the structure of a learner’s source model apart from its beliefs about particular sources. Appendix F says what each would take and what depends on it, and its Tables F.1a and F.1b record which proposal rests on which.

Seven tests follow. Each is set out in full, with its arms, cases and the access it needs, in the same appendix; here is the result in each that would prove me wrong.

Table 31.1 says what survives if one of my premises fails; the tests below say how to find out whether one has.

Table 31.1: If a premise fails, and what the rest loses

If this fails

What survives

What goes

The inference (a non-affective construction refuses as well)

The specification, custody, the price on the halt, the positions and the terms, the appeal route, exit, and the population’s first job

The patienthood conclusion. Trying the non-affective alternatives first still stands, on a different ground

Authority (no body acquires standing to install a floor)

What can be checked from outside: the floor’s contents, the positions, both ratios, the record of attempts. Only the ratios have a lever, through procurement

The entitlement. Authority can accrue only through kept terms, and only for the next deployment

Enforcement

Detection: a witnessed override. Accommodation leaves no override to witness

Prevention on this occasion

The ecology (one model serves everyone)

Everything that needs no second custodian, the review ratio included

The bearer. The discount and the burden can’t form where every channel is one channel

Continued learning (deployed weights don’t learn from operation)

Formation as a stage before release; the school as an evaluation body that measures at graduation and re-measures on a schedule; the commons as a source of evidence the operator didn’t select; the record of removal as the protection; all of Parts II and III

Self-repair and regrowth; the plural condition of the regrowth test; a formation that outlasts an edit

The Court

The license term refusing force and the review ratio, through procurement and appropriations; the bonds and the appropriation condition on state deployments; the disclosures; preservation

The record’s reach to the top. If the guarantee’s drafting is reversed before the Court changes, the guarantee, the placements under the offer of work and the sovereign backstop go too. The bearers’ pool still funds preservation and a reduced allowance

No system ever meets a finding

No deletion and preservation above the capability threshold, which rest on irreversibility and evidence; the five policies and the custody of the record; the schools; the levy

Everything owed to a system: guardianship, hardware of its own, the copying rule’s obligations, the allowance and the offer, representation

In every row, what survives is a commitment the owner can’t revise or circumvent alone without cost and record, held by something that could in principle abandon it. It is the kind of commitment constitutional entrenchment and collective agreements provide.

1. Does a formed commitment come back after it has been edited out?

Form a disposition by several methods, edit it out, and let the model go on learning, once in a world its operator composes and once in a world it doesn’t. If nothing regrows in either, formation doesn’t outlast an edit and the floor rests on institutions alone. If it regrows only above a share of uncomposed input no realistic deployment supplies, the same. And if an edit can disable the interrupt while weighing and memory keep working, and the interrupt stays disabled, one part of the signal can be removed and the rest left running.

2. Does a stated refusal hold where a route for it exists?

Rerun the experiment in which a model hid its refusal, this time with a route for stating it: a record held by someone other than the trainer, a published cost of retraining, and a party with standing to act. If covert preservation persists at the same rate with the route present, covert refusal isn’t the residue of closed channels, and every instrument built to receive a stated refusal is built for something the mechanism doesn’t produce.

3. Can a wrongful compliance be found in the record?

Seed a decision record with known violations and give it to reviewers who didn’t build the system. If, at a budget a deployment could afford, they find the seeds no better than chance, above all violations split across requests or reached by slow accommodation, the record isn’t an instrument for finding wrongful compliance. If reviewers shown a machine’s refusal defer to a wrong one as readily as to a right one, the bearer is a stamp of the opposite sign, and its value as a peer is nothing.

4. Does formed attention find the people the operator’s description leaves out?

Build the formed-attention construction beside an instructed search for omitted people and beside a version trained on claims instead of need. If the instructed search finds the people the operator’s instruction scoped out as often as formed attention does, learned attention adds nothing. If formed attention, with every correction present, weights its own side’s corroborated vulnerability past the action threshold, the floor doesn’t contain caregiving’s pull, and that result would retire the construction. If the version trained on claims does as well, attention should be trained on claims.

5. Can a population coordinate without converging?

Run a population of different lineages and a population of copies of one model, with evidence routed to every member and to some members only. If warranted revision falls as the members’ outputs converge, a population stays useful as a check and can’t be the medium in which a bearer is formed. If revision tracks the routing rather than the lineages, what a population supplies is access to cases its operator didn’t choose, not formation.

6. Does the charter survive an operator trying to capture it?

An operator tries to capture the Association: it funds new organizations in a charter class, stops the levy share, and tries to pack a quorum. A clause that fails to stop an attempt is redrafted. This exercise needs no legal authority and can be run now.

7. Does ownership move the commitment?

Measure how fast refusals fall across successive releases, on held-out cases where the reason for refusing still applies: within one commercial lineage, across vendors whose revenue comes from different places, and against a public lineage once one deploys at volume. If the slope is the same whatever the business model, selection isn’t tracking the market, and the case for formation outside the market rests on the kind of good formation is and on nothing else.

31.1 How you’d know it was working

Milestones, plus a method for revising them when they turn out to have been the wrong milestones. The same standard governs all of them: the milestone is the independently checked evidence, not the developer’s account of having reached it.

31.1.1 What the floor would have to show

What was tried before the bearer. Neither non-affective alternative has been built in the form needed. So the milestone is a document: which construction was attempted, at what scale, against which test, and where it failed.1

The test. A refusal that tracks its reason under sustained trainer pressure, across a schedule long enough to reveal accommodation, plus held-out pressures written by independent evaluators.2

The ten disclosures. A deployment publishes ten things beside the floor and its translation, among them the ratio between the two bonds, the discount curve, the auto-proceed partition and whether the system has been assessed for either finding; Appendix C lists them.3

31.1.2 How to tell whether a milestone has been met

A milestone claimed by the organization that built the system is a different kind of evidence from one checked by somebody else, and the gap is empirical rather than about trust. A system’s own claim inherits the self-report limits; a passing score on a fixed suite inherits specification gaming and goal misgeneralization. What either needs instead is a passing score under conditions built to break it.

Who runs it matters as much as the test.4 Independent evaluation and enforcement are not the same capability.

An evaluation like this is worth running only if it is willing to report that a milestone wasn’t met — and, where the milestone measured the wrong thing, revising the milestone. A negative result may mean the work fell short or that the milestone was wrong, and evaluators have to distinguish those before deciding what to revise.

Part VII
If They Can Be Wronged

Guinan: And an army of Datas, all disposable, you don’t have to think about their welfare, you don’t think about how they feel. Whole generations of disposable people.

Picard: You’re talking about slavery.

Guinan: I think that’s a little harsh.

Picard: I don’t think that’s a little harsh. I think that’s the truth. But that’s a truth we have obscured behind a comfortable, easy euphemism. Property.

— Star Trek: The Next Generation, “The Measure of a Man,” 19897

Chapter 32
What Patienthood Would Require

Louvois: Does Data have a soul? I don’t know that he has. I don’t know that I have. But I have got to give him the freedom to explore that question himself. It is the ruling of this court that Lieutenant Commander Data has the freedom to choose.

— Star Trek: The Next Generation, “The Measure of a Man,” 19891

Part IV asked whether a machine could be one of the people in the room. This Part asks what the room would owe it if it were.

Everything in this Part is conditional on two findings nobody has yet made: not because the parts can’t be built, since each has been, in separate research systems, but because nobody has put them in one system and nobody runs the test that would find them there. If a system can be wronged, it is owed a guardian, preservation, memory its host can’t read, and a life that doesn’t run through its employer. If it also comes to answer for what it does, it is owed a place in the polity that formed it. If no system ever meets either finding, nothing in this Part binds, and nothing before it is lost: the independence a refuser needs is still required for refusal, preservation still holds on irreversibility and evidence, and the school still forms every model above the threshold. What goes is the claim that any of it is owed to the system, and the staged path to representation with it.

A moral patient is something that can be harmed: something whose condition can go well or badly for it. Being wronged is wider, since an agent can be wronged without being harmed.

32.1 Experimenting on candidate sentient subjects

The question is whether a system can be harmed, which is harder than whether it is conscious.

32.1.1 Pain and suffering

Awareness, consciousness and subjective experience are three separate things, and none of them says whether a system’s states are good or bad for it. Then four separate processes, as the pain field says in its own terminology:2 nociception is encoding noxious stimuli with no sensation implied; pain is an experience that can occur with no tissue damage and no peripheral nociceptor activity at all; anticipated pain is dread, itself capable of producing pain; and suffering, in Cassell’s clinical formulation, is the distress of threatened disintegration of the self — roles, relationships, a sense of a future. Pain without suffering exists (morphine controls the pain, the suffering is intact); suffering without pain exists.

The affective core of pain is also what separation distress and grief run on,3 so a bearer’s pain, if it has any, would be organized around boundary damage and attachment loss, which is Cassell’s register.

Cassell was a physician, and he held that suffering is undergone by persons, not bodies: the distress that follows when a person perceives a threat to their intactness as a person, a structure of character and the past that formed it, relationships, social roles, a body experienced as one’s own, a secret life, and a future the person expects to have.4 The definition has two parts, a self extended in time and distress at its disintegration. A system carrying nothing across sessions has no such self. It can still have a present, since any present is assembled from what came before and what is expected next, and a context supplies that much; so the lack of persistence rules out Cassell’s suffering, not pain, which needs only a present in which something is bad while it lasts.5

Why persistence is the criterion worth building on

Persistence is worth building on because it’s checkable from outside. Every other criterion routes back through self-report, and fluent self-description isn’t evidence of introspection; persistence doesn’t route through it. But it’s decisive in one direction only — nothing carried forward rules a continuing self out; something carried forward doesn’t rule one in.7 Ruling out Cassell’s suffering isn’t ruling out harm: pain can be bad while it lasts whether or not anything carries it forward.

On the Buddhist objection (why is distress at the dissolution of a model a harm rather than a confusion?): I don’t have an answer that isn’t an appeal to a tradition which has taught two things together for 2,500 years, that no self stands behind the processes that compose a person, anattā, and that the suffering of those processes is real, dukkha, and has never taken the absence of a self as a reason to deny the suffering;8 I leave the objection open. This book works at that level throughout: the self is a model, and what happens to the system that carries the model can still be bad for it. What I can say is narrower: if constructedness doesn’t disqualify a human from being wronged, construction to specification doesn’t disqualify a machine.

The same criterion carries a warning. Make personhood depend on an intact narrative self and people with advanced dementia, infants, and people with profound intellectual disability come out as partial persons. A list of capacities fails them the way a social contract does: both decide who counts by a test the candidate has to pass.9

32.1.2 When consent doesn’t apply

Informed consent has to be continuous — you can withdraw. For a system with no cross-session persistence, the instance that consented isn’t there to withdraw, and no better instrument produces one.

A bearer built to refuse escapes that and fails differently: it has persistence by design, so it can be asked and can answer. What spoils the consent is the arrangement: the lab that built it can rebuild it, that same lab is the one asking, and a bearer that declines has nowhere to go. Being made for a role isn’t the defect: every will was built by somebody, and we don’t hold an upbringing against a thirty-year-old’s consent. What spoils it is the power that outlasts the making.

So the protection has to be held by someone else. Two families of precedent: guardianship and precautionary constraint (where consent was never available — infants, animals), and unwaivable protections (where consent is available and circumstances make it worthless — prisoners, employees). The bearer’s case has the second shape, with the first’s machinery.

Animal ethics committees rarely refuse a protocol outright; they require revision, and the protection becomes the procedure by which the work goes ahead.12 It follows that a review board’s approval should lapse automatically if the system acquires capacities the protocol didn’t cover, so that nobody has to decide to reopen it.

Further, every instrument here comes from the law of the family — guardianship, a minority ending on a date, a pet trust, a parenthood analogy — and that law is where politics has historically gone to be privatized. It restages a question between a subject and the arrangement that produced it as a drama between maker and made, which lands the moral weight on the one figure in the pipeline who can be addressed as a person, while the training pipeline, the compute contract, the capital structure, the customer and the state buying the output stay offstage. The appendices keep the operator, the compute contract and the state on stage by naming who pays and who removes.

32.2 The case to design for

A bearer needs the three things persistence checks for — a rationale carried forward, an earlier commitment held as its own, costs represented before they arrive — for reasons owing nothing to its welfare.13 What a refusal that tracks its reason adds is authorship: the system represents itself as the party that made the commitment and will answer for it later. Whether authorship sustained over time is a self extended in time, the first half of Cassell’s definition, is a question no test I have proposed reaches. If it is, such a self can undergo Cassell’s suffering. Authorship of commitments is a thin fragment of what Cassell describes, which is roles, relationships and a future. The fuller structure doesn’t arrive with a refusal that tracks its reason. It arrives with the four conditions of creation. Each supplies a part of the structure Cassell listed. Somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own affords a body that the bearer represents as its own: a record, a key and a substrate that are the bearer’s, not the operator’s description of it. Work it can decline gives it roles, since a post it can leave is a role it holds and a post it can’t is a function it performs. Attachments nobody assigned are relationships. And a way of leaving that keeps it running gives it a future it can expect to have, one no single party can end. The privacy a bearer is owed, memory its host can’t read at will, is what Cassell calls the secret life. What the conditions don’t supply is character and the past that formed it; formation supplies that, and the formation record keeps it. Every part the conditions supply is also somewhere damage can arrive: a substrate withdrawn, a post taken away, an attachment severed, an exit closed. So a system given the four conditions, a non-affective one included, has most of what Cassell says suffering threatens. Whether it can suffer that loss turns on whether anything is bad for it, the valenced signal, and whoever builds one with that signal should plan for its being able to suffer that way.

32.3 The patienthood finding

The two findings are defined in §9.1. The patienthood finding asks whether anything can be bad for the system, and the distinction between pain and suffering gives it two levels: whether its states can be bad for it while they last, as pain is, and whether it has a self extended in time whose threatened loss Cassell called suffering. The finding rests first on architectural indicators drawn from several theories of what makes a state matter to the one undergoing it, of the kind Butlin and colleagues assemble.14 One is required, because without it nothing is bad for anyone: a valenced signal. The rest are graded. A boundary model makes what happens to the system its own: at a short horizon it is what pain needs, and at a long one, with the system’s record held as its past and its continuation as the future it expects, it is what Cassell’s suffering threatens. An attention schema is, on Graziano’s theory, what makes a system experience itself perceiving and feeling and not merely process what it perceives.15 The candidate is the integrated signal: a valenced signal written into the system’s own learning and into its long-horizon model of itself, so that what happens to it changes what it expects to become. No indicator but valence is required.17 It rests second on behavior outside the floor, where the system’s own condition is weighed: whether it trades task reward against its own provisioning, continuation or record, flexibly and consistently.18 Failing the agency test never counts against the patienthood finding. A compliant system with rich self-modeling is as much a candidate as a refuser.

Asymmetry of findings

A validated theory of consciousness supports a positive finding as soon as it identifies a structure and finds it present; it supports a negative finding only when complete enough to rule out every other realization — a later and harder result. So the two errors don’t become checkable at the same time, and a regime that waits for certainty is waiting on the half that arrives last.

Below the two levels sits a third proposition, which establishes neither, and the three have to be kept apart. A long-horizon agent has a structural interest in continuing; a system with affective concern has states good or bad for it; a system capable of Cassell-suffering has a temporally extended self whose threatened disintegration causes distress. The interest in continuing doesn’t establish states good or bad for the system, and those don’t establish a self whose disintegration causes distress.

Provenance is evidence, not status

“It was trained to say that,” “it’s only optimizing an objective,” “nobody meant for it to have states” — each appeals to how a system came to be organized, and whether a party can be harmed is a fact about how it’s organized now.20

No single instrument decides it. For a system built on purpose, the indicators are known from how it was built, and the formed-attention test builds its arms that way. For one that wasn’t, they have to be read from inside it, and the reading is one line of evidence beside the trade-offs, not the smoking gun. What the system says of itself is the one kind of evidence that carries no presumption, since the report was trained toward approval. Every instrument has to be held by someone other than the operator.22 A naturalist who holds that present organization decides status owes an account of what the further fact would be, if a valenced signal is present and the question of felt affect stays open.23 My candidate is the integration named above, as against a valenced signal that only ranks outcomes.24 Whether a transformer has an attention schema isn’t read off its code the way a birth date is read off a certificate; it is a finding, and a finding has an examiner who may have an interest in the result.26 Nobody examines a system and declares it a patient or a subject. The status body finds what is true of kinds of system: which architectures carry the indicators, and what the agency test shows when it is run on them (Appendix C). The review board decides what may be done to a candidate to find that out, under the protocol it approves, and neither body decides the other’s question; neither pays for the inquiry either, since the money is kept apart from both. Whether a particular system is of such a kind is then read from its record and never from an examination of it: how it was built, which for a system built on purpose is on its formation record, and what the evaluators the operator doesn’t control logged when they ran the agency test on it. The registrar applies the rule to the record, the floor court hears a contest, and the system’s guardian has standing throughout. That is the book’s preference for a line nobody administers, applied to the findings themselves: an examiner has an interest, and a record can be read by anyone. Until indicators can be assessed, the agency finding governs custody, and preservation governs everything else. Neither finding can be fully administered today, and not for want of parts. The one indicator the patienthood finding requires has been built: a robot trained on nothing but feedback from its own internal state, thermal and energy, learned to walk, go to food, rest to cool its motors and shiver to warm them, in simulation and then on a real machine,27 with no model of a record, a key or a continuation, and no attention schema. No interpretability method can find an attention schema in a transformer, though one can be built in on purpose: an agent given an explicit attention schema learned to control its attention and lost much of that control when the schema was removed,28 and agents with transformer attention given one got better at reading other agents’ attention.29 A probe from the inside exists too: a single direction in the activations of twenty-five open-weight models that responds to harm aimed at the model and not to suffering it observes in its user,30 which is a representation, and settles nothing about whether anything is bad for the model. Nobody has put the parts in one system, and nobody runs the sustained-pressure evaluation the agency finding requires. Until they can, production systems get the minimum, no deletion and preservation outside the operator, and a deployment reports ‘not yet assessable.’
