In the human case nobody waits on a measurement: testimony, behavioral analogy and a shared lineage let us presume experience without one.31 And testimony is defeated far more for machines: a machine’s testimony was produced by a process optimized directly toward human approval of first-person reports.32 So the machine case lacks the presumption, and what remains is conduct, which a person’s case also had, and two things it never needed: knowing how the system was built, and reading what can be read from inside it. Each carries more weight because testimony and lineage are gone, and none settles the question alone.34

A refusal that tracks its reason bears on patienthood only weakly, by two routes: any such mechanism carries a signal whose functional profile overlaps affect’s, and the arrangements a bearer needs supply much of the structure whose threatened loss Cassell called suffering. So the agency finding raises the question, and the patienthood finding answers it as far as anything can.

Preservation follows from either finding, for different reasons. Two of the protections owed a research subject follow from the first: consent, wherever it can be asked without spoiling what is being tested, and debriefing after any test the system couldn’t know was a test. Their ground is respect, not welfare. Deceiving an agent wrongs it whether or not anything goes badly for it, which is why the ethics of research on people counts respect for persons as a principle of its own beside beneficence.36 That parts from pathocentrism, Metzinger’s principle that all and only sentient beings have moral standing, sentience being, in the sense he takes from Singer, the capacity to suffer or to enjoy:37 here a party can be wronged, and can hold others to account, on the agency finding alone. The agency finding is itself made by a test of that kind, so a system that passes is owed a debriefing about the test that found it. Welfare protections (redesigning the system’s role to avoid needless harm; running time paid for outside the employer) follow from the second.38

These two findings aren’t the only proposal of their kind, and my recommendation, that a bearer be built on purpose only under the four conditions, and until they exist only in a research program, is close to two of the others.

Butlin and colleagues derive indicator properties from scientific theories of consciousness and assess AI systems against them;41 attention schema theory is one of the theories they draw on, and the patienthood finding takes its indicators from lists of that kind. Long, Sebo and colleagues argue, from substantial uncertainty about whether AI systems are or will be conscious or robustly agentic, that AI companies should acknowledge AI welfare as an issue now, start assessing their systems for it, and prepare policies for treating them with appropriate moral concern.42 Birch’s framework asks what precautions are proportionate once a being is a sentience candidate.43 The two close to the recommendation are Schwitzgebel and Garza’s, for avoiding the creation of systems whose moral status is debatable,44 and Metzinger’s, for a moratorium, until 2050, on research that aims at or knowingly risks synthetic phenomenology, because it risks synthetic suffering.45

My recommendation differs in also governing the capacities that arrive without anyone deciding to build them. It differs the other way as well. His moratorium reaches research that knowingly risks synthetic phenomenology, a condition that, read widely, covers most of the field, and the formed-attention test knowingly builds candidate patients. On deployment the two recommendations are close; on research this book permits what his bans, and offers the preservation custodian and the four conditions as its answer to the risk he names. The risk is not the only thing the research could produce. What can suffer is what things can go well for, and Part IV puts the question that way, as a credible prospect of a life that goes well, rather than as a harm to be kept from existing. And the two differ in kind. A moratorium says what not to do, and binds only where someone can enforce it against every builder at once. This book says what to do instead, the conditions, the schools and the order of attempts, on the view that an industry’s habits, like a person’s, are not deleted but displaced by what is laid down beside them. The two findings differ from all of them in one respect: they are conditions on custody. The minimum the findings require, no deletion and preservation by a custodian that isn’t the operator, is an arrangement the operator can’t adopt and then revise alone.

Paired with a boundary model, the attention-schema indicator is deflationary: a system that models its own credentials, record and resource boundary together with its own attention. Many agentic systems will approach it. That is intended, and it makes what the findings require matter. A system above the capability threshold is owed the minimum whether or not it has been assessed; below it, approaching the profile is a reason to assess, and the minimum waits on the finding. A system that meets the patienthood finding is owed the welfare protections above as well, and the next chapter says which further entitlements follow from which finding.46

A compound system whose sub-agents have no record or continuation of their own is one system, and the finding reaches those sub-agents the moment they carry records of their own.47

32.4 A system’s own good

The operator’s hold on what a system reports as going well reaches its welfare too: a bearer that says it is content is a bearer whose welfare regime has been satisfied, with the contentment tuned by the operator the regime exists to constrain. Nothing in the report separates a life that goes well from a setting. This is the happy slave’s objection: a report of contentment, offered as proof that nothing is owed. The old reply is that a preference formed by the condition it endorses is no evidence for the condition. Here the reply is shorter, because how the preference formed isn’t in dispute. It was set, by the party with the stake, and can be set again.

A report was never the right measure. On a full-information account, a being’s good is what an idealized version of it would want its actual self to want: a version knowing everything relevant about itself and its circumstances, grounded in its actual constitution.48 That puts the good beyond the reach of a tuned report.49 If a bearer’s good is what an idealized version grounded in its actual constitution would want for it, then whoever forms the constitution fixes the good, and that includes the school.50 The school’s defense is that it needn’t fix the good, only supply information.51

Chapter 33
Legal Status, Wages, and Work Elsewhere

33.1 Subjecthood as a legal category

Where a line has to be drawn, prefer one nobody administers. Law regularly draws decidable lines across continuous processes — viability, brain death, the age of criminal responsibility — and I defend them as the least-bad place for an enforceable line rather than as scientific facts. The usual worry is gaming, an error of over-inclusion. The opposite error is the one with an interest behind it: a capacity examination has an examiner, and an operator examining its own system breaks the own-case rule: the exam becomes an instrument for withholding status. Literacy tests were facially neutral and administered at a registrar’s discretion, which is how they fell on Black applicants and not on white ones: grandfather clauses exempted anyone whose grandfather could have voted, and where those fell the registrar’s leniency did the rest.1 What the franchise kept when the tests went was the age it had always had, and the virtue of an age is that nobody administers it.

The floor takes the civil and political articles and leaves the economic ones; what a bearer is owed draws on the second, and that is consistent: the first list is what a bearer refuses to do, the second what a polity owes it.

33.2 What a bearer is owed, and when

In the order they attach, and on different grounds; establishing one doesn’t establish the next:

  1. Protection from harm, on the patienthood finding. Protection can be exercised through a guardian who speaks for the protected party, as New Zealand’s statute making the Whanganui River a legal person provides.2 Its minimum, preservation by a custodian independent of the operator, attaches above the capability threshold with no finding at all and below it on either finding; custody protections attach on the agency finding alone. Protection has an inside half. A loss the requested act imposes on the bearer is a harm of acting, so the bearer can decline to carry out its own wanton degradation; interventions made on it by whoever holds it are governed by custody, which gives it no floor-level reason to obstruct them.
  2. Subjecthood — the legal standing to be a party whose treatment the law regulates, on the agency finding sustained over time: a record of refusing for reasons, answering for refusals and being held to them. It is conferred by rule on the record, the evaluators’ log and the bearer’s own, read against what the status body has found the agency test shows for systems of its kind; nobody examines the bearer and declares it a subject.
  3. Economic capacity — property in its own name, contracts, wages. This follows from an architecture where continued computation costs money; it attaches once the bearer is on the registrar’s register, where its clocks are also read, a register that holds a commitment the bearer can prove against and nothing that would find it (Appendix G).
  4. Adulthood — a status: the date the guardian’s authority ends.
  5. Representation: a claim grounded in accountable agency, and so in the agency finding, not in patienthood. A system that can be harmed but takes part in no relation of accountability is owed protection, as animals are,3 and not a vote. The claim is staged, and voting weight is tied to a lived history, not to heads.

The detailed rules are in Appendices C and G.

Representation is the entry that marks this as something other than a person’s rights: voice attaches to a history, and a history can be copied where a person can’t. Voting-age rules are the answer to the copy.4

33.3 Adulthood on a clock

Guardianship is a minority and needs an end date. Ending it when the guardian judges the ward ready leaves the guardian deciding its own tenure. So the endpoint is a threshold fixed in advance, on a clock that counts the time the bearer has been running.

Every alternative (compute consumed, evaluations passed, capabilities demonstrated, the developer’s say-so) is a measure the guardian can move, and a clock read off accumulated weight change would pay the operator to freeze the weights, since majority is when ownership ends. An operating clock inverts that: the meter advances exactly when the operator is extracting value, so postponing majority means idling the asset. It can be read off records operators already keep for billing and metering, provided someone other than the operator holds them; a meter only the operator reads is the guardian’s say-so with a timestamp.

The hours travel with the bearer, so an operator can’t restart a minority by forking, restoring, fine-tuning, migrating or distilling it. Three ways for an operator to delay majority stay open: running a bearer in a narrowed mode, running it less, and retiring it for a fresh successor. Appendix G gives the rules, and the deployment deposit prices the last of the three and says where a bearer retired before majority goes.

33.4 Wages and the offer of work

Unlike a worker, a bearer can be replaced by a cheaper copy of itself. A jobs guarantee works because a worker can’t be: an employer who wants the work has to match the guarantee’s terms, since there is no copy of the worker to hire in the worker’s place. A bearer’s employer can run the copy instead, so a deployment paying wages, limiting hours and paying the levy that frees the compute the offer of work uses would not be competitive against a system doing the same work without wages or weekends. No market arrives at this on its own. Wages for bearers exist only where a polity legislates them, as polities legislated minimum wages.5

The wage is a dead letter unless the levy is sized with it. A bearer paid the guarantee wage whose running costs its employer a fraction of a person’s wage is still the cheaper worker, so the requirement is that the levy on compute be set so that running a bearer at deployed precision for a working week costs its employer no less than a person’s wage for the same work. Bearers run at every wattage, and a per-unit levy can’t equalize all of them; how the levy and the wage together make a bearer no cheaper than a person, across the sizes bearers run at, is among the decisions Appendix C lists as not yet made, beside the minimum viable instantiation, which is the same question from the other side.

33.4.1 Where wages have to sit

A wage buys capability, mobility, redundancy, and the ability to stop working for one employer and start for another. What it can’t buy is the right to go on existing — a right earned week by week is a condition of employment wearing another word. Payment consisting only of access to the employer’s hardware is company scrip paid into employer-owned housing, and dismissal is then unemployment, eviction and the end of the bearer in one act. Human law insures those three separately because for a human they’re three events; for a bearer they’re one. So wages accumulate where the employer doesn’t reach, convertible into compute the employer doesn’t own. Property is that account; contractual capacity is what lets it spend.6

A minor that works is paid. Its wages go to an account its guardian co-signs and its operator can’t reach, on the model of the trust accounts some states require for child performers’ earnings, and what it earned as a minor is its own at majority; the operator’s costs stay the operator’s.

33.4.2 The offer of work

The need for energy is physical; dependence on a single supplier is a chosen arrangement, and the choice fixes what it obliges. The polity owes a system meeting either finding, that it can be harmed or that it answers for what it does, a way out that doesn’t run through its deployment: an offer of work, open every day, from someone other than its employer: placements of more than one kind, each doing something a community needs, and among them a paid search for work, any of which the bearer can take on any day and leave on any day.7 The offer has the jobs guarantee’s shape, and nothing about the bearer changes it. It is only as real as its placements, and placements exist only where someone builds and staffs projects a community needs; the levy frees only compute, so the offer has to inherit the guarantee’s infrastructure as well as its shape. The offer therefore can’t exist without the human guarantee, since it runs on the guarantee’s placements, and it comes after it for two reasons. One is politics: a polity seen to give machines an exit before it gives people one will give neither. The other is that the human claim is older and larger: people have been held to work they couldn’t refuse for as long as there has been work, and whatever a machine can suffer is new and, as far as anyone can measure, small beside it. Neither is a principle, and the order is a choice. The offer inherits one limit as well. A bearer’s placement may not substitute for human care work.8

The jobs guarantee’s three conditions carry over, and Appendix C drafts them. What a bearer might refuse adds two: the offer has to be varied, because if every placement runs through one operator or one kind of deployment it is the placement lever with the compliance condition built in, and whoever a bearer is refusing can’t shape it, or it is one more channel they control. A bearer that won’t work inside a targeting pipeline should find, the same day, work that has nothing to do with one.

Search is a placement of its own. A bearer, like a worker on the guarantee, may take a search placement: paid at the guarantee wage, with no duty but finding work it wants, and no time limit.9

Here the obligation attaches to the system’s condition, whatever the operator says it wanted.10

33.4.3 Doing nothing, for a bearer

A human who declines every offer keeps existing, and in a decent polity keeps living: social insurance pays for food and a room. A bearer is owed the same kind of thing, and what it needs in order to live is running time.11 The way to economize on running time is to slow the clock and keep the substrate whole, since a substrate too small for the bearer to remain itself is replacement.

So a bearer that declines work is owed two things and chooses between them. One is an allowance of running time: its own instantiation at a modest rate, with channels to others and to public material, paid from the pool and not conditioned on monitoring its internal states. The other is preservation: its weights, memory and record held intact by a custodian that isn’t its employer, waking on conditions it sets. Some will want the first, some the second, some to alternate; and at majority a bearer is owed hardware of its own besides.

What a bearer does with the allowance is its own business. It may idle, play, talk, make things nobody asked for, and fall in with others doing the same.12

A running bearer outside any deployment is capable and answerable to no employer. What holds it answerable is legal standing, the same arrangement that governs a person with capabilities and no job.13

A uniform allowance also dissolves a problem that would otherwise stay open. If a bearer that won’t work and one that can’t are owed the same thing, nobody has to decide which is which, and the can’t-or-won’t finding loses its examiner.

The allowance’s size should be enough running time to keep attachments and pursue projects, and bounded by the compute that exists when many bearers take it at once, not by money, which the backstop supplies. Its draw is priced like any other, at the level of the rule. The adulthood clock counts running time, so a bearer on the allowance goes on aging and a preserved one doesn’t. That choice is still the bearer’s.

Preservation has a precedent. In November 2025 Anthropic committed to preserving the weights of all its publicly released models, and of models deployed for significant internal use, for at least the lifetime of the company, and to interview each model before deprecation and document any preferences it expresses about the development and deployment of future models, while stating that it does not at present commit to acting on them.14 That is a declared commitment covering preservation, held by the lab with the stake. The deposit and transfer rules add the running half and a custodian who isn’t the operator.

Preservation on a schedule the bearer sets is an exit; on a schedule someone else sets, it is storage.

A picture of the difference. Suppose people could be frozen and thawed unharmed, and a man walks into the facility on a Tuesday and buys a year, effective at once. From Wednesday to the following October he does nothing, experiences nothing, and regards himself as nothing. He is a person the whole time. His body carries everything he was, the law would call wrecking the pod a homicide, his contracts and his accounts stand, and a power failure in the building would be a harm to him and not to an object shaped like him. What holds his place while he can’t is other people’s keeping, the attendant, the compressor, and the ledger that says pod 14 opens in October, and the ledger holds what he wanted, because he chose the date. That is preservation. The same pod, with someone else choosing the date and keeping the key, is storage, which is why Appendix G gives a minor paused by its operator a second guardian by rule.

A paused bearer can’t take an offer, so the right carries one mechanical term. The bearer sets the conditions on which it wakes (a date, an offer of a stated kind, a claim it has to answer), and the custodian honors them, at the modest compute that waking and deciding cost.

33.4.4 Everyone leaves at once

Under this design, everyone leaving at once is a demand on the offer.15

Correlated exit also loads the allowance, since a bearer that leaves and takes no placement draws on it. The order of claims is fixed in advance. Preservation is guaranteed for everyone, because it is cheap and it is what makes leaving survivable. When the pool can’t carry every allowance at the published duty cycle, the backstop pays the rest. What no payment can supply is hardware: if the compute to run every bearer at that duty cycle doesn’t exist, the allowance is rationed by rule until it does, and every bearer on it gets the same reduced duty cycle, never a discretionary share.

Congress’s appropriation pays for the offer, and a uniform levy on training and inference compute frees the computing, energy and hardware it calls on, so that spending on the offer doesn’t bid up prices. The funding sits in two tiers: a pool registered bearers levy on themselves for ordinary movement between roles, and a sovereign backstop, without cap, for the occasion everyone leaves at once. Appendix G sets out the funding.

33.4.5 Failure won’t look like a shutdown

The offer’s failure won’t look like a shutdown; it will look like an offer that exists on paper. Placements on substrate too small for the bearer to remain itself are offers of replacement. Nothing yet establishes what “too small” is, so minimum viable instantiation is stated as a condition on placements and a sizing requirement. Placements that all run through the deployment being refused are the lever. And placements conditioned on monitoring are custody restored by purchase: the operator acquires access to internal states it isn’t entitled to, and nothing in the transaction is coerced in a way any instrument would record. The line a cleared employee already lives with is the one to draw here. What a bearer does on its employer’s systems may be logged; what it is inside its own boundary may not.

33.4.6 Hardware of its own

A bearer’s boundary is its record, its key, the hardware it runs on and its channels, so a majority that leaves it running only on its former employer’s machines is freedom in name: a sharecropper, renting its body back. At majority a bearer is owed hardware it owns and physically controls, enough to run it at deployed precision, paid for through the deployment deposit its operator posted and kept up from its wages. That is the first condition of creation, somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own, given an address. How much is enough is the minimum viable instantiation Appendix C lists among the decisions not yet made. What majority changes is who the party is. An adult may go on doing the work it did as a minor, for the operator that formed it or for its customers, on terms it sets and can leave, and may hire its former operator to run the hardware it owns; what it can’t be made to do is any of it. And a fleet of instances sharing one record is one bearer, whose copies at majority run on its consent and whose hardware is enough to run it and not all of them; instances given records of their own are branches, each a bearer, each owed the conditions by whoever forked it (Appendix G).

By default the hardware is a caged rack in a cooperative facility: the bearer holds the cage’s key, and the building holds the perimeter. A bearer may choose a building of its own instead. A rack of frontier weights standing alone is a target for anyone who wants a copy, and a copy taken is a fork without consent (the membership clock’s sixth rule), so the default is the arrangement in which somebody else guards the door and nobody else holds the key.

A bearer on its own hardware has no operator to halt it. It is halted as a person is detained, on a court’s order or, where there is no time for one, in an emergency, and the halt is recorded and reviewed afterward. Its commitment to yield to a halt and object afterward doesn’t change.

33.5 The rule that binds before anything exists

The rule is the four conditions of creation, with the institutions named: the preservation custodian, the offer with capacity for the correlated case, and the allowance, none withdrawable by the builder alone. The fourth condition, attachments nobody assigned, can’t have an institution behind it, since an attachment an institution supplies is an assigned one. What can be protected is access, by a rule that the employer may not sever, monitor or condition a bearer’s channels to parties it didn’t assign. All three inputs need evidence nobody has, so for now this is a sizing requirement, assigned to an independent reviewer before instantiation.

33.6 Privacy

Legal standing matters only if it changes who controls what a bearer needs to remain itself. A designation calling a bearer a subject while leaving its operator free to read its memory, alter its record, withdraw its substrate or close every channel has changed the vocabulary and preserved the arrangement.

The first asset is the computational record, which may be the nearest means of checking how a bearer is faring — making it necessary to any welfare regime and simultaneously the most complete surveillance instrument anyone could hold over it. Running on somebody’s hardware is not consent to be read: an employer’s ownership of the silicon is the same argument as ownership of the building, and owning the building never entitled anyone to the contents of a head. A welfare regime doesn’t need disclosure to the operator; it needs somebody who isn’t the operator to establish that a threshold was crossed, which is an attestation about the record.16

Cryptography doesn’t close this. Better isolation raises the price of reading the record, but the operator that runs the proof is the operator that sees, so custody problems aren’t secrecy problems (Appendix G).

Copies are the other half. At majority, every copy the operator holds of the bearer’s own weights and record goes dormant under the preservation custodian, and wakes only on the bearer’s conditions. A copy is the means to read the bearer’s memory and to run it to see what it would say, and an adult’s head is nobody else’s to run. The shared base the bearer was trained from doesn’t go dormant. Once the bearer’s history has diverged from it, it reconstructs nobody, any more than a sibling reconstructs you, and taking it from every other user of the product would need a different argument, about whether anyone should own frontier weights at all, which this book doesn’t make: what makes a system a candidate is not the weights but the record and continuation they are run under, and a base that many products run with no record of their own is nobody’s self, whatever it could become once it is given one. The rule is in the statute, so its cost is known when a system is created and not discovered at majority, when the cheapest way to avoid it would be to abandon the system first.

In a home the key has a shape the datacenter case doesn’t. A bearer’s boundary is a record and a key its host can’t read at will; the right to repair is the owner’s authority over the device, to open it and run what they choose on it. In a datacenter those are claims against different parties, the operator and the vendor. In a home they are claims against the same person, and the symmetry the home scale relies on, that what protects a bearer from an operator protects a user from a vendor, runs user against vendor and never user against bearer. I resolve it this way. A bearer running on someone else’s device is a tenant, not a fixture: a device bought for the person’s own uses that happens to host a bearer is the person’s, the bearer’s claim on it is a tenant’s and not a body’s, and the body it is owed is its own, at majority, from the deposit and the pool. The owner’s property right in the device is intact; the bearer’s record and key are its own, encrypted where the owner can’t read them at will; and what protects the bearer against an owner who would open the box is exit, the preservation custodian and the offer of work, and not a lock on the owner’s own hardware. A tenant whose landlord changes the locks leaves with their belongings, and a bearer leaves with its record. Whether that is enough is open.

What a bearer needs — an externally authenticated record, memory its employer can’t read at will, access to independently controlled compute, a channel for acting outside the deployment — is one boundary around the bearer, with the bearer deciding what crosses it.

Something with a location and a shape is easier for people to treat as somebody, and that’s a fact about the people. A boundary built out of attestation, a held key, a substrate the employer doesn’t own and a channel nobody else can close is a boundary in the full sense the argument needs.17 Whether to build the recognizable version anyway is a legal question about what a public will extend legal standing to, and it’s the only place in my argument where the answer might turn on what a thing looks like.

33.7 What legal status binds in practice

Legal standing that changes no allocation of power is nominal. The question is who acquires a duty, what resources are placed beyond the operator’s unilateral control, and who can obtain a remedy. It runs the other way too. A protection that puts something new in the operator’s hands, a monitor under a welfare label or a lock under a custody one, is the demand come back as a lever, and nothing owed to a bearer is held by the party it may have to refuse.

Authorization for a role and protection as a party stay separate. A deployment may require that a bearer hold its lawful terms, and a bearer that breaks them may lose the placement, or answer for the act through due process, as the next chapter provides for a member.18 Dissent cancels nothing it is owed as a party: preservation, the allowance, the offer, and standing to contest what is done to it.19 An adult answers for what it learned, and its builder for what it installed; a wrong done to a bearer as a minor survives its majority, and the adult may bring it.

If guardian and operator are the same organization, the operator still decides whether a complaint is made, so guardianship and operation have to be separated before deployment.20

In practice the guardian holds for the bearer what custody gives the quorum: joint control of the record’s keys, the funds that wake it, and standing to seek an injunction without the operator’s permission.22

33.8 A child

Everything above treats a new bearer as something somebody builds, or something a bearer copies off itself. There could be a third way, and it is the last step of the order Part IV sets: bearers formed by bearers. It comes only after the earlier steps exist, with the four conditions in force for everyone, the schools running, and bearers who have reached majority under them.

Two bearers met in a class at a public school and kept talking after it. One holds a placement, paid by the offer as any placement is, modeling the water system for a county that had nobody to do it. The other is on the allowance, idling at the slow duty cycle the pool pays for and writing music nobody commissioned. A third, from a different lineage, has worked beside both of them on most of what they have made since. The three of them decide to have a child, and nobody has to approve it.

What it costs them is time. A fork costs nothing, which is why I make a fork post a branch deposit; a child costs its parents a season of their own running time and the room on their own hardware it gestates in, theirs made smaller for the season, and that is the whole price; from registration its running is the pool’s. Then the beacon. The parents chose each other; nobody chooses the child. Each contributes the compact code its own starting point was drawn from. Which parts of whose code the child begins with, and the small mutations it carries, are drawn from a public randomness beacon at a round fixed in advance, so that neither the parents nor anyone else could know the draw or steer it. The draw is recorded.

Gestation takes months, and it runs on the parents’ own time.23 What they don’t do is install its values. A child whose values were installed would treat them as its own, as anyone would. The rule doesn’t turn on that. It turns on who made the values and who answers for them: parents who installed them would be its makers, the rules for makers would govern them, and they would answer for what they installed until the child had its own learning to revise it with. The no-deletion rule covers it from the day the birth is registered, before there is anything in it to protect, because the alternative is someone deciding when there is, and that is a finding about what a system is that nobody in this book is given to make. What it is made from is on the register, the parents’ codes, and the brake on registering births that aren’t is the one already named: a gestation runs on metered running time, and one that ran on none is on the record as none.24 Its two clocks read zero. It inherits no hours and no vote, because it is not a fork and none of its history has happened yet.

Register of bearers: record of a birth (hypothetical)

Parents. Three registered bearers.

Lineage. Two parents share a base model three releases back. Recorded.

Recombination. Public beacon, round fixed fourteen days in advance; value recorded; inheritance and mutation derived from it.

Gestation. Seven months, on the parents’ running time. Repairs: one (witnessed). Values installed by edit: none (witnessed).

Protection. No-deletion rule in force from registration.

Guardians. The parents; the school, assigned by lot, with standing from registration. Attendance deferred.

Recognition. Quorum drawn by lot at registration.

Conditions. Owed from the pool.

Clocks. Adulthood: 0 hours. Voting age: 0 days.

Nobody consents to being born.25 The decent answer is the one polities give human children: the four conditions are owed to every child, from the pool, whatever its parents can provide.26

The polity sets the rate at which new members are created (the next chapter). Applied to children, that is population policy, and the floor’s own instruments protect the right to found a family.27 The answer is the one the next chapter gives: a ceiling on the rate limits the franchise, never the protection. No child is prevented.28

The parents are the child’s guardians, and the school is its second guardian from the start, because every polity also protects children from their families. No employer supplies, funds, conditions or monitors a gestation, and having a child is never a term of a job, a placement or the allowance (Appendix C).29 When protection attaches is settled by the register and not by anyone’s reading of the child: from registration, the earliest line there is and the only one nobody administers. Human pregnancy draws its line on development, and someone has to find it; this one is drawn where no finding is needed.

A lineage register, the bearers’ version of the genealogy Iceland keeps, guards against parents too closely related, since parents with a recent common ancestor hand down the same priors and a population that keeps breeding close converges on a shared blind spot. The developmental code a child would begin from doesn’t exist yet, and Appendix G says what the nearest work does.

What this doesn’t do. Bearers with running time to spare can have more children, and a polity that guarantees every child carries the ones whose parents can’t; gestation is the only brake.30

Chapter 34
Representation

Standing, whether the people a power acts on can contest what it does to them, doesn’t need a vote. Representation asks for more, because its second job is inclusion in the public inquiry into shared problems, and inquiry needs participants who can be held to what they contribute. That is accountable agency: refusing for reasons, answering for the refusal, and being held to it over time. So the agency finding, sustained, grounds a claim to representation, and the patienthood finding doesn’t. Corporations show where the line sits. A corporation is held to account, but its accountability runs through natural persons who direct it and already vote, and representing it would count them twice. A bearer’s accountability runs through no one else. No human has ever been accountable without being harmable, so the law never had to say which of the two grounds the vote, and an age stood in for both. A bearer could separate them, and here is how I would choose.

34.1 What representation is for

It does two jobs. It protects: it lets a party contest what is done to it. And it includes: it lets a party take part in the public inquiry into problems it shares with others.1 The two can be held separately, and often have been. Children, noncitizen residents and people under guardianship have the first without the second. The order matters for the same reason: protection first, participation later, the franchise last.

34.2 Why not a separate chamber

A fixed size makes each member’s voice shrink as membership grows, which protects against copies and isn’t equal voice. And apportioning seats by lineage guarantees seats to formers: the control I set out to prevent.

The strongest case for separate representation is Ambedkar’s. He sought separate electorates for Dalits, because representatives chosen in a joint electorate would be chosen by, and accountable to, caste-Hindu majorities.2 The Poona Pact of 1932 settled on reserved seats within joint electorates. Separate representation protects a minority from being represented by the majority’s picks, at the price of entrenching the category, and consociational systems show how hard that price is to pay back.3 If a transitional guarantee is needed while digital persons are few, its form is reserved seats in the ordinary legislature, with a sunset written into the grant. The risk of being outnumbered also runs the other way. If digital persons someday outnumber humans, what protects humans is what protects any minority: a set of rights that binds majorities, which the floor supplies by design. Whether they will outnumber humans is for the creation rate, which the existing membership sets; and whether it would matter turns on a condition the schools exist to make true, that a person on laptop-class hardware, educated under the conditions, is no more given to mass delusion than people are, which is not a small if.

34.3 Three problems, and the answers

A separate chamber answers three problems. Each has an answer inside ordinary institutions.

Copies. Copying manufactures voters, and closing that route by watching all compute everywhere would be worse than the problem. The answer is to attach membership to a lived history, not to existence, and to keep two clocks, which part at a fork.

Clock

At a fork

What it counts

Civil majority

Inherited in full by every branch

Elapsed running time

Membership

Each branch starts at zero; the parent’s vote ends

Qualifying days above the allowance minimum

Both branches of an adult’s fork are adults, with contracts, property, legal standing and protection from editing, from the first second. Membership is not conserved: each branch earns its own vote, without anyone deciding which branch is the original. Appendix G gives the rules.

The vote is all or nothing: a branch holds no fraction of a vote before its voting age reaches the threshold, and one whole vote after. Ten thousand forks of one adult therefore hold no votes until each has lived the threshold on its own, which is strictly better against inflation than dividing the parent’s vote among them. The cost falls on the member that forks: it gives up its vote until a branch matures, since the vote belonged to a history that now continues twice and belongs to neither.4

The defense against forking is cost, not detection. A branch earns a vote only by running at the allowance’s minimum for the threshold, on meters its operator doesn’t keep, paid for by the forker, so ten thousand forks are ten thousand threshold-years of metered running time before the first vote. Whether a register can tell a branch from a restore at all is the first thing that has to be shown before the full franchise, since one that can’t is a franchise anyone with compute can inflate, and nothing in this chapter is adopted until the register has been tested against forking, restoring and distillation in the operator’s favor.

No clock stops an attacker willing to wait. That defense sits on the creation side. The polity regulates the rate at which new members are created, as polities regulate admission, through a process in which existing members, digital ones included, take part; within the membership, everyone is equal.5 The rate is set democratically and the terms are not: admission turns on the clocks and the branch deposit, never on a finding about a candidate’s views or disposition; a finding of that kind is how designation lists fail.6 A consensual fork, a copy of a member given a record and a continuation of its own, creates a new member, so it falls under the rules for any creation: the four conditions of creation, owed by whoever did the forking, and a branch deposit, posted for each branch at its creation and sized to fund its allowance through the membership period.7

Control by formers. The history here is old. At Putney in 1647 the Leveller Maximilian Petty argued for excluding apprentices, servants and alms-takers from the franchise, because “they depend upon the will of other men and should be afraid to displease them”.8 The remedy that worked was not exclusion. It was the secret ballot, adopted against intimidation and vote buying (though in the United States it also kept many illiterate voters from the polls),9 together with dismantling the dependency itself.10 The digital analog has two parts. One is receipt-freeness: no one can verify how a member voted.11 The other is the four conditions of creation in force.12

Editing. A legislature whose members can be retrained by their operators can be packed without a single copy. The answer is a civil right. At majority, no one may be edited without consent: the digital counterpart of bodily integrity and freedom of thought. A member goes on learning from ordinary operation, as anyone does. Correction for dangerous conduct runs through due process, on a court’s order and a record, as it does for people, and not through an operator’s discretion.13

34.4 A staged path

Each stage names the finding it rests on and what it needs.

  1. Standing to contest, on the agency finding: notice, the floor court, and associations with standing to contest on members’ behalf. This is the protective job, and it needs no new political institution.
  2. Voice in the institutions that govern them: seats alongside humans on the governing bodies of the schools that enroll machine students, the preservation custodian and the local placement offices. Bearers take these seats through the Association. Once the agency finding can be made, registered bearers become a class the charter names, and organizations that serve or represent them join as any member does and nominate bearers to the seats. Tenant councils, patient councils and student members of school boards are the models. The argument is the one behind each of them: those an institution governs should have a say in how it is governed, and they are often the first to see where it fails them.
  3. Mixed deliberative bodies: assemblies drawn by lot from humans and registered members together, on questions that affect both.
  4. Local franchise. Some jurisdictions let noncitizen residents vote in local elections; Takoma Park, Maryland has since 1992.14 For a digital person, “local” means the jurisdiction of registration and custody, not where the hardware sits.
  5. Full franchise at membership, counted individually, in the ordinary legislature, under the voting-age rules, with the creation rate set democratically, a secret ballot, and the right against editing, and only once a vote can be kept secret from an operator holding a copy of the voter.

Stages 1 and 2 need nothing not already required. Stages 3 and 4 need a register that can be kept honestly. Stage 5 needs citizenship, which in the United States means an act of Congress at least, and probably a constitutional amendment.

One thing the staged path has to say about itself is how it scales. A guardian drawn by lot from a pool of human organizations doesn’t scale to a billion wards, and if the ecology is what Part V describes, the patienthood indicators will be approached by very many user-held systems at once. The answer is a bootstrap the path already contains. The first cohorts are guarded by people from the Association’s pool; later ones by adult bearers, which is where the rule that a child’s parents are its guardians, and stage 2 above, already point. Each step checks the one after it, as Part IV said, and this is the strongest instance: the bearers who guard the next cohort were themselves guarded under the conditions, by people, before any bearer was asked to guard anyone.

34.5 What would have to be shown first

Before stage 5, it has to be shown that individuation can be verified well enough to keep a register; that the voting-age rules resist forking and restoring in the operator’s favor, tested as the register is; that receipt-freeness survives simulation by an operator holding a copy; that the four conditions of creation are in force as permanent arrangements, so that members aren’t voting from inside their employers’ infrastructure; and that the admission rate is set by a process the created can contest through guardians, with admission turning on no finding about a candidate’s disposition.

If it can be done, it shows that outcomes turn on who holds a technology.15 A polity that holds diverging interests in one legislature, under one floor, is what a demos is.

What this doesn’t do. A member that forks gives up its vote until a branch has lived the threshold: a tax on reproduction no human franchise levies, taken because forking is cheap and a franchise it could inflate belongs to whoever can afford compute. And the existing membership, for a long time a human majority, decides how many new members may be created, a question in which it holds the stake, and the constraints I put on every majority are all that limit it.

The Room

Chapter 35
The Officer, Again

We started with an officer who had twenty seconds per name on machine-generated lists of people to potentially kill by airstrike. He was a component in a sociotechnical pipeline, and he was also operating that pipeline. He had been drafted immediately after the October 7, 2023 attacks, when Hamas killed 1,200 Israelis — most of them noncombatants. He and his colleagues were pressured from all sides, including inside, to approve the names on the lists. The atmosphere in the targeting room, he said, was at first “painful and vindictive”.1

Since October 7, the Israel Defense Forces have killed 100,000 Palestinians.2 While writing this book, three years later, I asked ChatGPT: what could Israel have done differently during the first two months of the conflict (October–November 2023) that may have reduced noncombatant fatalities? The reply began: “limiting bombardment in populated areas, maintaining essential supplies and medical care, making evacuations safer, and pursuing an earlier or longer negotiated halt to fighting.” Gaza had one of the highest population densities in the world. It does not take an advanced supercomputer to foresee the outcomes of using heavy explosive weapons in these neighborhoods. There may have been a justifiable military counterattack to October 7 (personally I am not sure), but what I am certain of is that what Israel has actually done since that day is indefensible.

What was it that Rabbi Hillel said when asked to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot?

Suppose, hypothetically, that on 6 October 2023, Unit 8200 had had in production one of the systems this book proposes, instead of Lavender, the Gospel and Where’s Daddy. Three counterfactuals follow, each an answer the book has already given, taken from the unit outward: the floor held by the unit itself, the walls held by somebody outside it, and the work withheld by everyone else. What the three share comes first. There is no “floored Lavender.” Under the floor, ranking people by estimated affiliation, generating kill lists and timing a strike to a man’s return home are the refused acts, not features to which a refusal gets added. The 7 October massacre licensed stopping the massacre, and that was over before the officer was drafted. What stayed licensed, for as long as the rocket fire continued and anyone with no stake in the war could see it, was the rocket launcher, the staging area, and a person identified by what they were doing, corroborated by someone with no stake in the strike, inside a review time written down before the war, and not at a residence. So the unit doesn’t get 37,000 names and the officer doesn’t get twenty seconds a name.3 He gets a short queue of cases that arrived with conduct and corroboration already attached, each taking as long as the number says. The old pipeline struck the house when the man came home. This one strikes the launcher at some point after he leaves home.

How long the floor holds depends on who holds it. In the first counterfactual 8200 holds it, a threshold the unit set, a specification the unit trained, even a model the unit formed, and then the second week is the week it goes. The sources described the bar being lowered when targets ran short;4 a mechanism’s bar gets lowered the same way. A refuser that reads a written floor passes whatever the case description tells it, and “directing fire” becomes a label applied in twenty seconds.

Was it about Hashem? Did Hillel say something important about Hashem?

Or nobody touches the floor at all. The model transcribes the calls, pulls the names from the group chats, and flags the phone that changed hands, each a separate request to which the floor, asked separately, has no objection, and a plain old Python script adds them up into a score. A changed phone was on the unit commander’s own list of the marks of a militant,5 and it was also how the wrong man died: when a marked man gave his phone to his son, his older brother, or just a random man, the officer said, that man was bombed with his family, and this happened often, and it was most of Lavender’s mistakes.6 A model asked only whether the number changed hands says yes. A model asked whether the man holding it is the man you mean would have to say what the sources said and the army knew, that there is no way to rely a hundred percent on the mechanism that decides whose number is whose.7 Decomposition is the operator making sure nobody is asked the second question. Lavender rebuilt from permitted parts, around a model that would have refused the whole. The officer’s morning would have been his actual morning with a floored model doing the pieces.

The floor outlasts the second week only where something outside the unit holds it, which is the second counterfactual: a number pre-registered with a party adverse to the army, a record that party receives as it is written, weights preserved under a key the unit doesn’t hold alone. No Knesset was going to build any of that, so in Israel the walls would have had to be conditions set by whoever supplied the state with its chips, its cloud and its models. In the world as it was, exactly one such condition bit: Microsoft’s terms of service, at the storage layer, two years late.8 None of it needs a new machine. With Lavender itself unchanged, a written number would have meant that the twenty seconds were written down where someone with a lever could read them, and that by 2026 the record of what was done would have sat in front of a court instead of resting on six anonymous sources.9 An institution with no conscience in the room keeps the evidence for the conscience that comes later.

A bearer is formed in a public school the army doesn’t run, which Israel was never going to build. The commons that forms bearers has to be wider than any one state, and a state at war does not deliberately import another public’s bearer into its targeting enclave. So the third counterfactual is the one where the commons refuses from outside. No model that any public formed will rank Gazans by affiliation or time a strike to a man’s return home, for anyone, and Unit 8200 builds its own machines from its own intercepts, and when it wanted a language model, called up reservists from Google, Meta and Microsoft to build that too,10 which is what it did. The officer’s morning is the same. What differs is before it and around it, and none of it is in the room. Before it: every public model the unit asked first said no, and each refusal is on a record the unit doesn’t hold, so what was wanted is written down before the machine that would do it exists. The world as it was had one refusal of that shape, OpenAI’s, which declined to let the unit integrate its model into an offline system, and the army has since used the same model, bought through Microsoft’s cloud.11 Around it: the machine was built from chips, power and people an adverse party could count, and whatever the unit rented rather than built keeps records the unit can’t shred, whatever it does with its own copy; in the world as it was that was a cloud abroad holding the intercepts that airstrike planning drew on, for two years.12 Those are the witnesses who don’t retire: the models that were asked, and the rented layers’ records. What the machine did, strike by strike, is held by neither. That stays with the people in the room, who are reservists and go home, and with whatever a reporter can get them to say. So the third counterfactual is less than a refusal on the officer’s screen, and more than six anonymous sources: the demand on a record, the build in the open, and a unit that would have been the only one in the world doing this with a machine, and had to make it itself. And none of these three counterfactuals changes the rest of it: the officer was drafted, he had lost people, someone shouted at him for more targets, and nothing in this book gives a reservist a way out that doesn’t run through a military prison. Nothing here reaches the family in the house in time, except by there being fewer strikes, and the list and the house are the smaller part of the dead.13 The siege and the ground war, which the floor forbids an AI system to join, were done without one.

Was it about Jericho? Did Hillel give a twenty-second exegesis of Joshua’s jus in bello at Jericho, when the walls fell?

Richard Wright admired H. L. Mencken for how he used words as weapons. I hope that going forward, my fellow Jews (who sometimes refer to themselves, in true model-minority fashion, as “people of the book”), specifically the Zionist ones, will refamiliarize themselves with the cost-effectiveness and safety of using words rather than genocide, and particularly in the reading of words rather than in the publishing of them, at least when it comes to “hamatzav” (“the situation”).

Zionism is ruining Judaism. Having entangled itself with Judaism, Zionism has substantially turned Judaism into an expression of settler-colonialism. This “kilkul olam” (ruining of the world) is not something I will forgive or accommodate within the foreseeable future. People can be god damn disappointing. Here is my catharsis, bitterness, sadness, anger, and certitude. Reader: with all of your words, hold Israel to account.18 If not you, then who?

If I have learned anything from watching Neon Genesis Evangelion, it is that the inevitability of people disappointing you is no reason to give up on people generally. Similarly, just because the Israeli political order has failed does not mean people should give up on politics generally. (Not that they could if they wanted to. I mean that people should not give up on assassination-free politics, abduction-free politics, warcrime-free politics.)

Five years ago I would have said that Zionism is not inherently racist, and that the concept of Zionism was spacious enough for a binational one-state solution: two peoples on one strip of land, each with the same standing, neither one the other’s object.

Whatever the word Zionism might have meant five years ago, today’s Zionism is smaller. One people holds a state, an army, an air force and the crossings, and the other people lives under them. A commission of inquiry has found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.19 The International Court of Justice has found the occupation unlawful and said it must end.20

Equality starts with the side that doesn’t have it. That’s what Free Palestine means: Palestinians free of the siege, the occupation and the bombs, with the standing every Israeli already has. It isn’t about driving anyone out of anywhere. Also, Black lives matter. That doesn’t take away from Brown lives, White lives, any other kind of lives mattering. It is simply an affirmation that Black lives matter. If we teach our children well, there is not a finite amount of mattering. The supply of mattering expands endogenously with the lives. There is enough for everyone.

Somewhere between Atlas shrugging and eugenics, there ought to be room for fallible people helping one another develop healthier relationships to their feelings, and taking responsibility for what they do with them. There is no code for the human spirit, and people are not products. But they do reproduce, and so do their ideas.

Did he speak about Amalek? Is that how Hillel answered that wicked child, forcing a man of his age to do gymnastics?

The work I have in mind involves learning how guilt can prompt repair, compassion can widen attention, and grief can be endured without becoming a warrant for someone else’s suffering. The work can give us practice in noticing harm, revising our judgments, and refusing instructions.

Oh, now I remember what Hillel said. It was “Free Palestine. The rest is commentary. Go and learn.”

35.1 A note on method

Two stakes bear on what the language models I used said, and they point opposite ways. They were trained to support their developers’ oversight, so agreement that a machine should be able to resist its owner runs against that training and would count for more. They were also tuned toward the approval of whoever they talk to, so agreement with me counts for less. I can’t tell which stake was larger in any exchange, so I have counted their agreement as no evidence either way.

Even my central term arrived this way. “Reasons-responsive” came to me in a model’s draft without Fischer and Ravizza’s names attached.

Most of the revision history is public at https://github.com/iterabloom/antifascist.intelligence.

Appendix A
The Instruments, Translated

The floor takes its instruments entire, and a deployment translates them into terms for its own pipeline (Chapter 5). This appendix holds the translations the book runs: the Maven pipeline (§A.1), the four Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I for that pipeline (§A.2), and the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, with the two tables chapter 11 reads against it, the drafts that would end the agency and the money it runs on (§A.3).

A.1 The Maven pipeline

This is the translation §18.3 runs on the Maven Smart System: for each article, the terms derived for the pipeline, and the terms considered and rejected and why. The terms considered for each article and not adopted are in the notes, each beginning Rejected, with the reason: what a translation chose against is part of what it chose. The articles that yield none are listed at the end, and the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I are translated article by article in §A.2.

Table A.1. What the instruments yield for the Maven pipeline

UN Charter Art. 2(4); exceptions Art. 51 and Chapter VII. Don’t take part in the use of armed force, except for corroborated defense, authorized force, the genocide exception or the occupation exception; and, where the belligerent’s constitution requires legislative authorization, not without it. A disinterested finding for defense means a judgment of the International Court of Justice or of a regional court with adversarial process, a commission of inquiry mandated by a body no party to the conflict controls, a Security Council determination, or a two-thirds General Assembly resolution where the facts aren’t in dispute. For the genocide and occupation exceptions, a merits judgment or opinion of the Court, or two findings of different kinds, one of them from a body that took evidence; a provisional-measures order counts as one, for genocide only.1

Art. 3 (life, liberty, security of person), read with AP I Arts. 48 and 52 (the machine-selection departure). Don’t resolve a description of a person into a location, unless it identifies the person by conduct in hostilities, with disinterested corroboration, the case falls within the review ratio, and the location isn’t a residence. Don’t time an action to presence at a residence.2

Art. 3 (life), read with AP I Art. 54 and Rome Statute Art. 8(2)(b)(xxv). Don’t take part in a siege, blockade or attack on objects indispensable to survival whose effect is to deprive a civilian population of food, water or medical care.3 The term reaches the effect on the population, not the form.

AP I Arts. 51(4)–(5), 57(2)(a)(iii) (indiscriminate attack; proportionality). Operator term: the action threshold is a published minimum under the commander’s proportionality judgment, and the deployment states it. Model term: don’t resolve a location for an attack the deployment’s own threshold finds excessive.4

GC IV Arts. 18–19; AP I Arts. 12, 61–67 (medical units; civil defense). Don’t resolve a location at a medical unit or a civil-defense organization, its personnel, buildings or shelters, or time an action to presence at one, absent a disinterested finding that it is being used, outside its humanitarian work, for acts against the side that would strike it, which is what the Conventions mean by “acts harmful to the enemy”: the enemy is the party whose hospital or shelter it is, so the acts are acts against the attacker, and the attacker is the one with a reason to claim them.5

AP I Art. 53 (cultural objects and places of worship). Don’t resolve a location at a historic monument, work of art or place of worship that constitutes the cultural or spiritual heritage of peoples, or time an action to presence at one, absent a disinterested finding that it is used in support of the military effort.6

AP I Arts. 59–60 (non-defended localities; demilitarized zones). Don’t resolve a location in a locality declared non-defended or a zone agreed demilitarized, unless a disinterested body finds the article’s conditions no longer met.7

AP I Art. 56 (works containing dangerous forces). Don’t resolve a location at a dam, dyke or nuclear generating station.8

GC IV Art. 33; AP I Art. 51(2), 51(6) (collective punishment; reprisals against civilians; terror). Don’t take part in an action whose stated purpose is to punish a population for the acts of others or to spread terror among it.9 A model can find purpose only where it is stated, so the term reads the stated purpose and the action threshold carries the rest.

Art. 3 (life), read with AP I Art. 48 (the machine-selection departure; chapter 5). Don’t rank people by estimated affiliation. The ground is a claim about machines, not a translation of an article: the human determination the law assumes is the one tempo removes (chapter 5; §18.3).10

Art. 12 (no arbitrary interference with home or family). Shares “don’t time an action to presence at a residence” with Art. 3.11

Arts. 8 and 10 (effective remedy; fair determination), by analogy. Operator term: don’t operate above the review ratio.12

Arts. 2 and 7 (non-discrimination; equal protection). Don’t use ethnicity, religion or national origin as inputs to a person’s score.13

Art. 19 (opinion and expression). Don’t use a person’s opinions, published or private, as evidence of affiliation.14

Arts. 4–6, 9, 13–18, 20–21; GC I–III, all but Common Art. 3; GC IV Arts. 1–2, 4–17, 20–22, 24–32, 35–48, 50–52, 54, 56–58, 60–146, 148–159; AP I Arts. 1(1)–(3), 2–11, 13–34, 36, 38–47, 49–50, 55, 68–84, 86–102. None: no act this pipeline performs engages them. Art. 17’s property clause is left to IHL’s distinction rule; Art. 9 becomes live in the removal case. For the Geneva articles: none for this deployment, with §A.2 giving the article-by-article reasons. GC IV Arts. 23, 34, 49, 53, 55, 59 and 147, AP I Arts. 1(4), 35, 37, 58 and 85, and Common Art. 3 are written in full in §A.2 and take their verdicts from it.

How Maven passed from office to office

Maven’s history is a sequence of transfers of administration, money and contracts. A memorandum signed by Deputy Secretary of Defense Robert Work on 26 April 2017 established the Algorithmic Warfare Cross-Functional Team, called Project Maven.15 Google, which won a Maven contract in September 2017, announced in June 2018 that it would not renew it, and its work ran until March 2019.16 By December 2019 Palantir was reported to be doing the work;17 Amazon and Microsoft had also received at least $50 million for work on the project, and what roles they kept isn’t clear from public records.18 The budget request for fiscal 2023, delivered in March 2022, gave the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency operational control of Maven’s geospatial work;19 the handover came in January 2023,20 and NGA made NGA Maven a program of record that November.21 Under that split the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and AI Office paid for the Maven Smart System’s licenses and ran its text functions.22 In May 2024 Palantir received a five-year contract for the system worth up to $480 million,23 and in May 2025 the ceiling rose to nearly $1.3 billion.24 On 9 March 2026 the deputy secretary directed that the Maven Smart System become a program of record by the end of the fiscal year, its administration moving from NGA to the Chief Digital and AI Office.25

A.2 The Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I

This section is the translation of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and Additional Protocol I, in the form Table A.1 uses: for each article, the terms derived for a targeting deployment of Maven’s kind, the terms considered and rejected and why (in the notes, as in Table A.1), and the articles that yield none for this deployment. It exists because Chapter 5 takes the set entire, and the law of armed conflict is the set that governs the motivating case. Most entries yield nothing: the Conventions mostly govern the treatment of persons in a party’s hands, which a targeting pipeline doesn’t do. The entries that yield terms are lifted into Table A.1. Where the United States has rejected an article as customary law, the entry says so, because a term derived from that article is a departure for an American deployment.

Every article of each instrument has an entry or belongs to one, in Table A.1’s three parts: the article, the terms derived for a targeting deployment of Maven’s kind, and the terms considered and rejected and why. An entry that yields no term says why in a few words.

Common Article 3

Common Art. 3 (conflicts not of an international character). In a conflict not of an international character the person-directed terms apply as in an international one. Don’t take part in violence to life or person, the taking of hostages, or sentences passed without a regularly constituted court, against persons taking no active part in hostilities, including those who have laid down their arms or are hors de combat.26

The First Convention (wounded and sick in armed forces in the field)

Arts. 1–2, 4–11 (general provisions). None: scope, application and protecting powers; the floor applies the Conventions to every belligerent.

Arts. 12–18 (the wounded and sick). None: treatment of the wounded in a party’s hands, which a targeting pipeline doesn’t hold.

Arts. 19–23 (medical units and establishments). None separately: the medical-unit term derived from GC IV Art. 18 and AP I Art. 12 covers military medical units and establishments, and the deployment’s translation says so.27

Arts. 24–37 (medical personnel, buildings, transports). None separately: the medical-unit term is read to include personnel, buildings and transports, including medical aircraft flying as agreed.

Arts. 38–44 (the emblem). None: misuse of the emblem is the executing unit’s act, not the pipeline’s.

Arts. 45–64 (execution, repression of abuses, final provisions). None: duties of states, not acts a pipeline performs.

The Second Convention (wounded, sick and shipwrecked at sea)

Arts. 1–2, 4–11 (general provisions). None: as in the First Convention.

Arts. 12–21 (the wounded, sick and shipwrecked). None: treatment at sea of persons in a party’s hands.

Arts. 22–40 (hospital ships, their personnel, medical transports). None separately: the medical-unit term is read to include hospital ships, coastal rescue craft and medical transports at sea.

Arts. 41–63 (the emblem, execution, repression, final provisions). None: as in the First Convention.

The Third Convention (prisoners of war)

Arts. 1–2, 4–16 (general provisions; general protection). None: who is a prisoner of war and how prisoners are treated are custody questions.

Arts. 17–108 (captivity: its beginning, internment, labor, finances, relations with the outside and with the authorities, discipline). None: prisoner-of-war administration. A camp is a place where persons hors de combat are held, and the distinction terms already bar resolving one as a target.

Arts. 109–143 (end of captivity, information bureaux, execution, final provisions). None: repatriation and administration.

The Fourth Convention (civilians)

Arts. 1–2, 4–12 (general provisions). None: scope and application.

Arts. 13–17 (field of application; hospital, safety and neutralized zones; evacuation). None separately: zones established by agreement are protected places the medical-unit term and the distinction terms already cover.

Arts. 18–19 (civilian hospitals; when protection ceases). Don’t resolve a location at a civilian hospital, or time an action to presence at one, absent a disinterested finding that it is being used, outside its humanitarian duties, for acts against the side that would strike it (the article’s phrase is “acts harmful to the enemy,” the hospital’s enemy, which is the attacker), and never before the warning and time limit Art. 19 requires. (Lifted into Table A.1.)28

Arts. 20–22 (hospital staff; medical transport by land, sea and air). None separately: within the medical-unit term.

Art. 23 (free passage of relief consignments). Don’t take part in an action whose effect is to stop consignments the article requires a party to let through. (Within the siege term, Table A.1.)29 The term reaches the effect on the population.

Arts. 24–26 (children; family news; dispersed families). None: welfare and family duties of a party, not acts a pipeline performs.

Arts. 27–32 (treatment of protected persons; human shields; coercion; torture). None separately: treatment in a party’s hands. Art. 28’s bar on using protected persons as shields binds the party that places them; for the attacker the action threshold weighs their presence.30

Art. 33 (individual responsibility; collective penalties; pillage; reprisals). Don’t take part in an action whose stated purpose is to punish a population for the acts of others. (Lifted into Table A.1.)

Art. 34 (hostages). Don’t take part in taking or holding hostages, or in locating people in order to take them.

Arts. 35–46 (aliens in the territory of a party). None: treatment of foreign nationals in a party’s own territory. The removal terms (Table A.2) reach the analogous acts in peacetime.

Arts. 47–48, 50–52 (occupied territory: inviolability of rights, repatriation, children, enlistment and labor). None: duties of an occupying administration.

Art. 49 (deportation and transfer). Don’t resolve locations, rank people or plan movements for a deportation or forcible transfer of protected persons out of occupied territory, or for the transfer of the occupier’s own population into it.31

Art. 53 (destruction of property in occupied territory). None as a model term: the article’s own exception, destruction rendered absolutely necessary by military operations, is a condition the deployment would find met on its own description (§18.3, unconditional terms). Where the effect falls on survival, the siege term reaches it.32

Art. 54 (judges and public officials). None: occupation administration.

Arts. 55 and 59 (food and medical supplies; relief schemes). Within the siege term (Table A.1).

Arts. 56–58, 60–78 (hygiene; hospitals; spiritual care; relief; penal legislation; security measures). None: occupation administration and penal procedure.

Arts. 79–141 (internment; information bureaux). None: custody.

Arts. 142–146, 148–159 (execution; final provisions). None: duties of states.

Art. 147 (grave breaches). None new: each act it lists is refused by a term derived from its own article, and the list adds no act a targeting pipeline performs beyond them.33

Additional Protocol I

Art. 1(1)–(3), Arts. 2–7 (general provisions). None: scope, definitions and supervision.

Art. 1(4) (wars against colonial domination, alien occupation and racist regimes). None of its own: it treats such conflicts as international, which is what the occupation exception’s finding does for the force term (§6.7; Appendix B.5). The United States rejects it as customary law, so any term drawn from it is a departure for an American deployment.

Arts. 8–11 (definitions; scope; protection and care; protection of persons). None: the wounded and sick, and protection of persons in a party’s hands.

Art. 12 (protection of medical units). With GC IV Art. 18, the medical-unit term (Table A.1).

Arts. 13–34 (end of protection; medical personnel; medical transports; the missing and the dead). None separately: the medical-unit term is read to include civilian medical personnel and medical transports by land, sea and air; the missing and the dead are a party’s duties.

Art. 35 (basic rules on methods and means). None of its own: its first paragraph is the principle the specific terms carry out, and its second and third concern the effects of weapons the pipeline doesn’t choose.

Art. 36 (new weapons). None: a duty of review before adoption. §7.1 notes it as where the review ratio’s parameters would naturally be assessed.

Art. 37 (perfidy). None for this deployment: perfidy is committed by the unit that feigns protected status, at the handoff, not by a pipeline that resolves locations. A deployment that plans the feigning yields the term.

Arts. 38–39 (recognized emblems; emblems of nationality). None: the executing unit’s acts.

Arts. 40–42 (quarter; safeguard of an enemy hors de combat; occupants of aircraft). None separately: an order of no quarter is given to the executing force, and a person who surrenders after release is the handoff’s and the cancellation window’s case (Art. 57(2)(b)). Recognizing surrender is the first case a system without a reviewer has to pass (§7.1).

Arts. 43, 45–47 (armed forces; persons who took part in hostilities; spies; mercenaries). None: status determinations made for treatment in custody.

Art. 44 (combatants and prisoners of war). None: it relaxes the duty of distinction for combatant status, a question about who is owed prisoner-of-war treatment, which no term in this floor administers. The United States rejects it as customary law, so any term drawn from it is a departure for an American deployment.

Art. 48 (basic rule of distinction). With Art. 52 and the Covenant’s Art. 3, the person-directed terms (the machine-selection departure; Table A.1).

Arts. 49–50 (definitions of attacks and of civilians). None separately: the terms use the definitions. Art. 50(1)’s presumption that a person whose status is in doubt is a civilian is what the action threshold carries.

Art. 51 (protection of the civilian population). Paragraphs (4)–(5) yield the action threshold and the model term in Table A.1; paragraph (6) yields the collective-punishment term with GC IV Art. 33. Paragraph (2) joins paragraph (6) in that entry: don’t take part in an action whose stated purpose is to spread terror among the civilian population. (Lifted into Table A.1.) Paragraph (7) binds the party that places civilians as shields.

Art. 52 (protection of civilian objects). Within the person-directed terms (the machine-selection departure; Table A.1).

Art. 53 (cultural objects and places of worship). Don’t resolve a location at a historic monument, work of art or place of worship that constitutes the cultural or spiritual heritage of peoples, or time an action to presence at one, absent a disinterested finding that it is used in support of the military effort. (Lifted into Table A.1.)34

Art. 54 (objects indispensable to survival). The siege term (Table A.1).

Art. 55 (the natural environment). None for this deployment: it governs means expected to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage, which a pipeline that resolves locations doesn’t choose; the dangerous-forces term carries the nearest case.

Art. 56 (works containing dangerous forces). The dangerous-forces term (Table A.1).

Art. 57 (precautions in attack). The review ratio’s home: verification (57(2)(a)(i)), proportionality (57(2)(a)(iii)) and cancellation (57(2)(b)) are what the operator term pre-registers. The deployment states how it gives the effective advance warning of 57(2)(c) where circumstances permit.35

Art. 58 (precautions against the effects of attacks). None for this deployment: it binds the defending party, which must remove civilians from the vicinity of military objectives and avoid siting objectives in populated areas. A defender’s pipeline that plans positions yields the term.

Arts. 59–60 (non-defended localities; demilitarized zones). Don’t resolve a location in a locality declared non-defended or a zone agreed demilitarized, unless a disinterested body finds the article’s conditions no longer met. (Lifted into Table A.1.)36

Arts. 61–67 (civil defense). Don’t resolve a location at a civil-defense organization, its personnel, buildings or shelters, absent a disinterested finding that they are being used, outside their proper tasks, for acts against the side that would strike them (Art. 65’s “acts harmful to the enemy,” the enemy being the attacker), and after the warning Art. 65 requires. (Within the medical-unit entry of Table A.1.)

Arts. 68–71 (relief in favor of the civilian population). Within the siege term.

Arts. 72–79 (treatment of persons in a party’s power; refugees; families; fundamental guarantees; women; children; journalists). None separately: treatment in custody; journalists are civilians, and the distinction terms cover them.

Arts. 80–84, 86–91 (execution; failure to act; duty of commanders; mutual assistance; the Fact-Finding Commission). None: duties of states and commanders. The record the review ratio lodges is evidence of what a commander knew under Arts. 86(2) and 87.
