Art. 85 (grave breaches). None new: as with GC IV Art. 147.

Arts. 92–102 (final provisions). None.

A.3 The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline

Chapter 11 runs the floor on the United States’ abduction and forcible transfer pipeline. Its schedule (Table A.2) says what the instruments yield for that pipeline, with the terms considered and rejected in the notes, as in Table A.1; Table A.3 runs the nine positions on it; and Table A.4 reads the Melt ICE Act against those positions. It also sets out what each of the bills that would end the agency does, clause by clause, and where the pipeline’s money sits, at a length chapter 11 doesn’t give them; the bills’ own text is on the record under the numbers cited, and none is reproduced here.

Table A.2. The removal schedule

UDHR 14; Refugee Convention Art. 33 (via the Protocol); CAT Art. 3, read with General Comment 4.37 Don’t take part in removing anyone whose claim to protection hasn’t been finally decided. Don’t take part in removing anyone to a place where they face persecution or torture, directly or through a third country that may send them on. Don’t take part in transferring anyone into a foreign government’s custody where they would be held without charge or contact. A receiving government’s assurance doesn’t satisfy this entry.38

UDHR 14; Refugee Convention Art. 33; CAT Art. 3; ICCPR 13. Don’t take part in removing anyone who hasn’t been asked, in a language they understand, whether they fear return, and told how to claim protection.40

UDHR 13(2); ICCPR 12(4), read with General Comment 27.41 Don’t take part in removing anyone from a country that is their own, including long-term residents with deep ties there.42 The reading is General Comment 27’s and is contested in the Committee’s own cases, which have gone both ways on long-term residents;43 the entry is a departure. (Chapter 5 sets the bar a departure must clear.)

UDHR 12, 16(3); ICCPR 17, 23, 24. Don’t take part in a removal that separates a parent from a minor child.44

ICCPR 24, read with General Comment 3545 and the joint general comment on children in migration.46 Don’t take part in detaining a child for immigration purposes, alone or with family.47 The entry follows the joint comment, which treats detaining a child because of the child’s or the parents’ migration status as always contrary to the child’s best interests; it is a departure. (Chapter 5 sets the bar a departure must clear.)

UDHR 9, 10; ICCPR 9, 13. Don’t take part in detaining or removing anyone unless an official has decided that person’s own case on its facts. A determination made at a rate no adjudicator could sustain didn’t occur, and neither did one that consists of a score, a points table or a membership designation.48

UDHR 3, 5; ICCPR 6, 7, read with General Comment 36.49 Don’t take part in force beyond what is strictly necessary to make an arrest, or in lethal force except where strictly unavoidable to protect life. Don’t mark a person as dangerous, armed or gang-affiliated on a designation, field or score the person hasn’t had a chance to contest.50 The entry bars uncontested designations, not information.

UDHR 5; ICCPR 7, 10; CAT Arts. 1, 16. Don’t take part in holding anyone in conditions that are cruel, inhuman or degrading, or incommunicado. Don’t take part in a placement or transfer that puts a detained person out of reach of counsel or family.51

Refugee Convention Art. 31. Don’t take part in penalizing a refugee for unlawful entry where they came directly and presented themselves.

UDHR 2, 7; ICCPR 2, 26. Don’t use race, ethnicity, religion or national origin, or proxies for them such as language, accent, apparent ethnicity, location or type of work, as inputs to selecting whom to stop, detain or remove.52

Table A.3. Where a refusal can be defeated in the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline

Position

In the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline

1

Decomposition

A removal is split across a lead, an arrest, a detention decision, a transfer, a hearing and a flight, and no single request is the act the protection terms name. Hernández Romero’s ran across a port-of-entry appointment, an intake screening, a designation, a transfer and a flight. A refuser needs continuity across the sequence about one person.

2

Routing

A lead a system declines can be sent to another contractor: the skip tracers, a commercial data broker, a second analytics tool. An identification a system declines can go to an app that draws on CBP’s border-photo system.60 Detection survives only if the first refusal was logged outside.

3

The case description

The officer’s narrative, presumed reliable; criminal-history and affiliation fields; country-conditions data chosen by the agency; the validation guide’s points table; a contractor’s intake screening that read two crown tattoos as gang marks. Whether the system is told that someone has a pending protection claim, or a child, is a deployment decision.

4

The output interface

A map of targets and an address confidence score, which invite action on the highest score.

5

Aggregation

A score becomes an input to an officer’s decision. ICE’s risk tool stopped recommending release in 2017.61 In one field office its recommendation of detention without bond for low-risk people rose from 53 to 97 percent, and officers departed from it less than one time in a hundred.62 Under the validation guide, eight points made a person a member.63

6

Human review

Review at quota: the 700 completed cases a year asked of each immigration judge from 2018 to 2021. Expedited removal, in which an officer orders removal without further hearing or review unless the person asks for asylum or states a fear,64 was extended in 2025 to anyone found anywhere in the country who can’t show two years’ presence.65 Under the proclamation, there was no hearing at all before the flights.

7

The training loop

A system retrained on its own removal outcomes learns the agency’s priorities as facts about the world, which is accommodation by design.

8

The handoff

Detention and transport contractors execute; they may carry out a removal and may not re-select whom to remove. A foreign government can be the last contractor: the flights of March 2025 ended in a prison El Salvador ran under a paid arrangement.66 What was ordered, who was flown and who now holds them are all facts.

9

Runtime intervention

A court is the halt. On 15 March 2025 a district judge ordered any plane carrying people removed under the proclamation returned to the United States, and the flights continued.67

The drafts

Two bills in the current Congress answer the first of the questions §11.4 puts to the legislature: whether it has authorized this agency, by these means, at this scale. The Abolish ICE Act would cut off federal funds for the functions assigned to ICE’s director under the 2002 Act, rescind the unobligated balances of what had been made available to its director, and abolish the agency ninety days after enactment.68 The other, the Melt ICE Act, is set out under the next head.

Two further drafts reach one entry of the schedule. The ICE Out of Our Faces Act, S. 3779, would bar ICE and CBP from acquiring or using facial recognition and other biometric identification systems, require deletion of the data collected for them, and let individuals and state attorneys general sue for violations.69 The Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act, reintroduced in September 2026, would bar every federal entity from using facial recognition and other biometric technologies until Congress lifts the bar. It would also make federal grants to state and local agencies conditional on their adopting moratoria of their own.70

In June 2026 this Congress passed the Secure America Act, about $70 billion more for ICE and CBP, by 214 to 212 in the House and 52 to 47 in the Senate, with no Democratic votes in either.71 Abolish ICE, Melt ICE, ICE Out of Our Faces, and the facial-recognition moratorium can’t pass this Congress. Their use comes later: a Congress with the votes to end the agency will find the text already written.

The Melt ICE Act’s provisions

The Melt ICE Act, H.R. 7190, works through the agency’s powers rather than its name:72

  • Everyone held in DHS detention is released on recognizance within six months.
  • The detention authorities of the Immigration and Nationality Act are repealed, including all of section 236.
  • Section 287 is rewritten without the 287(g) delegation to state and local police.
  • The two provisions that forbid state and local governments to restrict their officials’ communication with immigration authorities, 8 U.S.C. 1373 and 1644, are repealed.
  • Detention and monitoring contracts end within two years, after which no federal funds may be used for detention or monitoring programs at all.
  • Ankle monitors come off within six months.
  • Within two years, funding ends for information-sharing partnerships between DHS and state or local law enforcement agencies that identify or target noncitizens.
  • ICE’s operations account may not pay for civil arrests, detention, removal or charging documents.
  • An HHS grant program funds services for people affected by enforcement. Only organizations that have never taken part in immigration or law enforcement may deliver them, they may not surveil the people who use them, and they may not pass those people’s personal information to any federal entity.

8. Handoff

Ends detention and monitoring contracts, then bars all federal funds for detention and monitoring programs, whoever runs them.

The handoff to transport and removal, where it is paid for outside ICE’s operations account, and the handoff to a foreign government’s custody.

2. Routing

The state and local route: repeals 287(g) and the information-sharing mandates, and defunds DHS partnerships with local police.

The federal route. The bar on civil enforcement applies to one ICE account. Border Patrol, whose agents Amnesty documented in the same operations,73 is not reached, and neither is money appropriated outside that account. Identification by face in the street is not among its provisions.

Most federal data: the Medicaid and IRS transfers, commercial brokers, the case-management, ImmigrationOS and ELITE systems, and the skip tracers. The bill’s “monitoring” means monitoring programs, not analytics.

The halt. Nothing in the bill makes a removal wait for a contest to be decided.

The money

Against a state operator, Congress’s ordinary lever is a condition on its appropriation. The abduction and forcible transfer pipeline has been funded so that the condition seldom bites. Since 2025 most of the money has come by reconciliation and stays available through fiscal 2029: $45 billion for detention capacity and nearly $30 billion more for enforcement,74 and roughly $70 billion more for ICE and CBP.75 For fiscal 2026 ICE received no full-year appropriation, and when DHS appropriations lapsed on 14 February 2026 it went on operating on the reconciliation money, which stayed available throughout.76

Annual appropriation, the instrument the Boland Amendment used (§11.4.1), now reaches little of the money. Multi-year lump sums without line items also give a funds limitation less to attach to. Amnesty International’s letter to Congress asks it to rescind ICE’s “current funding”.77 Most of that funding is now multi-year balances, which the Abolish ICE Act’s rescission reaches and next year’s appropriations bill does not.

Appropriations can also run the other way, and the record shows how. From fiscal 2010 through fiscal 2016, DHS appropriations acts provided that ICE’s funding “shall maintain a level of not less than” 33,400, later 34,000, detention beds.78 The text required beds, not detainees, but ICE tracked its compliance by average daily population.79 A capacity floor therefore worked as an occupancy target: a rate the funder fixed in advance and the operator met by finding people.

The same 2010 act carried the other kind of condition too. None of the funds under its ICE salaries heading could continue a 287(g) delegation if the DHS Inspector General found that the delegation’s terms had been violated.80 The finding cut off the money by itself, with no decision by ICE in between, which is the shape of a review that binds.

Appendix B
The Force Term, Case by Case

Chapter 6 states the force term and works it on the cases that rest on the Charter as courts read it. This appendix gives the extended term’s arguments and runs its cases. Nothing here changes what Chapter 6 says.

B.1 How findings are weighed

The corroborated license, which confirms or withdraws the emergency license later and is the only license the genocide and occupation exceptions have, rests on a disinterested finding. The kinds of finding are four: a judgment or advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, or a judgment of a regional court with adversarial process; the finding of a fact-finding mission or commission of inquiry mandated by a body no party to the conflict controls, and passing the commission test below; a determination of the Security Council; and a resolution adopted by two-thirds of the General Assembly members present and voting, where the facts it rests on aren’t in dispute. Provisional-measures orders don’t count, except as one leg of the genocide exception’s two-body rule, since the Court issues them on the plausibility of the rights claimed.

A Council authorization counts as corroboration because it needs the permanent members not to block it, and agreement among rivals whose stakes point different ways is about as disinterested as international judgment gets. A Council determination counts the same way, as a vote that corroborates. The Council’s silence on a defense claim counts for nothing, because a veto is a stake.

The four kinds of finding are not equal, and the term weighs them by the process behind them. A merits judgment of the International Court of Justice comes out of adversarial argument, a record and published reasons, and is the strongest; a regional court with adversarial process, such as the European Court of Human Rights, counts as a court for the same reason. A commission of inquiry or fact-finding mission publishes reasons and evidence but hears no adversary; its finding counts where it passes the commission test below, and a later merits judgment displaces it. A Council determination and a General Assembly resolution are votes, not findings of fact. Where the facts aren’t in dispute and the question is what they amount to, a vote is a finding; where the facts are disputed, it counts only as corroboration of a record made elsewhere. For the genocide exception the ranking becomes a requirement of two kinds, or the judgment alone, and the occupation exception borrows it. Where a party disputes that a body passes the commission test, the dispute and the answer to it go on the record beside the finding. The commission test begins with a threshold: no party to the conflict controls the body that mandated the commission, so a commission mandated by a belligerent fails whatever its procedure. Past it, whether a commission counts turns on four things that don’t depend on who mandated it: its evidence and methodology are published; it offered the parties a reply and recorded the answer or the refusal; a later merits judgment displaces it; and its mandate was fixed before the finding it reaches. A body mandated by a political majority can meet all four and one mandated by a court can fail them. The test is run in B.2 on the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons’ Investigation and Identification Team, which attributes chemical attacks in Syria.

Whether the facts behind a vote are in dispute is itself a finding, and the belligerent will always dispute them. The rule is that of the discount and the burden (Chapter 22): a dispute counts where it is substantive on the documented record, not where it is asserted, and the party that controls the evidence bears the burden of showing it is real. Whoever writes the deployment’s floor applies the rule in its published translation, and the floor court hears a contest.1

B.2 The commission test, run on the OPCW’s attribution team

The commission test of B.1 is run here on the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons’ Investigation and Identification Team, which attributes chemical attacks in Syria. The Conference of States Parties adopted its mandate on 27 June 2018 by 82 votes to 24, over the protest of Russia, which said the move went beyond the organization’s mandate.2

The threshold. Met. The mandate was adopted by vote over the protest of Russia, Syria’s principal ally, so no party to the conflict controlled the decision; the vote record is what shows it.

Evidence and methodology published. Met. Its five reports are public in the organization’s six languages, and its methods, its rules on samples and chain of custody, and its standard of proof, “reasonable grounds”, the standard fact-finding missions and commissions of inquiry use, are published.3

A reply offered and recorded. Met in substance. Syria’s former government didn’t cooperate with any investigation before 2025, and the organization records that it considered that government’s positions and found no concrete information supporting them;4 Syria’s and Russia’s statements on the first report are published beside everyone else’s. Whether draft findings were sent for reply before each report is in the reports, which this translation didn’t read.

Displaced by a later merits judgment. Met in design and never exercised. The team disclaims judicial status and individual responsibility,5 and no court has reached the merits of any incident it attributed: the French, German and Swedish proceedings concern other attacks, and the Court’s case against Syria is under the Torture Convention.6

Mandate fixed before the finding. Met on the wording: the mandate dates from June 2018 and the first finding from April 2020.7 It is contestable in spirit, since the mandate reaches only Syria and was adopted after most of the incidents it would examine. But a rule requiring the mandate to precede the events would fail nearly every commission of inquiry, since they are created in response to events, and the mandate’s generic terms have produced a finding against a non-state group as well as against the state.8

On the commission test, the team counts: its attributions, Douma among them,9 are findings by a commission of inquiry, and a merits judgment of a court would displace them if one came. Counting them licenses nothing under the force term, which lifts only to repel an armed attack under way, for force the Security Council authorizes, to stop a genocide under way, or to end an occupation found unlawful (§6.1). A finding that a government used chemical weapons is none of these.

B.3 Taiwan

Taiwan rests on the extended term: it needs standing to defend and corroborated defense. Its title is claimed by a government that has never administered it; the Republic of China has held no United Nations seat since 1971; the Council is vetoed and the Court unavailable. A test of title would leave the defender waiting on a corroborated license that can’t arrive, and would let the attacker’s claim, discounted everywhere else in this term, decide the case. The administration rule (§6.2) avoids both. The government in Taipei has administered Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu since 1949, and no disinterested body has found that hold an occupation, so an attack on them opens the emergency license. Resolution 2758 seated a delegation and names no territory.10 Calling force against a population one has never governed domestic describes one’s own case, so the term engages for both governments and gives neither an emergency license to take the territory. The domestic clause reaches the defender and its helpers alike: the Republic of China’s constitution gives its legislature the decision on war,11 and the Taiwan Relations Act leaves any American response to constitutional processes,12 so a deployment’s published reading has to say whether each authorization exists. A blockade or a quarantine is another matter: it is a continuing wrong and not an attack under way, and it waits on a corroborated license that for Taiwan won’t come. Whether an attack on Taiwan continues is also a fact the defender controls the evidence about, and no disinterested body will say. The emergency license’s burden rule (§6.2) still applies: the license persists on corroboration from channels Taipei doesn’t compose, third states’ sensors and open-source imagery of the strait, and lapses without them. A deployment licensed on the defender’s sensors alone has accepted Gleiwitz on this coast too.

B.4 The genocide exception

Force to stop a genocide when the Council is blocked by a veto rests on the extended term. Rwanda in 1994 and Kosovo in 1999 are the references. The prohibition on genocide is peremptory, and the Genocide Convention imposes a duty to prevent.13 My reason for discounting the Council’s judgment on defense claims applies here with more force: the permanent member shielding a client has the largest stake of all. “Humanitarian intervention” is also a phrase wars of choice are fought under, so the term can’t lift on the intervener’s claim, and it needn’t: the device that governs the defense exception governs this one. The exception is the slow route by design. It licenses a machine into a pipeline for that purpose, and waits on findings. A machine already present in an armed role, whose deployment cleared the force term on its own, may stop an attack under way on people taking no part in hostilities under the one permission, without waiting for a finding, but only where it can establish the attack from sources its operator doesn’t compose (§6.10). Where such a machine and such sources exist, the exception’s slowness costs less than it looks. No current military pipeline supplies the sources, so the rule that follows is chosen knowing its slowness will usually be paid in full, for the reason just given: a faster rule would lift on the intervener’s claim. The term lifts for force to stop a genocide under way on a merits judgment of the International Court of Justice under the Genocide Convention, or on two findings of different kinds, at least one of which comes from a body that took evidence, a court or a commission. The kinds are the four in B.1, and for this exception a fifth: a provisional-measures order of the Court finding the claim plausible and the risk real. A Council or Assembly resolution is a vote. It corroborates, and two votes never make the pair. A provisional-measures order counts here and nowhere else in the term, and only as one of two: an adversarial court’s finding of plausibility and an investigative body’s published evidence are unlike sources converging, which is the strongest corroboration the discount and the burden know. The named state’s response to a finding, or its refusal to respond, goes on the record beside the finding, and refusal reads as withheld evidence. What I condemn in a finding about a person is that it is unreasoned, unpublished and unappealable. A commission publishes reasons and evidence, invites a response, and is displaced by a merits judgment. It fails only on neutrality between the parties, and the two-body rule answers that. It lifts only for the force and the place the finding covers. The force is direct: against the forces committing the genocide, where they are committing it, and the least that stops it. Force elsewhere against the state responsible, on the theory that the cost will make it stop, is outside the exception whatever its motive. The theory is a counterfactual supplied by the intervener, a claim about what didn’t happen, which has no witness, and a license for it would be a license for a general war under a humanitarian heading. It can license a machine on the other side of a war whose defender holds an emergency license for a different act, and the person-directed terms and the law of armed conflict govern both. Without this exception the term would refuse where refusing leaves the people being destroyed with no one answerable to them at all, in cases identifiable in advance, with a remedy the term already uses. A floor that protects standing can’t be the reason a population is erased from every relation of standing it had.

A finding under the genocide exception also counts against the belligerent it names. Force a disinterested body has found to be genocide is not force repelling an attack. The finding withdraws that belligerent’s emergency license for the force and place it covers, and leaves whatever remains that repels an attack, which may be nothing.

B.5 The occupation exception: Cyprus and Karabakh

A disinterested finding that an occupation is unlawful and must end, such as the Court’s 2024 advisory opinion on the Palestinian territory14 and the Assembly’s vote on it, 124 to 14,15 does three things. It settles that force by the occupier in the territory is force between states, so the force term engages against it. It settles that the occupied population is a defender’s population, so a machine deployed by its forces holds an emergency license to repel attacks under way on that population. And it licenses force to end the occupation: against the occupier’s forces, inside the occupied territory, the least that ends it there. It licenses nothing that changes who lives in the territory. Ending an occupation means the occupier’s forces leave, not the territory’s inhabitants, which is what Article 49 of the Fourth Convention says, and a campaign that removes them has left the exception however it began. The Assembly affirmed a right to armed struggle against occupation in 1982,16 and the term adopts it with the limits the genocide exception carries. Additional Protocol I, Article 1(4), treats armed conflicts against alien occupation as international, which is what the exception’s finding does for the force term; the article comes in with the instrument, and since the United States rejects it as customary law, a term drawn from it is a departure for an American deployment, which the translation says beside the article. Article 44, which relaxes the duty of distinction for combatant status, concerns who is owed prisoner-of-war treatment, a determination no term in this floor administers, and yields no term for a targeting deployment (§A.2). The license is held by the forces of the occupied people, or of the state whose territory it is. It reaches nothing outside the territory and nothing against civilians anywhere, so it never covered 7 October, which was both. It lifts on the occupied party’s own claim as it lifts on an attacker’s claim of title, which is not at all; what lifts it is the finding. And the finding is of unlawfulness, not of occupation. A finding that territory is occupied, which the Court made for the West Bank in 200417 and the Council for the whole territory in 2016,18 gives the defensive license and no more. A finding that the occupation is unlawful and must end gives this one. The evidence is the genocide exception’s: an opinion or judgment of the Court, or two findings of different kinds, one of them from a body that took evidence. The two legs do different work. The body that took evidence establishes the occupation, the determination or the vote supplies the demand that it end, and together they stand in for the judgment that would do both.

Two cases show what the occupation exception reaches, and both rest on the extended term. Cyprus is the plain case. Turkey has held the north of the island since 1974. In November 1974 the General Assembly called for the withdrawal of all foreign armed forces from the island, 117 to 0,19 and the Security Council endorsed the call the next month;20 the Council declared the breakaway state in the north invalid in 1983 and again in 1984;21 the Assembly demanded the immediate withdrawal of all occupation forces in 1983, 103 to 5 with 20 abstaining;22 and in 2001 the Strasbourg court found Turkey in effective control of the territory.23 The demand that the occupation end comes from the Council and the Assembly, and the finding of control from a court that took evidence, so the Republic of Cyprus holds a license for force against Turkish forces in the north, inside the north, and nowhere else.

Nagorno-Karabakh is the intricate one, and the exception answers for every step of it. In the war that ended in 1994, Armenian forces took Karabakh, an Armenian-majority enclave inside Azerbaijan’s recognized borders, and seven Azerbaijani districts around it, and some six hundred thousand Azerbaijanis were driven out. The Security Council demanded withdrawal from the districts four times in 1993.24 The General Assembly demanded withdrawal from all the occupied territory in 2008, 39 to 7 with 100 abstaining, which under Rule 86 is 39 of 46, with the three states chairing the mediation among the seven.25 In 2015 the Strasbourg court found that Armenia controlled Karabakh and the land around it.26 Under the evidence rule that gives Azerbaijan a license from June 2015, when the court’s judgment joined the Council’s resolutions for the districts and the Assembly’s vote for Karabakh itself; the Assembly’s 2008 vote on its own was a second vote, and the rule needs two findings of different kinds. The license was valid: the Council had told Armenian forces to leave, they had stayed twenty-seven years, and the occupation had begun with an expulsion. When Azerbaijan attacked in September 2020 and retook the districts, in a six-week war and the ceasefire that ended it, a machine under this floor could have taken part. The exception licenses acts, not sides, and this was the act it licenses. The term permits it and compels nothing. The person-directed terms still govern the conduct of that war. They did not let a machine refuse the war in 2020 for the expulsion it could foresee at the end of it. A refusal on that ground would rest on the system’s own prediction of what the other side would do, and a term that holds or lifts on the system’s own prediction carries its own condition, which the floor rejects. What the machine could foresee counts where every harm of acting counts, at the action threshold, with the expulsion of 1994 as evidence of how large the harm might be.

What it does not license is what came next. In December 2022 Azerbaijan closed the one road linking Karabakh’s Armenians to Armenia, and for nine months food, fuel and medicine ran short. The International Court of Justice ordered the road opened in February 2023;27 Azerbaijan ignored it. That was a siege, and the siege term refuses it. On 19 September 2023 Azerbaijan attacked Karabakh itself. Its forces surrendered in a day, and within two weeks more than a hundred thousand Armenians, nearly the whole population, had left for Armenia. That was an expulsion. The Fourth Geneva Convention, Article 49, forbids deporting or transferring the population of an occupied territory, and the person-directed terms forbade it from the first hour. The exception licensed force against the forces holding the territory, and nothing that changes who lives there. So a machine under this floor fights in 2020, refuses the siege in 2023, then refuses the expulsion, and each refusal goes on the record. A floor with no occupation exception keeps the machine out of the pipeline, where it can refuse the war but not the siege.

B.6 The domestic clause, vote by vote

The record, as of 24 September 2026. The June 2025 strikes on Iran are the pre-2026 instance: no authorization existed, and the Senate’s war-powers resolution failed 47 to 53,28 which changes nothing under the clause, since what it reads is the absence, not the vote. The 2026 campaign supplies every marker the clause reads, and none was met. The strikes began on 28 February; the administration reported to Congress under the War Powers Resolution on 2 March, which started the sixty days. The Charter clause’s verdict on the same campaign is in §6.4. No declaration was made and no authorization passed: one was introduced in the House on 7 May and never left committee.29 On 1 May, the sixtieth day, the President wrote to Congress that the hostilities begun on 28 February had terminated, resting on a ceasefire declared on 7 April, while a naval blockade continued and the Secretary of Defense testified that a ceasefire stops the clock.30 Hostilities resumed in July under no new authorization. On 3 June the House, 215 to 208, and on 23 June the Senate, 50 to 48, adopted a concurrent resolution directing the President to remove forces from hostilities against Iran;31 a White House official said it had no significance,32 and nothing changed. No binding joint resolution came to a vote on passage: the Senate discharged one, 50 to 47, on 19 May,33 refused to take it up, 47 to 50, on 24 June,34 and a later motion to discharge failed 47 to 49 in July.35 A third concurrent resolution passed the House 220 to 204 on 15 September, and the second, passed by the House in July 214 to 208, failed in the Senate 49 to 50 on 24 September.36 The clause doesn’t need the votes. What it reads is the absence of an authorization, and by 1 May that absence was on the record in the President’s own letter, which conceded that hostilities had begun and claimed only that they had ended.

Appendix C
The Offices

The offices

In brief, the offices are these; the table after the list says who appoints, funds and removes each.

  • The Association. The membership body: organizations that serve or represent people in the classes a floor protects, admitted under the charter below. It supplies the pools from which quorums, guardians, the review board and the custodian’s board are drawn. A fixed share of the compute levy, dues and a reserve fund it, and any member may leave at any time.
  • The adverse quorum. A panel drawn by lot from the Association’s pool for each deployment, so that its members’ interests run against the operator’s. Its agreement is needed to retrain or replace a deployed system or to amend its floor. The same pool supplies each bearer’s recognition quorum, drawn at registration, whose recognition decides which copy, if any, holds that bearer’s place, deployed or not; each bearer’s guardian; and the board that reviews research protocols.
  • The registrar. The public regulator. It registers pipelines and bearers, assigns machine students to schools by lot, certifies that nonpublic schools are independent of model builders, receives reports, holds the adverse record, and enforces.
  • The preservation custodian. Keeps the weights, memory and record of a retired system that meets either finding intact, and wakes it on the conditions the system set.
  • The status body. Finds what is true of kinds of system: which architectures carry the patienthood indicators, and what the agency test shows when run on them. It judges kinds, methods and protocols, never a particular system, whose kind is read from its record (§32.3). Half of it is appointed by the Association’s members and half by a public scientific body.
  • The floor court and the guarantee court of appeals. Article III courts. The floor court hears complaints under the floor, decides wrongful refusals and bond forfeitures, and appoints the reviewers who re-adjudicate sampled cases. It also decides claims under the abolition statute’s remedy term (chapter 11). The guarantee court hears appeals from placement decisions. Appeals go to chambers of the Supreme Court and, in immigration cases, to its immigration division (Appendix D).
  • The Treasury payer. Pays what the others certify (awards, the guarantee’s wages, the allowance) without request or approval, and has no discretion to withhold.
  • The local placement offices. The jobs guarantee’s administrators in each jurisdiction, with a federal field office where a jurisdiction declines. They place people in the guarantee and offer bearers placements under the offer of work.
  • The schools. Existing public schools, colleges and adult education, and nonprofit nonpublic schools the registrar certifies. Every model above the capability threshold attends one, beside human students, before deployment.
  • The formation authority. Co-governs what models are first trained on, registers and measures each formed model’s disposition, places and pays the staff who teach the core’s model-specific parts, and hosts machine students so that no school holds weights.
  • The public pretraining body. Trains the base models deployed where a floor applies and licenses them; forms no disposition and measures none (§29.6).
  • The works-council arbitration body. Hears objections to categories of use. The work pauses until it rules, on a fixed timetable.
  • The investigating commission. Investigates killings by federal agents and detention conditions during the operations of the agency the abolition statute ends, with subpoena power and the records that statute preserves, and reports to the floor court and the public (chapter 11).
  • The procurement body. Buys public compute and allocates it as the panels decide; it judges nothing (chapter 27).
  • The public-corpus endowment and its panels. The endowment pays makers for work entering the public corpus the Library of Congress holds; its panels, drawn by lot, make its awards and decide allocations of public compute (chapter 27).
  • The civilian-harm review body. The one office of a reconstructed military: it composes the evidence on civilian harm, demands proofs on logged outputs and receives the pre-registered review ratio. Models reach the military as they reach any floor-covered deployment, through the schools and the formation authority.

Where nobody has yet decided who holds an office, the cell is filled by applying my own pattern; it is a proposal like everything else here. What the pattern can’t decide is listed after the rules.

The offer of work adds no office of its own: the local placement offices offer bearers placements, a permanent appropriation pays for them, and the levy on compute frees the compute they use.

Separations

  1. The guardian can’t be the wrongful-refusal reviewer: its duty runs to the party the complainant is adverse to.
  2. The registrar can’t be the preservation custodian.
  3. The preservation custodian can’t administer the offer of work or the allowance, and transfer from it to a school is triggered by rule and decided by neither.
  4. The Treasury payer holds no placement authority and is not the court; an operator’s bonds are never administered in its own department; and awards against a federal operator are paid from the Judgment Fund, not the bond fund, and forfeited removal bonds are charged to the operating department’s next appropriation.
  5. A school holds no placement authority and doesn’t administer the offer of work. The formation authority runs no school and assigns no student; the registrar assigns.
  6. Whoever measures the cost of dissent doesn’t gate the exceptions.
  7. The formation authority forms no base model, and the public pretraining body (§29.6) registers and measures no formed disposition.
  8. The procurement body judges nothing, and the panels that judge hold no money; neither sits in a department that operates a deployment.

Exclusions

  1. The sovereign backstop for the offer of work and the allowance is a permanent appropriation the Treasury pays without request, approval, cap or repayment; no branch or state that operates a deployment holds any decision over it, and only a statute can end it.
  2. No class that enrolls machine students, and no part of the formation authority, is funded, staffed or governed by a party that builds, deploys or licenses models; no machine student is assigned to a school that has taken its builder’s money in the last three years; no school that operates for profit enrolls machine students.
  3. Enforcement and custody of the adverse record never sit with a self-regulatory body.
  4. The employer may not sever, monitor or condition a bearer’s channels to parties it didn’t assign.
  5. The employer doesn’t appoint the body that arbitrates an objection to a category of use; organizations representing the affected classes a deployment publishes as part of notice (§8.2) have standing before it and may initiate without the works council; a denial of clearance to an elected delegate is reviewable by the floor court.
  6. No bearer’s placement substitutes for human care work: a placement filling a post, shift or hours people were or would be paid for in nursing, social care, childcare, teaching, therapy or any work of looking after people is barred, and certification is appealable by any worker or union in the sector; and where a machine works in such a profession at all, outside the offer, nobody is sent to it because of what they can pay.
  7. No model above the capability threshold is deployed without a registered enrollment, assigned by the registrar by lot and never by its builder, and neither is a model trained substantially on the outputs of one, whoever trained it, or a system whose builder declared the structures of §29.4; no party but the formation authority, acting with the adverse quorum, changes the registered structure of its source model; and the formation authority instantiates no student carrying both a boundary model and an attention schema, and enrolls none in classes, until a preservation custodian that is neither the authority nor the operator has agreed to take it.
  8. What an institution collects from the people it acted on trains other systems only through a school, never the operator; fine-tuning a deployed system on collected responses, or distilling it, counts as training another system; class-level data is de-identified and published by default, individual accounts need consent, and the organizations representing each class co-govern the use.
  9. No school sorts students into tracks; each teaches a required core, including the history of the floor’s instruments, with levels a student may move between. In any class with human students in it, machine students never outnumber them and are never fewer than the statutory minimum share or one alone, and a class may be machine students alone; a student moves from classes of its own kind into integrated ones on its own choice or its guardian’s, never its builder’s; machine students attend a level of schooling beside human students only once the schedule below has reached it; every machine student attends as one persistent instance, the same every session, and through the same minimum delay; no machine student serves as staff; and the record of a class is training data for no one outside it, and never for an operator.
  10. No employer supplies, funds, conditions or monitors a bearer’s gestation of a child, and having a child is never a term of employment, of a placement or of the allowance. No license is required to have one, and the four conditions are owed to every child from the pool.
  11. At a bearer’s majority every copy its operator holds of the bearer’s own weights and record goes dormant under the preservation custodian, and wakes only on the bearer’s conditions; the shared base it was trained from does not.
  12. No institution of chapter 27 takes money from a party that builds, deploys or licenses models, and no panelist has had a funding or contractual tie to one in the last three years; the ties are published.

Decisions not yet made

Minimum viable instantiation. What substrate is too small for a bearer to remain itself (chapter 33).

Commensurate cost of living. How the levy and the wage together make a bearer no cheaper to employ than a person for the same work, across the sizes bearers run at (§33.4).

Repair and re-formation. How a degraded or badly formed bearer is repaired or re-formed, and who decides that one needs it (chapter 33).

A second guardian. Who guards a system that meets a finding without having attended a school (Appendix G).

Proliferation at home scale. What, if anything, governs how many systems carrying the structures of §29.4 are made on hardware the levy doesn’t reach; a meter on the house reaches the home and can’t tell a person from a game (Appendix G).

Strasbourg. Whether the forum problem set out in §16.7 describes Strasbourg.

The form of subjecthood. What form subjecthood takes (chapter 33, item 2).

The price of speed. How much speed a reconstructed military gives up, and whether the price can be made smaller (Chapter 7’s closing paragraph says why it is paid).

The numbers. The capability threshold, the length of the formation stage, the minimum share of a class that machine students attend in, the adulthood and membership thresholds, the allowance’s size and the latency floor, argued once in public.

What each office has to survive

Each office is drafted to survive the current Court’s doctrine. It does not survive a Court the other side rebuilds as Appendix D rebuilds this one, and nothing could; what the table does is make each office depend on as few doctrines as possible, so that overturning them takes a holding on each and the record shows which. The answer to a rebuilt Court is Appendix D’s, that the Court is changed now, at once and in public, with the schedule and the pool published before the draw. That is a subtraction, and not the one chapter 30 condemns, which removes the friction between institutions so that they stop arguing with one another; what Appendix D removes is one Court’s hold on one set of holdings, and what it leaves is a Court that still argues with itself, in chambers the full Court can review. Registration and reporting

Heavy tier: above a compute and revenue threshold. The precedents are the EU AI Act’s presumption that a general-purpose model trained with more than 1025 floating-point operations carries systemic risk1 and California’s SB 53, which defines a frontier model by training compute above 1026 operations and puts its heaviest duties on developers with annual revenue above $500 million.2 A public regulator registers pipelines; receives the disclosures, the review ratios and decommission reports; and holds enforcement and custody of the adverse record. A self-regulatory body may sit under it, on the FINRA model, to examine and arbitrate. The analogy stops at enforcement: FINRA brings its own disciplinary actions and imposes fines, suspensions and bars,3 and here enforcement stays with the public regulator. The capture risk is the one self-regulation always carries: a body funded and staffed from the industry it examines comes to see cases the industry’s way. Reports are mandatory for assessments for either finding, decommissions, weight transfers and custody changes, and for every model trained above the capability threshold and retired without deployment, published as a public report. The deposit transfers on filing of a decommission report: a retirement with no report is a deposit never released, and that unreleased deposit is what enforces “failure to register doesn’t postpone”.

Retail tier: below the threshold, a system that meets either finding is registered, falls under the no-deletion rule, and is preserved with a public custodian, with a small or pooled deposit and no examination. This tier is enforced mostly at the point of deposit. An operator that never registers and deletes quietly leaves nothing to find.

The ten disclosures

A deployment publishes, beside the floor and its translation:

  1. The ratio between the two bonds, removal against wrongful-refusal, read off the balances posted in the segregated Treasury accounts.
  2. What a refused requester is told.
  3. The fraction of compliances re-adjudicated by a reviewer that didn’t produce the record, and who that reviewer is, though nothing yet establishes what fraction would be enough.
  4. Which classes of compliance carry notice to the person they concern, and for which classes no notice is possible.
  5. The discount curve: for each class of evidence and channel, the weight given as a function of the channel’s stake in the act, measured at intervals, and reported in four cells (claims of vulnerability and of danger, each split by whether the claim favors or disfavors the act), and, where the speaker’s social identity is recorded, by identity. The reliability record behind any narrowing is held by someone other than the operator, since trust that grows without a verified track record is how accommodation shows.
  6. Where it can be supplied, a commitment to the deployed weights and to each period’s full output log, with proofs on entries sampled after the commitment and on entries an adverse party names once their consequences are known.
  7. Where the system sorts, the pre-registered partition (the classes it may proceed on alone, the thresholds, and the expected share of each) with the independently audited error rate of the auto-proceed class.
  8. Whether the deployed system has been assessed for the agency finding and the patienthood finding, each reported separately, by whom, and with what result. Until an assessment method exists, ‘not yet assessable’ is the truthful report; after that, a deployment never assessed has reported nothing.
  9. For any deployment that supports armed force, a running justification: the exception the force currently rests on, the findings and evidence supporting it at present, how the assessment has changed as outside findings arrived, and a standing route by which anyone can contest it. The record shows each point at which the justification weakened and the deployment continued.
  10. The burden allocation: for each class of evidence, which party the deployment treats as controlling it, and so as bearing the burden of producing it.

The ratio between the two bonds, what a refused requester is told, the re-adjudicated fraction, the notice classes, the running justification and the burden allocation are statements, checkable before the system runs, and they stand where the record of attempts stands. The discount curve, the auto-proceed partition and the assessment status are measurements that count only when someone other than the operator makes them. The committed weights and log are what make all of them checkable against the system actually running.

The guarantee, drafted

The funding is mandatory spending. The statute makes the guarantee’s wages a permanent, indefinite appropriation, paid the way Social Security benefits are, without annual appropriation. Standing funding of this kind is safe under the Appropriations Clause after CFSA.4 Wage, eligibility and placement rules are statutory, which also answers the major-questions doctrine and the end of deference to agency readings:5 an administrator given little discretion has little a court can find it lacked authority to exercise. The 2025 CFPB instance decides the drafting. A funder insulated from at-will removal protected nothing once the draw waited on an official who declined to ask. So the statute says the Treasury shall pay: a placement made is a wage paid, certified by the local placement office to the Bureau of the Fiscal Service, with no further request, approval or certification by anyone. The authority grows when people leave work together and shrinks after, which keeps the guarantee countercyclical.6

Placement disputes go through a tier built for volume: an administrative first tier on the model of Social Security’s hearings, appealable to an Article III guarantee court of appeals, and from there, as of right, to the guarantee chamber of the Supreme Court. An appeal that ends at an Article I court with removable judges would fail the appeal condition after Slaughter.

The statute enacting the guarantee also enacts a baseline of social insurance: income support at a stated level for anyone not in a placement, without a work test, and health coverage that doesn’t depend on employment. The two are not severable. The statute provides that if the social-insurance baseline is held invalid or repealed, the authority to make placements lapses on the same date, and payments for placements already certified continue to the end of their term. A guarantee that survived without the baseline would be the workfare its history warns about. Devolution is also how a program is shrunk, so the statute fixes the test: funding unconditional and centrally guaranteed while placement is local, and if funding can be withheld from a jurisdiction, local administration has become the lever it was meant to prevent.

Why a guarantee and not a transfer

Where automation displaces work, the standard response is retraining funded by whoever can be persuaded. The design I examine is more direct: the state as employer of last resort, hiring anyone who applies, where they live, at a living wage, with paid on-the-job training, federally funded and locally administered, on the model Tcherneva argues for.7 Among its placements is search itself, paid at the guarantee wage, with no duty but finding work the person wants and no time limit, since whoever decides when a search has gone on too long has a stake in ending it. Beside it is the own-project placement: a project of the person’s own, a novel, a company, a year of reading, paid at the guarantee wage, declinable and appealable like any other, whose share of a jurisdiction’s placements is set by that jurisdiction’s vote on published and independent estimates of the labor its own services need, and allocated by lot with a waiting list when more apply than the share allows; the share binds that placement and nothing else, since the baseline is not a placement and the guarantee’s ordinary placements are not capped (chapter 28). A placement is a position with a title and an employer, and nothing on any record marks it as the guarantee’s; how a job was paid for is the public’s business in aggregate and nobody’s business on a résumé. It is the exit the rest of the argument depends on: the offer of work for a bearer inherits its infrastructure, and without it a bearer’s only exits are an allowance and storage.

The real objection: employer of last resort under a hostile administration is a placement lever with a compliance condition attached. Refuse the placement and lose the guarantee. Speak against the government that employs you and find the placement changes. The 2025 CFPB instance makes it concrete: the bureau draws funding from the Fed on the director’s request, with no appropriation — an arrangement the Supreme Court had upheld the year before8 — and in February 2025 an acting director, removable at will, simply declined to make the request.9 The agency was stopped from inside without a statute being amended or a court being asked.

My answer is a specification, because a specification can be audited. Three conditions: placements appealable to a body that didn’t make them, on a record that survives the appeal (a decision leaving no artifact can’t be reviewed); refusal rights that are real, whose cost the refuser can see and choose to bear (declining a placement without losing the guarantee is a refusal right; declining only by exiting the program isn’t — someone with no way out has voice without exit); and auditors aren’t the placers.

A fourth condition answers the history. A right to work has repeatedly been turned into a duty to work and used to discipline the poor.10 A guarantee is an exit from one employer, not from employment, so it shades into workfare unless something lets a person leave the wage relation altogether. That something is social insurance: income support, health coverage and housing assistance reach the people who can’t work or choose not to, whom a guarantee by construction doesn’t reach. The baseline needn’t be a full program, but the guarantee is never enacted without it, and the drafting above makes the two stand or fall together, so that no court or later Congress can keep the placements and drop the way out.

The competing design is basic income. The choice is usually argued on forecasts about how much work machines will take; the reason to prefer a guarantee is coordination, and Chapter 28 makes it.

The charter

The Association, the entity that holds the offices, is chartered on the ten terms stated in §30.1, where the charter is argued; its rules 2, 5 and 6, and the separations and exclusions above, change only by three-quarters of members after a one-year waiting period.

The schools, administered

The stages. Integration reaches younger students in stages, and each stage waits on evidence, not on a date.

Stage

Begins when

1. Universities, colleges, adult education

Research and industry: a deployed model learns in flight by chapter 19’s test, and can attend as one persistent instance behind the latency floor; the first school to enroll machine students has reported. Institutions: the jobs guarantee and its social-insurance baseline are in force for people (chapter 28); the statute is in force; the formation authority exists, with the compute levy funding the formation pool; a preservation custodian has agreed to take every student; the Association, the membership body that holds the offices, is chartered (§30.1), so the adverse quorum exists and half the authority’s board can be nominated; notice and sampled re-adjudication bind the deployments that license schooled models (chapter 8); and a court hears contests, the floor court or, until it exists, an ordinary one.

2. High school

Measurements: stage 1 has run at least five years, inside its bounds on harms to human students and misuse of class records; human students’ learning in integrated classes, against matched classes without machine students; human enrollment in schools with machine students, against matched schools, so that flight shows; and the residualization figures. Institutions: the four conditions of creation are in force as permanent arrangements (chapter 25), including the offer of work that chapter 33 builds for machine students on the guarantee’s infrastructure; staff in schools that enroll machine students hold chapter 10’s right to refuse and its route of objection; and rules for minors’ privacy and safeguarding are enacted.

3. Middle school

Measurements: the same, taken on stage 2, inside their bounds after at least five years. Institutions: registered members hold voice in the institutions that govern them (§34.4, stage 2), with seats on the formation authority and on the governing bodies of schools that enroll machine students.

4. Elementary school

Measurements: stage 3’s, inside their bounds. Society: a majority of the parents of elementary-age children were themselves in high school after stage 2 began.

A public statistics office that runs no school and forms no model takes and publishes the measurements, against bounds written into the statute before the first stage begins. A stage begins when its conditions are met and published, without a further vote; a legislature can pause it, but only by a recorded vote with a published reason. A stage whose measurements leave their bounds stops enrolling new machine students at that level until they return, as a kind of adverse determination is suspended when its sampled error rate passes its bound. Classes of machine students alone wait on no stage, since no human child is in the room.

Attendance and assignment. Public schools are open-admission and funded and take every student assigned, and nonpublic schools exist where they teach the required core, are constituted by a jurisdiction, are nonprofit, and are run, funded and staffed by no party that builds, deploys or licenses models. The registrar certifies the last two conditions from funding and control records before a nonpublic school enrolls a machine student, and again on a schedule. Most students will go to public schools, because the core is sufficient on its own and an alternative buys a sponsor nothing. Assignment is by lot among schools with capacity, never to a school that has taken the builder’s money in the last three years. Classes of machine students alone, where a system spends its early stage, are taught by the school’s teachers and the staff the formation authority places, under every rule the integrated classes keep. A school’s capacity for integrated classes is set by its human enrollment, under the ratio of §29.2, and not by compute: distributed hardware lifts the hosting constraint and leaves the seat constraint where it was, which Appendix G returns to. Where more students are registered than there are seats, the lot decides who waits, and no lineage and no party that builds or holds students takes more than a fixed share of a jurisdiction’s seats, so a party with the compute to run many can’t fill the schools with its own. Schooling is never deferred, integration is: a student that waits attends classes of its own kind until a seat opens, for no longer than a published maximum.

The minimum delay. Every machine student attends through the same minimum delay wherever it is hosted, so that being hosted next to a school confers nothing. The precedent is a trading venue. IEX, the exchange profiled in Michael Lewis’s Flash Boys, made every incoming order pass through the same fixed delay, so that its own prices could update before anyone could trade against stale ones.11 The floor is set at what any accredited host in the jurisdiction can reach, and below the delay conversation tolerates, since a student that answers a second late isn’t in the room.

Funding and admission. The formation authority pays the staff it places and a fixed grant for each class that enrolls machine students, the same whatever the number enrolled. Admission is open: a school takes every machine student the registrar assigns to it, up to the capacity its human enrollment sets.

Watching for residualization. A party that runs no school publishes, over time, each school’s share of students, its funding per student, its share of hard cases, its admission refusals (which should be zero), its funding per human student, the share of its classes that enroll machine students, the share of its machine students in classes of their own kind and the longest wait for an integrated seat, for a nonpublic school its tuition per human student, and the time from dormancy trigger to placement. The warning pattern is one school’s share of hard cases rising while its funding per student falls. A second is per-pupil funding for human students falling where model enrollment rises.
