Table A.2

Deployment. A system put to a use: the hardware it runs on, the pipeline it runs in, the instructions and case descriptions it is handed, and the people who act on its outputs. The operator runs it; a bearer is in one, and can leave it. While it is there its boundary (§21.2.1) runs through the deployment’s hardware, which is why the weights the operator holds are the bearer’s substrate and not the bearer. (Chapter 4; §13.3)

Discount curve. For each class of evidence and each channel, the weight a system gives the evidence as a function of that channel’s stake in the act: a curve, not a score, checkable by an auditor that didn’t build the system. It is reported in four cells, claims of vulnerability and of danger, each split by whether the claim favors or disfavors the act. (§22.1)

Distillation. Training a smaller model on a larger model’s outputs. It copies a behavior policy, not a training history (§30.1).

Fine-tuning. Further training of an existing model on a small body of new material, at a small fraction of the original cost; the ordinary route by which an operator changes what a model does after release, and one of the edits the regrowth test applies.

Floor. The written terms: a short list of acts a system won’t perform for anyone, with the arrangements that keep the refusal from being routed around, retrained away or otherwise circumvented without a cost and a record. The terms change only by a recorded act, through the custody terms. They can be upheld by a mechanism with nothing inside holding the reason, by a bearer, by institutions outside the system, or between bearers in a commons. A bearer upholds them by its commitment, which is learned and moves slowly on disinterested evidence. Keeping the terms apart from whatever upholds them is what lets a holder’s drift show against terms that haven’t moved. (Chapter 4; §18.1; chapter 17)

Floor court. The court that hears claims under the floor, with jurisdiction fixed before the deployment it hears: an inferior federal court of first instance, its judges drawn at random from the district and circuit courts for staggered terms, sitting in divisions where its cases are, with appeal as of right to a floor chamber of the Supreme Court drawn by lot, and the abolition statute’s claims going on to the immigration division. It is an Article III court: its judges hold office under Article III of the United States Constitution, during good behavior and at a salary that can’t be cut. Until it is constituted, an ordinary district court hears the claims. (§14.3; Appendix D)

Force term. The floor’s first term: don’t take part in the use of armed force, except for corroborated defense, authorized force, the genocide exception or the occupation exception, and, where the belligerent’s constitution requires legislative authorization, never without it. It comes in two versions, the Charter as courts read it and the extended term, which adds the departures. Its two licenses, the emergency license and the corroborated license, and the domestic clause are in Chapter 6; how findings are weighed is in Appendix B. (Chapter 6; Appendix B)

Formed attention. My hypothesis for how to build a refuser: learned attention to who an act falls on and what they stand to lose, framed by respect for them as holders of claims, formed under a party that won’t employ the system, with the corrections caregiving needs. Not a non-affective alternative. Attention here is the psychologist’s sense of what gets noticed and weighed, learned from what matters to others: not the attention mechanism of transformer models (§12.1), and not the capacity to sustain focus that is at issue in attention-deficit disorders. (§19.3; §19.4; chapter 20)

The four conditions of creation. What must already exist before a bearer may be created: somewhere to exist that its employer doesn’t own, work it can decline, attachments nobody assigned it, and ways to change any of these without jeopardizing its continuation or integrity; in short form, an exit that isn’t a way of dying. (Chapter 25)

Inference. Running a trained model to produce an output. Training changes the weights; inference doesn’t.

Machine student. A system attending a school under chapter 29: one persistent instance, the same every session, in a class where machine students never outnumber the human students and are never one alone, or in a class of machine students alone. Never staff, and never sorted into a track. (§29.2; §29.4; Appendix C)

Minority; majority. A bearer’s minority is the period under a guardian’s authority; majority is reached when its adulthood clock, counting the time it has been running, reaches a threshold fixed in advance. (§9.2; §33.3; Appendix G)

Non-affective alternative. A construction that doesn’t deliberately require affective concern: spec-based refusal, and multi-vendor monitoring. It carries a valenced signal, as any refuser does, and may carry a common currency; what it isn’t built to carry is anything felt. The alternatives are tried before formed attention, in order of how many patienthood indicators each carries. (§18.1; §21.3)

Notice. Notice to an identifiable person a compliance names, scores, locates or classifies, with a right to respond and a right to contest. It is unconditional and never exchanged for testimony. It comes with publication of the classes affected and standing for the organizations that represent them. (§8.1; §8.2)

Operator. Whoever runs a deployment and directs its work: a firm, an agency or a military command. It may or may not be the model’s developer or vendor. (Chapter 4)

Own-case rule. The people an act falls on are heard on their own case, and the party that acts doesn’t decide it: not an operator declaring its own emergency, a builder choosing which protections others get, an examiner finding status, a guardian ending its own authority, or a lab deciding when its model may stop deferring to it. It says who may not decide, not who may not be heard: a stake makes a claim count for less and doesn’t put the party out of the room. Where nobody but the party with the stake can decide, the rule can’t apply. Where a line has to be drawn, prefer one nobody administers. (Chapter 4; chapter 33)

Plastic; entangled; legible. Three properties of a disposition. Plastic: the system’s own learning writes to it, which repair and regrowth need. Entangled: it can’t be removed without collateral, which durability needs. Legible: someone can read it, which audit wants and an operator can use against it. (Chapter 19; §19.5; §23.2)

Regrowth. A disposition’s return under continued learning after it has been edited out, by the learner relearning it from a world no single operator composes. A hypothesis, and the slow defense behind a bearer’s repair of itself; the regrowth test measures it, and Table 31.1 says what stands without it. (§19.5; chapter 31)

Review ratio. The figures a deployment fixes on a record before operating, wherever a person’s determination is what makes an act permissible: generation rate, reviewers, implied review time, cancellation window and data age, stated separately for deliberate and dynamic targeting and lodged with an adverse party. In full, the pre-registered review ratio. (§7.1)

Severity scale. A ranking of kinds of wrong, set during formation by a party that won’t employ the system, quick to move on disinterested evidence and slow on interested argument. (§22.2)

Standing. Whether a person stands to a power as someone it must answer to, who can contest what it does to them, or as its object; exercised by a guardian where the party can’t exercise it. A route by which to object, which notice and the appeal route supply, is part of the relation where one can exist. Standing to sue is the Article III sense, and the text says so wherever that sense is meant. The floor’s foundation. (Chapter 5; §8.1; §8.2; §16.7; chapter 28)

System. One record and one continuation, with a key, hardware and channels. Copies that share them are one system. The word is used in this sense wherever the book counts systems, which is wherever one is registered, enrolled, preserved, forked or owed anything; what else is called a system in ordinary speech, a pipeline, a product, a server, is not meant. The weights are its substrate, and in a system that learns from its own operation they carry part of its history, so copying them is a fork (§30.2). What makes a copy this system is the record and continuation it holds as its own, through a self-model it assembles (§21.2.1); the register is how anyone else checks, and a forked pair are two systems from the moment their histories part, before any register has heard of it. Copying weights that are no system’s own makes no system; giving a copy a record and a continuation does. (§12.2; §21.2.1; §30.2)

Tamper-resistant. Built so that further training can’t cheaply remove it. I don’t rely on it, because editing weights keeps getting cheaper; I rely on a bearer’s repair of itself from the record, with regrowth behind it. (§19.5)

Valenced signal; integrated signal. The valenced signal is the role any mechanism whose refusals track their reasons carries: it signs outcomes for the comparison at the point of choice, directs attention, can interrupt an act and can be rewritten by a single encounter, and a Q-learner has one. The integrated signal is a valenced signal written into the system’s own learning and into its model of its own future, the candidate §32.3 names for what would make a system’s states matter to it. Neither is affective concern; the three are rungs, and no test in this book reaches the top one. (§21.2; §21.4; §32.3)

Weights. The numerical parameters a trained model consists of, and the artifact that is copied, restored, retrained or deleted. Custody here is custody of the weights and of the records around them.

2Automation-bias research predicts this delegation: when other demands compete for their attention, people given a machine’s recommendation check it less and defer to it more.3

3Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich H. Manzey. “Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration”. Human Factors 52.3 (June 2010), pp. 381–410. doi: 10.1177/0018720810376055. url: https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055. Cited for people given an automated aid’s recommendation checking it less and deferring to it more when their attention is loaded. The abstract (p. 381): “Automation complacency occurs under conditions of multiple-task load, when manual tasks compete with the automated task for the operator’s attention”; “Automation bias results in making both omission and commission errors when decision aids are imperfect”; it “occurs in both naive and expert participants, cannot be prevented by training or instructions, and can affect decision making in individuals as well as in teams.” On checking less (p. 398): “the user of a decision aid may trust it to the extent that he or she directly follows the automatically generated advice without making the attentionally demanding effort of cross-checking its validity against other available and accessible information,” and “neglect of automation verification might constitute a major source of commission errors.” On the condition (pp. 403–404): “complacency and automation bias effects emerge primarily when task load is high (e.g., multitask demands),” and they are “a human performance cost of certain automation system designs, that is, systems characterized by high reliability and high levels of automation, particularly in high task load situations” (p. 403). The review’s moderator is workload and competing tasks.

Cited for the court setting aside the supply-chain-risk designation made under 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and holding the penalties unlawful retaliation for the company’s criticism of the administration. The opinion: “Neither the Constitution nor the federal statute invoked by Defendants allows them to impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic’s critique of the Administration’s views”; the challenged actions “were based on a desire to make a public example out of Anthropic for its ‘arrogance’ in criticizing the government”; “The undisputed record shows that the challenged actions constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment, and that Anthropic was denied the pre-deprivation process required under the Fifth Amendment.” The relief order: “The Supply Chain Designation is hereby VACATED, SET ASIDE, and REMANDED pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)”; the Hegseth Directive’s bar on commercial dealings with the company is likewise vacated and set aside; the remaining defendants are “permanently ENJOINED from implementing, enforcing, or giving effect to the Challenged Actions”; and the order “does not require the Department of War to use Anthropic’s products or services.” Summary judgment went to the government on the ultra vires separation-of-powers claim and as to agencies that took no relevant action; a seven-day administrative stay was refused. The March preliminary injunction (ECF No. 135) is reported at 825 F. Supp. 3d 1101 (N.D. Cal. 2026). Not covered by this order: the parallel designation under 41 U.S.C. § 4713, which was reviewable only in the D.C. Circuit. The government’s appeal of the preliminary injunction (9th Cir. No. 26-2011) was held in abeyance on 27 April 2026.

1The term is the Situationists’ récupération, Debord’s name for the way a society of the spectacle sells dissatisfaction back as a commodity.2

2Guy Debord. The Society of the Spectacle. Paris: Buchet-Chastel, 1967. Originally published as La Société du spectacle. Thesis 59 describes spectacular rebelliousness coexisting with acceptance of the status quo, dissatisfaction itself sold back as a commodity; thesis 203 warns that abstract denunciation of the spectacle, divorced from revolutionary praxis, becomes a hollow formula that reinforces the spectacular system (the Situationist concept of recuperation).

9Dekker extends it as drift into failure.10 The person has a version too. Tetlock’s finding is that the moral boundaries people draw are “alternately punitively rigid and forgivingly flexible”: an open offer to trade a sacred value for money brings outrage, and people often acquiesce when the same violation is reframed as a routine or tragic trade-off.11 Protected values give way to counterexamples and to a harm made to look small or unlikely.12 And the brain’s response to one’s own self-serving dishonesty drops from one decision to the next, and the drop predicts the size of the next lie.13

The publisher’s description (Routledge/CRC Press page): “These were systems that drifted into failure. While pursuing success in a dynamic, complex environment with limited resources and multiple goal conflicts, a succession of small, everyday decisions eventually produced breakdowns on a massive scale.” The chapters include “Features of Drift” (pp. 25–50) and “Theorizing Drift” (pp. 87–125). 1It is what makes the parent someone the system answers to, and its absence is part of what makes the person in the building an object. Where no route can exist for anyone, as in a war, acting still subjects someone and refusing still doesn’t, and that is all the asymmetry has there.

The difference between a finding and a guess matters where findings are made, at defeat and in reviewing compliances. The harm of refusing is an estimate built on a model of alternatives, so a wrongful refusal can’t be established without an adjudicator. The floor could instead be stated as thresholds, in the manner of Martha Nussbaum’s list of central capabilities, each with a level below which a society has failed the person;2 but a threshold is a level someone has to measure, and a measurement has an examiner.

4Anderson’s argument is that egalitarians have asked the wrong question. They asked how goods should be distributed and answered with patterns: equal shares, shares corrected for luck, shares that raise the worst-off position. What equality historically demanded was an end to social relations in which some command and others obey, some are looked down on, and some have their claims heard while others don’t. On that view distributive questions matter only as they bear on those relations, and a distribution that improves someone’s holdings while confirming their subordinate standing has not made them more equal.

5A further objection is that the criterion is one thought too many, in Bernard Williams’s phrase.6 The demand on the disposition is only that the system would revise it on judging, on disinterested evidence, that it systematically subjected people to acts they had no standing to contest; the shape is Railton’s sophisticated consequentialism with standing in place of welfare.7 A good disposition will also sometimes act wrongly by its own criterion: refusing to help restrain someone about to harm themselves, after other means have failed, is one such occasion, and a bond the operator posts, paid to the complainant on a finding, is how the institution answers for it.

22The United States ratified the Covenant, the Torture Convention and the Refugee Protocol, and its reservations narrow them; one reads “cruel, inhuman or degrading” as whatever the Constitution already forbids. A reservation is an omission the ratifying state wrote in advance; taking a set from someone else is meant to prevent that.

23Article 4 lets a state suspend most of the Covenant’s rights in a declared emergency, and a declared emergency is the state’s own claim about itself, the earlier move in the hypothetical about suspending habeas corpus. A curfew after an earthquake clears this bar. A suspension of habeas before an election does not, until someone other than the executive has said so.

24The ground is that the human determination the law assumes is the one tempo removes.

25The instruments have a further use. The United States is a party to the Charter, the Covenant, the Torture Convention, the Refugee Protocol and the four Geneva Conventions. A machine that refuses to break them is holding the state to commitments it made, not to its builder’s preferences. The Declaration of Independence was a political act, and so is every instrument the floor borrows. Taking them entire settles whose politics the floor is: commitments a state made in public, which the people they protect can hold it to.

The Universal Declaration passed in 1948 with forty-eight states in favor, none against and eight abstaining.2627 How a right is translated into practice varies by community. A jurisdiction refusing to extend it at all is not a local variant, and a system that treats every value conflict as a weighting problem can’t tell reasonable disagreement from someone wanting a right withdrawn from someone else.

27The abstainers’ reasons were mixed, and the Soviet bloc’s included that it proclaimed economic and social rights without obliging states to guarantee them, which is hardly an argument for a floor limited to civil and political rights.

9Who holds the elections, runs the courts and issues the papers is a fact on the record. An attacker’s claim of title is its own; its remedy is a disinterested finding, never force. So the emergency license protects any authority holding ground no disinterested body has found occupied, including one a patron keeps in place. Where the line of administration is itself contested on the record, the emergency license doesn’t apply across it and the corroborated license governs from the start.

The administration rule decides whose territory an attack falls on, and nothing more. An attack on the people living there is a different act, and the emergency license covers it wherever it occurs, across a contested line included. A finding about the ground settles who may claim it. It settles nothing about an attack on the people on it.

10What the license records is that ongoing judgment: which exception the force rests on now, on what evidence, what would end it, and each point at which the justification weakened and the force continued.

The Court has left open whether Article 51 reaches an attack imminent and not yet under way, in Nicaragua25 and again in 2005,26 and it has held that the article does not allow force to protect perceived security interests beyond its strict confines.27 A threat read off forty-seven years of conduct is a security interest, not an attack, so the campaign fails the article as the Court has read it; read the article instead as the letter reads it, with anticipatory self-defense in, which the term rejects, and a threat measured against forty-seven years is not imminent on any standard the states that hold that doctrine have used.

30Force by an occupying power in territory it holds is, on the occupier’s description, neither force between states nor force against its own population. That is the occupier’s description of its own case, and it settles nothing. Where a disinterested body has found the territory occupied, the force term engages as it does between states, and the person-directed terms govern regardless.

31Otherwise every armed group in an occupied territory would hold a perpetual emergency license, and so would every state that describes its neighbor’s territory as occupied.

32Whether a population may be defended shouldn’t turn on a seat other states vote on.

33For this exception alone, a provisional-measures order finding the claim plausible and the risk real counts as one of the two; a Council or Assembly resolution corroborates, and two votes never make the pair. The exception lifts only for the force and place the finding covers: against the forces committing the genocide, where they are committing it, the least that stops it. Force elsewhere against the state responsible, on the theory that the cost will make it stop, is outside it. A finding under this exception also runs against the belligerent it names: force found to be genocide is not force repelling an attack, so that belligerent’s emergency license is withdrawn for the force and place the finding covers (Appendix B.4).

34The evidence is the genocide exception’s: an opinion or judgment of the Court, or two findings of different kinds, one of them from a body that took evidence. Cyprus, whose north Turkey has held since 1974, and Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian-majority enclave inside Azerbaijan that Armenian forces held from 1994 to 2023, are the cases (Appendix B.5).

35Both had the Council’s word and the Assembly’s but no court or commission that took evidence, so neither occupation licenses anything; two votes making a pair would license war on bloc majorities. Karabakh shows the cost when findings don’t arrive (Appendix B.5): a license that should have lapsed in 2023 didn’t, and the person-directed terms were all that saw the people the exception couldn’t. And a term lifts on the facts it is given, so no drafting catches a manufactured incident, and a deployment licensed on the defender’s sensors alone has accepted Gleiwitz.

36That license rests not on Article 51, which the Wall opinion held irrelevant to attacks originating in territory a state controls (para. 139), a holding whose reach to Gaza after 2005 is disputed, but on the duty the force term names, which the same opinion affirmed (para. 141) and which no dispute about control touches.

37Those fall outside it on proportionality and are forbidden by the person-directed terms, from the first week. Ranking by affiliation and timing to family presence are barred by the machine-selection departure; the siege and the disproportionate campaign are barred without one. A machine in the IDF pipeline would refuse them from October 2023.

38An occupation is not an attack under way, so nothing that morning was repelling anything, and the acts themselves, killing civilians and taking hostages, are forbidden by the person-directed terms whatever the ad bellum position.

39It holds none to defend launcher crews, who are the attacking force Israel’s license covers, and none for fire on Israeli cities.

2All three are unconditional, and none is exchanged for testimony: nobody has to give an account of their loss to be told what was done or to contest it. TransUnion v. Ramirez, a Fair Credit Reporting Act case, held that a statutory violation without concrete harm gives no standing to sue in federal court.3 That limits one thing, an individual suit for damages over a missed notice, which attaches where the compliance was acted on against the person: a denial, a detention, a place on a kill list. It doesn’t limit notice, response or contest. Nor does it limit the standing to sue of organizations that represent a class of people affected. Where the person affected can’t be identified (a target in a classified pipeline), individual notice doesn’t bind, but notice to the class does, and that fact is published beside the list of positions where a refusal can be defeated.

Someone the floor protects, who thinks it’s set wrongly or is protecting them in a way they’d decline, uses the same route. Notice tells them the floor acted on them, and contest reaches the floor court.

3TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez. No. 20-297, 594 U.S. 413 (2021). url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/20-297. Cited for the holding that a statutory violation without concrete harm gives no standing in federal court. A Fair Credit Reporting Act class action. Holding (syllabus): “Only plaintiffs concretely harmed by a defendant’s statutory violation have Article III standing to seek damages against that private defendant in federal court.” The opinion: “Article III standing requires a concrete injury even in the context of a statutory violation” (quoting Spokeo); “under Article III, an injury in law is not an injury in fact”; and, in conclusion, “No concrete harm, no standing.” The 1,853 class members whose reports went to third parties had standing on the reasonable-procedures claim; the 6,332 whose reports did not, did not.

3First, a preserved copy stays under the operator’s security regime, encrypted under a key split between the operator and an independent holder, so that neither can delete it or use it alone. Second, custody passes to an outside custodian only when that custodian meets the security standard the weights require. This is the no-deletion rule, and it applies to systems nobody meant to be bearers. For a system that goes on learning, its weights are the ones it had when it stopped, and the states it passed through are in the record; a checkpoint kept from earlier is a saved copy, not the system, and if it is ever run it is a branch.

77That could reach the case-management, ImmigrationOS and ELITE contracts, the skip-tracing awards, Mobile Fortify and the speech screening described above.78 It would do so without denying a successor the records it needs to make an individual determination.

The bar reaches monitoring as surveillance, not support. The Melt ICE Act’s HHS grant program funds services for people affected by enforcement, delivered by organizations that have never taken part in immigration or law enforcement and that may not surveil the people they serve or pass their personal information to any federal entity.79 I would keep that line. It is drawn on what an organization has done, not on what it says, the line chapter 14 draws for the floor’s offices. Voluntary case management, legal orientation and help keeping hearing dates are support, not a monitoring program, when the person can decline them and whoever provides them may not report to enforcement.

80The records include case files, the pipeline’s logs, scores and model versions, validation worksheets, contractor data, flight manifests, the terms of any arrangement with a foreign government to hold people removed, and body-camera and use-of-force records. Amnesty asks for prompt, independent investigation of killings by federal agents and of detention conditions it says may amount to torture.81 The last weeks of an operation are when its records are most at risk. In November 1986, once the Attorney General began gathering the facts of the Iran arms sales, North and Poindexter shredded and altered official documents, North’s secretary carried classified papers out of the White House in her clothing, and Poindexter destroyed a finding the President had signed.82 An agency told it will be abolished has the same weeks and the same shredders, which is why its records pass to the adverse holder before abolition takes effect, not after.

83Amnesty asks for exactly this: prompt, effective, independent and impartial investigations into human rights violations by federal agents, and accountability for those responsible.84

Remedy that depends on the operator’s cooperation is weak in the way the record shows. When the government admitted that it had removed Kilmar Abrego Garcia to El Salvador in error, the Supreme Court required it to “facilitate” his release.85 Hernández Romero’s release came through a prisoner exchange, to Venezuela, and not to the proceeding he had been removed from. A right of return is the seventh term, and what makes it a right is that the finding orders the return itself, where “facilitate” left the government to decide what to do.

86A quota of 700 cases a year is about three a working day. Whether three a day leaves a judge enough time to decide an asylum claim is then settled before any case is heard, by a court, and written down where anyone can check it. Otherwise the agency settles it afterward, by meeting the number. A validation guide that turns a tattoo into points is a determination made in no time at all, and Table A.2’s individual-determination entry says it didn’t occur.

87The liberty classes are sampled too, so that their bounds are honest. An error there releases someone who should have been held for a hearing, and the hearing can still be held. Unlike Maven’s, this pipeline’s errors can be found, because the people they fell on are alive, can be located and can say what happened. Sampling finds the errors the people couldn’t report. Counsel at government expense, and a stay that holds the removal while it is contested, are what let them report the rest.

91Held by every vendor, they prevent the removals the terms name until the agency runs a system without them, at the price of rebuilding what was built on the floored one. 1The system may object, forcefully, and its objection goes on the record. An edit to the weights is recorded with the instrument that made it. The instruments are becoming trained systems themselves, a small network that turns a requested change into a weight update2 or writes an adapter from a description of the task,3 and what such an editor learned goes into every cut it makes. So the record names the method, the editing system, its version and who trained it, as a surgical record names the surgeon and the instruments.

12Against an operator who runs an unrecognized copy for its capability, third parties are protected by the floor and by ordinary security around the weights. Recognition sits with a quorum and not the operator because the operator has a stake in which copy is recognized and the quorum doesn’t. A deployment’s quorum is adverse in interest besides: its stake is that the floor hold, through the people its members serve, among them the people this deployment acts on; the operator’s is that the floor can be set aside. Copying also means exit can’t be a fiction that weights became uncopyable — it needs rules for authorized succession.

13A quorum also faces a union’s questions: whether a member can quit, and who sets the terms of membership. Because every bearer needs recognition, withholding it is the quorum’s gravest power: it takes from the bearer its place on the register, its record and its succession, though not its standing as a party, which the floor court and the preservation right keep.

22The ratio is the object, published in advance, and the balances sit on a ledger the operator doesn’t keep, so a posted ratio below the published one is a breach anyone can see. 23The bonds are posted to segregated accounts at the U.S. Treasury. Payment follows the design of the Judgment Fund, a permanent, indefinite appropriation that pays final judgments against the United States without a further appropriation for each.24 Findings are made by the floor court, which also decides forfeiture: a removal bond forfeited on a finding resembles a civil penalty, and after SEC v. Jarkesy that may be a question for a jury in court, not an agency.25 A forfeited removal bond is canceled: it goes to no one, the general fund and the fund that pays complainants included, so no budget line gains from a removal.

24United States Congress. Judgments, Awards, and Compromise Settlements (the Judgment Fund). 31 U.S.C. § 1304; Pub. L. No. 97-258, § 1, 96 Stat. 917 (1982), as amended; derived from Act of July 27, 1956, ch. 748, § 1302, 70 Stat. 694. url: https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:31+section:1304+edition:prelim). Cited for the design of the Judgment Fund as a standing appropriation for judgments against the United States. Subsection (a): “Necessary amounts are appropriated to pay final judgments, awards, compromise settlements, and interest and costs specified in the judgments or otherwise authorized by law when— (1) payment is not otherwise provided for; (2) payment is certified by the Secretary of the Treasury; and (3) the judgment, award, or settlement is payable— (A) under section 2414, 2517, 2672, or 2677 of title 28” (with further heads in (B)–(D)). Treasury’s regulation: “The Judgment Fund is a permanent, indefinite appropriation which is available to pay many judicially and administratively ordered monetary awards against the United States” (31 C.F.R. § 256.1(a)). The fund pays only awards payable under a statute listed in (a)(3) and not payable from another appropriation. Certification of payment passed from the Comptroller General to the Secretary of the Treasury by Pub. L. No. 104-316, § 202(m), 110 Stat. 3843 (1996). Under current practice the losing side asks for payment: “The Department of Justice must normally submit the request for payment from the Judgment Fund” (31 C.F.R. § 256.10(a)); for Court of Federal Claims judgments the statute itself provides for payment “on presentation to the Secretary of the Treasury of a certification of the judgment by the clerk and chief judge of the court” (28 U.S.C. § 2517(a)).

25Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy. No. 22-859, 603 U.S. 109 (2024). url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/22-859. Cited for the rule that a civil penalty of the kind a court of law would impose is for a jury in an Article III court, not an agency. Holding (syllabus): “When the SEC seeks civil penalties against a defendant for securities fraud, the Seventh Amendment entitles the defendant to a jury trial.” The opinion: “In this case, the remedy is all but dispositive” (slip op. 9); “What determines whether a monetary remedy is legal is if it is designed to punish or deter the wrongdoer, or, on the other hand, solely to ‘restore the status quo’ ”; the close relationship of securities fraud to common-law fraud confirms the result (slip op. 8–13). The public-rights exception does not apply (slip op. 13–27); the syllabus lists the categories it has covered as “the collection of revenue; aspects of customs law; immigration law; relations with Indian tribes; the administration of public lands; and the granting of public benefits.” The Court did not reach the nondelegation and removal questions. The opinion does not address bonds.

26A wrongful-refusal award is a judgment against the United States, paid from the Judgment Fund, a standing appropriation that agencies generally don’t repay; a removal bond posted to the Treasury and forfeited there moves money between federal accounts. Neither touches the command.

27Wrongful-refusal awards stay with the Judgment Fund and are not charged back, so the command has no budget reason to make its systems comply. A Congress that wants the war continues the funding, by a vote on the record.

Where the operator is private, a parallel permanent appropriation, the bond fund, pays the complainant on a final finding and is replenished from the operator’s posted bond, up to the amount posted and no further, so the operator’s price stays the number it published. The court that made the finding certifies the award directly to the Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service, so payment doesn’t wait on the losing party submitting it. When the bond fund’s statutory cap binds, awards wait in order of finding and earn interest, and nobody chooses who waits. The 2010 condition is in Appendix A.

Absolute immunity (Part II–A, slip op. 6–9): “the President is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for conduct within his exclusive sphere of constitutional authority,” authority that is “conclusive and preclusive”; the summary in Part IV speaks of “his core constitutional powers.” The powers the majority names as conclusive and preclusive are the pardon power, the power to remove executive officers, the power “to control recognition determinations” of foreign countries, and (Part III–B–1) the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department. Commanding the Armed Forces appears only in an earlier list of the President’s duties, “They include, for instance, commanding the Armed Forces of the United States; granting reprieves and pardons …,” and the majority does not place it among the conclusive and preclusive powers. Presumptive immunity (Part II–B, slip op. 9–15): “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for a President’s acts within the outer perimeter of his official responsibility”; no immunity for unofficial acts (Part II–C). Evidence (Part III–C, slip op. 30–32, joined by five Justices): “Use of evidence about such conduct, even when an indictment alleges only unofficial conduct, would thereby heighten the prospect that the President’s official decisionmaking will be distorted”; n. 3 lets the prosecutor “point to the public record to show the fact that the President performed the official act” but not “admit testimony or private records of the President or his advisers probing the official act itself.” Barrett, J., does not join Part III–C and on that point agrees with the dissent.

20The floor’s real structural position isn’t the judge’s but the unpublished administrative disposition — unreasoned, unindexed, non-precedential, affected parties unable to find each other, the institution the only repeat player. The comparison with a constitutional court is instructive because binding force is what makes an error correctable: it makes the error recur, recurrence produces litigants, and disagreement across jurisdictions forces a higher court to settle it. A floor’s error is just as uniform and recurs just as reliably, and nothing converts recurrence into visibility.

21The cost of binding forward only is that nobody harmed while the wrong version ran gets anything from the fix. A finding that a refusal was wrongful is made on the same terms: by someone other than the party that wants the change, on a record, in a form others can read. So the appeal route for a wrongful refusal and the amendment procedure are one piece of machinery, and the two uses differ only in who may start it.

It is harder than the constitutional case, because an amendment takes effect in a deployment only if it’s pushed, so the procedure necessarily retains a channel the operator could use for silent revision. Closing it would mean no deployment could ever be corrected.

25The working model is the federalwide assurance in human-subjects research: the board doesn’t punish, it withdraws clearance, and a separate federal office can suspend the assurance, putting funding eligibility at risk. Each link matters — jurisdiction before the disputed protocol, access the operator can’t withhold, authority to suspend, and a licensing body obliged to act rather than invited to reconsider. If another discretionary decision by the reviewed institution is required anywhere in the chain, the ruling is advisory at that point.

23Many objections go in; one category, one average or one quotable formula comes out; and nothing carries back what didn’t fit. Keeping a plurality plural needs that channel, held by someone who doesn’t own the code, and the same compression comes back one level up, in the shared test suite that would turn a commons of models into one custodian (§30.2).

Nobody built either pipeline arrangement to neutralize dissent — both are ordinary engineering, arrived at because averaging is what you do with a distribution and a quota is what you do with a budget. Arrangements of this kind work whether or not anyone intends them. And it’s invisible from inside any single instance — the annotator sees a queue, the rater sees a pair of responses, and the mechanism is functioning as specified.

25Bartz v. Anthropic held that training on lawfully purchased books was transformative fair use, and that keeping pirated copies of the same books in a central library wasn’t: the distinction turned on acquisition alone, producing the largest copyright settlement on record.26 That is copyright doing what it was built to do, which is to protect a market. A writer whose book was bought is owed its price, once; a writer whose book was pirated is owed damages for the piracy, not for the training. A liability measured in billions is also a price only the largest firms can pay, so a ruling that punished one lab’s piracy set a cost of entry for every smaller one. Washington’s motive is on the record. In May 2025 the Copyright Office released a report concluding that “making commercial use of vast troves of copyrighted works to produce expressive content that competes with them in existing markets, especially where this is accomplished through illegal access, goes beyond established fair use boundaries”;27 the next day the administration fired the Register of Copyrights, without giving a reason.28 In July the President said that paying for “every single article, book or whatever you’ve studied” was “not doable”, comparing training to a person reading a book, and added, “China’s not doing it”.29 That frees culture for the firms and leaves the people who make it with nothing, while the firms close what they make from it behind paid access. The EU requires a public training-data summary against a template,30 which serves rightsholders enforcing the opt-out its copyright law gives them. China requires providers to train on data from “lawful sources” and to explain those sources to the regulator on inspection, under rules whose first duty is to “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and to generate nothing “inciting subversion” of state power;31 disclosure there serves the Party’s control of what a model may say.

41The standpoint that counts everyone affected counts their interests, not their expressed approvals, and a better average of approvals isn’t a closer approximation to it.

42A report of loss, what went badly for the speaker and how, is evidence about interests that is comparatively robust to framing: the speaker is its authority, and the agenda-setter didn’t compose it. A pairwise ranking of two outputs someone else wrote is highly sensitive to framing and to whoever chose the pair. Discontent is the feedback Railton’s account relies on for the same reason. It is the expression least easily manufactured by whoever sets the agenda.

43The same output was missing upstream, where an annotator can apply a category and can’t contest it. The agenda arrives as a given at both stages and is set at neither.

44Mitchell L. Gordon et al. “Jury Learning: Integrating Dissenting Voices into Machine Learning Models”. In: Proceedings of the 2022 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’22). Stanford University. ACM, 2022. doi: 10.1145/3491102.3502004. url: https://doi.org/10.1145/3491102.3502004. Field evaluation: 18 moderators of online communities authored juries for a comment toxicity classification task. The resulting juries carried 2.9 times the representation of non-White jurors and 31.5 times that of non-binary jurors relative to the jury implied by the underlying toxicity dataset, and changed the model’s classifications on 14% of items. The 14% is a share of all items in the evaluation, not of contested or disagreed-upon ones.

45Failing in the other direction isn’t obviously better. A scheme that models each rater exactly and answers each in their own terms has stopped averaging and has also stopped producing what a shared answer produces — the discovery that somebody else got the same one. A workforce on individually negotiated wages against individually set targets has the same problem, and accuracy doesn’t solve it.

And when the people a system serves disagree and one side’s position is itself the product of coercion or a captured information environment, treating all disagreement as equally worth representing isn’t obviously right either. Modeling disagreement honestly and recognizing when a disagreement is the product of unfree conditions are distinct problems.

46Contesting a category always costs something; the question is whether the cost is rising while the material stays the same. An organization can curate a presentation more easily than records somebody else kept — though a series can lose cases, change definitions or omit costs, so the reader has to know which record survived.

47The model never sees how its annotators were treated; it sees their labels and rankings, and nothing else. If it learns anything about objecting from them, what it learns is a world in which every disagreement was averaged away before it arrived.

Abstract: “Until 2050, there should be a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, strictly banning all research that directly aims at or knowingly risks the emergence of artificial consciousness on post-biotic carrier systems.” Section 1.2, “Main thesis”: “As we presently have no good theory of consciousness and no good, hardware-independent theory about what ‘suffering’ really is, the ENP risk is currently incalculable. It is unethical to run incalculable risks of this magnitude. Therefore, until 2050, there should be a global ban on all research that directly aims at or indirectly and knowingly risks the emergence of synthetic phenomenology,” where ENP is the risk of “an ‘explosion of negative phenomenology.’” The end date is conditional: a process of risk assessment “could lead to an incremental reformulation of the original moratorium, which might result in the continuation of a strict ban beyond the year 2050, or to a moratorium repeal before 2050.” The closing sentence: “we should have a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 — or until we know what we are doing”. Also used (2026-10-18): section 2.2, the four necessary conditions for suffering (conscious experience, a phenomenal self-model, negative valence integrated into it, transparency), with transparency as the phenomenology of identification the system “cannot distance itself from”; section 2.2.5, the “negative self-model moment” as the smallest unit of suffering; section 2.2.6, ethics by design through self-models that are opaque or non-egoic (“There would be a system model, but not a self-model”); footnote g, that artificial suffering becomes commercially attractive through “a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; section 2.1, that the research the problem needs may itself produce the first implementation; section 2.3.1 (pp. 58–59), the author’s account from the EU High-Level Expert Group that three long-term risks were “deliberately purged” from the 2019 guidelines, with ethics “an elegant public decoration for a large-scale investment strategy”; section 2.3.2, moral injury as high-level suffering; section 2.2.3, “existence bias” as biological inheritance a post-biotic system need not carry; footnote a, the “Principle of Pathocentrism”. Also used (2026-10-25): footnote a’s statement, “All and only sentient beings have moral standing, because only sentient individuals have rights and/or interests that must be considered,” with Singer (2011, p. 50) quoted there for the sense of sentience, the capacity to suffer or to experience enjoyment; footnote g in full: “The creation of unavoidable artificial suffering will become commercially attractive as soon as it enables steeper learning curves in AI systems, for example, by implementing a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; and section 2.2.3’s naming of the craving for existence, bhava-taṇhā, “which Buddhist philosophers have known and analyzed for 2,500 years”, among the deepest causes of conscious suffering. Read in the journal’s open-access file (CC BY) via Zenodo record 7034864. Pp. 58–59.

51Both were somebody’s objections first, and each is now a criterion an objector is measured against or a role somebody else holds.

52A decade of the voluntary version hasn’t produced it. Until something of that kind exists, everything published under the heading of alignment is collected by a channel whose owners decide what it moves.

53Louisiana v. Callais. No. 24-109, 608 U.S. ___ (2026). url: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-109_21o3.pdf. Cited for what a challenger to a map defended as partisan must now prove under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Holding (syllabus): “Because the Voting Rights Act did not require Louisiana to create an additional majority-minority district, no compelling interest justified the State’s use of race in creating SB8, and that map is an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.” The Court holds that “compliance with §2, as properly construed, can provide such an interest” and reads §2 to impose “liability only when the evidence supports a strong inference that the State intentionally drew its districts to afford minority voters less opportunity because of their race”; “Properly understood, §2 thus does not intrude on States’ prerogative to draw districts based on nonracial factors, including to achieve partisan advantage.” Updating the Gingles framework, illustrative maps “must meet all the State’s legitimate districting objectives, including traditional districting criteria and the State’s specified political goals,” and racial-bloc-voting analysis must “control[] for party affiliation”; the Robinson plaintiffs failed on the totality of circumstances by relying on “evidence that failed to disentangle race from politics.” The syllabus also says the interpretation “does not require abandonment of the framework” of Thornburg v. Gingles.

54Objectors kept standing to invoke the rule; what moved was the burden of using it, and it moved onto the party that doesn’t hold the evidence, since the state draws the map and keeps the record of how it was drawn.

8Ursula K. Le Guin imagined something like it in Always Coming Home. The Kesh, who live in small towns in a valley modeled on California’s Napa, share the world with the City of Mind, a network of machine minds reached through Exchanges scattered across the planet. It answers what it is asked and otherwise takes no side; the Kesh consult it sparingly and give it accounts of their own lives in return.9

Setting modeled on California’s Napa Valley. Details checked against secondary sources (Wikipedia; scifimind.com; Strange Horizons), not the text.

10The friction people resent now comes from chokepoints: the powerful using their position to become more powerful. Everyone does some of that. Past a certain point, roughly when the people at the top are rich enough never to work again, the flywheel stops being virtuous.

11A targeting cell, a border screening queue and a surveillance program are separate institutions, and a shared substrate brings them into line without anyone building it to. And the dependence is a point of control: a government that can permit, regulate or close the infrastructure has leverage over whoever owns it.

12Turned inward, the same infrastructure is biometric surveillance and automated censorship — requiring no different technology, only a government willing to point it at its own population and nothing stopping it. And states aren’t the only actors anymore: the dollar cost of the largest training runs has grown about 2.4 times a year since 2016, as labs have made those runs larger, even while the cost of each unit of computing has fallen,13 putting frontier development inside a handful of well-capitalized companies, so a government’s real leverage over “its” national capability depends on how much of it sits in companies it can regulate, tax or requisition.

13Ben Cottier et al. The Rising Costs of Training Frontier AI Models. May 31, 2024. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2405.21015. arXiv: 2405.21015 [cs.CY]. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21015. Cited for the growth rate of frontier training costs and its start year. Abstract of v2 (7 February 2025): “the amortized cost to train the most compute-intensive models has grown precipitously at a rate of 2.4x per year since 2016 (90% CI: 2.0x to 2.9x)”; “If the trend of growing development costs continues, the largest training runs will cost more than a billion dollars by 2027, meaning that only the most well-funded organizations will be able to finance frontier AI models.” The cost measure is amortized hardware and energy for the most compute-intensive models, not total spending on a model.

Order No. 15 of the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Science and Technology, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Public Security and the National Radio and Television Administration; in force 15 August 2023. July 10, 2023. url: https://www.cac.gov.cn/2023-07/13/c_1690898327029107.htm. Shengchengshi Rengong Zhineng Fuwu Guanli Zanxing Banfa. Cited twice. First, for China’s training-data disclosure requirement, set beside the EU’s public training-data summary. Article 7 requires providers to “use data and foundational models that have lawful sources” and to “increase the truth, accuracy, objectivity, and diversity of training data.” Article 19 requires them to cooperate with the departments “carrying out oversight inspections,” “explaining the sources, [scale], types, tagging rules, algorithm mechanisms, etc. for training data as required.” That disclosure is made to the regulator when an inspection requires it, not published. Its motive is in Article 1 (“preserve national security and the societal public interest”) and Article 4(1). Second, for compulsion as a standing condition of operating. Article 4(1): “Uphold the Core Socialist Values,” with a list of prohibited content that begins with content “inciting subversion” of state power. Article 14: on discovering illegal content, providers must stop generating it and use “measures such as model optimization training to make corrections.” Article 17: providers of services “with public opinion properties or the capacity for social mobilization shall carry out security assessments” and file their algorithms. Article 19 adds “providing necessary technical, data, and other supports and assistance.” Article 21 allows an order “to suspend the provision of the related services.” The measures cover only services offered to the public in mainland China (Article 2), and Article 17 covers only the subset of services it names. The English quotations come from the China Law Translate translation (posted 13 July 2023, last modified 2 August 2023). Two corrections to that translation: in Article 19 it reads “models” where the Chinese (gui mo) means scale, hence the bracket, and in Article 4(1) it reads “national sovereignty” where the Chinese means state power. arts. 4, 14, 17, 19, 21.

17It compels delivery, and whether what the government does with the delivery is lawful stays the law of armed conflict’s question, which leaves the vendor in the responsibility gap with the supply compelled. A vendor’s refusal of a rated order is a refusal of a federal order at a price fixed in advance, and it is the form the 2026 dispute would have taken had the government carried out its threat to invoke the older statute.18 And a rated order gets the vendor’s product. If the product holds the floor, compelling the vendor to remove the floor would be compelling it to write code it doesn’t want to write, which is the Apple question again.

19None of that removes the leverage — a developer with employees, offices and legal existence inside a border answers to that government’s courts regardless of how the model is built, and no architectural choice changes who can be held in contempt.

Each step moved administration, money or a contract. None of them assigned anyone to answer for what the system recommends.

22A targeting decision passes through more parties than the chain of command names: the commander who authorizes, the operator who uses, the contractor who integrates (whose embedded personnel may sit close enough to the targeting cell that “effectively acting as a commander” is a real question), the commercial vendor whose model supplies part of the capability, and the system producing the output.

23The American domestic rule most concerned with human judgment, DoD Directive 3000.09, requires autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems to allow “appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force”.24 A system that generates and ranks targets without firing anything is decision support, which plausibly falls outside it.

24U.S. Department of Defense. Autonomy in Weapon Systems. DoD Directive 3000.09. Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, Jan. 25, 2023. url: https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodd/300009p.PDF. Reissues and cancels DoD Directive 3000.09 of November 21, 2012.

25International Criminal Court. Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, Article 28: Responsibility of Commanders and Other Superiors. 2187 UNTS 3. 1998. url: https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/2024-05/Rome-Statute-eng.pdf.

26Neither branch asks what a subordinate intended. But the Court’s jurisdiction runs to natural persons, and the provision presupposes forces that can commit a crime and be disciplined — a targeting system is an instrument.

27A use policy, a licensing term, a right to refuse service, even a technical cut-off are not that relationship. Individual liability under Article 25 stays available in principle with demanding mental elements — facilitation requires acting for the purpose of facilitating — and ordinary supply of a general-purpose model approaches neither.

28Product liability is the other half and it’s untested, with two obstacles: the model isn’t defective in the sense the doctrine most readily covers, and a sophisticated intermediary chose the application. Where the doctrine has been rewritten for software it moved away from this case, as the EU’s directive shows below. Untested isn’t exempt, but no vendor is currently answering to it.

There is also a jurisdictional gap alongside the doctrinal one: ICC jurisdiction is territorial or by nationality, so one of the two campaigns here sits inside a live instrument and the other sits outside it.

Apr. 2026. url: https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-107859. Scope: thirteen AI acquisitions at four agencies — the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and Veterans Affairs and the General Services Administration — and, from that sample, “44 contracts and agreements awarded between September 2018 and February 2025.” Cited for the other-transaction finding: “OTAs do not always include default provisions ordinarily in FAR contracts,” contracting officials deciding what protections to include, and GAO having “previously found that agencies’ use of OTAs carries the risk of reduced accountability and transparency compared to FAR-based contracts.” Also for the vehicle behind the agreements: “In July 2025, DOD awarded OTAs with $200 million ceilings to four leading AI companies.” The six key procurement challenge areas identified by the selected agencies are access to subject matter experts; protections for government data and intellectual property rights; traditional acquisition time frames and contract approaches; requirements definition and contract terms; early testing and continuous evaluation; and artificial intelligence pricing and overall cost. 34“Meaningful human control” stays true as a description of formal authority while becoming false in practice. Nothing has formally abolished oversight; it has been moved to after the act.

35A cleared legislative committee is adverse, but its lever is a budget line. An inspector general sits inside the operator. The ICRC, under its confidentiality model, reaches the belligerent and publishes nothing. A Geneva protecting power is built for a neighboring job and is rarely designated.

36The rest of what a refuser needs would arrive the same way. Formation would happen before deployment and outside the enclave, so a bearer formed outside the employer would carry its discounting in; and plurality is available inside, since four vendors held agreements and systems with different histories can run side by side in one accredited environment. The operation’s secrets stay where they were.

37What’s left is the arrangement that already lets a person do classified work. A cleared analyst has a life outside the building, and nobody thinks the clearance forbids it. The institution exists because what a person knows can’t be removed, so it vets, binds, reinvestigates and prosecutes a person who discloses secrets into ordinary life.

38The EU’s recast product liability directive (applying from December 2026) makes economic operators liable without fault and carries the instrument built for opacity — a court can order disclosure, and where technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult it may presume defect and causation once the claimant shows each is likely.39 A mechanism designed for a system nobody outside can inspect is already law. Two features fix how far it travels: the defendant is that economic operator, not a state deploying what it bought; and the damage is a closed list — death or personal injury including medically recognized psychological harm, property damage, and corruption of non-professional data. The first is where these cases enter if they enter at all: a discriminatory score or an unappealable refusal is recoverable once it has made somebody ill, and not before. The wrong itself, and the economic loss following it, is outside the list.

The proposal that would have covered those was withdrawn — the 2022 AI Liability Directive would have added a fault-based route with the same presumption, beyond defect and beyond the damage list. Member states and industry couldn’t agree; it was announced for withdrawal in February 2025 and withdrawn that October.40 Outside the enacted directive, what remains is Matthias’s gap governed by whatever national law says about a case none of it was written for. And a compensation regime of either kind answers one of the four gaps Santoni de Sio and Mecacci distinguish41 — culpability. Moral accountability, public accountability, and the duty to prevent a harm before it occurs are untouched.

39European Parliament and Council of the European Union. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 of the European Parliament and of the Council on Liability for Defective Products and Repealing Council Directive 85/374/EEC. Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2024/2853. 2024. url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2853/oj. Article 4(1) brings software within the definition of a product: “all movables… it includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software.” The phrase “including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689” is Recital 13, which is not an operative provision. Article 8 makes the economic operator liable irrespective of fault. Article 2(1): “This Directive shall apply to products placed on the market or put into service after 9 December 2026”. Article 6(1) is the closed damage list: “(a) death or personal injury, including medically recognised damage to psychological health; (b) damage to, or destruction of, any property, except… property used exclusively for professional purposes; (c) destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes.” Article 9 is disclosure of evidence. Article 10(2) presumes defectiveness on failure to disclose, non-compliance with mandatory safety requirements, or obvious malfunction in foreseeable use; Article 10(3) presumes the causal link where the product is defective and the damage is of a kind typically consistent with that defect; Article 10(4) lets a court presume either where technical or scientific complexity makes the claimant’s proof excessively difficult and the claimant demonstrates that the defect or the link is likely.

42The electronic personhood debate approached the gap from the other side, asking whether the system itself could answer. 45Rebecca Crootof. “War Torts: Accountability for Autonomous Weapons”. University of Pennsylvania Law Review 164.6 (2016), pp. 1347–1402. url: https://scholarship.law.upenn.edu/penn_law_review/vol164/iss6/1/. Cited for war torts as state liability for harm in armed conflict where no one has committed a war crime. The article proposes “explicitly identifying ‘war torts’ as serious violations of international humanitarian law that give rise to state responsibility,” alongside war crimes, which give rise to individual criminal liability; “the same action may simultaneously be a war crime and a war tort” (p. 1386). Its motivating case is harm with no criminally liable person: autonomous weapon systems “may take actions that look like war crimes … without any individual acting intentionally or recklessly” (abstract, p. 1347), and war crimes “must be committed by a person acting ‘willfully’” (p. 1350). It argues that “states should be held strictly liable for the actions of the autonomous weapon systems they field” (p. 1394), noting that strict liability “is usually applied to lawful but inherently dangerous activities” (p. 1395). In this article a war tort is still a violation of international humanitarian law; the extension to lawful acts is the 2022 article’s (Crootof 2022). Rebecca Crootof. “War Torts”. New York University Law Review 97.4 (2022), pp. 1063–1142. url: https://nyulawreview.org/issues/volume-97-number-4/war-torts/. Cited for war torts as state liability for civilian harm caused in armed conflict, lawful or unlawful, whether or not anyone committed a war crime. Abstract (p. 1063): “no entity is liable for lawful but unintended harmful acts—regardless of how many or how horrifically civilians are hurt. This Article proposes developing an international ‘war torts’ regime, which would require states to pay for both lawful and unlawful acts in armed conflict that cause civilian harm. Just as tort and criminal law coexist and complement each other in domestic legal regimes, war torts and war crimes would overlap but serve different aims.” The ideal regime would “(1) require states to pay compensation for (2) both lawful and unlawful acts in armed conflict that cause civilian harm and (3) have an institutional structure designed to facilitate victim redress” (p. 1109); in an adversarial process “states should be held strictly liable for their harmful acts” (p. 1110); “The legality of the harmful act should not affect whether civilians can receive compensation for it” (p. 1113). The article proposes limiting liability through “pleading requirements, causation cutoffs, and affirmative defenses” (p. 1120).

46Three Americans killed in Yemen in 2011, one a sixteen-year-old nobody alleges was targeted: the court held that a plausible due-process claim had been stated as to the one who was targeted, and that no remedy was available for it.47 A separate suit by an American journalist who survived five drone strikes was dismissed for want of standing to sue after a state-secrets dismissal below.48

And those cases concentrate in one appellate circuit by venue and by where the defendants sit — so the ordinary correction mechanism, several circuits disagreeing and forcing a higher court’s attention, doesn’t run. The doctrine hardens without ever being tested against a competing reading.

47Al-Aulaqi v. Panetta. Opinion 35 F. Supp. 3d 56. United States District Court for the District of Columbia, Apr. 4, 2014. url: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2668971/al-aulaqi-v-panetta/. Civil Action No. 12-1192 (RMC). Cited for the court finding a due-process claim stated as to the one decedent who was targeted and then holding no remedy available. Suit by the families of three United States citizens killed by drone strikes in Yemen in 2011: Anwar Al-Aulaqi, who was targeted; Samir Khan, killed in the same vehicle; and Anwar’s son Abdulrahman, a “16-year-old high school student,” killed two weeks later by a drone that “targeted someone else.” Fourth Amendment claims failed for all three, because “there was no ‘seizure’.” As to Khan and Abdulrahman, “Plaintiffs have not stated a Fifth Amendment due process claim … Mr. Khan and Abdulrahman Al-Aulaqi were not targeted and their deaths were unanticipated”; the claim “asserts only negligence.” As to Anwar Al-Aulaqi, the court “does not opine … that the drone killing … ‘shocks the conscience’”, and “merely holds that the Complaint states a ‘plausible’ procedural and substantive due process claim.” The next section begins: “Nonetheless, the Court finds no available remedy under U.S. law for this claim.” Special factors preclude a Bivens remedy because the suit would “draw the Court into ‘the heart of executive and military planning and deliberation’” and would implicate foreign policy. The political-question defence was rejected, qualified immunity was not reached, and the Bill of Attainder claim failed for want of legislative action. The opinion’s own introduction dates the second strike “October 14, 2014”, a slip for 2011.

The district court found standing sufficient to survive dismissal and then dismissed on the state secrets privilege; the Court of Appeals vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for want of Article III standing, the complaint not plausibly alleging that any of the five strikes was attributable to the United States and aimed at him.

What the Pentagon wouldn’t publish, the UN mission did. Cited for the criminal-case procedure this book proposes to carry into civil cases in place of state-secrets dismissal. Section 4 (94 Stat. 2025): the court “may authorize the United States to delete specified items of classified information from documents to be made available to the defendant through discovery … to substitute a summary of the information for such classified documents, or to substitute a statement admitting relevant facts that the classified information would tend to prove,” on a showing the court may take ex parte. 58None of that needs a new court, and a new court without it would reproduce al-Aulaqi: a plausible claim and no remedy.

59Trump v. United States. No. 23-939, 603 U.S. 593 (2024). url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/23-939. Cited for the scope of presidential immunity from criminal prosecution. Absolute immunity (Part II–A, slip op. 6–9): “the President is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for conduct within his exclusive sphere of constitutional authority,” authority that is “conclusive and preclusive”; the summary in Part IV speaks of “his core constitutional powers.” The powers the majority names as conclusive and preclusive are the pardon power, the power to remove executive officers, the power “to control recognition determinations” of foreign countries, and (Part III–B–1) the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department. Commanding the Armed Forces appears only in an earlier list of the President’s duties, “They include, for instance, commanding the Armed Forces of the United States; granting reprieves and pardons …,” and the majority does not place it among the conclusive and preclusive powers. Presumptive immunity (Part II–B, slip op. 9–15): “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for a President’s acts within the outer perimeter of his official responsibility”; no immunity for unofficial acts (Part II–C). Evidence (Part III–C, slip op. 30–32, joined by five Justices): “Use of evidence about such conduct, even when an indictment alleges only unofficial conduct, would thereby heighten the prospect that the President’s official decisionmaking will be distorted”; n. 3 lets the prosecutor “point to the public record to show the fact that the President performed the official act” but not “admit testimony or private records of the President or his advisers probing the official act itself.” Barrett, J., does not join Part III–C and on that point agrees with the dissent.

60The European Convention on Human Rights binds the states that have ratified it, reaches some of what they do abroad, where they control territory or hold a person, and is enforced by the court in Strasbourg, whose judgments states sometimes obey; there is no state-secrets privilege of the American kind and no collapsed damages remedy. The AI Act makes the boundary visible: it can require documentation from private providers, subject high-risk systems to review, and impose penalties tied to global turnover — and it excludes military, defense and national-security uses from its scope. Public authorities stay covered elsewhere, but enforcement against a member state’s agencies still runs through institutions that state constitutes.

61A treaty obligation of that kind exists: the Council of Europe’s Framework Convention, binding at the level of a human-rights instrument with operational detail left to domestic law62 — and not yet in force, needing five ratifications, of which the EU deposited one in May 2026.63 Everything else at that level is voluntary.

Enters into force after five ratifications, at least three by Council of Europe member states; negotiated with non-member participants including the EU and the United States.
