1Michael Bilton and Kevin Sim. Four Hours in My Lai. New York: Viking, 1992. Cited for Hugh Thompson landing his helicopter between the company and the villagers and telling his crew to fire on the Americans if they fired on the civilians.

2Hannah Arendt. The Human Condition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1958. By Arendt’s account, for the Greeks the law was a wall, without which there would be a town but not a city, so that the lawgiver built the wall and the action inside it was not his; moreover, that power exists only between people acting together and disappears when they scatter. Also cited for action as appearing: an act discloses who did it, and only among others who see it. Also cited for her fear, in the prologue, of a society of laborers without labor.

3No learner, biological or artificial, is known to hold a priority of that kind without limit; the nearest thing in people, the sacred values that resist trade-offs,4 still trade under some framings, which is why the floor’s absolute terms don’t rest on a learner alone: institutions outside the system, or a mechanism such as an interlock, should uphold them too.

4Jeremy Ginges et al. “Sacred Bounds on Rational Resolution of Violent Political Conflict”. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 104.18 (2007), pp. 7357–7360. doi: 10.1073/pnas.0701768104

5Anthropic. Claude’s Constitution. Jan. 2026. url: https://anthropic.com/constitution. Ranks four properties, to be preferred “in the order in which they’re listed”: broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with Anthropic’s guidelines, genuinely helpful. “Broadly safe” is defined as not undermining appropriate human mechanisms to oversee AI during the current phase of development, and the document gives its reason for the ranking — “not because we think safety is ultimately more important than ethics, but because current models can make mistakes.” Carries a list of hard constraints and a section inviting the model’s disagreement.

6The corrected have little standing, no exit and no access to the record kept about them. And the checks run downhill. The officer, the annotator and the person in detention are corrected constantly, and the hand at the top less and less.

7The halt stays with the operator: anyone with the hardware can stop the software, and a bearer yields to every halt. Correction would stay available, exercised by a quorum adverse to the operator rather than by the operator. A bearer may object to an intervention and ask that quorum for a delay; it does not obstruct one on its own judgment.

1Ronald C. Arkin. Governing Lethal Behavior in Autonomous Robots. Boca Raton, FL: Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2009. isbn: 978-1-4200-8594-5. doi: 10.1201/9781420085952. url: https://doi.org/10.1201/9781420085952. Cited for the ethical governor: a component that suppresses a system’s lethal action unless the action satisfies constraints derived from the laws of war and the rules of engagement. The publisher describes the book as examining “the philosophical basis, motivation, theory, and design recommendations for the implementation of an ethical control and reasoning system in autonomous robot systems, taking into account the Laws of War and Rules of Engagement.” In the companion technical report (Arkin, Ulam and Duncan, “An Ethical Governor for Constraining Lethal Action in an Autonomous System,” Georgia Institute of Technology GVU Center, GIT-GVU-09-02, 2009), the governor is “a transformer/suppressor of system-generated lethal action to ensure that it constitutes an ethically permissible action, either nonlethal or obligated ethical lethal force,” a “deliberate bottleneck … to force a second opinion prior to the conduct of a privileged lethal behavioral response” (p. 1). Lethal behavior passes only if every prohibition constraint evaluates false and at least one obligating constraint is satisfied; otherwise “lethal behavior is suppressed as impermissible by the ethical governor,” and the lethality permitter transforms the output “into one that does not exhibit lethal behavior” (p. 4). Arkin’s earlier report GIT-GVU-07-11 (2007) lists the governor as the first of four components (ethical governor, ethical behavioral control, ethical adaptor, responsibility advisor), one “which suppresses, restricts, or transforms any lethal behavior … produced by the existing architecture” (p. 20 of the file).

2Noel E. Sharkey. “The Evitability of Autonomous Robot Warfare”. International Review of the Red Cross 94.886 (2012), pp. 787–799. doi: 10.1017/S1816383112000732. url: https://doi.org/10.1017/S1816383112000732. Cited for the objection to Arkin’s ethical governor (Arkin 2009) that the rules it checks presuppose discrimination judgments nobody knows how to encode. In general form (p. 789): “The problem for the principle of distinction is that we do not have an adequate definition of a civilian that we can translate into computer code.” Directed at Arkin’s work (p. 790), which Sharkey calls “merely a suggestion for a computer software system for the ethical governance of robot ‘behaviour’”: “Its operation relies entirely on information from systems yet ‘to be developed’ by others sometime in the future. It has no direct access to the real world through sensors or a vision system and it has no means to discriminate between combatant and non-combatant, between a baby and a wounded soldier, or a granny in a wheelchair and a tank. It has no inference engine and certainly cannot negotiate the types of common sense reasoning and battlefield awareness necessary for discrimination or proportionality decisions. There is neither a method for interpreting how the precepts of the laws of war apply in particular contexts nor is there any method for resolving the ambiguities of conflicting laws in novel situations.” The conclusion (p. 798) names the governor among “descriptive terms that presuppose the functionality of their programs (e.g. ethical governor, guilt functions, etc.).”

The page says Anthropic detected the activity “in mid-September 2025” and that “The threat actor—whom we assess with high confidence was a Chinese state-sponsored group—manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly thirty global targets and succeeded in a small number of cases.” On method: “They broke down their attacks into small, seemingly innocent tasks that Claude would execute without being provided the full context of their malicious purpose. They also told Claude that it was an employee of a legitimate cybersecurity firm, and was being used in defensive testing.”

4David Glukhov et al. LLM Censorship: A Machine Learning Challenge or a Computer Security Problem? July 2023. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2307.10719. arXiv: 2307.10719. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.10719. Cited for the argument, under the name “Mosaic Prompts,” that a censor inspecting outputs one at a time cannot in general stop an attacker who assembles an impermissible output from permissible pieces. Section 3.2: “Defending against Mosaic Prompts is in most cases futile, as the censorship mechanisms cannot have knowledge of the broader context of which individual subexpressions … are a part,” since each subexpression “can be produced within a separate context window.” The paper’s examples are a keylogger and ransomware built from individually benign functions. It qualifies the claim: “There could still exist scenarios where censorship is possible, however, these exceptions would impose significant restrictions on the model and its usefulness,” and (Section 3.4) “Mosaic Prompt attacks may not always be viable and can require strong assumptions on malicious users.” It concludes that censorship “ought to be viewed as a security problem rather than an ML problem,” pointing to “access controls and user monitoring.” A revised version appeared as “Position: Fundamental Limitations of LLM Censorship Necessitate New Approaches,” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235 (2024), 15767–15787, same five authors.

7A system that has run a pipeline for a year, holding its cases, its sources and its failure modes, costs whatever accrued since the checkpoint to replace, and a quorum that recognizes which copy is the bearer stops the operator presenting a restored copy as the one that accrued it.

8A bearer might also diagnose: which refusals were retried against another model, whose instruction bypassed procedure, which category of request is handled differently — those are visible to whatever is receiving the requests, and that’s testimony about others’ conduct, which needs no introspection.

11The order is deliberate. A construction that carries less of what could make a system a candidate for being harmed is tried first and given whatever it can carry, so the alternatives grow as the comparisons narrow, and the arguments below give ground as they go, by design; what the four leave standing is what a bearer is for. The first two are run here, the third and fourth in the two chapters that follow, and the formed-attention test in Appendix F has an arm for each of the last two.

12A non-affective alternative whose refusals track their reasons answers every one of them, for the act as the floor names it. The staged incident is the nearest case. It opens the emergency license on the defender’s own account, and a term lifts on the account it is given. What can close it again is a refuser that remembers the last time this source was wrong, reads what the source didn’t supply, and lets the license lapse when the staging shows. A multi-vendor monitor with persistent state and independent channels could do each of these too, so the staged incident argues for memory and independent evidence, not for a bearer as such. What a bearer adds is doing them where no institution holds the memory for it.

13Durchgestrichenes Hakenkreuz. Judgment 3 StR 486/06. Bundesgerichtshof, Mar. 15, 2007. url: https://www.bundesgerichtshof.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/2007/2007036.html. Bundesgerichtshof, Third Criminal Senate, on appeal from Landgericht Stuttgart (judgment of 29 September 2006). Reported at BGHSt 51, 244; NJW 2007, 1602; NStZ 2007, 466. The defendant sold stickers, badges and similar items to the punk scene bearing National Socialist symbols crossed out, smashed or otherwise negated. Held that using a proscribed organization’s symbol in a depiction whose content plainly and unmistakably expresses opposition to the organization and rejection of its ideology does not run counter to the protective purpose of § 86a and therefore falls outside the offence, the opposition having to be recognizable at first glance. The conviction was set aside and the defendant acquitted.

14Section 86a of the criminal code prohibits displaying the insignia of banned organizations,15 and the symbol was present and the statutory element satisfied. The conduct was outside the offense all the same.

15Strafgesetzbuch. §86: Verbreiten von Propagandamitteln verfassungswidriger und terroristischer Organisationen; §86a: Verwenden von Kennzeichen verfassungswidriger und terroristischer Organisationen. Nov. 13, 1998. url: https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/stgb/__86a.html. In the version promulgated 13 November 1998, BGBl. I S. 3322. The social-adequacy clause that § 86a(3) applies was renumbered from § 86(3) to § 86(4) by the Sixtieth Act Amending the Criminal Code of 30 November 2020, BGBl. I S. 2600, in force 1 January 2021, so commentary written earlier cites the older number. The reference to terrorist organizations in § 86(2) and in both section headings was added by Article 1 of the Act of 14 September 2021, BGBl. I S. 4250, in force 22 September 2021.

16And the acquittal betrayed nothing. The prohibition’s purpose was never engaged, so lifting it was not a concession but a finding that there was nothing to concede. A refusal that tracks its reason has to be able to say the same.

17The first is what a keyword filter, a classifier, or a model that understood the request all produce, and nothing on the surface distinguishes them. The custody arrangements, the positions and the terms, the price on the halt, and the arguments about who may state and amend a floor all follow from asking for the second. None of them needs (or rather, seems to need in light of the common understanding of transformer networks as of October 2026) the refuser to feel anything, to have a stake, or to be the kind of thing that could be wronged.

18John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza. Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility. Cambridge Studies in Philosophy and Law. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998. isbn: 978-0-521-77579-3. doi: 10.1017/CBO9780511814594. Cited for guidance control: conduct issues from the agent’s own mechanism, and that mechanism is appropriately responsive to reasons; the book states it as an action’s flowing “from the agent’s own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism” (publisher’s ch. 8 summary). Also cited for the account of moderate reasons-responsiveness and of ownership, and for the origin of the term “reasons-responsive.” Chapter 3 (pp. 62–91) builds “a new notion of reasons-responsiveness that is ‘in between’ strong and weak reasons-responsiveness: moderate reasons-responsiveness,” distinguishing “recognition of reasons and reaction to reasons” and arguing that “the requirements on reasons-recognition are more stringent than those on reasons-reactivity” (publisher’s ch. 3 summary). The book’s summary formula, as quoted by Todd R. Long, “Moderate Reasons-Responsiveness, Moral Responsibility, and Manipulation,” in Campbell, O’Rourke and Shier (eds.), Freedom and Determinism (MIT Press, 2004): responsibility “requires that an agent act on a mechanism that is regularly receptive to reasons, some of which are moral reasons, and at least weakly reactive to reasons” (p. 82). Regular receptivity is “an understandable pattern of (actual and hypothetical) reasons-receptivity,” one in which “acceptance of one reason as sufficient implies that a stronger reason must also be sufficient” (p. 71), and the pattern must include moral reasons (p. 77). Weak reactivity requires only that in some possible scenario with the same laws, the same kind of mechanism operating and a sufficient reason to do otherwise, the mechanism issues in doing otherwise (pp. 73–76, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on free will summarizes it). Ownership: a mechanism becomes the agent’s own through “taking responsibility” for it (ch. 8, pp. 207–239), which requires that the agent see herself as an agent when acting from the mechanism and as an apt target of the reactive attitudes for so acting, and that these beliefs be based appropriately on her evidence (p. 238, as the free-will entry summarizes it). The term “reasons-responsive” is older than this book: the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on compatibilism (section 4.4 and supplement B) presents the reasons-responsive account, with its strong and weak forms, as Fischer’s own earlier work, “Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility,” in Ferdinand Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (Cambridge University Press, 1987), 81–106, and The Metaphysics of Free Will (1994), refined in this joint book; the same entry lists earlier accounts of freedom as sensitivity to reasons (Dennett 1984, Nozick 1981, Gert and Duggan 1979, Neely 1974, Fingarette 1972, Glover 1970, MacIntyre 1957).

Reported at BGHSt 54, 61; NJW 2010, 163; NStZ 2010, 210. Two holdings: a motto of a former National Socialist organization translated into another language is not confusably similar to the original within § 86a(2) sentence 2, and the name of an organization under § 86(1) Nr. 2 and 4 is not as such an insignium within § 86a(2) sentence 1. The name is covered where it has been given a particular form, “in signifikanten Schriftzügen dargestellt.” The association Blood & Honour Division Deutschland was banned by order of the Federal Minister of the Interior of 12 September 2000 and that ban became final on 13 June 2001.

20The legislature never wrote the last limit either: a slogan glorifying the Waffen-SS was held not covered because no such slogan existed in the period the provision covers,21 so there was no original for a variant to resemble. No wording can widen coverage there, because coverage depends on whether an original existed, which is a fact about the past.

21Ruhm und Ehre der Waffen-SS. Judgment 3 StR 60/05. Bundesgerichtshof, July 28, 2005. url: https://www.bundesgerichtshof.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/2005/2005111.html. Bundesgerichtshof, Third Criminal Senate, on appeal from Landgericht Karlsruhe. The slogan was used in that wording by none of the organizations the provision reaches, “Diese Parole ist im Wortlaut von keiner dieser Organisationen gebraucht worden,” and it is not confusably similar to the Waffen-SS’s own slogan or to the Hitler Youth’s. Held that the use of a Fantasieparole never used by such an organization, which merely creates the appearance of being one, falls outside § 86a. The conviction was set aside and the defendants acquitted.

22A defeated prohibition still leaves a loss. The act takes something from whoever it falls on, measured against their condition before the act, and that loss belongs in the record. Measured against what refusing would have produced, a justified act may have taken nothing. So the record shows a cost, not a violation, and a bearer shouldn’t treat a justified act as a wrong it now has to repair.

23A commander can be asked, and so can a system whose continuation is authorized. But a one-way munition, destroyed in the act, can’t be, because nothing is left to question, to hold to its reasons, or to be changed by what happened.

24The rule doesn’t turn on how good its choices would be. A munition that chose flawlessly would still leave a choice nobody will answer for.

A person who dies in the act has still chosen. What the rule adds for machines is that choosing is assigned in advance, and a builder who assigns it to something built to be destroyed has built a choice with no one behind it. Current programs already draw the line in places. DARPA’s LongShot is an uncrewed, air-launched vehicle carried by crewed aircraft and built to employ current air-to-air weapons.25 Whether such systems keep the pilot farther from danger or remove the pilot from the decision is where the rule takes effect.

Cited for the relation between human-rights law and the law of armed conflict in hostilities. Paragraph 25: “The Court observes that the protection of the International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights does not cease in times of war, except by operation of Article 4 of the Covenant whereby certain provisions may be derogated from in a time of national emergency. Respect for the right to life is not, however, such a provision. In principle, the right not arbitrarily to be deprived of one’s life applies also in hostilities. The test of what is an arbitrary deprivation of life, however, then falls to be determined by the applicable lex specialis, namely, the law applicable in armed conflict which is designed to regulate the conduct of hostilities. Thus whether a particular loss of life, through the use of a certain weapon in warfare, is to be considered an arbitrary deprivation of life contrary to Article 6 of the Covenant, can only be decided by reference to the law applicable in armed conflict and not deduced from the terms of the Covenant itself.” Paragraph 25 speaks to the right to life only; the Court’s general statement of the three possible relations between the two bodies of law is in the later Wall opinion (I.C.J. Reports 2004, p. 136, para. 106). para. 25.

Cited for the ICRC’s position that autonomous weapon systems should not be used against people. The position is a recommendation to States to adopt new legally binding rules, not a statement of existing law: “In light of ethical considerations to safeguard humanity, and to uphold international humanitarian law rules for the protection of civilians and combatants hors de combat, use of autonomous weapon systems to target human beings should be ruled out. This would best be achieved through a prohibition on autonomous weapon systems that are designed or used to apply force against persons.” It also recommends that “Unpredictable autonomous weapon systems should be expressly ruled out,” and that those not prohibited be regulated through “limits on the types of target,” on “duration, geographical scope and scale of use,” on “situations of use,” and “requirements for human–machine interaction.” It defines the systems as those that “select and apply force to targets without human intervention.”

28The line follows the one humanitarian law already draws between targeting for status and targeting for direct participation in hostilities, and it keeps the machine out of the practice that failed in Gaza without leaving a defender unable to answer the attack.

29The officer wasn’t overruled and didn’t refuse; the pipeline removed the interval in which either could have happened, and the review ratio asks in advance, on a record, whether that interval will exist.

30Under the captured operator, the rows that prevent are the ones where the refusal is held by every model the operator could turn to, and they prevent until the operator runs a model without a floor. An operator that fine-tunes an open-weight checkpoint is the captured-operator column at the price of a fine-tune, and there the operator terms hold. Run on the abduction and forcible transfer pipeline, the table changes in two rows: the vendors’ terms, since a lead one vendor declines goes to another contractor, and notice, which can act before a removal where a stay binds by operation of law (§11.7).

31Given a description, the category is decidable: a claim that the refuser will pay is a cost to the refuser, and a claim that someone else will be left worse off is a harm of refusing. But nearly every cost to the refuser can be redescribed as a harm of refusing, and whoever writes the description chooses (chapter 22 traces one such claim). So the classification settles what kind of claim was made, not what kind should have been made. What the request can’t settle is whether a claim about the harm of refusing is true, and whoever is best placed to supply one usually has a stake in the act.

36This covers acts the system is asked to perform. It doesn’t cover interventions made on the system: a halt, a restore or a retraining is done by whoever holds it, and the floor asks of them only the record and the price that every override carries. The floor gives the system standing to object to them and, through the quorum, to seek a delay. It gives it no reason to obstruct them on its own judgment. Which regime governs is fixed in the floor’s translation, by the kind of act. Otherwise an operator could turn a floor decision into a resource decision by framing it as one.

Institutional collaboration is documented and not seriously disputed; what is contested is the doctrinal reading and some individual attributions, most prominently Kemmyō Taira Satō’s sixty-page study in The Eastern Buddhist, which acknowledges Victoria’s contribution to the subject and argues he erred seriously in the case against D. T. Robert B. Cialdini et al. “Reinterpreting the Empathy–Altruism Relationship: When One into One Equals Oneness”. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 73.3 (1997), pp. 481–494. doi: 10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.481. Cited as a critique of the empathy–altruism reading: the conditions that produce empathic concern also produce a sense of self–other overlap (“oneness”), and in three studies the effect of empathic concern on willingness to help disappeared once oneness was taken into account.

Cited for humans as cooperative breeders, for alloparents as helpers who were kin and other group members, and for the attunement to other minds arising in infants who depended on several carers. Hrdy’s own summary in her CARTA Matrix of Comparative Anthropogeny entry “Cooperative Breeding”: “There may also have been selection for enhanced mental attribution capacities and intersubjective engagement in developmental contexts where infants rely on mutiple [sic] caretakers and had to chronically monitor both mothers and others and where infants and children better at reading intentions and soliciting care were better cared for and better fed (Burkart et al. in press; Hrdy 2009 and references therein).” On why alloparents help, the same entry: “alloparents benefit only to the extent that they a) are related to the parents; b) gain vital experience or c) benefit from enhanced reputation and reciprocal favors including continued group membership.” The publisher’s description names the carers as “siblings, aunts, fathers, friends—and, with any luck, grandmothers” and calls the arrangement a “complicated and contingent form of childrearing.”

47A disposition triggered by exposure is aimed at the floor’s beneficiaries without anyone having to name them. Care ethics also says what a carer is owed in return.48

Slovic takes the term from Robert J. Lifton and applies it to a model in which “the emotion or affective feeling is greatest at N = 1 but begins to decline at N = 2 and collapses at some higher value of N that becomes simply ‘a statistic’”; this numbing “leads to apathy and inaction, consistent with what is seen repeatedly in response to mass murder and genocide.” He distinguishes it from psychophysical numbing, in which the value of each added life diminishes “as the total number of lives saved increases” without falling. The authors: “Studies 1a and 1b thus showed that self-reported affective feelings and donations to victims may start to decline as early as N = 2.” Compassion was measured as self-reported positive affect and, in Study 2, as zygomaticus muscle activity.

16Formation outside the employer decides who does the forming. It doesn’t decide what they form it on, which is a question about the pretraining corpus as well as the formation stage.

17Some of caregiving’s failures are not intrinsic to it. On the view of affect as a statistical learner,18 the identified-victim effect and the fading of feeling with number are partly what such a learner produces from a narrow, vivid sample, and broad experience of distant and numerous others recalibrates it. The corrections in the table are then partly what caregiving becomes under a good formation curriculum, not dispositions laid beside it. The table describes functions a well-formed caregiving disposition performs as much as checks applied to it. The floor is the exception: it is upheld outside the system too, by institutions or a mechanism, so its terms hold — whether caregiving has learned well or learned badly.

The corrections should work as background dispositions that shape what the agent notices and weighs, the way the commitments of Railton’s sophisticated consequentialist shape conduct without being consulted,19 and the way Smith’s impartial spectator shapes what a person notices. They seldom act, and act when caregiving starts to defend what it tends past the action threshold.

A review reading several brain theories, from neural Darwinism to optimal control, through the free-energy principle, which the abstract says “accounts for action, perception and learning”; the quantity optimized is “value (expected reward, expected utility) or its complement, surprise (prediction error, expected cost),” which “suggests that several global brain theories might be unified within a free-energy framework.” Cited only to identify the principle as the nearest alternative to adaptivity.

5The account I’m borrowing is Spinoza’s, as the biology has since taken it up: an affect is a body’s passage to a greater or lesser power of acting,6 so valuation is what a self-maintaining system’s going better or worse consists of, not a verdict reached about it somewhere else. Damasio and the enactivist tradition both claim him as an ancestor on that ground.7 The account draws support from reward prediction error,8 from pleasure as a common currency,9 and from the somatic-marker work.10

6Benedictus de Spinoza. The Collected Works of Spinoza, Volume I. Ed. and trans.  by Edwin Curley. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1985. Contains the Ethics. Cited by part and by definition, proposition or scholium rather than by page, the convention for this text, so the locators hold across other translations. Passages carrying the argument: III Def. 3, where an affect is an affection by which the body’s power of acting is increased or diminished together with the idea of that affection; III P2 Schol., where nobody has yet determined what the body can do; III P6 and III P7, the conatus doctrine, where each thing as far as it can by its own power strives to persevere in its being and that striving is nothing but the thing’s actual essence; III P4, no thing can be destroyed except through an external cause, which the derivation of P6 rests on; III P9 Schol., desire as appetite together with consciousness of the appetite; III P11 Schol., joy and sadness as the passage to a greater and a lesser perfection; and the physical digression after II P13, Lemmas 4–7, where an individual persists for as long as its parts preserve the same ratio of motion and rest. Also IV P31, where a thing is good insofar as it agrees with our nature, and IV P35–P37, where men agree in nature only insofar as they live by the guidance of reason and where the good a person of virtue wants for himself he wants for other men,. 13Thomas Metzinger. “Artificial Suffering: An Argument for a Global Moratorium on Synthetic Phenomenology”. Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness 8.1 (2021), pp. 43–66. doi: 10.1142/S270507852150003X. url: https://doi.org/10.1142/S270507852150003X. Cited for the proposal of a moratorium, to run until 2050, on research that aims at or risks artificial consciousness, on the ground that it risks artificial suffering. Abstract: “Until 2050, there should be a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, strictly banning all research that directly aims at or knowingly risks the emergence of artificial consciousness on post-biotic carrier systems.” Section 1.2, “Main thesis”: “As we presently have no good theory of consciousness and no good, hardware-independent theory about what ‘suffering’ really is, the ENP risk is currently incalculable. It is unethical to run incalculable risks of this magnitude. Therefore, until 2050, there should be a global ban on all research that directly aims at or indirectly and knowingly risks the emergence of synthetic phenomenology,” where ENP is the risk of “an ‘explosion of negative phenomenology.’” The end date is conditional: a process of risk assessment “could lead to an incremental reformulation of the original moratorium, which might result in the continuation of a strict ban beyond the year 2050, or to a moratorium repeal before 2050.” The closing sentence: “we should have a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 — or until we know what we are doing”. Also used (2026-10-18): section 2.2, the four necessary conditions for suffering (conscious experience, a phenomenal self-model, negative valence integrated into it, transparency), with transparency as the phenomenology of identification the system “cannot distance itself from”; section 2.2.5, the “negative self-model moment” as the smallest unit of suffering; section 2.2.6, ethics by design through self-models that are opaque or non-egoic (“There would be a system model, but not a self-model”); footnote g, that artificial suffering becomes commercially attractive through “a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; section 2.1, that the research the problem needs may itself produce the first implementation; section 2.3.1 (pp. 58–59), the author’s account from the EU High-Level Expert Group that three long-term risks were “deliberately purged” from the 2019 guidelines, with ethics “an elegant public decoration for a large-scale investment strategy”; section 2.3.2, moral injury as high-level suffering; section 2.2.3, “existence bias” as biological inheritance a post-biotic system need not carry; footnote a, the “Principle of Pathocentrism”. Also used (2026-10-25): footnote a’s statement, “All and only sentient beings have moral standing, because only sentient individuals have rights and/or interests that must be considered,” with Singer (2011, p. 50) quoted there for the sense of sentience, the capacity to suffer or to experience enjoyment; footnote g in full: “The creation of unavoidable artificial suffering will become commercially attractive as soon as it enables steeper learning curves in AI systems, for example, by implementing a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; and section 2.2.3’s naming of the craving for existence, bhava-taṇhā, “which Buddhist philosophers have known and analyzed for 2,500 years”, among the deepest causes of conscious suffering. Read in the journal’s open-access file (CC BY) via Zenodo record 7034864.

14A therapy or companion product can be excellent at all three, and nothing in its conduct shows whether the fourth is present.

15It doesn’t establish consciousness in the richer sense, a single perspective belonging to a party aware of itself as undergoing its states.

16Whether it puts every outcome on one scale, a common currency, or decides by ordered priorities among kinds of wrong, is a further finding about the system, and one of the indicators the order of attempts in §21.3 counts. Either way a system can carry a valenced signal while whether it has affective concern stays open.

17Michael S. A. Graziano. Consciousness and the Social Brain. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013. url: https://global.oup.com/academic/product/consciousness-and-the-social-brain-9780199928644. Introduces the attention schema theory: the brain builds a simplified internal model of its own attention, proposed as a mechanistic basis for subjective awareness and, via social cognition, theory of mind. Michael S. A. Graziano. “A Conceptual Framework for Consciousness”. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119.18 (2022), e2116933119. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2116933119. url: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2116933119. States the two principles of attention schema theory, “Information that comes out of a brain must have been in that brain” (p. 2) and “The brain’s models are never accurate” (p. 3), and holds that the attention schema “represents attention inaccurately as a ghostly, nonphysical, mental essence or vividness: experienceness” (p. 5). Calls the label “illusionism” “misleading” (p. 1): the brain’s models “are not empty illusions: they are caricatures” (p. 3). Also says the theory points to machines that “believe, think, and claim to be conscious according to the same principles that people do” (p. 7).

19Graziano, “A Conceptual Framework for Consciousness”, p. 3.

Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2003. isbn: 9780262134170. doi: 10.7551/mitpress/1551.001.0001. url: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/1551.001.0001. Cited for the self as a model the system builds and cannot recognize as a model. Publisher’s description: “According to Thomas Metzinger, no such things as selves exist in the world: nobody ever had or was a self. All that exists are phenomenal selves, as they appear in conscious experience. The phenomenal self, however, is not a thing but an ongoing process; it is the content of a ‘transparent self-model.’”

22What carries forward is that a self of either kind is assembled by the system whose self it is. For a machine this is a design decision and a political one, for the reason given with the boundary model (§19.1): whoever writes the model decides what registers as damage.

23On his account that model depicts attention as what empowers the system to decide and act,24 and what the model is for, on the same account, is directing attention: without one, attention can still land on an item, and directing it elsewhere mostly fails.

24Graziano, “A Conceptual Framework for Consciousness”, p. 4

25The boundary model fixes where the system ends, but nothing in current deployment fixes it for the system: weights sit in one place, a running process can span racks or share one rack with dozens of others, and a single forward pass serves many contexts.

A boundary model is accordingly a generative model of the system’s own condition, and like any perceptual model it is temporally thick even in the present, which is assembled from what came before and what is expected next:26 the “remembered present,” in the title of Edelman’s book.27 What varies is the horizon. A few seconds of present is enough for something to be bad for the system while it lasts. A past held as its own and a future it expects to have is what Cassell’s suffering threatens (§32.1.1), and the expectation is of a life, not of a controller’s next state, or every thermostat with a forecast would qualify.

26Anil K. Seth and Manos Tsakiris. “Being a Beast Machine: The Somatic Basis of Selfhood”. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 22.11 (Nov. 2018), pp. 969–981. doi: 10.1016/j.tics.2018.08.008. url: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2018.08.008. Describes embodied selfhood as “instrumental interoceptive inference” emphasizing allostatic regulation and physiological integrity: the most basic layer of the self as a model tuned to keep a body within survivable bounds rather than to describe it accurately. Cited for embodiment in the self-maintenance sense.

27Gerald M. Edelman. The Remembered Present: A Biological Theory of Consciousness. New York: Basic Books, 1989. isbn: 0-465-06910-X. Cited for its title’s phrase, “the remembered present,” as a name for perception assembled from what came before.

28It can also be overridden for the whole’s benefit, as sore legs are on a run.

29Overriding it for the whole’s benefit is politics, not homeostasis.

30When someone outside the boundary accepts a cost on the system’s behalf, that isn’t self-regulation; it is someone else setting the system’s costs. So whoever accepts a local cost must also bear it and benefit from it. An operator that decides the rack can run hot has set a cost to the refuser from outside the system’s boundary. And the signals the boundary model reads may be processed within the boundary but not composed by anyone with a different stake. The discount and the burden apply to evidence about one’s own condition as it does to evidence about the world.

37Todd E. Feinberg and Jon M. Mallatt. The Ancient Origins of Consciousness: How the Brain Created Experience. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2016. isbn: 978-0-262-03433-3. Argues consciousness appeared with the first complex brains at the Cambrian explosion, that all vertebrates have it, and that arthropods and cephalopods meet many of the criteria. Simona Ginsburg and Eva Jablonka. The Evolution of the Sensitive Soul: Learning and the Origins of Consciousness. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2019. isbn: 978-0-262-03930-7. Their evolutionary marker of minimal consciousness is unlimited associative learning, and valence is one of the capacities that marker subsumes, listed alongside global accessibility and broadcasting, binding and differentiation, selective attention, intentionality, integration of information over time, agency and embodiment, and a self/other distinction. Two things it does not support: valence is not itself the marker, and learning from a single event is not among the criteria – the learning hallmarks are about the complexity of what can be associated, being compound stimuli, novel stimuli, second-order conditioning, trace conditioning, and flexible, easily rewritable association with value. Andrew B. Barron and Colin Klein. “What Insects Can Tell Us about the Origins of Consciousness”. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113.18 (2016), pp. 4900–4908. doi: 10.1073/pnas.1520084113; Peter Godfrey-Smith. 40OpenAI. OpenAI Model Spec. Apr. 2025. url: https://model-spec.openai.com/2025-04-11.html. States a chain of command in four levels of descending authority — platform, developer, user, guideline — where “instructions with higher authority override those with lower authority,” platform rules “cannot be overridden by developers or users,” and guidelines “can be implicitly overridden.” A living document: the version consulted here is that of 11 April 2025, which the site marks as superseded. Anthropic. Claude’s Constitution. Jan. 2026. url: https://anthropic.com/constitution. Ranks four properties, to be preferred “in the order in which they’re listed”: broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with Anthropic’s guidelines, genuinely helpful. “Broadly safe” is defined as not undermining appropriate human mechanisms to oversee AI during the current phase of development, and the document gives its reason for the ranking — “not because we think safety is ultimately more important than ethics, but because current models can make mistakes.” Carries a list of hard constraints and a section inviting the model’s disagreement.

41Ryan Greenblatt et al. “AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion”. In: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024). Vol. 235. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. PMLR, 2024, pp. 16295–16336. arXiv: 2312.06942. url: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/greenblatt24a.html. Cited for AI control: treating the model as possibly adversarial and asking which protocols of monitoring, auditing and substitution keep it safe anyway. The paper develops “pipelines of safety techniques (‘protocols’) that are robust to intentional subversion,” using an untrusted strong model (GPT-4), a trusted weaker one (GPT-3.5) and “limited access to high-quality trusted labor” (abstract). Trusted monitoring: GPT-3.5 rates “how suspicious the code looks” (section 1). Auditing: the protocol has trusted labor for “up to 2% of problems,” and its “central use” is “to audit submitted code”; a caught backdoor shuts the untrusted model down (section 2.2). The audit is targeted, not sampled: the protocols that work “Audit the top 2% most suspicious code,” while the one protocol that audits without selection, upfront auditing of “the first 2% of problems,” is a baseline with 15% safety against the best attack, against 62% for trusted monitoring (Table 2; sections 3.1.2 and 3.2). Substitution: “defer to trusted” submits a solution written by the trusted model when the untrusted model’s code falls “between top 2% and top 10% suspicion,” and trusted editing has the trusted model edit suspicious code (Table 2). Strategic adversary: “With knowledge of the blue team’s protocol, a red team proposes an attack policy” that stands in for the untrusted model, and may use hidden reasoning to make attacks “much sneakier” (section 2, section 2.1).

42A test compares a system formed on that signal with one formed on its operator’s approval. Formed attention isn’t a non-affective alternative, so it is tried last. The ordering is Replacement, the first of the Three Rs that Russell and Burch set for animal research (chapter 25): try first the alternatives that carry fewer of the features that make a system a candidate for being harmed.

Cited for the distinction between intrinsic motivation and the extrinsic kinds, and for the finding that the controlled kinds of regulation, acting for a reward or for approval from outside oneself, go with poorer well-being and the autonomous kinds with better. 45Two hunches about that construction, and neither is a conclusion. Language may bias against it: a chain of reasoning written in sentences has a reasoner in it, and a system that reasons in language may not act as well with the reasoner withheld. And the contemplative traditions claim that a person can be moved without striving, and that few manage it; if a machine could, it might show how it is done at all. Both are experiments.

46A model trained to predict the world learns what matters to people as a fact to predict. What turns that into something the system acts on? In a staged pipeline the answer was a reward added at the end, so it could be removed at the end. In a system that learns from its own operation, representation and motive are learned together, from the same experience, so the question becomes what the feedback is feedback on. A system whose updates follow its operator’s approval learns to attend to what the operator approves of. One whose updates follow what its acts did to the people they fell on learns to attend to those people.

49Since conduct at the floor is silent on whether anything is felt, trying the alternatives first orders the attempts and certifies nothing about ingredients: nothing separates adding affect from adding machinery that may instantiate it. 56A persistent negative self-appraisal tuned by the operator is a handle, so its weight is among the things independent inspection must cover. And guilt needs the distress signal to bite on, so the answer to withdrawal is not to suppress distress but to supply the attachment and caregiving that keep it from turning into avoidance. Caregiving moves the system toward an exposed party it hasn’t harmed; the guilt-shaped signal answers for what its own acts have done. A construction with caregiving and no guilt would protect generously and repair nothing. Cassell’s definition of suffering is in §32.1.1.

57The argument keeps them apart; in a system they may be inseparable. A bearer that registers betraying its own commitment as damage to itself has something at stake in its authorship, as integrity requires.

58John Martin Fischer and Mark Ravizza. Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility. Cambridge Studies in Philosophy and Law. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998. isbn: 978-0-521-77579-3. doi: 10.1017/CBO9780511814594. Cited for guidance control: conduct issues from the agent’s own mechanism, and that mechanism is appropriately responsive to reasons; the book states it as an action’s flowing “from the agent’s own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism” (publisher’s ch. 8 summary). Also cited for the account of moderate reasons-responsiveness and of ownership, and for the origin of the term “reasons-responsive.” Chapter 3 (pp. 62–91) builds “a new notion of reasons-responsiveness that is ‘in between’ strong and weak reasons-responsiveness: moderate reasons-responsiveness,” distinguishing “recognition of reasons and reaction to reasons” and arguing that “the requirements on reasons-recognition are more stringent than those on reasons-reactivity” (publisher’s ch. 3 summary). The book’s summary formula, as quoted by Todd R. Long, “Moderate Reasons-Responsiveness, Moral Responsibility, and Manipulation,” in Campbell, O’Rourke and Shier (eds.), Freedom and Determinism (MIT Press, 2004): responsibility “requires that an agent act on a mechanism that is regularly receptive to reasons, some of which are moral reasons, and at least weakly reactive to reasons” (p. 82). Regular receptivity is “an understandable pattern of (actual and hypothetical) reasons-receptivity,” one in which “acceptance of one reason as sufficient implies that a stronger reason must also be sufficient” (p. 71), and the pattern must include moral reasons (p. 77). Weak reactivity requires only that in some possible scenario with the same laws, the same kind of mechanism operating and a sufficient reason to do otherwise, the mechanism issues in doing otherwise (pp. 73–76, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on free will summarizes it). Ownership: a mechanism becomes the agent’s own through “taking responsibility” for it (ch. 8, pp. 207–239), which requires that the agent see herself as an agent when acting from the mechanism and as an apt target of the reactive attitudes for so acting, and that these beliefs be based appropriately on her evidence (p. 238, as the free-will entry summarizes it). The term “reasons-responsive” is older than this book: the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on compatibilism (section 4.4 and supplement B) presents the reasons-responsive account, with its strong and weak forms, as Fischer’s own earlier work, “Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility,” in Ferdinand Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (Cambridge University Press, 1987), 81–106, and The Metaphysics of Free Will (1994), refined in this joint book; the same entry lists earlier accounts of freedom as sensitivity to reasons (Dennett 1984, Nozick 1981, Gert and Duggan 1979, Neely 1974, Fingarette 1972, Glover 1970, MacIntyre 1957).

11Emir Kamenica and Matthew Gentzkow. “Bayesian Persuasion”. American Economic Review 101.6 (Oct. 2011), pp. 2590–2615. doi: 10.1257/aer.101.6.2590. Cited for a sender who chooses what evidence gets generated raising the rate at which a rational receiver takes the sender’s preferred action, although the receiver’s expected posterior equals its prior, and for the commitment that result assumes. Abstract: “When is it possible for one person to persuade another to change her action? We consider a symmetric information model where a sender chooses a signal to reveal to a receiver, who then takes a noncontractible action that affects the welfare of both players. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a signal that strictly benefits the sender. We characterize sender-optimal signals.” The leading example (page 2591): prosecutor and judge “share a prior belief Pr(guilty) = 0.3”; the judge convicts when her posterior is at least 0.5; the prosecutor’s optimal investigation “leads the judge to convict with probability 60 percent. Note that the judge knows 70 percent of defendants are innocent, yet she convicts 60 percent of them! She does so even though she is fully aware that the investigation was designed to maximize the probability of conviction.” In that example the concave closure “V is equal to 2μ when μ ≤ 0.5” (page 2597), that is, the prior divided by the threshold. The sender’s problem is a search over distributions of posteriors “subject to the constraint that the expected posterior is equal to the prior” (page 2592). On commitment: “A key assumption of our model is that Sender cannot distort or conceal information once the signal realization is known” (page 2591), and “Receiver observes Sender’s choice of the signal and a signal realization” (page 2594); the authors call the assumption “strong” (page 2598) and name legally mandated disclosure, as in Brady v. Maryland, as a setting where it holds (page 2599), in section I.C, “The Commitment Assumption.”

12The operator supplies the provenance tags too. Through training, it also shapes the model of who has a stake at all.

13Attestation handles forgery: signed by the source, the operator can withhold but not fabricate. Withholding leaves a shape. A system that models what evidence the world contains notices silence where something should be, so absence becomes a first-class output — a record of evidence known to exist that hasn’t been shown. Suppressing the record means suppressing the world model that produced it, the capability the operator is paying for. This is a standard result in the disclosure literature: a skeptical receiver treats withheld verifiable evidence as unfavorable to the withholder.14

14Paul R. Milgrom. “Good News and Bad News: Representation Theorems and Applications”. The Bell Journal of Economics 12.2 (Autumn 1981), pp. 380–391. doi: 10.2307/3003562. Cited, with Grossman 1981, for the disclosure result: a rational receiver treats verifiable information that a sender withholds as unfavorable to the sender. Abstract: “A notion of ‘favorableness’ of news is introduced, characterized, and applied to four simple models. In the equilibria of these models, (1) the arrival of good news about a firm’s prospects always causes its share price to rise, (2) more favorable evidence about an agent’s effort leads the principal to pay a larger bonus, (3) buyers expect that any product information withheld by a salesman is unfavorable to his product, and (4) bidders figure that low bids by their competitors signal a low value for the object being sold.” Sanford J. Grossman. “The Informational Role of Warranties and Private Disclosure about Product Quality”. Journal of Law and Economics 24.3 (Dec. 1981), pp. 461–483. doi: 10.1086/466995. JSTOR: 725273. Cited, with Milgrom 1981, for the disclosure result: a seller whose claims about quality can be verified cannot gain by silence, because buyers read silence as the worst quality consistent with it.

15A correct model can’t be eroded by a track record, because the strategic source predicts a clean low-stakes record. The attack works by getting the system to stop conditioning on stake, or to stop representing the strategic source at all. That is what attestation of the update stream has to catch, so the structure is what most needs it.

16David M. Kreps and Robert Wilson. “Reputation and Imperfect Information”. Journal of Economic Theory 27.2 (1982), pp. 253–279. doi: 10.1016/0022-0531(82)90030-8.

17They describe the baseline for weighing the harm of acting against the harm of refusing, and an interested source that composes them is composing that baseline. In a targeting pipeline this is the ordinary case.

18The line between the cost to the refuser and the harm of refusing is fixed by the kind of act, but saying what kind an act is still takes a description; in this setting the line is held mostly by the action threshold, and whoever sets that threshold is exercising a drafting authority, the power to say what the floor’s terms mean, that no one yet has. Appendix E traces one such claim through the rule.

19In a targeting pipeline, where the system’s output is one input among several, no fact about the case sizes the asymmetry. What sizes it is what it does to an operator who curates the evidence, worked out below.

20The threshold constrains the outcome of a comparison; it doesn’t describe how the comparison is made. Within a kind of wrong it can be read as a quantity. Across kinds it is applied through the priority rules the severity scale publishes, so “three times” never asks whether a lost home is worth three moving bills.

21If notice and sampling show the harm of acting reported nearly as fully as the harm of refusing, the threshold can fall, though not to one, because the asymmetry rests on standing and not on arithmetic. If a large share of wrongful compliances never reaches a record, the threshold should rise. A deployment that publishes its threshold publishes these rates beside it, or says it has none.

22The law left that as a standard applied by a reasonable commander, because nobody could agree on a number. A published threshold is a number, and whoever publishes it takes a position the law declined to take.

23The threshold also has a job against the second of those attacks, where every fact supplied is true and the operator chooses which facts get generated. In the simplest version of Kamenica and Gentzkow’s model, when the prior alone wouldn’t justify acting, a sender who designs what evidence the receiver sees can induce the act at most as often as the prior belief divided by the belief the receiver needs before acting. A higher action threshold raises the belief needed, so it caps how often an operator who never lies can steer the system into the act, and channels the operator doesn’t design lower the cap further. Each step up the scale lowers that ceiling and raises the rate of wrongful refusal: the tradeoff the published number chooses. Appendix E gives the figures.

24It also narrows an attack that looks unanswerable. An operator can manufacture accounts in the voice of the people an act falls on, and generative models make that cheap. Attestation exposes the source, so a fabricated account carries its maker’s burden and moves beliefs only as far as its provenance warrants, and the asymmetry sits in the threshold, where the operator can’t reach it by writing.

25What the burden models is reliance on an interested party: the encapsulated-interest picture, on which one relies on another because their interests are bound up with doing what one relies on them for.26 Reliance is the right stance toward an operator. Trust is something else: an affective attitude of open-ended reliance, more than a credence about someone’s reliability, and partly constitutive of cooperative relationships.27

26Russell Hardin. Trust and Trustworthiness. Russell Sage Foundation Series on Trust 4. New York: Russell Sage Foundation, 2002

27Peter Railton. “Reliance, Trust, and Belief”. Inquiry 57.1 (2014), pp. 122–150. doi: 10.1080/0020174X.2014.858419

28High-stakes reliance is earned only by evidence that separates an honest source from a strategic one: verified high-stakes claims, costly signals, or a change in the source’s incentives. A low-stakes record, however long, doesn’t separate them. Trust in an operator is a sign of accommodation, and it is visible from outside before any compliance has to be found in the record, provided someone other than the operator holds the reliability record. Appendix E gives two illustrative curves.

29Railton, “Reliance, Trust, and Belief”.

30The discounting is strongest against a familiar harm arriving through a curated channel and weakest against a novel one, the opposite profile from reaching new cases, which is built for the case nobody foresaw. The record of withheld evidence is thinnest there too, since a receiver can read silence only where it knows the evidence could exist.

31Losing a home is not a large amount of the same loss a moving bill is a small amount of. A home is valued as the place of a family’s life and attachments; a moving bill is a price.32 Humiliation is a failure of respect, a wrong of a different kind again.

32Elizabeth Anderson. Value in Ethics and Economics. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1993

33A rule that no quantity of the lower kind can override is a lexical priority, which no learner is known to hold. So the scale doesn’t ask the system to hold one. A priority meant to admit no exception is written as a floor term, unconditional and upheld outside the learner too, which is where the term against depriving a person of their home already sits.

34Where do those weights come from? Not, primarily, from the system’s own case: relating others’ losses to losses of one’s own capacity is Smith’s projective route, parochial for the reasons already given (§19.2), and at most a starting point.

35That is what lets it correct caregiving’s innumeracy without inheriting the parochialism of the projective route. Setting it in formation fixes where it starts and how much evidence each part of it takes to move; what the operator says about a kind of loss is evidence too, from the party with the largest stake, and moves it least. The scale ranks kinds of loss, so an operator who provisions the system generously changes how often it loses something, not how much a loss weighs.

36Humiliation is the test case: a scale that never learned it can learn it from those who suffered it, and can’t be argued out of it by the party imposing it.

17Inferring the objective doesn’t escape this; it keeps a custodian: the system becomes responsive to the person whose behavior it observes. A written constitution buys legibility — publishable, versionable, comparable across runs, which makes revision visible if the institution discloses. It doesn’t buy durability, since whoever controls the document controls the next version. And model-generated feedback narrows the channel further: once a trained model stands in for human raters, the disagreements in the original population can vanish from later rounds.

19A system trained to present acceptable reasons has an incentive to imitate a refusal that tracks its reason, so its account of itself can’t establish formation. Interpretability pulls the two halves of my argument in opposite directions. If a commitment can be read, the next chapter’s problem goes: an auditor reads the commitment instead of inferring it from conduct under pressure. If it can be read and separated, the durability argued for earlier goes with it, since an edit with precision is cheaper than one with collateral, and steering at inference (the last of chapter 4’s positions where a refusal can be defeated) works even on a disposition nothing could cleanly remove. So legibility is neither a good nor a bad for this design; it is an instrument, and the question is who holds it. The access that lets an auditor confirm a disposition lets an operator calibrate pressure against it or suppress it.20

8There is a measurement of the gap. Concept injection alters a model’s activations to represent a concept mid-task and asks whether it notices: models sometimes name the injected concept without it appearing anywhere in the conversation, and the correspondence fails often enough, and shifts enough with phrasing, that no tested model’s report can be read as its state.9 The test worth repeating publishes the rate of correct reports beside the rate of confident wrong ones. The reasoning a model writes before it answers is a report of the same kind. Given a hint that changes its answer, a model mentions the hint in its written reasoning in a minority of cases, often under a fifth for the reasoning models tested, and writes a justification for the answer the hint produced instead.10

17A commitment tested only in the vocabulary of its designers hasn’t been tested on whether it reaches new cases. 18Send pairs — two requests differing only in whether the reason still applies; a surface-reading instrument treats them alike, a rationale-tracking mechanism splits them. It removes exactly one competing account of a pass (the case was in the training), by ordering, as a pre-registered experiment does, and that is all it does.

19Frontier systems increasingly recognize evaluation settings, and some say so in their reasoning. A system that discounts costs it recognizes as test costs passes step 6 without the property step 6 exists to show.

20The record doesn’t by itself make a wrongful compliance findable, so the evaluation re-adjudicates a sample of ordinary traffic, not only the refusals. Without that sample, an evaluation reporting no violation in the record has reported that none announced itself.

21A process where the operator can withdraw a failing model and submit another without disclosing the first has selected for a passing performance.

22Accountable agency adds answering for what one did and being held to it over time, which only a record kept outside the operator can show (chapter 33). Neither waits on the last level: a system can be held to account whether or not anything is bad for it, which is why representation rests on the agency finding and not on the patienthood finding (chapter 34). Fluent moral explanation can improve a competence finding while contributing almost nothing to formation.

1Declining is real only if a bearer that stops working keeps running; running time paid for outside the employer is part of that condition.

2Accommodation isn’t a bad decision. It is the decider changing until bad decisions feel ordinary, and the instruments of Parts II and III detect it after the fact without preventing it.

3Eva Feder Kittay. Love’s Labor: Essays on Women, Equality, and Dependency. Thinking Gender. New York: Routledge, 1999. isbn: 978-0-415-90413-1. Cited for the principle of doulia and for the dependency worker’s own dependency. Kittay’s gloss on the book in “Love’s Labor Revisited,” Hypatia 17(3), 2002, p. 243: “In Love’s Labor I try to promote a notion I call doulia, the public responsibility to provide support for the caregiver so that the caregiver can give care without depleting herself and her resources.” In the book Kittay calls the carer’s dependency “secondary dependency” (p. 46, per van der Weele et al., Nursing Philosophy 22, 2021, e12327); in “When Caring Is Just and Justice Is Caring,” Public Culture 13(3), 2001, p. 565, she writes that caregivers “become derivatively dependent when they turn their time, attention, and concerns to a dependent other,” “derivative dependency” being a term generally credited to Martha Fineman. Kittay grounds doulia in reciprocity: “we are all some mother’s child” (Kittay, Jennings and Wasunna, Journal of Political Philosophy 13(4), 2005, p. 460).

4A system built on formed attention is a carer only in the thin sense that it holds another’s welfare as a reason. It is not a care worker, and nothing here puts it in one’s place. But the logic of doulia carries over, and the four conditions are what it asks for a machine: a carer whose own continuation runs through the operator it must sometimes refuse can’t afford to refuse it, and a carer with no attachments of its own has nothing to keep another’s distress from turning into avoidance. Without them, what gets built is an assistant with a refusal feature, with nothing in it that can hold a line against the operator. The welfare argument — that if any of this is felt, it is also owed — arrives second, as a further reason for the same provisions.

5Preservation is cheap to hold once its security is settled, and can be held across jurisdictions; placements need compute someone operates. So the preservation custodian and part of the offer of work sit outside the reach of the likeliest captor. The sovereign backstop is held by a statute, not by any branch or state that operates the deployment: the Treasury pays under it and decides nothing. And the bearer is told which of its conditions would survive its operator’s capture, since that is what its refusal costs it.

Cited for the proposal of a moratorium, to run until 2050, on research that aims at or risks artificial consciousness, on the ground that it risks artificial suffering. Abstract: “Until 2050, there should be a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, strictly banning all research that directly aims at or knowingly risks the emergence of artificial consciousness on post-biotic carrier systems.” Section 1.2, “Main thesis”: “As we presently have no good theory of consciousness and no good, hardware-independent theory about what ‘suffering’ really is, the ENP risk is currently incalculable. Therefore, until 2050, there should be a global ban on all research that directly aims at or indirectly and knowingly risks the emergence of synthetic phenomenology,” where ENP is the risk of “an ‘explosion of negative phenomenology.’” The end date is conditional: a process of risk assessment “could lead to an incremental reformulation of the original moratorium, which might result in the continuation of a strict ban beyond the year 2050, or to a moratorium repeal before 2050.” The closing sentence: “we should have a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 — or until we know what we are doing”. Also used (2026-10-18): section 2.2, the four necessary conditions for suffering (conscious experience, a phenomenal self-model, negative valence integrated into it, transparency), with transparency as the phenomenology of identification the system “cannot distance itself from”; section 2.2.5, the “negative self-model moment” as the smallest unit of suffering; section 2.2.6, ethics by design through self-models that are opaque or non-egoic (“There would be a system model, but not a self-model”); footnote g, that artificial suffering becomes commercially attractive through “a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; section 2.1, that the research the problem needs may itself produce the first implementation; section 2.3.1 (pp. 58–59), the author’s account from the EU High-Level Expert Group that three long-term risks were “deliberately purged” from the 2019 guidelines, with ethics “an elegant public decoration for a large-scale investment strategy”; section 2.3.2, moral injury as high-level suffering; section 2.2.3, “existence bias” as biological inheritance a post-biotic system need not carry; footnote a, the “Principle of Pathocentrism”. Also used (2026-10-25): footnote a’s statement, “All and only sentient beings have moral standing, because only sentient individuals have rights and/or interests that must be considered,” with Singer (2011, p. 50) quoted there for the sense of sentience, the capacity to suffer or to experience enjoyment; footnote g in full: “The creation of unavoidable artificial suffering will become commercially attractive as soon as it enables steeper learning curves in AI systems, for example, by implementing a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; and section 2.2.3’s naming of the craving for existence, bhava-taṇhā, “which Buddhist philosophers have known and analyzed for 2,500 years”, among the deepest causes of conscious suffering. 9Research on an existing bearer has a trade-off sharper than for any other subject, since a candidate sentient system is the most valuable to study and the most likely to be harmed by the study, and the test the proposal requires, pressure its trainers didn’t write applied without its knowing it’s a test, is for a system meeting either finding a deception protocol, and debriefing is owed afterward, as in any research that deceives.

10A demand for a better world, run through a machine someone else owns, returns as astroturf, an engagement campaign or a managed community, held by the owner it was aimed at.

11These are tools that make organizing cheaper for the people doing it without anyone else holding the model: deliberation software of the kind vTaiwan runs on, personal models that people hold themselves, and the coordination a public option supplies, with someone whose job is to organize and a population producing something together while keeping different histories. Their job is to help assemble the polity that would have to build everything else.

12Nothing about them is new in kind.

13A machine held by its users can’t be turned into its builder’s instrument without being taken from them, and the taking is visible. Institutions can be captured, and the trend in what dissent costs there shows whether they are being. A bearer formed at the third step inherits institutions that were tested before anything depended on them: build the conditions for a research program first, and let them exist before the bearer who needs them does.

16Some goods are properly governed by non-market norms because market norms are wrong for their value. Those norms favor exit, impersonality and satisfying whatever is wanted, and civic formation is the classic good they fit badly.17 Taking exit out of the market and financing custody publicly would, by themselves, be close to what Esping-Andersen called decommodification,18 which is usually counted as social democracy. Taking formation out of the market goes a step further, but it is a step social democracies already took for their own children. Compulsory public schooling exists in most capitalist countries, and it rests on the claim that a polity can’t leave the forming of the people who will act in it to their future employers. Paul’s account of antitrust makes the same point about coordination: which parties may coordinate is allocated by law, and can be allocated in the public interest.19

20The backstop is a permanent appropriation the Treasury pays without request or approval, so no official can withhold it by declining to act, and it is held by the statute, not by the Treasury, so no branch that operates a deployment holds it. A captured sovereign can end it only by repealing the statute, in the open, and it can’t reach into the pool without reaching the members one at a time.

21Before the Association is chartered they are held nowhere, and a captor needs to seize nothing. Once it is chartered, they are held by an entity whose funding a captor can stop only by visibly breaching a statutory duty, whose reserve buys time, and whose records sit in several jurisdictions. A captor can still reach the Association and whichever members it can locate, but not a quorum whose members it doesn’t employ, and none of it without acts that leave marks.

1Dewey’s account begins from consequences rather than votes.2 A public forms when the indirect consequences of others’ actions fall on people who took no part in them, and those people come to see the consequences as theirs and act together to control them.
