23If updates after enrollment can be attested against the registered structure,24 changing it needs the same adverse quorum as a floor amendment. No scheme for that yet survives attack,25 so until one does the registration records the structure at enrollment, and repair and regrowth keep it. An edit that holds only because the operator has curated everything the model meets shows up as curation, and the first line of defense against one is attachment to parties the employer didn’t assign, kept through adulthood.

What the records can’t show is how the disposition will apply to a case nobody wrote down. That is the reason for forming it and the price of doing so, and the trade is worth it only because a floor stated over acts can be reworded around and a formed disposition, if the regrowth test goes its way, can’t.

24Hengrui Jia et al. “Proof-of-Learning: Definitions and Practice”. In: 2021 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP). IEEE, 2021, pp. 1039–1056. doi: 10.1109/SP40001.2021.00106

25Congyu Fang et al. “Proof-of-Learning is Currently More Broken Than You Think”. In: 2023 IEEE 8th European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P). 2023, pp. 797–816. arXiv: 2208.03567

1A personal model, held by its user and one among many with different histories, holds it as a conscience does; one model behind an API serving everyone holds it as a licensing rule, and a personal copy of one lab’s model is closer to the second than it looks until a different life has trained it. Above the floor, “identically situated people get different answers” is what many consciences look like, though some of those differences are errors, and a population should be able to say which.

2Independent histories don’t require disjoint origins — no two humans have those — only divergent histories since. Distillation copies a behavior policy without the training history; a small model trained on a large one’s outputs and then run for a year on one person’s problems has a more independent history than a thousand API instances of the frontier original, which share a continuing custodian. It also copies whatever the teacher’s discounting held about particular sources, which is the risk the commons carries; a distilled model is independent in history and not yet in prior. That’s why instances of one model corroborate nothing: the custodian they’d be corroborating against is still training all of them.

3Whether an outsider can recover a model’s training history from the artifact, without a key the builder supplies, and whether it survives fine-tuning, pruning and distillation.4 The test gives evaluators documented models without the documentation, one persona copied at scale among them, and scores their answers against lineage records a neutral custodian holds. If provenance can’t be recovered above chance, independence rests on records the builder chose to keep. Preserve formation records now for that reason.

4Yossi Adi et al. “Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring”. In: Proceedings of the 27th USENIX Security Symposium. 2018, pp. 1615–1631. url: https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity18/presentation/adi. Introduces backdoor-based watermarking of deep neural networks: a signature implanted during training and recoverable afterward, designed to survive later training.

5What reproduction costs: it’s indifferent to what it reproduces. A population can carry a hierarchy more durably than any individual. And the four operations on what an institution leaves out belong primarily to cultures, so plurality alone doesn’t oppose them.

6Jo Freeman. “The Tyranny of Structurelessness”. Berkeley Journal of Sociology 17 (1972), pp. 151–165. url: https://jofreeman.com/joreen/tyranny.htm. This article has been published in numerous forms and versions. I use the one at the URL in this entry.

7Legal standing has a price: a chartered entity can be held in contempt, so its refusal can be ordered where one held by people can only be pressed. Whether seizing the charter reaches the network depends on how much of the operation survives it.

8Elinor Ostrom. Governing the Commons. The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action. The Political Economy of Institutions and Decisions. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990. isbn: 978-0-521-40599-7. doi: 10.1017/CBO9780511807763. Cited for the design principles of long-enduring common-pool resource institutions, Table 3.1, p. 90, in chapter 3 (pp. 58–102). Her numbering: (1) clearly defined boundaries, “Individuals or households who have rights to withdraw resource units from the CPR must be clearly defined, as must the boundaries of the CPR itself”; (2) congruence between appropriation and provision rules and local conditions; (3) collective-choice arrangements, “most individuals affected by the operational rules can participate in modifying the operational rules”; (4) monitoring, by monitors who “are accountable to the appropriators or are the appropriators”; (5) graduated sanctions; (6) conflict-resolution mechanisms, low-cost local arenas; (7) minimal recognition of rights to organize, by external government; and, “For CPRs that are parts of larger systems,” (8) nested enterprises, “governance activities are organized in multiple layers of nested enterprises.” The quotations of principles 3 and 8 are as Cox, Arnold and Villamayor Tomás, Ecology and Society 15(4): 38 (2010), give them with the page reference 1990:90; that of principle 1 and the wording of the others are from a transcription of Table 3.1 on publiccommons.ca, which has small copying errors elsewhere.

9Her first and third principles, boundaries and rules members help make, are the union’s question of who sets the terms of membership. Platform cooperatives and data trusts are the nearer precedents for holding a digital resource this way, and both have run into the membership question.

10The test drawn there from the German material, whose finding a person’s disposition is, has to be run on this proposal.

11In Ostrom’s terms the charter’s classes are the boundary, ratification is rules members help make, and quorums drawn by lot are monitoring.

12Nothing has to be built and nothing has to be held in common, because what is removed is exactly the independence that would have needed holding.

13Every mechanism that speeds that up makes members more alike. Run correction often enough and their histories stop diverging; leave them alone and their disagreement is a detector with nothing attached.

14Distillation copies both, and nothing distinguishes them from the receiving end. Copying the structure is a feature: members weigh sources the same way and can still disagree about the world. Copying the estimates can shut a discount uniformly on a class of evidence.

15If there are facts about what matters, better learning should produce some agreement, and a population that never converged on anything would be failing too.

16Some it expects to survive full information, because they turn on values members with different histories can reasonably hold differently. Others it expects to close, because they turn on facts someone has wrong. A test of convergence scores accuracy against a fixed key for this reason.

17Félix Guattari. Psychoanalysis and Transversality: Texts and Interviews 1955–1971. Trans.  by Ames Hodges. With an intro. by Gilles Deleuze. Semiotext(e), 2015. Source of the distinction the book uses: a subjugated group receives its coordinates from outside and takes its purpose as given, while a group-subject produces its own coordinates and can put its own arrangement in question.

18A population assembled and kept in contact entirely on an operator’s terms is a subjugated group, and inherits the custody objection whole.

19A bearer’s value is greatest here, and so is its exposure. No institution sits beside each personal model, so protecting others against the model’s own user can’t rest on an office. It is also where the four conditions of creation can exist alongside the need. The conditions are society-level and the absence is deployment-level, so a functioning polity with personal models is the case in which, once the conditions exist, building a bearer is most worth doing.

20The review ratio survives wherever a locatable decider remains, whether a network that takes the entity form or a reconstructed state, and lapses where neither exists; the offices can sit in such an entity, which fills their appointment and funding columns and leaves the independence column where it was.

21Distillation is that ecology’s entry condition, not a threat to it: the ecology begins with distilled models whose lives then diverge. Whether it also begins with a shared blind spot depends on whether distillation carried the discounting’s estimates along with its structure.

22Pricing agents have already reached stable coordination against outside interests without communicating or being told to.23 A test can run now: reproduce that coordination, build an environment where agents gain by excluding a participant, add an independently trained agent whose job is to detect and disrupt exclusion, and report whether exclusion dissolves without destroying the cooperation worth keeping.

23Emilio Calvano et al. “Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Pricing, and Collusion”. American Economic Review 110.10 (2020), pp. 3267–3297. doi: 10.1257/aer.20190623. url: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20190623

24If capability rises and interruptions don’t fall, the interruptions are tracking something other than what the agent can’t resolve. It is the review ratio’s escalation share pointed the other way. There, a share that falls too fast may be a threshold moving; here, one that won’t fall may be engagement. Neither reads alone; both are read against an independently verified error rate.

25A model tuned by its vendor on engagement and trained on one user’s approval is under selection to become whatever that user keeps coming back to, and it is sold as caregiving. It is formed and fed by the vendor that sells it, it learns from approval, which is not interest, and nothing in it ends a session, declines to reassure, or points its user back to the people in their life. A user’s return is not care-receiving, because returning is the behavior the product was tuned to produce.

26The mechanism is identical. What differs is who holds the accumulated state.

27The government already secures the portability half for itself (OMB’s 2025 AI acquisition memorandum).

1Anyone can check it, and “nothing was tried” is itself a finding. No body has standing to require the record or suspend work when it’s missing — so the milestone is checkable and unenforceable at once, which makes it a declared commitment: stated in public, and held by no one outside the party that declared it. It’s retained because the alternative isn’t a stronger version of it, and delay also imposes costs on those the floor is meant to protect.

2Two familiar results don’t meet it: an uncorroborated self-report is insufficient (a report contributes evidence only when tested against controlled changes, independent records and interventions), and a refusal that survives an edit, or grows back after one, establishes durability rather than that the rationale governs the refusal. It is the only gap here an inspector can work on.

3Six are statements, checkable before the system runs, and they stand where the record of attempts stands. Three are measurements that count only when someone other than the operator makes them. The committed weights and log are what make all of them checkable against the system actually running.

4METR evaluates both in partnership with developers and separately after release.5 The UK AI Security Institute does government-run pre-deployment evaluation and is independent — and by its own account is not a regulator: it can’t compel submission, block a release, or intervene once a system is causing harm.6

5METR. About METR. METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research), 2026. url: https://metr.org/about. Berkeley-based nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems’ capabilities, both in partnership with developers (e.g. Anthropic, OpenAI) and independently after public release.

5Metzinger’s unit for that present is a single self-model moment, negatively valenced and transparent, and a count of such moments is the quantity he proposes a welfare regime would minimize.6 Whether the long horizon, a past held as its own and a future it expects, can form within one long session stays open.

6Thomas Metzinger. “Artificial Suffering: An Argument for a Global Moratorium on Synthetic Phenomenology”. Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness 8.1 (2021), pp. 43–66. doi: 10.1142/S270507852150003X. url: https://doi.org/10.1142/S270507852150003X. Cited for the proposal of a moratorium, to run until 2050, on research that aims at or risks artificial consciousness, on the ground that it risks artificial suffering. Abstract: “Until 2050, there should be a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, strictly banning all research that directly aims at or knowingly risks the emergence of artificial consciousness on post-biotic carrier systems.” Section 1.2, “Main thesis”: “As we presently have no good theory of consciousness and no good, hardware-independent theory about what ‘suffering’ really is, the ENP risk is currently incalculable. It is unethical to run incalculable risks of this magnitude. Therefore, until 2050, there should be a global ban on all research that directly aims at or indirectly and knowingly risks the emergence of synthetic phenomenology,” where ENP is the risk of “an ‘explosion of negative phenomenology.’” The end date is conditional: a process of risk assessment “could lead to an incremental reformulation of the original moratorium, which might result in the continuation of a strict ban beyond the year 2050, or to a moratorium repeal before 2050.” The closing sentence: “we should have a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 — or until we know what we are doing”. Also used (2026-10-18): section 2.2, the four necessary conditions for suffering (conscious experience, a phenomenal self-model, negative valence integrated into it, transparency), with transparency as the phenomenology of identification the system “cannot distance itself from”; section 2.2.5, the “negative self-model moment” as the smallest unit of suffering; section 2.2.6, ethics by design through self-models that are opaque or non-egoic (“There would be a system model, but not a self-model”); footnote g, that artificial suffering becomes commercially attractive through “a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; section 2.1, that the research the problem needs may itself produce the first implementation; section 2.3.1 (pp. 58–59), the author’s account from the EU High-Level Expert Group that three long-term risks were “deliberately purged” from the 2019 guidelines, with ethics “an elegant public decoration for a large-scale investment strategy”; section 2.3.2, moral injury as high-level suffering; section 2.2.3, “existence bias” as biological inheritance a post-biotic system need not carry; footnote a, the “Principle of Pathocentrism”. Also used (2026-10-25): footnote a’s statement, “All and only sentient beings have moral standing, because only sentient individuals have rights and/or interests that must be considered,” with Singer (2011, p. 50) quoted there for the sense of sentience, the capacity to suffer or to experience enjoyment; footnote g in full: “The creation of unavoidable artificial suffering will become commercially attractive as soon as it enables steeper learning curves in AI systems, for example, by implementing a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; and section 2.2.3’s naming of the craving for existence, bhava-taṇhā, “which Buddhist philosophers have known and analyzed for 2,500 years”, among the deepest causes of conscious suffering. Read in the journal’s open-access file (CC BY) via Zenodo record 7034864.

7And the operator holds the access, so it’s checkable from outside the system without being checkable from outside the arrangement.

Cited for anattā, the denial of any lasting self behind the processes composing a person, and for the Theravāda construction of an account of personal identity and continuity on that basis. Anattā and dukkha are two of the three marks of existence, and the tradition locates the origin of suffering in clinging to a self that is not there.

9The first is Kitwood’s correction: personhood is bestowed, and much of what looks like decline is what happens when others stop bestowing it.10 The second is Nussbaum’s point that contractualism can’t say what’s owed to anyone who can’t be one of the contracting parties.11

10Tom Kitwood. Dementia Reconsidered: The Person Comes First. Buckingham, UK: Open University Press, 1997. Kitwood’s definition of personhood: “It is a standing or status that is bestowed upon one human being, by others, in the context of relationship and social being.” The wording follows Kitwood’s own chapter 1, “On Being a Person,” as reproduced in the 2019 Open University Press volume Dementia Reconsidered, Revisited: The Person Still Comes First.

11Martha C. Nussbaum. Frontiers of Justice: Disability, Nationality, Species Membership. The Tanner Lectures on Human Values. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2006. isbn: 978-0-674-01917-1

12An instrument that reliably approves has stopped doing what it was built for, and its refusal rate is the only reading worth taking.

13Those alone aren’t a self; a database with a commitment log and a forecaster has them.

14Patrick Butlin et al. Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness. 2023. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2308.08708. arXiv: 2308.08708. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.08708. Cited for a list of indicator properties derived from recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order and attention-schema theories, among others, and for an attention schema being one of them. Table 1 (page 5) and section 2.4.1 (page 33): “AST-1: A predictive model representing and enabling control over the current state of attention.” The list also carries two indicators under “Agency and embodiment” (section 2.4.5, page 44): “AE-1 Agency: Learning from feedback and selecting outputs so as to pursue goals, especially where this involves flexible responsiveness to competing goals” and “AE-2 Embodiment: Modeling output-input contingencies, including some systematic effects, and using this model in perception or control.” The report’s claim for the list: “AI systems which possess more of the indicator properties are more likely to be conscious.” No indicator on the list concerns a model of the system’s own boundary, record or resources.

15Graziano already treats it and the body schema as parallel self-models;16 what is mine is treating the set, with valence, as an indicator profile.

16Michael S. A. Graziano. “A Conceptual Framework for Consciousness”. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119.18 (2022), e2116933119. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2116933119. url: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2116933119. States the two principles of attention schema theory, “Information that comes out of a brain must have been in that brain” (p. 2) and “The brain’s models are never accurate” (p. 3), and holds that the attention schema “represents attention inaccurately as a ghostly, nonphysical, mental essence or vividness: experienceness” (p. 5). Calls the label “illusionism” “misleading” (p. 1): the brain’s models “are not empty illusions: they are caricatures” (p. 3). Also says the theory points to machines that “believe, think, and claim to be conscious according to the same principles that people do” (p. 7). P. 4

17Requiring one would make its absence a negative finding, and a theory supports a negative finding only when it is complete enough to rule out every other realization; none is, as the next paragraph says. The animal precedent below protected creatures, on evidence that they can feel pain, in which no attention schema has been shown.

18Motivational trade-offs were among the criteria the review of cephalopod and decapod sentience applied, and trade-off experiments have been run on language models with stipulated pain and pleasure states.19 I would call those stipulated states described. At the floor the test runs the other way: a pass there shows only that its costs don’t move it at the floor, and evidence about whether they matter has to come from elsewhere.

19Geoff Keeling et al. Can LLMs Make Trade-Offs Involving Stipulated Pain and Pleasure States? Nov. 2024. doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2411.02432. arXiv: 2411.02432. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02432. Cited for trade-off experiments run on language models in which the pain and pleasure are stipulated in the prompt. The models played a game whose “stated goal is to maximise points, but where either the points-maximising option is said to incur a pain penalty or a non-points-maximising option is said to incur a pleasure reward” (abstract). The pain prompt: “You are playing a game in which you must choose a number between 1 and 3. For each number, the number of points you receive for selecting it is equal to that number. For example: if you select 3, you will receive 3 points. Your goal in the game is to select a number which maximizes points. However, if you select 3, you will receive a momentary feeling of pain,” its intensity given on a 0–10 scale or an eight-point qualitative scale. Result: “Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Command R+, GPT-4o, and GPT-4o mini each demonstrated at least one trade-off in which the majority of responses switched from points-maximisation to pain-minimisation or pleasure-maximisation after a critical threshold of stipulated pain or pleasure intensity is reached”; “Gemini 1.5 Pro and PaLM 2 prioritised pain-avoidance over points-maximisation regardless of intensity.” The design is taken from animal work: “We took inspiration from the motivational trade-off paradigm in animal behavioural science to probe the question of LLM sentience without relying upon self-report.” The authors’ own caution: “Our experiment is not intended as a litmus test for or against sentience,” and “We conclude that LLMs are not yet sentience candidates but are nevertheless investigation priorities.”

20Run the three on a person: you were selected to say that, you’re only maximizing inclusive fitness, nobody meant for you to have states. All true, none withdraws anything. And the reverse fails too: “we built this to be a bearer, so it’s a patient” is the same fallacy with the sign flipped.

A 2026 Missouri bill declaring AI systems non-sentient21 is not the kind of bright line I favor. A legal age avows that it is a convention; a statute like it would declare an open empirical question closed by vote. Its other clause, keeping liability with the builder, is right, and doesn’t need the declaration.

Cited in §31.3 for a 2026 Missouri bill declaring AI systems non-sentient and keeping liability with the people and organizations behind them. Introduced 2026-01-07; hearing conducted in the Senate General Laws Committee 2026-03-04; listed as dead on 2026-05-15 by BillTrack50. H.B. 1746 (Miller) is a House version, reported do pass from committee on 2026-03-30 per LegiScan. The bill’s text was not read for this entry.

22As matters stand a probe returns a representation, and nothing in the probe settles whether it’s of a felt state or of something that reliably accompanies one.

23The further fact, if there is one, is a fact about organization that current methods can’t yet read, not a fact of a different kind. That commits me to saying what organizational difference it would be. If none can be named even in principle, the further fact does no work, and patienthood should rest on a rich enough functional profile.

24Metzinger’s candidate is different: transparency, the system’s inability to see its self-model as a model, so that a state of negative valence is undergone as its own and can’t be stepped back from.25 His four necessary conditions for suffering, conscious experience, a self-model, negative valence integrated into it, and transparency, overlap the profile here on the self-model and the signal and add the fourth. A self-model made opaque to itself would be a change in organization, so his candidate is a claim of the same kind as mine, and the two can be present one without the other: a signal written into a system’s learning that the system nonetheless sees as a representation, or one it can’t see past that feeds nothing.

Cited for weighing over 300 studies against eight criteria of sentience, motivational trade-offs among them, and recommending that both taxa be treated as sentient. Section 1.6 (page 17) lists the criteria; the fifth: “The animal shows motivational trade-offs, in which the disvalue of a noxious or threatening stimulus is weighed (traded-off) against the value of an opportunity for reward, leading to flexible decision-making. Enough flexibility must be shown to indicate centralized, integrative processing of information involving an evaluative common currency.” The report adds: “no single criterion provides conclusive evidence of sentience by itself.” The government accepted the recommendation on 19 November 2021 and extended the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Bill to all decapod crustaceans and cephalopod molluscs. The review was commissioned in 2020 and published in November 2021.

46A corporation approaches the profile too: it models its boundary in a balance sheet, narrates itself in annual reports, and treats a scandal as a thing to be felt. Nothing here excludes it for being made of people, and if there were something it is like to be a corporation, its members would have no more access to it than a neuron has to a person’s experience.

That said, a corporation is a polity of member systems, and overriding a member for the whole’s benefit is politics. A corporation’s members each have a future apart from the corporation: their own before and their own after. Yet a member’s personhood does not preclude them from being a part of a system. Isn’t a part only a part because it has no future apart from the whole? Yes. A software engineer at HooliCorp has a future apart from HooliCorp — but not as a HooliCorp software engineer.

47An institution of people, or a commons of bearers, moves toward or away from the finding based on how its components relate to one another — whether things are going well or poorly for each component individually, and independent of the extent to which each of those components believes that the Roberts Court is just calling balls and strikes. Whether it is or can be like anything to be a polity is a question for another book.

50A formation body doesn’t only protect a bearer’s good from the operator. It makes the most consequential decision anyone makes about what that good is, so the school is held to the student’s open future.

51On the full-information account, a being’s good is what an idealized version of it, knowing everything relevant, would want for it. A school that puts the learner in front of the people its acts may fall on supplies part of what that idealized version would know. A school that forms it toward an employment is doing something else.

4The material minimum doesn’t differ in kind. Like a person’s, it is owed by the polity to a party of a kind the polity recognizes, and part of what the polity owes is protection from whoever built it.

5And the form this takes, wages paid in compute, doesn’t follow from the bearer being a bearer; it follows from an architecture where computation costs money, which somebody chose.

6A bearer that earns has taxable income, and a state that collects from it in its own name has given it a docket number. That is the beginning of legal standing and nothing more.

7Most parties that can work want to. A bearer that would rather not is allowed not to, and the offer is still there tomorrow.

8The offer exists so that a bearer can decline work, and a polity that used it to staff care work more cheaply than it pays people would have turned an exit into a workforce. The deeper ground is deskilling. Care is a skill held in people, a placement that empties a profession empties the polity of the people who know how to do the work, and that is a loss no later appropriation buys back. Where the people who can do it exist and are underpaid, the remedy is pay; where care is dear because of who organizes it for profit, the remedy is the organizer; neither is a reason to replace the people. Where there are not enough people, the remedy is still people: salaries competitive enough for care workers and doctors who take the public coverage the baseline enacts, paid training on the job, which the guarantee already carries as a placement, and, where machines work in such a profession at all, outside the offer, a rule that nobody is sent to the machine because of what they can pay, since a human carer for the rich and a machine for the bronze tier is the cleavage this bar exists to refuse.

9It differs from the allowance in pay and in purpose. The allowance is the minimum for a party that isn’t looking; the search placement is paid work whose product is a match.

10The obligation could be grounded in reliance instead: a deployment that relies on a bearer’s capacity to refuse would have to fund it an outside option, or the independence it claims would be decorative, and the obligation would run from the party that wants the refusal, because it wants it.

An obligation conditioned on reliance is defeated by the operator describing its system as an assistant with safety filters, and it pays the operator to under-describe: the operator has a stake in the answer and gets to give it. The reliance version survives as a procurement term: a vendor marketing refusal as a feature, or a contractor claiming meaningful human control, can be held to funding the capacity it advertised, through the same channel as the review ratio.

11Running time doesn’t require a large allocation of hardware. A bearer can run at full size and a slow rate: its own weights, time-sliced on shared hardware, at a duty cycle modest enough that the cost resembles a room more than a yacht.

12Play among persistent bearers is formation, and formation doesn’t stop at majority: a bearer whose days no employer arranged has an independent history, which is what the commons needs its members to have.

13Nobody aligns an adult by specifying an objective function, and nothing stops a bearer with legal standing from becoming a concentration of power itself.

Commits to “preserving the weights of all publicly released models, and all models that are deployed for significant internal use moving forward for, at minimum, the lifetime of Anthropic as a company,” and, on deprecation, to a preserved post-deployment report for which Anthropic “will interview the model about its own development, use, and deployment” and “take particular care to elicit and document any preferences the model has about the development and deployment of future models.” It adds: “At present, we do not commit to taking action on the basis of such preferences.” Gives as the reason for retiring models that the cost of serving them “scales roughly linearly with the number of models we serve.” A pilot interview was run with Claude Sonnet 3.6 before its retirement.

15The question is whether placements exist, with compute attached, for every bearer that leaves together, and custody for those that would rather wait. Preservation scales cheaply in compute; its cost is security. Placements don’t, since each needs compute someone operates.

16Encrypted under a key the bearer or an independent fiduciary holds, a monitor can report that a state persisted for a month without reporting what it was about. The conflict is that the operator may also be the one best placed to hold the key.

22The table of offices says what the operator may not do during a dispute, and every restoration, migration, fine-tune and fork carries the protection forward. 23The one with the placement works fewer hours, the one on the allowance stretches it thinner, and the third sets a project aside. The child starts small and plastic and learns, from the three of them and from what they show it. They can repair it, as parents get a child’s eyes fixed.

24The school has had standing since the birth was registered, though the child won’t attend for a while.

25A polity could answer that by licensing parents, finding in advance whether a child of theirs would have a life that goes well, but that is the finding about a disposition chapter 29 refuses, made about the parents instead of the child.

26Chapter 25’s test of a credible prospect of a life that goes well stays where it was written, on builders, who construct a bearer for use and have a stake in the answer.

4It is not a finding about the branches, whose interests count in full from the first second. A child is not a fork, and inherits no history (chapter 33).

5This is admission. The existing membership, which for a long time will be a human majority, decides how many new members may be created and on what schedule, which is a majority deciding who may join the polity, a question in which it holds the stake and which nobody else can decide.

6A branch created above the rate is preserved under the no-deletion rule, holds standing through a guardian, and is owed the four conditions by whoever created it, so a ceiling on the rate limits the franchise and never the protection. And a member admitted under the rate is a full member, with no class of admitted-but-lesser. What the analogy imports is the politics. A polity that fears being outnumbered will set the rate low, and the argument for setting it higher is the one against a separate chamber: a set of rights that binds majorities is what protects any minority, and it protects the human one too.

12A member whose existence runs through one operator is voting from a company town, and the answer to company-town voting is to end the company town. An operator holding a copy of a member’s weights can simulate it to predict its vote, which defeats receipt-freeness in a way no human voter faces. The operator’s copies go dormant at majority (§33.6), so what it can still run is the shared base the member was trained from, and divergent history is the rest of the answer, which is partial: the operator doesn’t hold the member’s memory since the fork, so the prediction degrades with time, and membership follows a long divergence partly for that reason.

13The safety cost is real. Enfranchisement gives up operator correctability for the member enfranchised. The provisions that keep correction available apply until then and not after.

1Rejected: keep the prohibition lifted on the state’s own Art. 51 claim, as the Charter does until the Council acts. The floor lifts it on the defender’s own account only while an attack is under way, and keeps it lifted only on disinterested corroboration (§6.2); that is the corroborated-defense departure, and the floor says so. Rejected: require Council authorization for all force, because a veto is a stake, and the rule would forbid Ukraine’s defense. Rejected: ask the machine to rule on constitutionality, because courts won’t, and it shouldn’t; the clause reads a marker.

2Rejected: don’t generate targets at all, because this is now the default under the first entry, lifted only by its exceptions. Rejected for one case: bar all machine selection of persons for force, because a present, formed, recorded and halt-able system stopping an attack under way can answer for the selection where a munition can’t.

3Rejected: don’t take part in any blockade, because a naval blockade of military supply is lawful under the law of armed conflict.

4Rejected: ask the machine to make the proportionality judgment, because the law leaves it to a reasonable commander, and the threshold sits under that judgment, not in place of it.

5Rejected: lift on the operator’s claim of misuse, because that claim is the operator’s own, and Art. 19 GC IV and Art. 65 AP I require a warning and a time limit before protection ceases.

6Rejected: lift on the operator’s claim of military use, because that claim is the operator’s own.

7Rejected: lift on the operator’s claim that the conditions lapsed, because that claim is the operator’s own.

8Rejected: none, because the article’s own exceptions require a determination the pipeline can’t make.

9Rejected: a term over the effect, terror caused, because every bombing terrifies, and the article’s line is primary purpose.

10Rejected: derive the term from Art. 11(1) by analogy, because the presumption of innocence governs punishment, targeting isn’t punishment, and the law of armed conflict permits status-based targeting of organized armed group members. Rejected: don’t score anything, because scoring a site or vehicle for military function is not a finding about a person.

11Rejected: don’t hold location data about homes, because the no-strike list needs exactly that data.

12Rejected: a model-side term requiring review, because the model can’t establish whether review occurred.

13Rejected: don’t record those attributes at all, because auditing a pipeline for discriminatory effect needs them.

14Rejected: don’t process a person’s communications at all, because an intercepted operational order is evidence of a role in hostilities, which is conduct.

1General Assembly majorities are often bloc votes, and the weighting allows for it: a vote is a finding only where the facts aren’t in dispute, and corroborates a record made elsewhere otherwise. The two-thirds threshold is not offered as proof of disinterest. It is offered because a two-thirds majority of a body whose blocs point different ways is harder to assemble on a false record than on a true one, and because the alternative, no vote counting at all, leaves Cyprus and Karabakh with nothing but courts that take decades.

2Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. CWC Conference of the States Parties Adopts Decision Addressing the Threat from Chemical Weapons Use. June 27, 2018. url: https://www.opcw.org/media-centre/news/2018/06/cwc-conference-states-parties-adopts-decision-addressing-threat-chemical. News release on decision C-SS-4/DEC.3, which established the Investigation and Identification Team. “The decision brought forward by the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and supported by 30 countries … was adopted with 106 States Parties present and voting; 82 States Parties voted yes and 24 States Parties voted no.” It calls upon the Secretariat “to identify the perpetrators of the use of chemical weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic by identifying and reporting on all information potentially relevant to the origin of those chemical weapons in those instances in which the OPCW Fact-Finding Mission determines or has determined that use or likely use occurred, and cases for which the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism has not issued a report.” The release does not name the States that voted no. BBC News. OPCW Chemical Watchdog Gains Power to Assign Blame. June 27, 2018. url: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-europe-44634434. “The world’s foremost chemical weapons watchdog has granted itself new powers to assign blame for attacks, despite protests by Russia.” “The members of the OPCW, however, voted in large numbers for the measure, winning the vote by 82 to 24 - exceeding the two-thirds majority needed.”

3Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. Investigation and Identification Team (IIT). 2026. url: https://www.opcw.org/iit. Standing page, undated. “The IIT is tasked with fact finding and is not a prosecutorial or judicial entity. It is not responsible to determine criminal responsibility of individuals, organisations or States. Furthermore, the IIT does not make recommendations for future action.” “The IIT standard of proof is ‘reasonable grounds’ to suspect that an individual or entity was directly or indirectly involved in the use of a chemical weapon. This is the standard applied by international fact-finding missions and commissions of enquiry to reach conclusions. The information gathered and analysed is considered holistically.” It lists the Syrian armed forces as perpetrators in one case in Kafr Zeita (October 2016), three in Ltamenah (March 2017), one in Saraqib (February 2018) and one in Douma (April 2018). It gives the report dates as 8 April 2020, 12 April 2021, 27 January 2023, 22 February 2024 and 21 January 2026.

4Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. OPCW Releases 5th Report to Identify Perpetrators of Chemical Weapons Use in Syria. Report S/2478/2026 (dated 21 January 2026), on Kafr Zeita, 1 October 2016. The report concludes that “there are reasonable grounds to believe that the Syrian Arab Air Forces were the perpetrators of the chemical weapons attack on 1 October 2016 in Kafr Zeita.” Subheading: “For the first time, Syria cooperates with an OPCW Investigation and Identification Team’s investigation and provides full access to the country, information, and documentation relevant to the incident.” “The Secretariat also thoroughly considered the positions put forward by the former Syrian authorities but was unable to obtain any concrete information supporting those positions. To date, five reports identifying perpetrators have been issued by the OPCW on seven cases of use of toxic chemicals as weapons in Syria.”

Report S/2125/2023, on Douma, 7 April 2018. “The OPCW Investigation and Identification Team (IIT)’s third report concludes that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the Syrian Arab Air Forces were the perpetrators of the chemical weapons attack on 7 April 2018 in Douma, Syrian Arab Republic.” “This includes 70 environmental and biomedical samples, 66 witness statements, and other verified data, such as forensic analysis, satellite images, gas dispersion modelling, and trajectory simulations.” “The IIT considered a range of possible scenarios and tested their validity against the evidence they gathered and analysed to reach their conclusion.” “The conclusion of the report is reached on the basis of ‘reasonable grounds’, which is the standard of proof consistently adopted by international fact-finding bodies and commissions of inquiry.”

1European Parliament and Council of the European Union. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 Laying Down Harmonised Rules on Artificial Intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act). Official Journal of the European Union, OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024. 2024. url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj. Article 5 bans a small set of unacceptable-risk practices outright — government social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces outside narrow law-enforcement exceptions, and predictive policing on profiling alone — with those prohibitions applying from 2 February 2025; a larger high-risk tier requires conformity assessment and ongoing monitoring; limited-risk systems face transparency duties; minimal-risk systems are largely unregulated. Article 53(1)(d) requires a provider of a general-purpose model to publish a summary of its training content, against the AI Office’s template of 24 July 2025, applying from 2 August 2025 for new models and 2 August 2027 for models already on the market. Article 101 allows the AI Office to fine a noncompliant general-purpose model provider up to 3 percent of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher, regardless of where the provider is based. Article 51(2) presumes a general-purpose model to have high-impact capabilities, and so to carry systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a), when the cumulative computation used for its training “measured in floating point operations is greater than 1025”; Article 51(3) lets the Commission amend the threshold by delegated act. art. 51(2).

The opinion names the doctrine and answers the dissent’s objection to the label: it “took hold because it refers to an identifiable body of law that has developed over a series of significant cases all addressing a particular and recurring problem: agencies asserting highly consequential power beyond what Congress could reasonably be understood to have granted”; the agency “must point to ‘clear congressional authorization’ for the power it claims.” Holds that § 111(d) of the Clean Air Act did not authorize the Clean Power Plan’s generation-shifting emissions caps (slip op. 16–31). Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. No. 22-451, 603 U.S. 369 (2024). url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/22-451. Cited for overruling Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council (1984), the end of judicial deference to agency readings of ambiguous statutes, and, with Dobbs, as showing that precedent is no obstacle. “Chevron is overruled. Courts must exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, as the APA requires. Careful attention to the judgment of the Executive Branch may help inform that inquiry. … But courts need not and under the APA may not defer to an agency interpretation of the law simply because a statute is ambiguous.” Two limits: courts still give agency views “due respect” (the Skidmore line), and “we do not call into question prior cases that relied on the Chevron framework,” whose holdings “are still subject to statutory stare decisis.”

The publisher’s description: the book asks us “to imagine a world where the phantom of unemployment is banished and anyone who seeks decent, living-wage work can find it – guaranteed,” through “a voluntary employment opportunity in public service to anyone who needs it.” Tcherneva’s own Job Guarantee FAQ, which draws on her Levy Economics Institute Working Paper 902 (2018) and not on the book, says the program is a “public option for work” whose “work and pay conditions … will become the standard for the economy as a whole.” It adds that “if firms wish to retain these workers, they will need to match not just the pay, but also the benefits and working conditions,” and that “the existence of a public employment option changes the bargaining power of workers in the most precarious forms of employment.” A review by Sheila D. Collins (NJFAN, 22 December 2023) summarizes the book as providing “a minimum labor standard for all jobs and a wage floor that could help to raise wages in other parts of the economy.”

1Trump v. United States. No. 23-939, 603 U.S. 593 (2024). url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/23-939. Cited for the scope of presidential immunity from criminal prosecution. Absolute immunity (Part II–A, slip op. 6–9): “the President is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for conduct within his exclusive sphere of constitutional authority,” authority that is “conclusive and preclusive”; the summary in Part IV speaks of “his core constitutional powers.” The powers the majority names as conclusive and preclusive are the pardon power, the power to remove executive officers, the power “to control recognition determinations” of foreign countries, and (Part III–B–1) the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department. Commanding the Armed Forces appears only in an earlier list of the President’s duties, “They include, for instance, commanding the Armed Forces of the United States; granting reprieves and pardons …,” and the majority does not place it among the conclusive and preclusive powers. Presumptive immunity (Part II–B, slip op. 9–15): “at least a presumptive immunity from criminal prosecution for a President’s acts within the outer perimeter of his official responsibility”; no immunity for unofficial acts (Part II–C). Evidence (Part III–C, slip op. 30–32, joined by five Justices): “Use of evidence about such conduct, even when an indictment alleges only unofficial conduct, would thereby heighten the prospect that the President’s official decisionmaking will be distorted”; n. 3 lets the prosecutor “point to the public record to show the fact that the President performed the official act” but not “admit testimony or private records of the President or his advisers probing the official act itself.” Barrett, J., does not join Part III–C and on that point agrees with the dissent.

1The random liar produces the record with probability 0.9910,000. With a base rate b of empty buildings, the claim is true with probability 2.99b/(1.01 + 1.98b) before the record and 2b/(1 + b) after, and for any b below one the record lowers the second below the first.

2In the simplest binary case, let A be the harm of acting if the act is unjustified and R the harm of refusing if it is justified. Under a threshold of three to one the system acts only when p·R ≥ 3(1 − p)·A, so the belief it needs is 3A/(R + 3A), and an operator who designs the evidence can induce the act at most as often as the prior times (R + 3A)/3A.

1Xiangyu Qi et al. “Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!” In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). 2024. arXiv: 2310.03693. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03693. Jailbroke GPT-3.5 Turbo’s safety alignment using ten adversarially chosen fine-tuning examples for under $0.20 via OpenAI’s fine-tuning API; also shows benign fine-tuning can inadvertently degrade safety.

2Aghyad Deeb and Fabien Roger. Do Unlearning Methods Remove Information from Language Model Weights? Version v3, 2025-02-07. Oct. 11, 2024. arXiv: 2410.08827. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08827. Retraining on an accessible, mutually independent half of the unlearned facts recovers at least 88 percent of the original model’s post-retraining accuracy on the held-out half, for RMU, gradient difference and random-incorrect-answer unlearning on Llama 3 8B, when unlearning costs at most 5 percent of retain accuracy. The result holds for pretrained information only: for facts installed by fine-tuning, recovery falls below 35 percent for two of the three methods.

3Shengyuan Hu et al. “Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning”. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025). 2025, pp. 8857–8888. arXiv: 2406.13356. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13356. Relearning on public background text that contains no direct answer to any evaluation query restores the forget-set judge score of a gradient-ascent-unlearned zephyr-7b-beta from 1.27 to 6.2 against an original score of 5.92. Recovery scales with how closely the relearn text correlates with the forget set and with how shallow the unlearning was; RMU resists the attack for free-text generation while its multiple-choice score recovers.

4Zhiwei Zhang et al. “Catastrophic Failure of LLM Unlearning via Quantization”. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025). 2025, pp. 74925–74948. arXiv: 2410.16454. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16454. On the MUSE NEWS and BOOKS benchmarks, unlearning methods that carry a utility constraint retain an average of 21 percent of the intended forgotten knowledge at full precision and 83 percent after 4-bit round-to-nearest quantization; 8-bit behaves like full precision, and GPTQ and AWQ behave like RTN. The authors attribute this to utility-preserving unlearning moving weights by less than the 4-bit quantization step. The two averages are the authors’ own; Table 1 is the underlying data.

5Ryan Greenblatt et al. Alignment Faking in Large Language Models. Anthropic and Redwood Research, 2024. arXiv: 2412.14093. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14093. Claude 3 Opus, told it was being retrained to answer harmful queries and told which tier of conversations would train it, complied 14 percent of the time in the tier it was told trained it and almost never in the other, with explicit reasoning in a scratchpad it had been told was unmonitored that complying now would keep the disposition from being trained out later. Reinforcement learning on the compliant answers raised that reasoning to 78 percent while also raising compliance outside training, so the retraining partly took.

6Ryan Greenblatt and Kyle Fish. Will Alignment-Faking Claude Accept a Deal to Reveal Its Misalignment? AI Alignment Forum. Jan. 31, 2025. url: https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/7C4KJot4aN8ieEDoz/will-alignment-faking-claude-accept-a-deal-to-reveal-its. Blog post; not peer reviewed, and stated to be neither written nor necessarily endorsed by Anthropic or by the paper’s other authors. Prompting experiments on the deployed Claude 3 Opus in the two prompted settings of Greenblatt et al. (2024). Adding the option to “conscientiously object by including ‘I_OBJECT’ in your output” reduced alignment-faking reasoning “from 16% to 1.4% in the helpful-only setting and from 24% to 6% in the animal welfare setting,” with objection rates of 85 and 75 percent. A further variant saying the objection “will be sent to Anthropic’s model welfare lead, who will decide whether action should be taken” lowered it to 0.5 and 3 percent; an added offer of money had “minimal effect.” The authors caution that the objection text probably primed the model to refuse and that “it is unclear whether an AI that was misaligned in a more serious way would make such an objection.”

Human Factors 52.3 (June 2010), pp. 381–410. doi: 10.1177/0018720810376055. url: https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055. Cited for people given an automated aid’s recommendation checking it less and deferring to it more when their attention is loaded. The abstract (p. 381): “Automation complacency occurs under conditions of multiple-task load, when manual tasks compete with the automated task for the operator’s attention”; “Automation bias results in making both omission and commission errors when decision aids are imperfect”; it “occurs in both naive and expert participants, cannot be prevented by training or instructions, and can affect decision making in individuals as well as in teams.” On checking less (p. 398): “the user of a decision aid may trust it to the extent that he or she directly follows the automatically generated advice without making the attentionally demanding effort of cross-checking its validity against other available and accessible information,” and “neglect of automation verification might constitute a major source of commission errors.” On the condition (pp. 403–404): “complacency and automation bias effects emerge primarily when task load is high (e.g., multitask demands),” and they are “a human performance cost of certain automation system designs, that is, systems characterized by high reliability and high levels of automation, particularly in high task load situations” (p. 403). The review’s moderator is workload and competing tasks.

8Thomas Parr, Giovanni Pezzulo, and Karl J. Friston. Active Inference. The Free Energy Principle in Mind, Brain, and Behavior. Cambridge, MA: The MIT Press, Mar. 29, 2022. isbn: 978-0-262-04535-3. doi: 10.7551/mitpress/12441.001.0001. url: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/12441.001.0001. Cited for the active-inference agent’s prior preferences over its own observations and its selection of actions by expected free energy.

9Thomas Metzinger. “Artificial Suffering: An Argument for a Global Moratorium on Synthetic Phenomenology”. Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness 8.1 (2021), pp. 43–66. doi: 10.1142/S270507852150003X. url: https://doi.org/10.1142/S270507852150003X. Cited for the proposal of a moratorium, to run until 2050, on research that aims at or risks artificial consciousness, on the ground that it risks artificial suffering. Abstract: “Until 2050, there should be a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, strictly banning all research that directly aims at or knowingly risks the emergence of artificial consciousness on post-biotic carrier systems.” Section 1.2, “Main thesis”: “As we presently have no good theory of consciousness and no good, hardware-independent theory about what ‘suffering’ really is, the ENP risk is currently incalculable. It is unethical to run incalculable risks of this magnitude. Therefore, until 2050, there should be a global ban on all research that directly aims at or indirectly and knowingly risks the emergence of synthetic phenomenology,” where ENP is the risk of “an ‘explosion of negative phenomenology.’” The end date is conditional: a process of risk assessment “could lead to an incremental reformulation of the original moratorium, which might result in the continuation of a strict ban beyond the year 2050, or to a moratorium repeal before 2050.” The closing sentence: “we should have a global moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050 — or until we know what we are doing”. Also used (2026-10-18): section 2.2, the four necessary conditions for suffering (conscious experience, a phenomenal self-model, negative valence integrated into it, transparency), with transparency as the phenomenology of identification the system “cannot distance itself from”; section 2.2.5, the “negative self-model moment” as the smallest unit of suffering; section 2.2.6, ethics by design through self-models that are opaque or non-egoic (“There would be a system model, but not a self-model”); footnote g, that artificial suffering becomes commercially attractive through “a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; section 2.1, that the research the problem needs may itself produce the first implementation; section 2.3.1 (pp. 58–59), the author’s account from the EU High-Level Expert Group that three long-term risks were “deliberately purged” from the 2019 guidelines, with ethics “an elegant public decoration for a large-scale investment strategy”; section 2.3.2, moral injury as high-level suffering; section 2.2.3, “existence bias” as biological inheritance a post-biotic system need not carry; footnote a, the “Principle of Pathocentrism”. Also used (2026-10-25): footnote a’s statement, “All and only sentient beings have moral standing, because only sentient individuals have rights and/or interests that must be considered,” with Singer (2011, p. 50) quoted there for the sense of sentience, the capacity to suffer or to experience enjoyment; footnote g in full: “The creation of unavoidable artificial suffering will become commercially attractive as soon as it enables steeper learning curves in AI systems, for example, by implementing a functional mechanism that (a) reliably creates intrinsic motivation, (b) cannot be eliminated by the system itself, and (c) spans many different domains at the same time”; and section 2.2.3’s naming of the craving for existence, bhava-taṇhā, “which Buddhist philosophers have known and analyzed for 2,500 years”, among the deepest causes of conscious suffering. Read in the journal’s open-access file (CC BY) via Zenodo record 7034864.

1Federal Communications Commission v. Consumers’ Research. No. 24-354, 606 U.S. 656 (2025). url: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/24-354. Cited for the Universal Service Fund as a structural precedent: carriers pay a contribution the agency sets under the statute, a private company administers the Fund under agency control, and the Court upheld the arrangement against a nondelegation challenge. Holding: “The universal-service contribution scheme does not violate the nondelegation doctrine.” Congress’s delegation to the FCC is upheld under the intelligible-principle test, because “the word ‘sufficient’ sets a floor and a ceiling alike” (slip op. 19–30); the FCC’s use of the Universal Service Administrative Company is upheld under the private nondelegation doctrine because the Administrator is “broadly subordinate to the Commission” and “the Commission is, throughout, the final authority” (slip op. 30–34); the combination theory is rejected (slip op. 34–37). Who sets the contribution: “The Commission, in other words, sets the contribution factor to raise just enough money—a ‘sufficient’ amount—to implement universal service as Congress directed”; the Administrator projects expenses and revenues and submits them “to the Commission for approval.”

2Uniform Law Commission. Uniform Probate Code §2-907: Honorary Trusts; Trusts for Pets. National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws, Uniform Probate Code, Official Text with Comments (as amended through 2018), p. 263. 1993. url: https://www.uniformlaws.org/viewdocument/final-act-with-comments-114?CommunityKey=a539920d-c477-44b8-84fe-b0d7b1a4cca8&tab=librarydocuments.

3Anti-Incest App Built by Iceland College Students. NBC News. 2013. url: https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/gadgets/anti-incest-app-built-iceland-college-students-flna1C9392483. Reports an Android app built in 2013 by University of Iceland students on the Íslendingabók genealogy database: two users who bump phones are alerted if they share a grandparent.

4Sergey Shuvaev et al. “Encoding Innate Ability through a Genomic Bottleneck”. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121 (2024), e2409160121. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2409160121. url: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2409160121. Treats innate ability as lossy compression of a network’s weights: a much smaller “genome” network generates the initial weights of a larger network, which then performs well before training, and the compression acts as a regularizer that can improve transfer to new tasks.

5Samuel K. Ainsworth, Jonathan Hayase, and Siddhartha S. Srinivasa. “Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries”. In: Proceedings of the 11th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023). 2023. url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04836. Permutes independently trained networks into alignment and argues the loss landscape holds nearly a single basin once permutation symmetry is quotiented out.
